turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: We'll hear argument first this term in Case 25-170, Suncor Energy versus County Commissioners of Boulder County. Speaker B.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Thank you, [ADDRESS] This case involves an unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct. Boulder is suing Petitioners under Colorado law on the theory that their global conduct increased the global use of fossil fuels, which led to an increase in global greenhouse-gas emissions, which contributed to global climate change, which resulted in global harms. Our constitutional system does not permit state law to be used in that manner. The Constitution bars the application of state law to certain inherently federal areas. When the states entered the Union, the plan of the Convention required them to surrender certain preexisting powers in order to ensure each state's equal sovereignty. Because of the ambient nature of air and water and the conflicting rights of states, this Court has held for over a century that federal law governs interstate pollution claims. That principle applies with even greater force to claims involving global climate change. In addition, the Constitution's prohibition on extraterritorial regulation precludes a state from extending its law beyond its borders to regulate global conduct with global effects. A state does not have the power to regulate out-of-state conduct based solely on attenuated effects on the state. What is more, the use of state law to regulate global climate change would substantially interfere with the nation's foreign policy. And far from authorizing the application of state law, the Clean Air Act independently preempts any effort by one state to impose its law on emissions originating in others. If Boulder's claims are allowed to go forward, some 90,000 municipalities across the country will have the ability to make national and international energy policy by asking juries to impose catastrophic damages on selected fossil-fuel producers. Put simply, that is not the constitutional scheme that the Founders adopted. The Colorado Supreme Court's judgment should accordingly be reversed. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Sure, [PERSON]. Our view is that the Court has both statutory and constitutional jurisdiction. I'll address those in turn. On statutory jurisdiction, our view is that Atlantic Richfield is directly on point. It could not be clearer as a matter of Colorado law that the proceeding below was a self-contained original proceeding, which gives rise to jurisdiction in this Court under Section 1257. Boulder's argument to the contrary is that because this case did not involve a formal writ proceeding directed at the lower court, that it falls outside the scope of Atlantic Richfield. But, in Atlantic Richfield itself, this Court attached no weight to the form of the underlying proceeding. Instead, the Court relied on the fact that it was a self-contained proceeding. In fact, this proceeding contained many of the hallmarks of a writ proceeding. The Colorado Supreme Court ordered the trial court to respond to its order to show cause and then discharged the order to show cause at the end of the proceeding. And the Colorado Supreme Court's move away from formal writs is not unusual. As the brief of the state -- former state supreme court justices points out, many states have made that move toward a more informal label for their proceedings. The key point is that in Colorado, as elsewhere, these original proceedings are distinct from ordinary appellate proceedings, even interlocutory appellate proceedings. In Colorado, there are separate rules, Rule 21 and Rule 4.2, that govern each. As to constitutional jurisdiction, I think our submission here is a straightforward one. Because this case is coming from a state court, you look to the injuries suffered by the Petitioners, who were the defendants in the lower court proceeding. The decision below definitively adjudicated our legal rights, and it did so in a way that was binding not just in this case but in other cases in Colorado as well. So not only are my clients exposed to a greater risk of liability as a result of the fact that one of our central defenses has been knocked out, but, in a very real sense, we have lost the right to be free from state regulation, which was how this Court characterized the loss of a preemption defense in NCAA versus Murphy, and as a result, we will suffer an injury. So that personal stake, in our view, is sufficient for Article III purposes.

turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS], you would concede that there are some situations in which an individual who engages in conduct in State B, causes harm to somebody in State A, can be sued under the law of State A, right?

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS], we would concede that. And so the principle of no extraterritorial regulation that I articulated in my opening does admit of exceptions. There are cases in which the Court has permitted that, where a defendant can be said to be constructively present in the state by virtue of their conduct.

turns_pm15.speaker: B

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Well, yeah, if you throw a rock over the border and hit him, that person can be --

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Correct. And we have no truck with those cases. Our point is that this goes further than any of those cases, and I would submit that that's really for three reasons. First, none of the conduct that is at issue here can really be said to have been directed at Colorado. Second, the harm at issue here is a harm that is diffuse nationwide and, indeed, worldwide. And, third, any causal nexus here is severely attenuated.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Well, just --

turns_pm15.speaker: B

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Well, it -- it certainly is true that if you are, say, across a state border and you direct your conduct across the state border, many of the cases on which my friend relies fall into that paradigm. I think what makes this case different is that, in this case, not only do you not have any sort of direction of the conduct towards Colorado, but, again, the causal chain here is severely attenuated. And there is no case on which my friend relies where, in the face of such an attenuated chain of causation, this Court has said that the exception to the venerable prohibition against extraterritorial regulation applies. And I would submit that if you accept Respondents' theory, the exception would swallow the rule. Now, just to be clear, as I indicated at the outset, we are relying on two strands of federalist principle here. The second is extraterritoriality. The first is the principle of equal sovereignty, the notion that in an area like this, there are uniquely federal interests that dictate the application of federal law. Now I think the virtue of that approach is that it underlies the entire line of cases from this Court involving interstate pollution going all the way back --

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Sure.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Sure. So, [PERSON], I'll give you our bottom line and then the explanation. Our bottom line is that, in fact, no state's law can apply here and that before you get to the question of choice of law, you've got to determine which state's laws potentially could apply here. Our view is that under either the equal sovereignty principle or the closely related extraterritoriality principle, there is no justification for Colorado's law applying, the law of the affected state to apply.

turns_pm15.text: We would object to Colorado applying Texas law as well, but I think the answer to that is a little more complicated. We acknowledge under our equal sovereignty principle that Congress can authorize state law to apply. Congress has done that in a limited way in the Clean Air Act by, in the saving clause, authorizing the law of the source state to apply.

And the last thing -- can I say one last thing to [PERSON]? And I'll be very brief.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Sure.

turns_pm60.speaker: B

But it would still get you to the same result. So, yes, these are separate strands, but I think, ultimately, the conclusion under each is the same.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Thank you, [ADDRESS] This case involves an unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct. Our constitutional system does not permit state law to be used in that manner. The Constitution bars the application of state law to certain inherently federal areas. When the states entered the Union, the plan of the Convention required them to surrender certain preexisting powers in order to ensure each state's equal sovereignty. Because of the ambient nature of air and water and the conflicting rights of states, this Court has held for over a century that federal law governs interstate pollution claims. That principle applies with even greater force to claims involving global climate change. In addition, the Constitution's prohibition on extraterritorial regulation precludes a state from extending its law beyond its borders to regulate global conduct with global effects. A state does not have the power to regulate out-of-state conduct based solely on attenuated effects on the state. What is more, the use of state law to regulate global climate change would substantially interfere with the nation's foreign policy. And far from authorizing the application of state law, the Clean Air Act independently preempts any effort by one state to impose its law on emissions originating in others. If Boulder's claims are allowed to go forward, some 90,000 municipalities across the country will have the ability to make national and international energy policy by asking juries to impose catastrophic damages on selected fossil-fuel producers. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Thank you, [ADDRESS] This case involves an unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct. Boulder is suing Petitioners under Colorado law on the theory that their global conduct increased the global use of fossil fuels, which led to an increase in global greenhouse-gas emissions, which contributed to global climate change, which resulted in global harms. Our constitutional system does not permit state law to be used in that manner. The Constitution bars the application of state law to certain inherently federal areas. When the states entered the Union, the plan of the Convention required them to surrender certain preexisting powers in order to ensure each state's equal sovereignty. Because of the ambient nature of air and water and the conflicting rights of states, this Court has held for over a century that federal law governs interstate pollution claims. That principle applies with even greater force to claims involving global climate change. In addition, the Constitution's prohibition on extraterritorial regulation precludes a state from extending its law beyond its borders to regulate global conduct with global effects. A state does not have the power to regulate out-of-state conduct based solely on attenuated effects on the state. What is more, the use of state law to regulate global climate change would substantially interfere with the nation's foreign policy. And far from authorizing the application of state law, the Clean Air Act independently preempts any effort by one state to impose its law on emissions originating in others. If Boulder's claims are allowed to go forward, some 90,000 municipalities across the country will have the ability to make national and international energy policy by asking juries to impose catastrophic damages on selected fossil-fuel producers. Put simply, that is not the constitutional scheme that the Founders adopted. The Colorado Supreme Court's judgment should accordingly be reversed. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Sure, [PERSON]. Our view is that the Court has both statutory and constitutional jurisdiction. I'll address those in turn. On statutory jurisdiction, our view is that Atlantic Richfield is directly on point. It could not be clearer as a matter of Colorado law that the proceeding below was a self-contained original proceeding, which gives rise to jurisdiction in this Court under Section 1257. Boulder's argument to the contrary is that because this case did not involve a formal writ proceeding directed at the lower court, that it falls outside the scope of Atlantic Richfield. But, in Atlantic Richfield itself, this Court attached no weight to the form of the underlying proceeding. Instead, the Court relied on the fact that it was a self-contained proceeding. In fact, this proceeding contained many of the hallmarks of a writ proceeding. The Colorado Supreme Court ordered the trial court to respond to its order to show cause and then discharged the order to show cause at the end of the proceeding. And the Colorado Supreme Court's move away from formal writs is not unusual. As the brief of the state -- former state supreme court justices points out, many states have made that move toward a more informal label for their proceedings. The key point is that in Colorado, as elsewhere, these original proceedings are distinct from ordinary appellate proceedings, even interlocutory appellate proceedings. In Colorado, there are separate rules, Rule 21 and Rule 4.2, that govern each. As to constitutional jurisdiction, I think our submission here is a straightforward one. Because this case is coming from a state court, you look to the injuries suffered by the Petitioners, who were the defendants in the lower court proceeding. The decision below definitively adjudicated our legal rights, and it did so in a way that was binding not just in this case but in other cases in Colorado as well. So not only are my clients exposed to a greater risk of liability as a result of the fact that one of our central defenses has been knocked out, but, in a very real sense, we have lost the right to be free from state regulation, which was how this Court characterized the loss of a preemption defense in NCAA versus Murphy, and as a result, we will suffer an injury. So that personal stake, in our view, is sufficient for Article III purposes.

turns_pm60.text: Thank you, [ADDRESS] This case involves an unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct. Boulder is suing Petitioners under Colorado law on the theory that their global conduct increased the global use of fossil fuels, which led to an increase in global greenhouse-gas emissions, which contributed to global climate change, which resulted in global harms. Our constitutional system does not permit state law to be used in that manner. The Constitution bars the application of state law to certain inherently federal areas. When the states entered the Union, the plan of the Convention required them to surrender certain preexisting powers in order to ensure each state's equal sovereignty. Because of the ambient nature of air and water and the conflicting rights of states, this Court has held for over a century that federal law governs interstate pollution claims. That principle applies with even greater force to claims involving global climate change. In addition, the Constitution's prohibition on extraterritorial regulation precludes a state from extending its law beyond its borders to regulate global conduct with global effects. A state does not have the power to regulate out-of-state conduct based solely on attenuated effects on the state. What is more, the use of state law to regulate global climate change would substantially interfere with the nation's foreign policy. And far from authorizing the application of state law, the Clean Air Act independently preempts any effort by one state to impose its law on emissions originating in others. If Boulder's claims are allowed to go forward, some 90,000 municipalities across the country will have the ability to make national and international energy policy by asking juries to impose catastrophic damages on selected fossil-fuel producers. Put simply, that is not the constitutional scheme that the Founders adopted. The Colorado Supreme Court's judgment should accordingly be reversed. I welcome the Court's questions.

The first is the principle of equal sovereignty, the notion that in an area like this, there are uniquely federal interests that dictate the application of federal law. Now I think the virtue of that approach is that it underlies the entire line of cases from this Court involving interstate pollution going all the way back --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Sure.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Sure. So, [PERSON], I'll give you our bottom line and then the explanation. Our bottom line is that, in fact, no state's law can apply here and that before you get to the question of choice of law, you've got to determine which state's laws potentially could apply here. Our view is that under either the equal sovereignty principle or the closely related extraterritoriality principle, there is no justification for Colorado's law applying, the law of the affected state to apply.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: We would object to Colorado applying Texas law as well, but I think the answer to that is a little more complicated. We acknowledge under our equal sovereignty principle that Congress can authorize state law to apply. Congress has done that in a limited way in the Clean Air Act by, in the saving clause, authorizing the law of the source state to apply.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It is the --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It is the constitutional principle that dictates --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: As a matter of --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: As a matter of constitutional structure, federal law and only federal law can apply. We point to this Court's cases starting with Missouri versus Illinois --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: A Texas court can apply Texas law --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- to ordinary interstate pollution claims by virtue of the Clean Air Act. So our view as to how this is supposed to work, [PERSON] --and I recognize that there are --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: This case is certainly a little bit complicated.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes. So --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah, there's one --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- there's one caveat that --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- in our view, prevents Texas law from applying, but it's an important one. Here's how the analysis, in our view, should work. Step one, as a matter of constitutional law, as this Court's cases involving interstate pollution say, this is within the field of the uniquely federal interest. We'd go all the way back, again, to Justice Holmes and Missouri versus Illinois and his explanation as to why, as a matter of constitutional structure, that is so. Second, under our approach, it is for Congress to authorize state law to apply if it wishes to do so. Our --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I do want to get to point three, but --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Like my children, I love both of our theories equally, [PERSON].

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But let me explain --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: They both get you to the same result in this case, and let me explain why. As I was saying to [PERSON], under our equal sovereignty theory, Congress has the authority to authorize state law to apply. There's nothing anomalous about that. That is just Congress saying that in this uniquely federal area, we can prescribe as the federal rule of decision that state law applies. It's no different from a court applying federal common law borrowing state law. Now my caveat, which I think is an important one, is that in the context of these sorts of climate change claims, it really doesn't make a lot of sense to talk about the source state law. Remember that my clients are not emitters, as was the case in American Electric Power. My clients are producers of fossil fuels. And these sorts of claims -- I said at the outset that these claims -- that the application of federal law follows a fortiori from the interstate pollution cases. Unlike in the traditional interstate pollution cases like Ouellette, where you have two states, the source state and the affected state, here, because the claim runs through global climate change, the claims here necessarily depend on the emissions of anyone who uses fossil fuels worldwide. All 50 states and --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS], can I bring you back -- can I bring you back --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- foreign countries have an interest.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- to the point? I have a starting problem, which is I don't see anywhere below where you argue the extraterritoriality principle at all. And in this case, you raised it only on reply. And yet you come here and start arguing it as your first argument. Haven't you forfeited? It's a defense like any other. If you didn't raise it below -- I didn't see anywhere in your briefs this argument. But putting that aside, I'm trying to disentangle them. You are really staying away from the word that seemed to control the briefing below and even here, which is preemption, all right? Are you claim -- you --you don't win unless you get us to say that federal law preempts state law in this area, period, correct?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That is correct, which is to say this is --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But you can't say that for the reasons that just the [PERSON] pointed out, which is there are nuisance suits that we have permitted under state law in both the -- in the Clean Water Act, and I don't see why we wouldn't permit it under the Clean Air Act either.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. Let me answer that question. And I do want to finish off my answer to [PERSON]. But let me address your question first, Speaker A. I respectfully disagree with your suggestion that this issue was not fully preserved. And I would note that we made all these arguments in our petition for certiorari. There was never any suggestion by Respondent that these arguments were not made below. Now I will acknowledge that I think that the two strands of our argument are closely related, and the reason that they are closely related is that the constitutional source for our arguments is essentially the same. Our constitutional source is that when the states went into the constitutional system, the states sacrificed certain rights that they would have had as independent sovereigns, and they went into the Union on an equal footing. That is really the source for the extraterritoriality principle, which goes all the way back to Justice Marshall and Justice Story. I would point this Court to the various amicus briefs, including the amicus brief of Professor Prakash, as well as the amicus brief of Tennessee, which set out the originalist history for these principles in some detail. Now, to answer, Speaker A, the last part of your question, yes, it is true in both Ouellette and in American Electric Power that the Court recognized that there is some room for state law to operate at least in the context of a bilateral interstate pollution dispute. But that is because the Clean Water Act and the Clean Air Act contain these saving clauses, which this Court --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: What do you do with Watson? What do you do with Watson that didn't -- it wasn't a bilateral situation?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: With --with, sorry?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Watson. Watson versus Employer Liability. That was a multi-state case.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Oh, I'm not sure I'm remembering which case you're --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, that was a constructive presence case.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Oh. Well, look, I think what I would say as to the constructive presence cases more generally, not just Watson but any other constructive presence case, is that there is no case comparable to this one. I actually think that the closest case on which my friend relies is State versus Lord, which was not a case from this Court. But, even in that case, what you were dealing with was the diversion of water into the affected state. It was much easier to say in that context that the nuisance existed in the affected state than here. And, again, I would just say that in Ouellette, in AEP, the Court was plainly construing and definitively construing the scope of the savings clauses to apply only to source state law. And the last thing -- can I say one last thing to [PERSON]? And I'll be very brief.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: [PERSON], on the extraterritoriality principle, I think what I would say is that if you accept our view that this goes too far under the extraterritoriality principle, I think your analysis is at an end. I suppose that one could make an additional argument that even as to the extraterritoriality principle, a state could -- Congress could authorize the application of state law. But it would still get you to the same result. So, yes, these are separate strands, but I think, ultimately, the conclusion under each is the same.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I want to go back to jurisdiction. I don't want to leave it. As I look at Article 21 of the Colorado system, which is very different than the one that we looked at in Atlantic Richfield, it has two strands. And our amicus tell us that very directly. They tell us that the first strand is like Atlantic Richfield, has to do with writs of prohibition or some sort of writ of that sort, but that it also encompasses appellate jurisdiction. And we don't have a right to take certiorari over appellate jurisdiction cases. How do we know, since the court below didn't tell us, that this was an original writ or just an interlocutory appeal?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Sure. So I don't think, with respect, that that characterization of Rule 21 is correct. I think it is true that Rule 21, which is labeled Original Jurisdiction Under the Constitution, sweeps in two constitutional provisions in Colorado: Article VI, Section 2, which grants the supreme court superintending control, and Article VI, Section 3, which grants the supreme court power to issue certain writs. But I think that the key fact here is that whichever strand of the Constitution you're proceeding under, the rule itself is talking about original jurisdiction in the Colorado Supreme Court, and it could not be clearer --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: If we're unsure --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- that the rule provides for self-contained proceedings. I'm sorry.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- if we're unsure of your characterization, because there's certainly a number of amici brief who disagree with that characterization, shouldn't we be certifying this question to the Colorado court instead of us deciding it? We have to be sure of our jurisdiction before we take it.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: You do, Speaker A, but we cite numerous decisions from the Colorado Supreme Court that characterize the proceeding in exactly this fashion. And if you have --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: And the other side gives us numerous statements completely to the contrary that describe it just as an appellate process.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That is -- with respect, I don't think that that is accurate. I think the best thing that my friend on the other side has pointed to is the fact that the decretal language in this case remanded. But I think the problem with that argument is that in Atlantic Richfield itself, the Montana Supreme Court's decision not only remanded but affirmed the lower court, and yet the court said this is the exercise of original jurisdiction. And can -- if I could add --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: With respect to the Cox stand of your --the Cox strand of your statutory argument, you still have federal defenses below that are available, aren't there?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: We do. But we cite --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: You still have personal jurisdiction. That's usually how we protect against extraterritoriality, correct?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But that provides very limited protection in a context like this, as evidenced by the fact that the trial court rejected that defense and then used --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I mean, you still have an appeal of that.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- and then used personal jurisdiction to bootstrap jurisdiction worldwide.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: You also have causation arguments to raise. The indirectness of this could be a defense to any of the public nuisance arguments.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But the very point of the fourth exception under Cox is that it provides for review in circumstances where the party seeking review might still prevail on non-federal grounds. And we point to Fort Wayne Books for the proposition that the --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, that one, we took great pains to say that it was because there was a second constitutional principle at issue, which was a First Amendment right, where the injury was immediate. Here, the injury is not immediate to you. You still have appellate rights below that can protect any federal claims you have.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: We would submit that the injury to us is immediate for the reasons that I said earlier in response to [PERSON].

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Because you're spending money that -- in litigation. But I don't know that we've ever talked of spending money on litigation as a constitutional injury.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But we are doing so involuntarily as a result of the adverse ruling on a question of federal law. The Court need only get to Cox if it disagrees with the application of Atlantic Richfield, a unanimous decision that is on all fours here. And the last thing I would say, to the extent that there is any doubt, and there really shouldn't be, about Colorado procedure, is, again, that in Colorado, the best evidence that this is in the self-contained original proceeding category is that Colorado provides for two avenues in a circumstance like this. You can take an interlocutory appeal under Colorado Appellate Rule 4.2. That rule looks a lot like Section 1292 in the federal context. And that goes to the Colorado court of appeals first, as you would expect. Or you can go directly to the Colorado Supreme Court. The standard is quite high. You've got to show that you have an extraordinary question. But, if you do, the proceeding begins and ends in the Colorado Supreme Court. And the rules distinguish explicitly between the original proceeding in the Colorado Supreme Court on the one hand and the underlying proceeding in the trial court on the other.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I don't think so. I would submit that this is, in fact, a very different book, and that is for the simple reason --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Book, not the same -- not a chapter in the same book, and that is because, in the tobacco litigation, as your question illustrates, that feels a lot more like a traditional misrepresentation claim where you have representations that are being made about a product, you have consumers relying on those representations and, as a result, suffering injury quite directly if you accept the claims. And in that case, the remedies are --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, I -- I think, in an effort to avoid what would obviously be the preemptive force of our constitutional arguments and, indeed, also our Clean Air Act arguments, Respondent has attempted to back up one step to the misrepresentation. But I want to make clear what is different here. What is different here is that the injury is not suffered by the Colorado consumer in the traditional sense. The claim here, if you look at the misrepresentation strand of the claims -- and it's not very clearly defined in the complaint, but take a look, for instance, at paragraph 411 of the complaint at page 105. It's not really like any sort of misrepresentation claim that you would be familiar with. It's a claim that --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That is basically what we're saying. And we rely on this Court's decision in Kurns for the proposition, when you're engaging in this type of analysis, you've got to look at the gravamen of the claim. And our core submission for this Court is that whatever state law label you attach to the claims -- and, again, I would direct you to the paragraphs that talk about misrepresentation. The gravamen of the claim here is that some marginal increase in greenhouse-gas emissions attributable to my clients' conduct caused the harm.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Kurns -- Kurns makes clear that that is relevant to damages.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Sure. We talked about this Court's cases on interstate pollution, but let me provide, I think, a very concrete grounding for each of the constitutional principles we've been discussing. For the equal sovereignty principle, I would point to [PERSON]'s opinion for the Court in Franchise Tax Board versus Hyatt, which I think established three very important premises for the argument. There, the Court stated that the equal sovereignty of each state imposed -- implied certain limitations on the sovereignty of other states. Second, that there were certain areas involving conflicting rights where states could not supply the applicable rule of decision. The Court cited borders, water rights, and interstate compacts.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So I think that Hyatt establishes the premise for this mode of constitutional interpretation, and the cases that applied federal common law before the enactment of the Clean Air Act apply that principle in the context of interstate pollution. And if I could point you to any cases from this Court, the two I would select are Missouri versus Illinois and Georgia versus Tennessee Copper, two decisions written by Justice Holmes within two years of each other that talk about the fact that states no longer have the right to abate forcible nuisances. And on the extraterritoriality principle, but I -- which I know we were discussing earlier, I can actually do no better than this Court's decision in National Pork Producers, which recognized that there are certain territorial limitations on state power as a matter of constitutional structure that are embodied to some extent in the Due Process Clause and the Full Faith and Credit Clause but that exist more broadly beyond those specific applications.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That is undoubtedly true with regard to the --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I -- I'm not resisting that. I took --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Sure. There's no flaw in that with regard to our equal sovereignty principle because the equal --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And -- and that is dispositive in our view.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So what we would say is that when you're dealing with air and water and their ambient aspects, that is what implicates the conflicting rights of states. And, boy, in the context of climate change, do you ever have conflicting rights because states have wildly divergent views on the correct approach.

Milwaukee I, Milwaukee II, Ouellette, and AEP, which, as I read them together, make crystal-clear that interstate air and water pollution are matters for federal law unless Congress specifically preserves state law. That is through and through those four cases. So I -- maybe there's a flaw in that. And, actually, there is one wrinkle I'm going to raise, but you tell me why you're just resisting that.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Sure. There's no flaw in that with regard to our equal sovereignty principle because the equal --

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Well, isn't that -- I mean --

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: And -- and that is dispositive in our view.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Exactly.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: So what we would say is that when you're dealing with air and water and their ambient aspects, that is what implicates the conflicting rights of states. And, boy, in the context of climate change, do you ever have conflicting rights because states have wildly divergent views on the correct approach.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: So why -- we don't have to reinvent the wheel because we've said this multiple times, and Congress presumably, when doing the Clean Air Act and doing the Clean Air Act amendments, has relied on this Court's precedents establishing that this kind of pollution is a federal law matter unless Congress speaks otherwise.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Correct. And --

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Okay. Now the wrinkle -- and this is -- I think, goes back to [PERSON]'s question -- the one wrinkle, it's a little -- and [PERSON]'s --a little bit of a problem for you -- is that Ouellette did allow the Vermont affected party to sue the New York polluter under New York State law. What do we do with that? Give me the explanation you would provide for how we deal with that if your side is to prevail and not to go back on choice of law.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: So the easiest answer to that, Speaker A, is that it is clear that my friend, [PERSON], is relying on Colorado law, the law of the affected state. So, if you --

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Okay. That resolves this case. If he weren't, what's your answer?

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Yes. And that's very important for us given the fact that there are dozens of these cases out there. So I think what I would say is that if, say, a plaintiff in the next town over tried to bring a claim against Exxon Mobil under, say, Texas law, what we would say is that it still is not a claim that really involves the source state in any meaningful sense because we're not talking about --

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: How about if it was against an emitter, a Texas emitter under Texas law by a Texas affected party for --

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: That is --

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: -- for greenhouse-gas emissions?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Like my children, I love both of our theories equally, [PERSON].

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But let me explain --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: They both get you to the same result in this case, and let me explain why. As I was saying to [PERSON], under our equal sovereignty theory, Congress has the authority to authorize state law to apply. There's nothing anomalous about that. That is just Congress saying that in this uniquely federal area, we can prescribe as the federal rule of decision that state law applies. It's no different from a court applying federal common law borrowing state law. Now my caveat, which I think is an important one, is that in the context of these sorts of climate change claims, it really doesn't make a lot of sense to talk about the source state law. Remember that my clients are not emitters, as was the case in American Electric Power. My clients are producers of fossil fuels. And these sorts of claims -- I said at the outset that these claims -- that the application of federal law follows a fortiori from the interstate pollution cases. Unlike in the traditional interstate pollution cases like Ouellette, where you have two states, the source state and the affected state, here, because the claim runs through global climate change, the claims here necessarily depend on the emissions of anyone who uses fossil fuels worldwide. All 50 states and --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- foreign countries have an interest.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That is correct, which is to say this is --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. Let me answer that question. And I do want to finish off my answer to [PERSON]. But let me address your question first, [PERSON]. I respectfully disagree with your suggestion that this issue was not fully preserved. And I would note that we made all these arguments in our petition for certiorari. There was never any suggestion by Respondent that these arguments were not made below. Now I will acknowledge that I think that the two strands of our argument are closely related, and the reason that they are closely related is that the constitutional source for our arguments is essentially the same. Our constitutional source is that when the states went into the constitutional system, the states sacrificed certain rights that they would have had as independent sovereigns, and they went into the Union on an equal footing. That is really the source for the extraterritoriality principle, which goes all the way back to Justice Marshall and Justice Story. I would point this Court to the various amicus briefs, including the amicus brief of Professor Prakash, as well as the amicus brief of Tennessee, which set out the originalist history for these principles in some detail. Now, to answer, [PERSON], the last part of your question, yes, it is true in both Ouellette and in American Electric Power that the Court recognized that there is some room for state law to operate at least in the context of a bilateral interstate pollution dispute. But that is because the Clean Water Act and the Clean Air Act contain these saving clauses, which this Court --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: With --with, sorry?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Oh, I'm not sure I'm remembering which case you're --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Oh. Well, look, I think what I would say as to the constructive presence cases more generally, not just Watson but any other constructive presence case, is that there is no case comparable to this one. I actually think that the closest case on which my friend relies is State versus Lord, which was not a case from this Court. But, even in that case, what you were dealing with was the diversion of water into the affected state. It was much easier to say in that context that the nuisance existed in the affected state than here. And, again, I would just say that in Ouellette, in AEP, the Court was plainly construing and definitively construing the scope of the savings clauses to apply only to source state law. And the last thing -- can I say one last thing to [PERSON]? And I'll be very brief.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: [PERSON], on the extraterritoriality principle, I think what I would say is that if you accept our view that this goes too far under the extraterritoriality principle, I think your analysis is at an end. I suppose that one could make an additional argument that even as to the extraterritoriality principle, a state could -- Congress could authorize the application of state law. But it would still get you to the same result. So, yes, these are separate strands, but I think, ultimately, the conclusion under each is the same.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Sure. So I don't think, with respect, that that characterization of Rule 21 is correct. I think it is true that Rule 21, which is labeled Original Jurisdiction Under the Constitution, sweeps in two constitutional provisions in Colorado: Article VI, Section 2, which grants the supreme court superintending control, and Article VI, Section 3, which grants the supreme court power to issue certain writs. But I think that the key fact here is that whichever strand of the Constitution you're proceeding under, the rule itself is talking about original jurisdiction in the Colorado Supreme Court, and it could not be clearer --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- that the rule provides for self-contained proceedings. I'm sorry.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: You do, [PERSON], but we cite numerous decisions from the Colorado Supreme Court that characterize the proceeding in exactly this fashion. And if you have --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That is -- with respect, I don't think that that is accurate. I think the best thing that my friend on the other side has pointed to is the fact that the decretal language in this case remanded. But I think the problem with that argument is that in Atlantic Richfield itself, the Montana Supreme Court's decision not only remanded but affirmed the lower court, and yet the court said this is the exercise of original jurisdiction. And can -- if I could add --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: We do. But we cite --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But that provides very limited protection in a context like this, as evidenced by the fact that the trial court rejected that defense and then used --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- and then used personal jurisdiction to bootstrap jurisdiction worldwide.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But the very point of the fourth exception under Cox is that it provides for review in circumstances where the party seeking review might still prevail on non-federal grounds. And we point to Fort Wayne Books for the proposition that the --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: We would submit that the injury to us is immediate for the reasons that I said earlier in response to [PERSON].

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But we are doing so involuntarily as a result of the adverse ruling on a question of federal law. The Court need only get to Cox if it disagrees with the application of Atlantic Richfield, a unanimous decision that is on all fours here. And the last thing I would say, to the extent that there is any doubt, and there really shouldn't be, about Colorado procedure, is, again, that in Colorado, the best evidence that this is in the self-contained original proceeding category is that Colorado provides for two avenues in a circumstance like this. You can take an interlocutory appeal under Colorado Appellate Rule 4.2. That rule looks a lot like Section 1292 in the federal context. And that goes to the Colorado court of appeals first, as you would expect. Or you can go directly to the Colorado Supreme Court. The standard is quite high. You've got to show that you have an extraordinary question. But, if you do, the proceeding begins and ends in the Colorado Supreme Court. And the rules distinguish explicitly between the original proceeding in the Colorado Supreme Court on the one hand and the underlying proceeding in the trial court on the other.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I don't think so. I would submit that this is, in fact, a very different book, and that is for the simple reason --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Book, not the same -- not a chapter in the same book, and that is because, in the tobacco litigation, as your question illustrates, that feels a lot more like a traditional misrepresentation claim where you have representations that are being made about a product, you have consumers relying on those representations and, as a result, suffering injury quite directly if you accept the claims. And in that case, the remedies are --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, I -- I think, in an effort to avoid what would obviously be the preemptive force of our constitutional arguments and, indeed, also our Clean Air Act arguments, Respondent has attempted to back up one step to the misrepresentation. But I want to make clear what is different here. What is different here is that the injury is not suffered by the Colorado consumer in the traditional sense. The claim here, if you look at the misrepresentation strand of the claims -- and it's not very clearly defined in the complaint, but take a look, for instance, at paragraph 411 of the complaint at page 105. It's not really like any sort of misrepresentation claim that you would be familiar with. It's a claim that --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That is basically what we're saying. And we rely on this Court's decision in Kurns for the proposition, when you're engaging in this type of analysis, you've got to look at the gravamen of the claim. And our core submission for this Court is that whatever state law label you attach to the claims -- and, again, I would direct you to the paragraphs that talk about misrepresentation. The gravamen of the claim here is that some marginal increase in greenhouse-gas emissions attributable to my clients' conduct caused the harm.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Kurns -- Kurns makes clear that that is relevant to damages.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Sure. We talked about this Court's cases on interstate pollution, but let me provide, I think, a very concrete grounding for each of the constitutional principles we've been discussing. For the equal sovereignty principle, I would point to [PERSON]'s opinion for the Court in Franchise Tax Board versus Hyatt, which I think established three very important premises for the argument. There, the Court stated that the equal sovereignty of each state imposed -- implied certain limitations on the sovereignty of other states. Second, that there were certain areas involving conflicting rights where states could not supply the applicable rule of decision. The Court cited borders, water rights, and interstate compacts.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So I think that Hyatt establishes the premise for this mode of constitutional interpretation, and the cases that applied federal common law before the enactment of the Clean Air Act apply that principle in the context of interstate pollution. And if I could point you to any cases from this Court, the two I would select are Missouri versus Illinois and Georgia versus Tennessee Copper, two decisions written by Justice Holmes within two years of each other that talk about the fact that states no longer have the right to abate forcible nuisances. And on the extraterritoriality principle, but I -- which I know we were discussing earlier, I can actually do no better than this Court's decision in National Pork Producers, which recognized that there are certain territorial limitations on state power as a matter of constitutional structure that are embodied to some extent in the Due Process Clause and the Full Faith and Credit Clause but that exist more broadly beyond those specific applications.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: On the tobacco and opioid question that [PERSON] asked, and she alluded to this, I thought the answer was that this Court has consistently said that air and water pollution are different in our federal enclaves.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That is undoubtedly true with regard to the --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: What -- why are you resisting that? I just thought --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I -- I'm not resisting that. I took --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I mean, there's a lot of constitutional theory being tossed around, but we have four precedents on point. Let me finish.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Let me finish. Milwaukee I, Milwaukee II, Ouellette, and AEP, which, as I read them together, make crystal-clear that interstate air and water pollution are matters for federal law unless Congress specifically preserves state law. That is through and through those four cases. So I -- maybe there's a flaw in that. And, actually, there is one wrinkle I'm going to raise, but you tell me why you're just resisting that.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Sure. There's no flaw in that with regard to our equal sovereignty principle because the equal --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, isn't that -- I mean --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And -- and that is dispositive in our view.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Exactly.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So what we would say is that when you're dealing with air and water and their ambient aspects, that is what implicates the conflicting rights of states. And, boy, in the context of climate change, do you ever have conflicting rights because states have wildly divergent views on the correct approach.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So why -- we don't have to reinvent the wheel because we've said this multiple times, and Congress presumably, when doing the Clean Air Act and doing the Clean Air Act amendments, has relied on this Court's precedents establishing that this kind of pollution is a federal law matter unless Congress speaks otherwise.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Correct. And --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Okay. Now the wrinkle -- and this is -- I think, goes back to [PERSON]'s question -- the one wrinkle, it's a little -- and [PERSON]'s --a little bit of a problem for you -- is that Ouellette did allow the Vermont affected party to sue the New York polluter under New York State law. What do we do with that? Give me the explanation you would provide for how we deal with that if your side is to prevail and not to go back on choice of law.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So the easiest answer to that, Speaker A, is that it is clear that my friend, [PERSON], is relying on Colorado law, the law of the affected state. So, if you --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Okay. That resolves this case. If he weren't, what's your answer?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes. And that's very important for us given the fact that there are dozens of these cases out there. So I think what I would say is that if, say, a plaintiff in the next town over tried to bring a claim against Exxon Mobil under, say, Texas law, what we would say is that it still is not a claim that really involves the source state in any meaningful sense because we're not talking about --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: How about if it was against an emitter, a Texas emitter under Texas law by a Texas affected party for --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That is --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- for greenhouse-gas emissions?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- that is the very question that the Court left open in AEP. It suggested that as to emitters, you might be able to bring a claim under the source state law. The Court didn't definitively resolve that. It just left it open in the way that this Court often does. But we would say that in this context of climate change, when you're suing producers, you cannot do that. And I would say that the most telling thing is that neither Respondent nor any of their 28 amici suggest that the saving clause in the Clean Air Act affirmatively authorize claims in this context.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Under Colorado law?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: At least under Colorado law. But I didn't see an argument anywhere as to why this -- it makes sense to say that there is a source state for claims of this variety.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Okay. A different point now. The Clean Air Act is very significant in terms of the responsibilities it puts on states. We've had the cross-state air pollution rule. I had that multiple times on the D.C. Circuit. It came up here. EME Homer sets forth the good neighbor provision, tells the states what they can do. Explain as clearly as you can the conflicts or the inconsistencies or the -- or the like that would result if states could do tort suits and were no longer constrained by the good neighbor provision in the way that the Clean Air Act constrains them.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. So, certainly, as this Court has recognized, we believe that the Clean Air Act establishes a comprehensive scheme for the regulation of air quality in the United States.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right. I got that.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But I don't want to --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Just very precisely, what are the states' responsibilities that would be in tension with allowing tort suits? If you could answer that specifically.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think the best place to look is to Section 7411, which is Section 111 of the Clean Air Act, which makes the EPA the primary regulator of stationary sources and gives secondary authority to source states because the states submit plans that specify emissions reductions for point sources within their jurisdiction. You alluded to the good neighbor provision, which is in the previous section, which, for certain pollutants, requires states to take into account the effects on neighboring states in submitting plans. This regime that Boulder is positing, this liability regime runs directly contrary to that because it is a scheme that gives EPA primary authority and source states secondary authority. And, again, when we're talking about source states, under the Clean Air Act, the Clean Air Act reflects the judgment that it is the emitters who are going to be regulated and not the producers. And so I think all of these arguments dovetail with each other. The only other thing I would say, just to close the loop on where you started, Speaker A, is that when I was answering [PERSON]'s question, I was really answering it with regard to the extraterritoriality principle because I think that's where it's clearest that the effects here are much more attenuated --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: No, I would just answer it with respect to our precedent.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Our precedent says air and water pollution are different. But there is a wrinkle there on choice of law. And that's the -- that's the tension I see.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, the wrinkle is --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I guess the wrinkle's resolved under your extraterritoriality.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And the wrinkle is that it isn't so much choice of law as that Congress has authorized state law to apply in a very specific context. That having been said --and, again, we think that both of these principles point to the same result. But the virtue of the Court potentially relying on the equal sovereignty principle is that it is certainly not writing on a blank slate. It wouldn't be doing that even with extraterritoriality. We have this line of cases culminating in the Court's unanimous decision in AEP rejecting claims against the actual emitters. This case just represents an effort to back up one step, and that's on the --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Last question. Real succinctly, do you think that our precedents that I mentioned before come from the equal sovereignty principle or the extraterritoriality principle? I would have thought the former.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think the former.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Okay. That's all I need.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes. And the cases that the Court relies on -- the principles the Court relies are on the Hyatt principles.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I -- I do slightly quibble with that, [PERSON], in that, although the Court may not have used the specific term "authorize," I do think it's the implication of the Court's reasoning. Remember that in Ouellette, the Court cited not just Congress's pervasive regulation under the Clean Water Act but also, "the fact that control of interstate pollution is primarily a matter of federal law." And then the Court went on to construe the saving clause of the Clean Water Act. And I think the implication of recognizing the constitutional principle is that what the Court was effectively saying, again, even though it didn't use the word "authorize," was that Congress has -- has authorized state law to operate where it otherwise would not have been able to authorize -- to -- to apply.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But I think that the problem with that is that I think one of two things would have to be true for that characterization to be correct. One of them would be that state law previously would have operated for a claim of this variety. In other words --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, it was incredibly circumscribed because, if you look at the cases that Boulder cites on page 36 of their brief, I think that the best they can do is the case that I alluded to earlier involving water diversion, where it's much easier to say the nuisance is physically present in the state. But the alternative -- and I think that this is the real upshot of the argument that Boulder is making -- is to say that when Congress enacted the Clean Water Act and the Clean Air Act, that state law somehow sprung into effect.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- and that can't possibly be --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- correct.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And -- and --and the last thing I would say on this line is that when it comes to the federal common law, I think at least in its brief -- we'll see what my friend says at oral argument --Boulder suggests that the -- that the way to think about this is to think about whether or not there would have been a federal common law cause of action. But I think this Court, both in the context of interstate pollution cases and beyond, has made clear that a federal court can decide for any number of reasons not to recognize a federal common law claim, even in an area where uniquely federal interests are implicated. So the mere fact that this Court limited federal common law to cases where states were bringing claims either against other states or even against private parties doesn't really tell you anything about the field that is covered by the constitutional --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- principle.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So I think what we would say as to that is that any decision that EPA makes as to whether and how to regulate greenhouse-gas emissions -- and that's obviously subject to ongoing litigation -- but any decision that EPA makes has no bearing on our argument concerning constitutional structure. Our arguments concerning constitutional structure apply with full force regardless of what EPA says --

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: So I -- I want to pick up on some of the questions [PERSON] was asking you. As I read those four precedents, the Milwaukee and Ouellette and AEP, they do say, drawing on other older precedents, that this is a field, interstate pollution, air and water, is a field that's an enclave of federal common law because it is not suited to the law of any one state, bracketing for one moment source state, state law, you know, suits in the -- under the state law of the source state. Right?

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: Yes.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: Okay. So then, when you get to AEP -- so tell me if -- if I'm going wrong in any spot here -- when you get to AEP, what the Court says is, yes, before, this was an area of law which needed nationally uniform federal rules, and in the absence of congressional speak -- a statute, federal common law is what governed. But now we have the Clean Air Act, and Massachusetts versus EPA interpreted 7411 to say that the EPA is the one that has the authority to regulate greenhouse-gas emissions. So, to the extent there is a national rule, Congress has given it to the EPA to set it. Now I think where I would quibble with you is about where the state law comes in. I do not read either Ouellette or AEP to say that they are authorizing states to apply state common law rules or apply their own law otherwise. What I read it to be saying is, if you think of a Venn diagram, there was this center where it always had to be an enclave of federal common law, where federal courts were developing the rules for interstate air and water pollution, but even under that old pre-Clean Air Act system, there was this outer ring where states had authority. So maybe in some of these cases that we're talking about where you had the source state and you were suing for, you know, emissions and you were suing in Texas for emissions from a Texas source or maybe some of these cross-border suits where there was a tight connection, I understand what the Court said in AEP to simply say: Congress preserved some state authority. It -- it displaced --to the extent we need national rules, federal courts, you're out of the business. But it did not disturb some of that state authority. And then the Court just didn't decide how much of that state authority it might have preempted or not because it wasn't before it. But it's not that it said Congress authorized states in any way. It just left alone some of that preexisting authority, maybe some of which might be affected by the Clean Air Act. Do you quibble with any of that?

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: I -- I do slightly quibble with that, Speaker A, in that, although the Court may not have used the specific term "authorize," I do think it's the implication of the Court's reasoning. Remember that in Ouellette, the Court cited not just Congress's pervasive regulation under the Clean Water Act but also, "the fact that control of interstate pollution is primarily a matter of federal law." And then the Court went on to construe the saving clause of the Clean Water Act. And I think the implication of recognizing the constitutional principle is that what the Court was effectively saying, again, even though it didn't use the word "authorize," was that Congress has -- has authorized state law to operate where it otherwise would not have been able to authorize -- to -- to apply.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: Well, I --

turns_pm60.speaker: B

And if you accepted Respondents' contrary functional view of does this feel like an interlocutory proceeding, does it feel kind of appellatee, I don't know what remains of the Court's traditional conception of its 1257 jurisdiction. You respect the state supreme court's framing of these things. And it seems clear that that's what the Colorado Supreme Court did.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Let me put it this way. In all of those state court -- tort cases, of course, you can regulate the out-of-state injury directed at your state. What it's not doing is saying what Colorado is doing here: You're banned from making that product anywhere nationwide. And so that's why this case falls more in the BMW v -- v. Gore side of the line, where the Court nicely illustrates the distinction.

turns_pm60.text: Again, you only allow that just as in BMW it's not a question of remedy. turns_pm60.text: Ms. -- Speaker A --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- let alone across the world.

turns_pm60.text: -- can I just ask on the -- that's a very complicated inquiry: direct effects, predictable effects. Doesn't that take care of the issue? What -- I mean, I guess I'm not sure why you're leading with this more difficult inquiry than the one that our precedents have set forth since 1972.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: We agree that both paths are available and have no problem if you consider the -- the equal sovereignty arguments of --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: What's -- you're leading with the other one, which makes me think there's a problem with the precedent, interstate air pollution one. So what -- what's the problem with that? Why are you leading with the other one?

turns_pm60.text: Because we think there are two complementary theories in this case that are good to expound. But we are a hundred percent on board with what Petitioners are saying, so --

turns_pm60.text: Sure.

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.text: Okay.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- above and beyond.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That's beyond our precedent. Okay, thank you.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: If you prevail, is there a limiting principle to whom you can -- as to whom you can sue?

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: There are a number. So there's the constitutional limitations on choice of law, which require a sufficient nexus between the state whose law is to be applied and the conduct at issue. There's the Dormant Commerce Clause. There's personal jurisdiction limitations. The question here is not whether anything in the Constitution prohibits this lawsuit but whether the specific theories that they raised and the -- the Colorado Supreme Court passed upon below are valid.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: So you could just as easily sue large retailers of -- of --of these products?

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: I think nothing in the Constitution would prevent that. I think that we would have --

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: But nothing in your theory prevents that either, right?

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: Nothing in our theory prevents that. It could be that the Colorado courts would have a different idea that it is first and foremost a question of --of state tort law. But, in terms -- but, you know, when lots of people act together to cause widespread harm, it is not uncommon for multiple different defendants to be potentially liable. But the principal, I think, protection, to the extent that seems unreasonable, is that Congress stands at the ready to intervene and to enact federal law that preempts unreasonable state laws with undesirable national effects.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] Since the Founding, states have had the power to provide tort remedies for injuries occurring within their borders even when the conduct causing those injuries occurred elsewhere. When somebody in New York defames a citizen of Boulder on national television or somebody in California releases a computer virus on the Internet or a biological virus into the world and it causes mass damage in Colorado, it has never been thought that only federal law can provide a remedy simply because the tortious conduct and the injury occurred in different states, because the harm was widespread, the damages were large, or the defendants were part of an important industry. And applying state law to such cases has never been viewed as one state impermissibly projecting its law nationwide. To be sure, specific constitutional provisions limit choice of law and place other constraints on the extraterritorial effects of state law. But Petitioners invoke none of those provisions here. Instead, they invite this Court to find in the structure of the Constitution a judicial power to declare some subject matters inherently federal and, therefore, preempted not by Congressional enactments but by Congressional silence. That claim inverts the constitutional structure and risks preemption being driven by judicial policy intuitions rather than anything in the Constitution itself. The structure of the Constitution places residual authority to preempt state laws with undesirable nationwide effects in Congress, not the courts. Accordingly, in AEP, this Court held that preemption of global warming nuisance claims is governed by the preemptive force of the Clean Air Act, citing Ouellette, which applied ordinary statutory preemption principles and concluded that state law could apply. Here, the statute does not preempt Respondents' deception and other claims against non-emitters not subject to the Act. But all of this must await another case because Petitioners have failed to establish this Court's jurisdiction to hear this interlocutory appeal. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.text: Even Ouellette recognized that it was all right to bring the state law claim there. So what do you do with that?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] Since the Founding, states have had the power to provide tort remedies for injuries occurring within their borders even when the conduct causing those injuries occurred elsewhere. When somebody in New York defames a citizen of Boulder on national television or somebody in California releases a computer virus on the Internet or a biological virus into the world and it causes mass damage in Colorado, it has never been thought that only federal law can provide a remedy simply because the tortious conduct and the injury occurred in different states, because the harm was widespread, the damages were large, or the defendants were part of an important industry. And applying state law to such cases has never been viewed as one state impermissibly projecting its law nationwide. To be sure, specific constitutional provisions limit choice of law and place other constraints on the extraterritorial effects of state law. But Petitioners invoke none of those provisions here. Instead, they invite this Court to find in the structure of the Constitution a judicial power to declare some subject matters inherently federal and, therefore, preempted not by Congressional enactments but by Congressional silence. That claim inverts the constitutional structure and risks preemption being driven by judicial policy intuitions rather than anything in the Constitution itself. The structure of the Constitution places residual authority to preempt state laws with undesirable nationwide effects in Congress, not the courts. Accordingly, in AEP, this Court held that preemption of global warming nuisance claims is governed by the preemptive force of the Clean Air Act, citing Ouellette, which applied ordinary statutory preemption principles and concluded that state law could apply. Here, the statute does not preempt Respondents' deception and other claims against non-emitters not subject to the Act. But all of this must await another case because Petitioners have failed to establish this Court's jurisdiction to hear this interlocutory appeal. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.text: There are a number. So there's the constitutional limitations on choice of law, which require a sufficient nexus between the state whose law is to be applied and the conduct at issue. There's the Dormant Commerce Clause. There's personal jurisdiction limitations. The question here is not whether anything in the Constitution prohibits this lawsuit but whether the specific theories that they raised and the -- the Colorado Supreme Court passed upon below are valid.

But, in terms -- but, you know, when lots of people act together to cause widespread harm, it is not uncommon for multiple different defendants to be potentially liable. But the principal, I think, protection, to the extent that seems unreasonable, is that Congress stands at the ready to intervene and to enact federal law that preempts unreasonable state laws with undesirable national effects.

turns_pm60.speaker: B

This case is not about emissions. It's about deception and -- and producers. But, even assuming that this case was exactly about the same subject matter, I think the Court has treated this as, look, there was a body of federal common law. Set to the side for the moment whether that body of common law reflected this Court's determination that only federal law could apply there or that the Court had some degree of flexibility for deciding that some subject matters of special federal interest should be subject to federal common law. But there was this federal common law. Congress steps in and displaces it. And when Congress steps and displaces it, it displaces all of the policy decisions that were previously made by courts, including on the proper role of state law. turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] Since the Founding, states have had the power to provide tort remedies for injuries occurring within their borders even when the conduct causing those injuries occurred elsewhere. When somebody in New York defames a citizen of Boulder on national television or somebody in California releases a computer virus on the Internet or a biological virus into the world and it causes mass damage in Colorado, it has never been thought that only federal law can provide a remedy simply because the tortious conduct and the injury occurred in different states, because the harm was widespread, the damages were large, or the defendants were part of an important industry. And applying state law to such cases has never been viewed as one state impermissibly projecting its law nationwide. To be sure, specific constitutional provisions limit choice of law and place other constraints on the extraterritorial effects of state law. But Petitioners invoke none of those provisions here. Instead, they invite this Court to find in the structure of the Constitution a judicial power to declare some subject matters inherently federal and, therefore, preempted not by Congressional enactments but by Congressional silence. That claim inverts the constitutional structure and risks preemption being driven by judicial policy intuitions rather than anything in the Constitution itself. The structure of the Constitution places residual authority to preempt state laws with undesirable nationwide effects in Congress, not the courts. Accordingly, in AEP, this Court held that preemption of global warming nuisance claims is governed by the preemptive force of the Clean Air Act, citing Ouellette, which applied ordinary statutory preemption principles and concluded that state law could apply. Here, the statute does not preempt Respondents' deception and other claims against non-emitters not subject to the Act. But all of this must await another case because Petitioners have failed to establish this Court's jurisdiction to hear this interlocutory appeal. I welcome the Court's questions.
