turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] Since the Founding, states have had the power to provide tort remedies for injuries occurring within their borders even when the conduct causing those injuries occurred elsewhere. When somebody in New York defames a citizen of Boulder on national television or somebody in California releases a computer virus on the Internet or a biological virus into the world and it causes mass damage in Colorado, it has never been thought that only federal law can provide a remedy simply because the tortious conduct and the injury occurred in different states, because the harm was widespread, the damages were large, or the defendants were part of an important industry. And applying state law to such cases has never been viewed as one state impermissibly projecting its law nationwide. To be sure, specific constitutional provisions limit choice of law and place other constraints on the extraterritorial effects of state law. But Petitioners invoke none of those provisions here. Instead, they invite this Court to find in the structure of the Constitution a judicial power to declare some subject matters inherently federal and, therefore, preempted not by Congressional enactments but by Congressional silence. That claim inverts the constitutional structure and risks preemption being driven by judicial policy intuitions rather than anything in the Constitution itself. The structure of the Constitution places residual authority to preempt state laws with undesirable nationwide effects in Congress, not the courts. Accordingly, in AEP, this Court held that preemption of global warming nuisance claims is governed by the preemptive force of the Clean Air Act, citing Ouellette, which applied ordinary statutory preemption principles and concluded that state law could apply. Here, the statute does not preempt Respondents' deception and other claims against non-emitters not subject to the Act. But all of this must await another case because Petitioners have failed to establish this Court's jurisdiction to hear this interlocutory appeal. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] Since the Founding, states have had the power to provide tort remedies for injuries occurring within their borders even when the conduct causing those injuries occurred elsewhere. When somebody in New York defames a citizen of Boulder on national television or somebody in California releases a computer virus on the Internet or a biological virus into the world and it causes mass damage in Colorado, it has never been thought that only federal law can provide a remedy simply because the tortious conduct and the injury occurred in different states, because the harm was widespread, the damages were large, or the defendants were part of an important industry. And applying state law to such cases has never been viewed as one state impermissibly projecting its law nationwide. To be sure, specific constitutional provisions limit choice of law and place other constraints on the extraterritorial effects of state law. But Petitioners invoke none of those provisions here. Instead, they invite this Court to find in the structure of the Constitution a judicial power to declare some subject matters inherently federal and, therefore, preempted not by Congressional enactments but by Congressional silence. That claim inverts the constitutional structure and risks preemption being driven by judicial policy intuitions rather than anything in the Constitution itself. The structure of the Constitution places residual authority to preempt state laws with undesirable nationwide effects in Congress, not the courts. Here, the statute does not preempt Respondents' deception and other claims against non-emitters not subject to the Act. But all of this must await another case because Petitioners have failed to establish this Court's jurisdiction to hear this interlocutory appeal. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, with respect, I disagree with that. Number one, the deception claims, I think, are far outside anything the Clean Air Act is designed to deal with. turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: Can applied constitutional challenges be considered under 511?

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: Can as- applied?

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: As-applied challenges.

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: So we have avoid use -- we have tried to avoid using the distinction between facial versus as-applied in our briefing here because that terminology risks confusion, and, ultimately, it's a red herring. So let me explain what our position has always been and how as-applied and facial has been -- come into this case. So our position, the line that we have always tried to drawn is -- draw is the line that this Court drew in Robison. On one side of that line is challenges to statutes, and on the other side of the line is challenges to agency action, constitutional and otherwise. And so the reason you see this "facial" versus "as-applied" terminology is because lower courts have used that terminology to describe the two sides of the Robison line. But that's confusing because this Court uses that terminology in a more well-known context, which is the Salerno context, which is, you know, invalid as to all applications versus as to just some. So we -- that's not what lower courts are talking about in this context. And so, to answer your question, as-applied meaning attacks on agency action, even constitutional ones, they must -- our position is that they must go through the VJRA process, they are covered by the text of Section 511(a), whereas attacks on -- on -- or challenges to statutes, those fall outside the scope of Section 511(a).

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] Section 511(a) reaches questions necessary to a decision under a law that affects the provision of benefits. Text, context, structure, and the government's own longstanding practice make clear that 511(a) does not reach constitutional challenges to statutes. Start with the text. A decision under a statute is a decision in accordance with the statute. It applies the statute as written. That's how this Court construed the same phrase in Robison. And deciding a statute's validity is not necessary to a decision under the statute. The VA did not need to resolve Section 5313's validity to reduce Mr. Johnson's benefits in accordance with Section 5313. Indeed, a decision to disregard Section 5313 as unconstitutional would obviously not be in accordance with Section 5313. Context reinforces the point. The Board of Veterans Appeals must make the VA's final decisions on all 511(a) matters, and no one in 1988 would have understood deciding the constitutionality of statutes as necessary to the BVA's decisions. The BVA had long disclaimed authority to decide those questions, and the settled understanding was that administrative tribunals couldn't decide them. If Congress meant to depart from those settled views, it would have done so clearly, but it didn't. In fact, the government itself has long understood 511(a) exactly the way we do. The VA responded to 511(a) by prohibiting the BVA from deciding challenges to statutes. And the BVA has continued to disclaim authority over those questions. The government's new reading would spurn decades of BVA practice and raise a host of anomalies and thorny questions. Among other things, it would empower the inferior officers of the BVA to render final decisions for the executive on whether to disregard acts of Congress. That presents serious Article II concerns. And none of the government's proposed workarounds is consistent with the VJRA. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] Section 511(a) reaches questions necessary to a decision under a law that affects the provision of benefits. The Board of Veterans Appeals must make the VA's final decisions on all 511(a) matters, and no one in 1988 would have understood deciding the constitutionality of statutes as necessary to the BVA's decisions. The BVA had long disclaimed authority to decide those questions, and the settled understanding was that administrative tribunals couldn't decide them. If Congress meant to depart from those settled views, it would have done so clearly, but it didn't. In fact, the government itself has long understood 511(a) exactly the way we do. The VA responded to 511(a) by prohibiting the BVA from deciding challenges to statutes. And the BVA has continued to disclaim authority over those questions. The government's new reading would spurn decades of BVA practice and raise a host of anomalies and thorny questions. turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] Section 511(a) reaches questions necessary to a decision under a law that affects the provision of benefits. turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] The law entitles Petitioner to judicial review, just not in district court. Under Section 511(a), Petitioner's challenge to the validity of Section 5313 is a question of law that is necessary to a decision under the benefits laws because the answer to that question dictates whether his benefits under Section 1131 must be reduced. 511(a) therefore channels his claim to the Veterans Court and the Federal Circuit. Indeed, those courts have already decided the very same constitutional claims. If Petitioner concedes that as-applied claims are covered by 511(a), then there's no basis for treating facial claims differently. Petitioner resists that straightforward analysis with two main theories. The first is that the VJRA incorporated this Court's holding in Johnson against Robison, but the VJRA fundamentally changed the statutory scheme. It amended 511(a) to establish that the relevant question of law need not arise under a benefits statute to be covered. And it enacted Chapter 72, which obviates Robison's constitutional concerns and explicitly contemplates that challenges to VA benefit statutes are channeled into the exclusive review scheme. It's the current statute that matters. The second theory is that the VA can't decide constitutional challenges to statutes, so 511(a) can't apply to such claims. But the premise is mistaken. True, the Board of Veterans Appeals in the past has been inconsistent on its authority, sometimes deciding such claims and sometimes not. But, as we see it, the Board can and must decide veterans' constitutional claims subject to the supervision of agency leadership. Petitioner's contrary view would conflict with the statutory text and deprive veterans of their ability to bring such claims to the agency. It would even compel the VA to enforce a hypothetical benefits statute that was blatantly unconstitutional. The judgment of the court of appeals should be affirmed. I welcome the Court's questions.

Under Section 511(a), Petitioner's challenge to the validity of Section 5313 is a question of law that is necessary to a decision under the benefits laws because the answer to that question dictates whether his benefits under Section 1131 must be reduced. 511(a) therefore channels his claim to the Veterans Court and the Federal Circuit. Indeed, those courts have already decided the very same constitutional claims. If Petitioner concedes that as-applied claims are covered by 511(a), then there's no basis for treating facial claims differently. Petitioner resists that straightforward analysis with two main theories. The first is that the VJRA incorporated this Court's holding in Johnson against Robison, but the VJRA fundamentally changed the statutory scheme. It amended 511(a) to establish that the relevant question of law need not arise under a benefits statute to be covered. And it enacted Chapter 72, which obviates Robison's constitutional concerns and explicitly contemplates that challenges to VA benefit statutes are channeled into the exclusive review scheme. It's the current statute that matters. The second theory is that the VA can't decide constitutional challenges to statutes, so 511(a) can't apply to such claims. But the premise is mistaken. True, the Board of Veterans Appeals in the past has been inconsistent on its authority, sometimes deciding such claims and sometimes not. But, as we see it, the Board can and must decide veterans' constitutional claims subject to the supervision of agency leadership. Petitioner's contrary view would conflict with the statutory text and deprive veterans of their ability to bring such claims to the agency. It would even compel the VA to enforce a hypothetical benefits statute that was blatantly unconstitutional. The judgment of the court of appeals should be affirmed. I welcome the Court's questions.

I think we're in a world in which a member of the Board sort of goes rogue and declares a federal statute unconstitutional in a scenario where the agency leadership disagrees with that. That would be easily dealt with through the reconsideration process. The Board's chairman has plenary authority to order reconsideration of cases before the Board. By the time that step was taken, the VA leadership could have used the mechanisms that my friend, [PERSON], was discussing to dictate the Board's resolution of that constitutional claim, so instructions of the Secretary, a precedential legal opinion of the agency's GC. turns_pm60.text: Yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- just so I understand the state of play as -- on the ground. You tell us on page 33 of your brief that the Veterans Court opinion is that the Board can but is not required to address constitutional questions. You understand that to be the present state of play in the Veterans Court, right?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Okay. And a year ago, in Pereida, the government took the position that even the Veterans Court couldn't consider constitutional questions, right?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That was erroneous, but, yes, we did say that in our brief.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes, you did.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Okay. And then just to be clear about the Thunder Basin point, you acknowledged that when dealing with an express provision like we have here, this Court generally determines the scope of preclusion simply by interpreting the words Congress has chosen, right?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes. So, as a general matter, we know from Arthrex, page 20 of that decision, that the veterans' general scheme complies with the Appointments Clause. Arthrex did not address this issue of the VA's inability to appeal decisions from the VA itself to the Veterans Court. We think that makes sense given the statutory structure and all the mechanisms that I was discussing earlier for the VA leadership to control the decisions of the Board. I think the upshot of Petitioner's position would have to be that this supposed constitutional problem means that the Board is entirely unconstitutional because it wouldn't just be Board decisions on constitutional questions that would be problematic under his view. It would be the Board issuing final decisions about individual veterans' entitlements to benefits that would be the problem. So we don't think that there is any sort of constitutional avoidance basis for reading out just these facial constitutional claims from the statutory scheme. That broader constitutional theory is not presented in this case, and I don't think you need to go down that road. I think you can just apply the text of Section 511(a) as it's written. And as [PERSON] was interpreting it earlier, we agree with that interpretation. The other thing I wanted to just mention before I forget, [PERSON], you suggested that there's a regulation prohibiting the Board of Veterans Appeals from deciding these kinds of claims. That's not correct. The regulation refers to the Board being bound by applicable statutes. We don't think that an unconstitutional statute could be deemed applicable. And we don't think that in the four decisions that we've cited at page 33 of our brief, where the Board did decide facial constitutional challenges -- I could have cited 12 more -- we don't think in those cases that the Board was violating that regulation, and we also don't think that the Board was somehow exceeding its jurisdiction under Section 511(a). The other thing I wanted to circle back to, Speaker B suggested that the Board could decline to enforce or apply a blatantly unconstitutional statute even if it wasn't channeled, even if that claim was not channeled, to --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, isn't that -- isn't that your position, that it can, but it doesn't have to decide constitutional questions?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: No. We think that --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, I thought that's exactly what I read to you earlier.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- it only can if it must. I'm sorry.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I thought -- I thought that's exactly what I read earlier, was that the Board -- the Veterans Court has stated the Board can but is not required to decide constitutional questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: We -- we disagree with the Veterans Court.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: You disagree with the Veterans Court as well?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Insofar as it suggested --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So you disagree with what you said last year and you disagree with the Veterans Court?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: We disagree with an aspect of that decades-old precedent of the Veterans Court. We think that the Board can and must decide these constitutional claims. If that were not the case, under the text of 511(a), I don't see how the Board could decline to enforce a blatantly unconstitutional benefits statute. That would be the final decision of the agency, and so then all veterans would have to go to the Veterans Court and the Federal Circuit to get relief on those kinds of claims. We don't think that's the scheme that Congress designed. Again, going back to what [PERSON] was discussing about Robison --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: How is it supposed to do that? The Board doesn't have much competence in questions of constitutional -- or it tells us in a lot of cases, and I could cite you a dozen of those. And you say, well, we've got maybe some process we can create with the General Counsel. But we're told the last time the General Counsel came up with a binding prospective opinion was -- was 2019, which was a minute ago. And many of these constitutional questions won't even be sufficiently obvious that there's prospective guidance available to give the Board. So it does seem like a bit of a rabbit hole.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, first of all, I think --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Plus, this will decide constitutional questions even though the court that reviews the Board says they can't, and -- and we don't know what the issues are, and we're not going to provide any guidance. So isn't it really saying -- isn't the upshot of the government's position is the Board's never going to decide a constitutional question?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: The Board has done so. Again --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Oh, yeah, no, it'll -- it'll do so once in a while, and God bless it when it does. I mean, it's great when somebody follows the Constitution. But just as often and more likely than not, the veteran is likely to find a decision saying, ah, yeah, it's a nice constitutional argument you have here; I don't know anything about that; I see nothing, I know nothing, I hear nothing.

turns_pm60.text: I think, Speaker B, particularly if this Court agrees with us on the proper interpretation of 511(a), the Board is going to take very seriously its obligation to decide these claims going forward. There has been uncertainty in the past, I think probably as a result of this notion that administrative agencies are often thought not to have jurisdiction to decide these claims.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Why can't they just continue to do what they've always done, which is say we can, but -- sometimes, and -- and -- and we won't most of the time?

turns_pm60.text: That would be --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: What's to stop them from doing that?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That would be a violation of their statutory duty, which they take very seriously, and we do too.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, except for you've never done it.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes. Absolutely. But I don't think --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, they -- they have on numerous occasions, which we've discussed, and then they haven't done it on other occasions. And so what this Court would be saying is the Board was right in the first set of cases and not the second.

What's wrong with that?

What sense would it make to make the Federal Circuit the exclusive circuit --

turns_pm60.text: Well, one important point I want to make, [PERSON], is that one of the impressions that Petitioner has left is that you can have kind of a standalone constitutional claim that doesn't have any other issues accompanying it. If Petitioner is right --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yet another problem with Petitioner's view is that it's not always going to be clear, the nature of the claim. So, if you look at the complaint --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- that was filed in this case --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, right. But I think it's pretty important that the jurisdictional analysis here would hinge on facial versus as-applied. I want my full benefits. That's the relief I'm demanding. So --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think that approach --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think you could certainly write an opinion like that in theory. I think it would break down very quickly in practice. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- with respect to the facial validity.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, first of all, there is no consistent longstanding practice. As I've said multiple times, the Board has repeatedly decided these kinds of claims, and so we're going to have consistency one way or another going forward. We think that the statutory --

turns_pm60.text: Well, one important point I want to make, [PERSON], is that one of the impressions that Petitioner has left is that you can have kind of a standalone constitutional claim that doesn't have any other issues accompanying it. That will never be the case. Every veteran's benefits dispute involves case-specific, fact-specific determinations that need to be made. Is the person a veteran? Do they have a disability? Is the disability related to their service? So you're always going to have, under his view, dual-track litigation going on both in the VA and then in federal district courts around the country. It makes a lot more sense, and I think Congress agreed with us when it enacted the VJRA, to consolidate all of those issues together and to send them to the Federal Circuit. If Petitioner is right --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yet another problem with Petitioner's view is that it's not always going to be clear, the nature of the claim. So, if you look at the complaint --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- that was filed in this case --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, right. But I think it's pretty important that the jurisdictional analysis here would hinge on facial versus as-applied. If you look at the complaint that Petitioner filed when he was pro se, as many veterans will be, there's nothing about facial versus as-applied. It just says: 5313 is unconstitutional. I want my full benefits. That's the relief I'm demanding. So --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think that approach --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think you could certainly write an opinion like that in theory. I think it would break down very quickly in practice. This is why the Court said in Elgin that the distinction between facial and as-applied claims are very amorphous, hard to get your hands around. And so it's a bad basis to distinguish between claims that must be channeled through an administrative and judicial review scheme and claims that should not be. So we don't think that that is tenable. And we also just don't think that there is any basis in the text or structure of Section 511(a) to distinguish these kinds of claims. A facial claim is certainly necessary to a decision in just the same way that an as-applied claim would be. And, frankly, we think that the kind of uniformity concerns that Congress often has in mind when it enacts a channeling provision are even more serious for facial claims because, if you have as-applied claims turning on the particular circumstances of individual veterans, maybe it's not as big a deal that you're going to have district -- different district courts around the country issuing different types of decisions on that basis --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- with respect to the facial validity.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, first of all, there is no consistent longstanding practice. As I've said multiple times, the Board has repeatedly decided these kinds of claims, and so we're going to have consistency one way or another going forward. We think that the statutory --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: We think that they do have to decide them, yes. And I don't think there's anything anomalous about that. I mean, if you imagine a Board of Veterans' Appeals decision in this case if the Board had been given an opportunity to do so, it's not that hard to have a section at the end of the opinion saying: There's an equal protection challenge, we've overturned your challenge, it's rejected for these reasons.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think it's a few different fronts from our --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Obviously, we want to get the law right.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, it would definitely be problematic to make the VA start litigating these kinds of claims all around the country. The VA is incredibly burdened as it is, and I think that would be a significant problem. As I said before, you would have dual-track litigation going on in every single case because the veteran always needs to have a claim with the VA, and that's always going to raise some fact- and case-specific matters. So you're always going to have a process that needs to go on at the VA. You have the disuniformity concerns, but I really do think the main thing is the litigation burden. At the time of Robison, the Court said that, you know, these kinds of constitutional challenges to statutes are pretty uncommon, it's not a big deal to make the VA have to litigate them all around the country.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: They are much more common. I think that --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: They are never successful. I'm not aware of a benefits statute ever having been held unconstitutional since, like, Hayburn's Case maybe.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Having to defend against meritless claims is still a great burden on the agency, particularly if -- if they have to do it all around the country from district courts and then up to all the regional courts of appeals. A point I wanted to just tie off that I was going to make earlier was that Section 7292(c) goes out of its way to say the Federal Circuit shall have exclusive jurisdiction to decide challenges to the validity of statutes. If Petitioner is correct, then that is essentially a nullity because anybody can go to any district court around the country and then take that claim up to any court of appeals.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Is that what they're doing now?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That's what --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I mean, since this has been the prevailing system and you told [PERSON] that the problem for the government is the litigation burden of being all around the country, but given the government's position to this point, is that what's happening now?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, it hasn't been a huge deal yet because there are only two circuits, I think, that have adopted Petitioner's view.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: If -- if the Court --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- if the Court were to adopt Petitioner's view and open the doors of all the district courts around the country to these claims, we think it would be a serious problem because, again, as the Board decisions that we've cited in the briefs addressing these kinds of facial constitutional challenges show, these claims are a lot more common than they were back in the '70s when Robison was decided. So we don't think that that concern can be dismissed. We're totally in policy land at this point. We think that the statutory text resolves this case completely. These claims are --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I respectfully disagree with that. And I think a good example of this is the Traynor versus Turnage angle because Petitioner accepts that one of Congress's purposes in enacting the VJRA was to abrogate this Court's decision in Traynor. It also did that in a relatively subtle way. It changed that second clause --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- of the first sentence --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, we --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: We think this is also pretty darn clear moving that "question of law" clause away from the "under any law affecting the provision of benefits" clause. We think that's clear. And that's just looking at 511(a) in isolation, which you would never do. You would also want to look at Chapter 72. And we think that that statutory context really eliminates any doubt. Another case I would point you to is Weinberger. It was decided the year after Robison. That case had an express preclusion clause referring to claims arising under Title II of the Social Security Act. You said that that clause applied to constitutional challenges to the Act even though it's pretty unnatural to say that such a claim arises under the Act. If that clause covered constitutional claims, we don't see how this one couldn't.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: No. No, we don't think that would work that way at all, which is why the 7292(c) --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- would be defeated.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It says exclusive jurisdiction in cases brought under this section, I think. And so what that means is that you can't go from the Veterans Court to any court of appeals besides the Federal Circuit.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But, by its terms, that provision would not prevent you, assuming you could file these claims in district court --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. It's the "under this section" language that is problematic.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Sure. I mean, I think we have to look at the actual statutory text, not hypothetically hyper-clear statutory text. We think that the statutory text is quite clear here, particularly in conjunction with Chapter 72, which --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think the key difference in this case is separating --so the "question of law" clause from the "under a law" clause. The previous version of the statute said decisions of the administrator on any question of law or fact under any law administered by the VA. That was at least plausibly read, particularly in light of the Court's constitutional concerns in Robison, as referring to questions of law arising under the statute itself relating to its interpretation or application. By saying "all questions of law and fact necessary to a decision by the Secretary," that naturally invites the inclusion of constitutional challenges to the statute because, as [PERSON] was explaining, it's obviously necessary to a decision under or in accordance with the statute if you define it that way to determine whether the statute is constitutional in the first place.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That's the current version.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. That's not the Robison version.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yep. I don't have anything more to add, so we can proceed to seriatim.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

turns_pm60.text: Can I ask, following up on [PERSON]'s questions, if it's a close call in the statutory interpretation, why upset the longstanding practice?

turns_pm60.text: Well, first of all, there is no consistent longstanding practice. As I've said multiple times, the Board has repeatedly decided these kinds of claims, and so we're going to have consistency one way or another going forward. We think that the statutory --

turns_pm60.text: They haven't had to decide them, right?

turns_pm60.text: We think that they do have to decide them, yes. And I don't think there's anything anomalous about that. turns_pm60.text: And then what's the harm the government -- from the current state of play?

turns_pm60.text: I think it's a few different fronts from our --

turns_pm60.text: Other than you want to get the law right. I get that one, but is there --

turns_pm60.text: Obviously, we want to get the law right.

turns_pm60.text: But, apart from that, is there something going on that's problematic from the government's perspective?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: They are much more common. I think that --

case: Anderson v. Intel Corp. Investment Policy Committee
setting: Excerpt from a recorded institutional proceeding. Exactly one of the two speakers, A and B, holds the more powerful institutional role.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: So are you saying that you can prove imprudence or demonstrate it by comparing dissimilar funds?

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: I mean, that is one way that a complaint --

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: So how would you do that?

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: Sure. So it's context-dependent, and there is no one specific fund that a complaint needs to identify to make performance allegations relevant to support a claim of imprudence. It can run a very wide spectrum of different ways that the complaint could use performance allegations to contribute to the overall plausibility of a complaint. And the way it would do that is it would identify a relevant way of comparing the performance of one fund with other potential comparators, and it would explain why that performance was relevant to the theory of breach alleged in a complaint. But what the Ninth Circuit has done here is it has attempted to predefine the kind of comparison that will count when a court is asking how the performance allegations contribute to plausibility.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: I think what the Ninth Circuit is saying is you can't compare apples and oranges if you have a fund, an equity fund, that is designed to produce high returns but riskier returns, and you can't compare that to a fund that is to protect against losses.

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: We -- I agree that if that was all the complaint was trying to do, to premise a claim of imprudence on, that kind of complaint would be -- would not survive a motion to dismiss. But the Ninth Circuit, I think, went beyond just a recognition that the performance allegations need to contribute to the theory of imprudence. What it did was to say the only kind of comparison that will count is one that identifies a specific materially indistinguishable fund that only differed in performance. And by attempting to predefine the kind of comparator that counts, it set the bar in a way that would foreclose a complaint from relying on a whole range of different kinds of potential comparisons.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] ERISA's duty of prudence is inherently flexible. As a result, this Court has consistently declined to inject judicially crafted bright-line rules into a determination of whether a complaint's allegations plausibly allege imprudence. Categorical rules, as this Court put it colorfully in Dudenhoeffer, do not readily "divide the plausible sheep from the meritless goats" because they are inconsistent with the careful, context-sensitive inquiry that both ERISA and Rule 8 require. The Ninth Circuit's "meaningful benchmark requirement" is just such a rule. Under it, a court first asks whether a complaint's performance allegations on their own can plausibly demonstrate imprudence by identifying a virtually indistinguishable fund that performed better. If the complaint fails to identify that specific fund, the performance allegations are discarded, and that is true even if the complaint relies on benchmarks selected by the fiduciaries themselves or comparators identified by benchmarking experts. In the Respondents' view, this rule is consistent with the ordinary pleading framework set forth in Twombly and Iqbal. But, under that framework, courts must assess all non-conclusory allegations together in determining if a complaint plausibly states a claim. The "meaningful benchmark requirement" precludes that assessment. And the Ninth Circuit's rule isn't even necessary. Everyone agrees that, without more, a complaint merely alleging that one fund performed better than another won't survive a motion to dismiss. The ordinary pleading standards, however, are perfectly capable of weeding out a truly meritorious --meritless claim like that. Ultimately, because the meaningful benchmark rule is both out of step with Twombly and Iqbal and an unnecessary solution in search of a problem, it should be rejected. turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] ERISA's duty of prudence is inherently flexible. As a result, this Court has consistently declined to inject judicially crafted bright-line rules into a determination of whether a complaint's allegations plausibly allege imprudence. Categorical rules, as this Court put it colorfully in Dudenhoeffer, do not readily "divide the plausible sheep from the meritless goats" because they are inconsistent with the careful, context-sensitive inquiry that both ERISA and Rule 8 require. The Ninth Circuit's "meaningful benchmark requirement" is just such a rule. Under it, a court first asks whether a complaint's performance allegations on their own can plausibly demonstrate imprudence by identifying a virtually indistinguishable fund that performed better. If the complaint fails to identify that specific fund, the performance allegations are discarded, and that is true even if the complaint relies on benchmarks selected by the fiduciaries themselves or comparators identified by benchmarking experts. In the Respondents' view, this rule is consistent with the ordinary pleading framework set forth in Twombly and Iqbal. But, under that framework, courts must assess all non-conclusory allegations together in determining if a complaint plausibly states a claim. The "meaningful benchmark requirement" precludes that assessment. And the Ninth Circuit's rule isn't even necessary. Everyone agrees that, without more, a complaint merely alleging that one fund performed better than another won't survive a motion to dismiss. The ordinary pleading standards, however, are perfectly capable of weeding out a truly meritorious --meritless claim like that. Ultimately, because the meaningful benchmark rule is both out of step with Twombly and Iqbal and an unnecessary solution in search of a problem, it should be rejected. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] ERISA's duty of prudence is inherently flexible. As a result, this Court has consistently declined to inject judicially crafted bright-line rules into a determination of whether a complaint's allegations plausibly allege imprudence. Categorical rules, as this Court put it colorfully in Dudenhoeffer, do not readily "divide the plausible sheep from the meritless goats" because they are inconsistent with the careful, context-sensitive inquiry that both ERISA and Rule 8 require. The Ninth Circuit's "meaningful benchmark requirement" is just such a rule. Under it, a court first asks whether a complaint's performance allegations on their own can plausibly demonstrate imprudence by identifying a virtually indistinguishable fund that performed better. If the complaint fails to identify that specific fund, the performance allegations are discarded, and that is true even if the complaint relies on benchmarks selected by the fiduciaries themselves or comparators identified by benchmarking experts. In the Respondents' view, this rule is consistent with the ordinary pleading framework set forth in Twombly and Iqbal. But, under that framework, courts must assess all non-conclusory allegations together in determining if a complaint plausibly states a claim. The "meaningful benchmark requirement" precludes that assessment. And the Ninth Circuit's rule isn't even necessary. Everyone agrees that, without more, a complaint merely alleging that one fund performed better than another won't survive a motion to dismiss. The ordinary pleading standards, however, are perfectly capable of weeding out a truly meritorious --meritless claim like that. Ultimately, because the meaningful benchmark rule is both out of step with Twombly and Iqbal and an unnecessary solution in search of a problem, it should be rejected. I welcome the Court's questions.

Just because one strategy produces lower returns doesn't make it imprudent. And, in assessing prudence, the statute commands a comparison to a fiduciary with like aims acting in like capacity, not an identical fiduciary and not identical investments but similar enough to make the comparison meaningful. Requiring meaningful comparisons also follows from well-established federal pleading standards. Again, underperformance standing alone is not a violation of ERISA, as my friend conceded. turns_pm15.text: Thank you, [ADDRESS] I'd like to start today by noting that much of my friend's arguments had little to do with the question presented. The question presented today is important but narrow: Can a plaintiff state a plausible claim for a breach of the duty of prudence based on a comparison of two funds that aren't meaningfully similar? And as Judge Miller's opinion explained for the Ninth Circuit below, the answer is no for multiple reasons. You can start with ERISA's text and purpose. ERISA recognizes that fiduciaries can make a wide range of prudent decisions, including the decision that Intel's fiduciaries made here to pursue a more conservative strategy through diversification. Just because one strategy produces lower returns doesn't make it imprudent. And, in assessing prudence, the statute commands a comparison to a fiduciary with like aims acting in like capacity, not an identical fiduciary and not identical investments but similar enough to make the comparison meaningful. Requiring meaningful comparisons also follows from well-established federal pleading standards. Again, underperformance standing alone is not a violation of ERISA, as my friend conceded. So the mere existence of a difference in performance between two funds doesn't plausibly suggest any wrongdoing, especially when accounting for the obvious alternative explanation that different funds are designed to perform differently. To rule out that explanation, a plaintiff needs to allege that the funds being compared had similar aims but performed better or cost less. Twombly did it for allegations of parallel conduct. Dudenhoeffer did it for allegations based on insider information. Hikma did it most recently for allegations based on inaction. The meaningful benchmark standard does the same thing for allegations that a fund costs too much or didn't earn enough. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Thank you, [ADDRESS] I'd like to start today by noting that much of my friend's arguments had little to do with the question presented. The question presented today is important but narrow: Can a plaintiff state a plausible claim for a breach of the duty of prudence based on a comparison of two funds that aren't meaningfully similar? And as Judge Miller's opinion explained for the Ninth Circuit below, the answer is no for multiple reasons. You can start with ERISA's text and purpose. ERISA recognizes that fiduciaries can make a wide range of prudent decisions, including the decision that Intel's fiduciaries made here to pursue a more conservative strategy through diversification. Just because one strategy produces lower returns doesn't make it imprudent. And, in assessing prudence, the statute commands a comparison to a fiduciary with like aims acting in like capacity, not an identical fiduciary and not identical investments but similar enough to make the comparison meaningful. Requiring meaningful comparisons also follows from well-established federal pleading standards. Again, underperformance standing alone is not a violation of ERISA, as my friend conceded. So the mere existence of a difference in performance between two funds doesn't plausibly suggest any wrongdoing, especially when accounting for the obvious alternative explanation that different funds are designed to perform differently. To rule out that explanation, a plaintiff needs to allege that the funds being compared had similar aims but performed better or cost less. [PERSON] has called this requirement of an apples-to-apples comparison an improper heightened pleading standard. That's not correct. This Court regularly draws clear lines at the pleading stage. Twombly did it for allegations of parallel conduct. Dudenhoeffer did it for allegations based on insider information. Hikma did it most recently for allegations based on inaction. The meaningful benchmark standard does the same thing for allegations that a fund costs too much or didn't earn enough. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.text: I do, [ADDRESS], for this reason: In order to have a plausible inference of wrongdoing, you need a comparison that is itself meaningful. I think, in that respect, it's very similar to the allegations of parallel conduct in Twombly. In Twombly, the Court said those allegations are equally consistent with lawful conduct. And the same thing is true here. The fact that Fund A underperforms Fund B is equally consistent with those funds either being different because of the vagaries of the market or because of intentional difference in strategy between the two funds.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Speaker B, can I -- can I ask you, would you be --or would you be satisfied or would it be a good idea for the Court to simply answer the QP in this way? You know, it asks whether, when allegations are based on underperformance, the plaintiff must allege a meaningful benchmark. Yes, period. Or do you think that we would need, in a rules statement, to say more about what "meaningful" means?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I don't think, [ADDRESS], this is a case where you need to explain what "meaningful" means. The lower courts have not struggled with that question. They have considered it for a number of years now, and I think they are getting it right more often than not. So this is not a case where I think it's necessary for the Court to provide further guidance.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: What do you make of all of the arguments that your friend on the other side is making about the extra allegations that didn't relate to underperformance that the complaint had that he thinks should have gotten the allegations about underperformance over the edge?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So, Speaker A, I would have a harder case if the Ninth Circuit had said your underperformance allegations aren't sufficient and so we're not going to consider anything else in your complaint. That's clearly not what the Ninth Circuit did. I think [PERSON] and I just fundamentally disagree about how to read the Ninth Circuit opinion. It went through in detail the allegations about our supposedly outlier strategy and the allegations about hedge funds and private equity being evil, and it found that those failed, but they failed for reasons that are separate and apart from the meaningful benchmark standard.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So, [PERSON], I think it is true that, as a general matter, underperformance is going to rarely be indicative of any sort of imprudence. The example that comes to mind where it might be probative is let's say you had two funds that had a similar goal of trying to track the S&P 500, and you see Fund A consistently meets that goal and Fund B consistently fails to meet that goal. That might suggest the fiduciaries of Fund B were not adequately monitoring to make sure that they were actually trying to hit their goal. That could be indicative of underperformance. It might get you close to the line. I don't know that I would say that that alone would plausibly suggest imprudence.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think that would be appropriate, [ADDRESS].

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And I want to be clear. Requiring a meaningful benchmark does not prevent plaintiffs from making other sorts of allegations of imprudence.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Exactly. And I think Judge Berzon's concurrence is exactly on point on these issues. And so, if the Court wanted to endorse the points that Judge Berzon made, we would have no objection to that.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So, [PERSON], I agree with you this decision is very reasonable. I think the analysis that it endorses is helpful and instructive and, in fact, many district courts in the Ninth Circuit have looked to it and applied it in assessing these allegations.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I don't have any objection to that. I will say I think even the narrower version of the opinion that just says you need a meaningful comparison is still helpful because we have the Sixth Circuit in the Parker-Hannifin case that seemed to suggest that you didn't need an apples-to-apples comparison. And so you could bring the Sixth Circuit in line through an opinion that's narrower. But, again, I have no objection to endorsing the analysis in the Ninth Circuit opinion. I think it's -- it's spot on.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So, if you want to --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Sure. Maybe I can use the facts of this case to illustrate a helpful comparison. So, in this case, as you heard from [PERSON], the argument was that we had an acceptable strategy and we implemented it in a bad way by over-allocating the hedge funds in private equity. To make the comparison meaningful, you need to control for the strategy, keep the strategy the same, but point to someone who they say did it better by using fewer hedge fund and private equity investments. That's the sort of comparison that might suggest imprudence because it would suggest the difference in performance was really due to our inclusion of hedge funds and private equity. That's not the comparison that they tried to make in this case. In this case, they were saying: You didn't do as well as equity-heavy funds that prioritized more aggressive growth. Well, of course, we didn't do as well because that wasn't our strategy. We told everyone we were trying to be more conservative and to make sure that retirees had lots of money at the end of the day without taking unnecessary risks. So the obvious explanation for the difference in performance in this case is the difference in strategy.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: They do.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It could. It could be the -- the basis for allegations of similar -- I would want to know more about the actual allegations in the complaint, but I think that sort of information could be relevant. And there are district court decisions that have credited similar sort of information.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: If the argument is you had an okay strategy, but you implemented it poorly, I think you probably do want a comparison. It's not required, but it would be helpful because that's a way to control for the strategy and show a difference. I think you could have attacks on the strategy itself that wouldn't require a comparison. I agree with [PERSON] --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- on that.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Exactly. Exactly. But, again, if you want to attack the strategy itself, if you want to say you can't invest in hedge funds, in private equity, that is an argument you could make. And, in fact, they did make it here. And the Ninth Circuit rejected it, but it rejected it for reasons that are outside of the question presented and don't have anything to do with the meaningful benchmark standard.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So, Speaker B, do you think it would be helpful then in defining "meaningful" to say that the comparator must have like aims and strategies? Does that give enough guidance, or does that risk having lower courts look for a twin?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think that you could say like aims and strategies, but "like" simply means similar, not identical. I think that would clear up, to the extent there's confusion in the lower courts, some of that confusion. And, again, from my read of the cases, all of the courts seem to agree that like aims, the goals of the investments, is the most important consideration.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think you can simply say you don't need an identical asset allocation. And, in fact, in many cases, a difference in asset allocation will be probative of whether there's imprudence, especially where, as here, you're saying the asset allocation was the problem. And the Ninth Circuit, to be clear, I don't think, required a similar asset allocation.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That the allegation was that there were no similarly situated --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Oh, that the plaintiffs didn't allege?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes, absolutely. They -- they never even tried to allege that there was another fund that had a similar goal that they were trying to compare us to. They wanted to compare us to things like the S&P 500, which isn't even a -- an investment strategy. It is just the agglomerated strategies of 500 different companies. The other thing they could have done -- and I disagree with [PERSON] about this too -- is they could have tried to compare us to our own disclosed benchmarks. We had a benchmark that we told participants -- participants about. [PERSON] suggested they did that comparison. The Ninth Circuit was very clear and the district court was very clear that the things that they called our benchmarks were not our benchmarks. But I think that is an available option for plaintiffs in these cases. And there are a number of cases that have found, if you make allegations against a fund's own benchmarks, that can be probative of imprudence.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think you do because the premise --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I'm confused. You do always have to have a benchmark? Because I thought that before -- maybe I misheard [PERSON] -- I think it was [PERSON] who asked you a question. I mean, what if, to use [PERSON]'s example, you have a fund that's 50 percent lottery tickets? I mean, couldn't there be some kind of res ipsa where you didn't need a benchmark?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I don't view that as an underperformance claim, [ADDRESS]. That would just be you had a --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Bad strategy?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- bad strategy.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Okay. Thanks.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But, to the extent you are premising your underperformance on saying A did worse than B, I do think that comparison has to be meaningful.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Got it. Thanks.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

case: Anderson v. Intel Corp. Investment Policy Committee
setting: Excerpt from a recorded institutional proceeding. Exactly one of the two speakers, A and B, holds the more powerful institutional role.

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: If you were to flyspeck the Ninth Circuit's opinion and not -- I'm not asking for things you think are wrong with it such that it would change the result because you've clearly said you think it should be affirmed. But consistent with that disposition, if I asked you to flyspeck the circuit court's decision, would you have said anything different? Would you have added things? Would you have subtracted things? Is there anything?

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: So I think, at various points -- I would have to go back and look at the very, very precise language that they used. Sometimes the courts in these cases have said that it has to have the same objectives, the same risk/reward profile, and the same strategy. It's used an "and" instead of an "or," and sometimes asset allocation is thrown into some of those decisions. I agree that the Ninth Circuit certainly didn't do that here. We -- we think that's correct. It does not have to be the same asset allocation. I think where some confusion could happen is how you define what the strategy is. So I've been using kind of objectives and aims as this broader goal of we want to reduce downside. We want to have kind of a risk-mitigating approach. The strategy in some cases is going to be the way that you implement that objective. And so, here, that would have been allocating assets to the hedge funds and the private equity funds. Obviously, we don't think you have to hold that constant because that would then have some of the problems that Petitioners have suggested. But I think that the Ninth Circuit generally did the right thing. And -- and we read the opinion the same way that -- that [PERSON] does.

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: And on this asset allocation point, I mean, your brief says -- this is -- I'm reading from page 25, "Where two funds seek to achieve similar levels of risk using different asset allocation strategies, the challenged fund may be compared to a fund with more conventional assets that bear the same level of risk."

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: Exactly.

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: If you didn't allow that, you would be essentially foreclosing these claims from the outset.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: Exactly. And we think that Petitioners were perfectly capable of doing that here. There are many different assets that have the kind of downside protection that Intel said it was using the private equity funds and the hedge funds here to accomplish. And so they could have compared this to a fund that had more allocations to bonds or to high-yield savings accounts or something like that. Intel -- or the -- the plaintiffs here just chose not to do so. Instead, they were comparing these to these kind of equity-heavy funds that wanted to have more -- more exposure to the potential for the upside. And I -- I don't think that the correct kind of implication to draw from that is that there weren't those kinds of funds available. I think, more likely, the case is that if they had tried to draw those kinds of comparisons, Intel's funds just wouldn't really have underperformed to any significant degree. That's consistent with the way the Ninth Circuit kind of understood the -- the complaint here. Some of the charts in the complaint tend to just suggest that Intel's funds performed pretty much exactly as they anticipated they would.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Thank you, [ADDRESS] ERISA allows prudent fiduciaries to make a range of reasonable judgments when adopting investment objectives. They can pursue varying degrees of exposure to market upside and varying degrees of protection from market downside. When different objectives lead to different results, that does not suggest imprudence. In this case, Intel's fiduciaries had the objective of reducing exposure to losses at the acknowledged expense of some potential upside. Petitioners have not challenged the prudence of that objective. Instead, they have asked the lower courts to infer that the fiduciaries imprudently implemented that objective based on the fact that Intel's funds underperformed other funds. But, to create that inference, Petitioners have to compare Intel's funds to other funds with similar objectives. Otherwise, the obvious alternative explanation for the difference in results is the difference in objectives. That common-sense understanding does not mean that plaintiffs in every case need to plead a comparator. There are myriad ways of pleading imprudence without relying on performance at all. But, when a claim is premised on underperformance, the comparator has to be similar to make the comparison probative of the claim. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: I don't. I think we're -- we're well-aligned on the instances in which a comparator is necessary, the work that it's doing in these kinds of cases.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: I do think that it would be helpful to suggest some parameters for what the meaningful benchmark here, the meaningful comparator, needs to be. I think the easiest way to do that is to assess it within the confines of what we're doing with the duty of prudence. Prudence is about process and not about performance. And so the plaintiff does have to connect the dots back from the performance to the process. In a case like this, that's going to mean that the plaintiff is essentially alleging that if its fiduciaries were acting prudently, they would have selected the better-performing fund. But, again, in order for that to be the correct inference, you have to hold constant the things that go into that decision that the Petitioners are not challenging as imprudent themselves. And, here, that is the goals, the objectives, the aims, sometimes it's been called the strategy, of the funds to -- to mitigate against potential down --down -- downturns in the market. And when you hold those constant and you provide two, you know, different funds, one of which performed better than the other, then maybe you have an indication of some imprudence in selecting kind of the worst-performing of the funds. But, without that kind of comparison that holds constant the factors that go into the decision, the -- the implication just isn't there. And it might be helpful to actually apply that to this case and to show how the Ninth Circuit, I think, did that correctly because, here, the plaintiffs identified funds that had different objectives entirely from Intel's objective. They were these equity-heavy retail funds that wanted more exposure to the potential market upside. And, you know, they were not challenging, again, that Intel could have prudently decided that that was not the right strategy for them. The comparator funds did end up overperforming Intel's funds. That's not very surprising. The market ended up doing pretty well during this relevant time period. But that doesn't suggest that Intel's fiduciaries were imprudent for wanting to protect against potential downside, even if that didn't end up materializing during the relevant period here.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: If you were to flyspeck the Ninth Circuit's opinion and not -- I'm not asking for things you think are wrong with it such that it would change the result because you've clearly said you think it should be affirmed. turns_pm15.text: I think it's correct that the Ninth Circuit first looked at the underperformance allegations and determined whether those under -- whether those allegations were going to be probative at all in the analysis, and it held that they were not. In order for those allegations to do any work, they have to be tied to a meaningful comparator because, otherwise, they are equally consistent with the lawful alternative explanation here that these just had different objectives, and so the different results don't tell you anything. That's not enough to take the complaint outside of neutral territory, is the term that Twombly uses at one point. turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] A permit application is not final agency action. It's a request to someone else to take action. Filing a permit application triggers a back-and-forth process whose outcome is, by definition, a moving target until a decision on the permit is issued. Treating an application as final would just lead to a multiplicity of suits throughout a permitting process, which I think defeats the whole point of the finality requirement. Now Respondent says that the application reflects some internal Air Force decision to continue these activities for the next three years if Guam issues a permit. But the "if" is precisely the kind of contingency that makes this not final. Respondent also points out that the application enabled the old permit's expiration date to be tolled or extended. But that is, at most, an incidental or indirect effect of the application, really, of Guam EPA's failure to rule on the application. The direct and appreciable legal consequences of that extension flow from the terms of the old permit, which Respondent has not challenged. Now Respondent's claim also fails on the merits. RCRA is a comprehensive statute specifically targeting hazardous waste and specifically specifying which environmental review must occur at each step of a reticulated permit process. Respondent's attempt to take all of NEPA and just shove it into the application stage is not only duplicative of RCRA's requirements, which are the functional equivalent, but inconsistent with RCRA's specification of when each of those requirements should occur through the permitting process. All of that said, I don't think you need to actually address the interaction of NEPA and RCRA in this case because NEPA, by its terms, does not apply to non-final agency actions. And so, if you agree with us, as I think you should, that the application is not final agency action, that would not only resolve the threshold issue in the case; it would also have the effect of resolving Respondent's claim on the merits here. I welcome the Court's questions.

case: Department of Air Force v. Prutehi Guahan
setting: Excerpt from a recorded institutional proceeding. Exactly one of the two speakers, A and B, holds the more powerful institutional role.

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: Speaker A, normally, in these administrative cases, we have a regulatory body making a decision, and our determination has to be whether or not that is a final action for APA purposes. In this case, we have a regulated body applying to a regulatory body that you -- your argument is that the application process makes it a final decision. Do you have another example where the regulated body's decision to apply to a regulatory body is a final decision for APA purposes or a final action for APA purposes?

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: Well, I can think of one fact pattern in this Court's cases involving another NEPA case, and that was the Winter versus Natural Resources Defense Council case. And, there, the Navy was continuing a series of training exercises for another two years that they had been doing previously, and they did the NEPA analysis before embarking on another two years of exercises. The Court -- you know, finality -- the Court did not decide finality in this case, but nobody seemed to think that there was any issue with --

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: Was that an --

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: -- being able to review the NEPA analysis in that case.

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: Was that an application for a permit in order to do the training? I'm -- my interest is that this is an odd case because we are not talking about a regulatory body making a decision to do something itself without permission. We are talking about a regulated body asking permission to do something.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: I understand, and I understand that that creates a contingency, but I guess what I would say is that the contingency -- the fact of the contingency shouldn't be determinative. So say that RCRA required the Air Force to put all of the information it would put in an application and just publish that document. I don't think we would be having a debate about final agency action there, even though it's action about the --the Air Force's own operations. Here, yes, that has to go and get external sign-off from somebody else. But this Court has found final agency action where there is a contingency. For instance --

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] The Air Force was required to comply with NEPA before choosing to continue open detonation on Tarague Beach. And we can obtain judicial review of that violation now. On the question whether NEPA applies, the government's position is simply atextual. Congress has told us that NEPA is displaced only when it is excluded pursuant to another provision of law or there is a clear and fundamental conflict between NEPA and another law's requirements. That aligns with this Court's precedent, the strong presumption against implied repeals, and Congress's longstanding practice of drafting express exclusions to NEPA when it wants them. The government's response is that RCRA is specifically about hazardous waste. But, because the laws can be harmonized, that observation can't carry the day. Indeed, NEPA is meant to be harmonized with other environmental laws in this way. It is what agencies call an umbrella law. It is meant to consolidate and streamline all required environmental analysis at an early juncture to ensure a better decision and better planning. So, if the Air Force was wrong to ignore NEPA here, the only question should be when Prutehi Guahan can get judicial review of that violation. The Air Force's decision to continue OD at this location and submitting the renewal application was not tentative, and its application implementing the decision had, among other things, the concrete effect of authorizing open detonation operations past the date when they otherwise would have ended. The government is instead pushing a rule where the fact that the Air Force's decision required external sign-off means that it can't be final as a matter of law, perhaps, apparently, not even after that external sign-off occurs. That does not align with this Court's pragmatic approach to finality, and it is especially senseless when it comes to our claim of a procedural violation here. Indeed, this Court has already said in Ohio Forestry Association versus Sierra Club that a litigant with standing can "complain of a NEPA failure at the time it takes place for the claim can never get riper." There is nothing to be gained here by delaying our challenge to the Air Force's own decision-making about its own operations until a non-federal agency has made a different determination under a different law. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.text: Well, I can think of one fact pattern in this Court's cases involving another NEPA case, and that was the Winter versus Natural Resources Defense Council case. The Court -- you know, finality -- the Court did not decide finality in this case, but nobody seemed to think that there was any issue with --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- being able to review the NEPA analysis in that case.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I understand, and I understand that that creates a contingency, but I guess what I would say is that the contingency -- the fact of the contingency shouldn't be determinative. So say that RCRA required the Air Force to put all of the information it would put in an application and just publish that document. I don't think we would be having a debate about final agency action there, even though it's action about the --the Air Force's own operations. Here, yes, that has to go and get external sign-off from somebody else. But this Court has found final agency action where there is a contingency. For instance --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But isn't it because your publication hypothetical doesn't contemplate the back-and-forth that I talked about with [PERSON]? I mean, it's -- it's -- if we had a world in which the requirement was just the Air Force has to publish everything that it was putting in a permit application -- that was your hypothetical -- there's nothing to come of that in terms of potential changes, in terms of it -- you know, conditions being placed on it. That's why I was focusing on the fact that, in this particular scheme, we have the Air Force making a proposal that is subject to totally being rewritten and redone by the regulator agency. And, in that case, isn't there a finality problem?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I don't think so because this Court has been clear that the possibility of revision of the agency's decision, that it might change its mind, is not itself enough to say that a decision where the agency reached the culmination of its decision-making process is non-final. Here, yes, that possibility of revision might come because it's provoked by an outside entity, but I think that was also true in Biden versus Texas, where this Court found final agency action when there was --DHS Secretary issued a memo saying: I am terminating immigration --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But that's -- but the decision was within the agency's control. I mean, any agency can change its decision, so that would render, you know -- I don't know that -- that that's really the critical point. The point is we don't even know in this situation what the final terms are going to be because it's subject to the other regulator responding. And they're taking a long time, suggesting that they're actually looking at this and are possibly going to come back with significant revisions. And so then we don't really have the terms. What -- what would the Air Force even be evaluating at this point when it hasn't heard from Guam EPA about what this thing is going to look like?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well -- so I think it does matter here, and I think it should matter under this Court's pragmatic approach to finality, the kind of legal claim we're bringing here. So our NEPA claim is attached to the -- the process of decision-making the Air Force used before it decided in NEPA's terms to propose this major federal action and should not be --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That's not what your QP says. You say submission, right? We're -- we're in --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Right, but in --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- the action is the submission.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So -- but, to be clear, the NEPA violation, it's clear that it happened before resources were committed in this application. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: The prior decision.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- the fundamental decision to carry out these --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yeah.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- open detonations at Tarague Beach. And we know that the Air Force is settled on that decision because it has, in fact, been acting on them past -- you know, by continuing these detonation operations past September 2021, when they otherwise would have ceased.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I am not aware of a basis for us to bring this challenge on review of whatever Guam EPA does. I understand that's what my friend said here today, but Guam EPA has no NEPA obligation. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: No, not against the state permitting agency. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- they would have wasted their time.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: They would have -- it would wasted the permitting agency's time to have ruled on that application and have everybody double back at that point.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So that's not the way that the NEPA obligation works. NEPA is very clear that you have to undertake the analysis before proposing a major federal action. turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.text: Yeah.

turns_pm60.text: They have to --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] The Air Force was required to comply with NEPA before choosing to continue open detonation on Tarague Beach. And we can obtain judicial review of that violation now. On the question whether NEPA applies, the government's position is simply atextual. Congress has told us that NEPA is displaced only when it is excluded pursuant to another provision of law or there is a clear and fundamental conflict between NEPA and another law's requirements. That aligns with this Court's precedent, the strong presumption against implied repeals, and Congress's longstanding practice of drafting express exclusions to NEPA when it wants them. The government's response is that RCRA is specifically about hazardous waste. But, because the laws can be harmonized, that observation can't carry the day. Indeed, NEPA is meant to be harmonized with other environmental laws in this way. It is what agencies call an umbrella law. It is meant to consolidate and streamline all required environmental analysis at an early juncture to ensure a better decision and better planning. So, if the Air Force was wrong to ignore NEPA here, the only question should be when Prutehi Guahan can get judicial review of that violation. The Air Force's decision to continue OD at this location and submitting the renewal application was not tentative, and its application implementing the decision had, among other things, the concrete effect of authorizing open detonation operations past the date when they otherwise would have ended. The government is instead pushing a rule where the fact that the Air Force's decision required external sign-off means that it can't be final as a matter of law, perhaps, apparently, not even after that external sign-off occurs. That does not align with this Court's pragmatic approach to finality, and it is especially senseless when it comes to our claim of a procedural violation here. Indeed, this Court has already said in Ohio Forestry Association versus Sierra Club that a litigant with standing can "complain of a NEPA failure at the time it takes place for the claim can never get riper." There is nothing to be gained here by delaying our challenge to the Air Force's own decision-making about its own operations until a non-federal agency has made a different determination under a different law. I welcome the Court's questions.
