turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] The Air Force was required to comply with NEPA before choosing to continue open detonation on Tarague Beach. And we can obtain judicial review of that violation now. On the question whether NEPA applies, the government's position is simply atextual. Congress has told us that NEPA is displaced only when it is excluded pursuant to another provision of law or there is a clear and fundamental conflict between NEPA and another law's requirements. That aligns with this Court's precedent, the strong presumption against implied repeals, and Congress's longstanding practice of drafting express exclusions to NEPA when it wants them. The government's response is that RCRA is specifically about hazardous waste. But, because the laws can be harmonized, that observation can't carry the day. Indeed, NEPA is meant to be harmonized with other environmental laws in this way. It is what agencies call an umbrella law. It is meant to consolidate and streamline all required environmental analysis at an early juncture to ensure a better decision and better planning. So, if the Air Force was wrong to ignore NEPA here, the only question should be when Prutehi Guahan can get judicial review of that violation. The Air Force's decision to continue OD at this location and submitting the renewal application was not tentative, and its application implementing the decision had, among other things, the concrete effect of authorizing open detonation operations past the date when they otherwise would have ended. The government is instead pushing a rule where the fact that the Air Force's decision required external sign-off means that it can't be final as a matter of law, perhaps, apparently, not even after that external sign-off occurs. That does not align with this Court's pragmatic approach to finality, and it is especially senseless when it comes to our claim of a procedural violation here. Indeed, this Court has already said in Ohio Forestry Association versus Sierra Club that a litigant with standing can "complain of a NEPA failure at the time it takes place for the claim can never get riper." There is nothing to be gained here by delaying our challenge to the Air Force's own decision-making about its own operations until a non-federal agency has made a different determination under a different law. I welcome the Court's questions.

Now, you know, it's possible we could just bring the same suit but wait to bring it in federal court against the Air Force until after the permit issues. I think it would be odd to say that that's the point of finality because it would make finality turn on the decision of a non-federal actor. It would somehow make the previous decision by the Air Force non-final. But we do think that there has to be final agency action by the Air Force at some point given that there is a NEPA obligation here and we need to be able to enforce it. We don't think waiting to sue until after the permit issues serves anybody because, if the NEPA, you know, review produces a different application or, in our view, produces a determination not to seek a application from Guam at all because the Air Force decides to treat its waste somewhere else that's not in this location --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- they would have wasted their time.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: They would have -- it would wasted the permitting agency's time to have ruled on that application and have everybody double back at that point.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So that's not the way that the NEPA obligation works. NEPA is very clear that you have to undertake the analysis before proposing a major federal action. And it also talks about bringing entities like Guam EPA to the table as what NEPA calls cooperating agencies, and those are agencies who have jurisdiction by law over some part of the project or some environmental effects involved. And so, if this had been done properly, the Air Force would do its NEPA analysis, bring E -- or Guam EPA in on the process, get their views then, and then, if they decided to go forward with a permit for open detonation on Tarague Beach, submit that permit, which, given that Guam EPA had already been involved, I would assume would -- could be approved readily. But this is exact -- I mean, NEPA, the whole point of NEPA is to make sure that these -- this kind of evaluation is happening before resources -- resources are committed, such as resources in the form of teeing up a plan for an application and before the die is cast. So, no, it would not satisfy NEPA for that to all happen after the Air Force bakes its plan, tees it up, and then says: Okay, wait, now we're going to decide whether -- or we're going to evaluate the environmental effects of what we have already -- you know, the ball we've already started rolling.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But aren't NEPA challenges often made after the conclusion of the process? I'm just thinking about the posture of Seven County, which we decided in 2025. I mean, I agree with you that if the obligation applies, it's something that has to happen at the front end, but it seems to me like NEPA challenges do sometimes happen at the back end.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So a NEPA challenge, because the route for challenging a NEPA violation is through the APA, it requires final agency action. And so, yes, it often happens that a NEPA analysis is concluded at the same time a decision is made on the major federal action that is the subject of NEPA. Here, we think that is what happened because the Air Force decided it wanted to continue these operations.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But I'm just saying that it wouldn't be unusual. [PERSON] and [PERSON] and [PERSON] too were talking about the waste of time having the whole process run before a court addressed whether the NEPA obligation was complied with. And I'm just saying it seems to me as I understand it that that is often what happens.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So -- well, I guess I'm not sure -- I'm not familiar with situations that would happen like this, where a plan is devised and the Air Force decides to put it forward and then acts on that plan by continuing open detonation at the site by virtue of the extension and then doubles back and does a NEPA analysis after the fact.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But I'm glad you raised the extension because [PERSON] pointed out that the legal consequence actually didn't -- wasn't triggered by the application itself but, rather, by the Guam EPA's failure to act on the application before the expiration date of the prior permit. What is your response to that?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So both are necessary conditions. But I think the fact that the submission of the application is a necessary condition is all that is required for a legal consequence for purposes of Bennett prong 2. I don't think this Court's cases have said it has to be a completely sufficient condition on its own. And I think one case that illustrates this is Dalton versus Specter. So, there, of course, the Court ruled that the Secretary's action recommending certain military bases for closure was not final agency action, but the Court did find that the President's action was final action. It's just that he's not an agency. And, there, the process didn't end with the President. There was also -- the President had to submit the base closures to Congress, and there was a 45-day time built in for Congress to essentially veto what the President wanted to do by joint resolution. So, there, you still had a period of -- there was required inaction by another actor, but this Court still found the President's decision to be final action. But I think -- I think it's hard to dispute that the actual operations themselves, once they're being carried out, is final agency action. And so I don't think that is a route to avoid the text of NEPA, which is very clear that NEPA is not displaced in the absence of something like a clear and fundamental conflict or an express exclusion of the kind that Congress has repeatedly done over the years but did not do for -- for RCRA.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes. So I don't -- so, if we were to challenge Guam EPA's decision on a permit, whenever that decision happens, that is done under Guam -- the equivalent of Guam administrative law, so like the Guam APA. And I don't see how we could go --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yeah.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: The Guam EPA has no obligation to police the Air Force's compliance with NEPA. They don't enforce NEPA. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes, I think the same is true of a state EPA because they also don't have a NEPA obligation. And they have the --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: They have to --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So they have to fulfill all of RCRA's requirements. And I am just saying that because NEPA's a --

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think, if this Court found that there was no finality here because there was still some kind of a contingency, I would -- we would respectfully ask that the Court say that there is final agency action once that contingency is resolved so that we could file our federal APA suit against the Air Force then.

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] The Air Force was required to comply with NEPA before choosing to continue open detonation on Tarague Beach. And we can obtain judicial review of that violation now. On the question whether NEPA applies, the government's position is simply atextual. Congress has told us that NEPA is displaced only when it is excluded pursuant to another provision of law or there is a clear and fundamental conflict between NEPA and another law's requirements. That aligns with this Court's precedent, the strong presumption against implied repeals, and Congress's longstanding practice of drafting express exclusions to NEPA when it wants them. The government's response is that RCRA is specifically about hazardous waste. But, because the laws can be harmonized, that observation can't carry the day. Indeed, NEPA is meant to be harmonized with other environmental laws in this way. It is what agencies call an umbrella law. It is meant to consolidate and streamline all required environmental analysis at an early juncture to ensure a better decision and better planning. So, if the Air Force was wrong to ignore NEPA here, the only question should be when Prutehi Guahan can get judicial review of that violation. The Air Force's decision to continue OD at this location and submitting the renewal application was not tentative, and its application implementing the decision had, among other things, the concrete effect of authorizing open detonation operations past the date when they otherwise would have ended. The government is instead pushing a rule where the fact that the Air Force's decision required external sign-off means that it can't be final as a matter of law, perhaps, apparently, not even after that external sign-off occurs. That does not align with this Court's pragmatic approach to finality, and it is especially senseless when it comes to our claim of a procedural violation here. Indeed, this Court has already said in Ohio Forestry Association versus Sierra Club that a litigant with standing can "complain of a NEPA failure at the time it takes place for the claim can never get riper." There is nothing to be gained here by delaying our challenge to the Air Force's own decision-making about its own operations until a non-federal agency has made a different determination under a different law. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] The Air Force was required to comply with NEPA before choosing to continue open detonation on Tarague Beach. And we can obtain judicial review of that violation now. On the question whether NEPA applies, the government's position is simply atextual. Congress has told us that NEPA is displaced only when it is excluded pursuant to another provision of law or there is a clear and fundamental conflict between NEPA and another law's requirements. That aligns with this Court's precedent, the strong presumption against implied repeals, and Congress's longstanding practice of drafting express exclusions to NEPA when it wants them. The government's response is that RCRA is specifically about hazardous waste. But, because the laws can be harmonized, that observation can't carry the day. Indeed, NEPA is meant to be harmonized with other environmental laws in this way. It is what agencies call an umbrella law. It is meant to consolidate and streamline all required environmental analysis at an early juncture to ensure a better decision and better planning. So, if the Air Force was wrong to ignore NEPA here, the only question should be when Prutehi Guahan can get judicial review of that violation. The Air Force's decision to continue OD at this location and submitting the renewal application was not tentative, and its application implementing the decision had, among other things, the concrete effect of authorizing open detonation operations past the date when they otherwise would have ended. The government is instead pushing a rule where the fact that the Air Force's decision required external sign-off means that it can't be final as a matter of law, perhaps, apparently, not even after that external sign-off occurs. That does not align with this Court's pragmatic approach to finality, and it is especially senseless when it comes to our claim of a procedural violation here. Indeed, this Court has already said in Ohio Forestry Association versus Sierra Club that a litigant with standing can "complain of a NEPA failure at the time it takes place for the claim can never get riper." There is nothing to be gained here by delaying our challenge to the Air Force's own decision-making about its own operations until a non-federal agency has made a different determination under a different law. I welcome the Court's questions.

And, there, the Navy was continuing a series of training exercises for another two years that they had been doing previously, and they did the NEPA analysis before embarking on another two years of exercises. The Court -- you know, finality -- the Court did not decide finality in this case, but nobody seemed to think that there was any issue with --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- being able to review the NEPA analysis in that case.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I understand, and I understand that that creates a contingency, but I guess what I would say is that the contingency -- the fact of the contingency shouldn't be determinative. So say that RCRA required the Air Force to put all of the information it would put in an application and just publish that document. I don't think we would be having a debate about final agency action there, even though it's action about the --the Air Force's own operations. Here, yes, that has to go and get external sign-off from somebody else. But this Court has found final agency action where there is a contingency. For instance --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I don't think so because this Court has been clear that the possibility of revision of the agency's decision, that it might change its mind, is not itself enough to say that a decision where the agency reached the culmination of its decision-making process is non-final. Here, yes, that possibility of revision might come because it's provoked by an outside entity, but I think that was also true in Biden versus Texas, where this Court found final agency action when there was --DHS Secretary issued a memo saying: I am terminating immigration --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well -- so I think it does matter here, and I think it should matter under this Court's pragmatic approach to finality, the kind of legal claim we're bringing here. So our NEPA claim is attached to the -- the process of decision-making the Air Force used before it decided in NEPA's terms to propose this major federal action and should not be --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right, but in --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So -- but, to be clear, the NEPA violation, it's clear that it happened before resources were committed in this application. And because -- excuse me --so, because the NEPA claim there is nothing -- or, sorry, I should say, because any revision that happens by Guam EPA with respect to, you know, particular procedures or something like that, that will not affect whether --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- the fundamental decision to carry out these --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- open detonations at Tarague Beach. And we know that the Air Force is settled on that decision because it has, in fact, been acting on them past -- you know, by continuing these detonation operations past September 2021, when they otherwise would have ceased.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I am not aware of a basis for us to bring this challenge on review of whatever Guam EPA does. I understand that's what my friend said here today, but Guam EPA has no NEPA obligation. It has no obligation to enforce the Air Force's NEPA obligations. So whatever -- if, you know, we have a basis -- if this permit is granted and we have a basis to challenge it before Guam EPA, that is a separate question.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: No, not against the state permitting agency. Now, you know, it's possible we could just bring the same suit but wait to bring it in federal court against the Air Force until after the permit issues. I think it would be odd to say that that's the point of finality because it would make finality turn on the decision of a non-federal actor. It would somehow make the previous decision by the Air Force non-final. But we do think that there has to be final agency action by the Air Force at some point given that there is a NEPA obligation here and we need to be able to enforce it. We don't think waiting to sue until after the permit issues serves anybody because, if the NEPA, you know, review produces a different application or, in our view, produces a determination not to seek a application from Guam at all because the Air Force decides to treat its waste somewhere else that's not in this location --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- they would have wasted their time.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: They would have -- it would wasted the permitting agency's time to have ruled on that application and have everybody double back at that point.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So that's not the way that the NEPA obligation works. NEPA is very clear that you have to undertake the analysis before proposing a major federal action. And it also talks about bringing entities like Guam EPA to the table as what NEPA calls cooperating agencies, and those are agencies who have jurisdiction by law over some part of the project or some environmental effects involved. And so, if this had been done properly, the Air Force would do its NEPA analysis, bring E -- or Guam EPA in on the process, get their views then, and then, if they decided to go forward with a permit for open detonation on Tarague Beach, submit that permit, which, given that Guam EPA had already been involved, I would assume would -- could be approved readily. But this is exact -- I mean, NEPA, the whole point of NEPA is to make sure that these -- this kind of evaluation is happening before resources -- resources are committed, such as resources in the form of teeing up a plan for an application and before the die is cast. So, no, it would not satisfy NEPA for that to all happen after the Air Force bakes its plan, tees it up, and then says: Okay, wait, now we're going to decide whether -- or we're going to evaluate the environmental effects of what we have already -- you know, the ball we've already started rolling.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So a NEPA challenge, because the route for challenging a NEPA violation is through the APA, it requires final agency action. And so, yes, it often happens that a NEPA analysis is concluded at the same time a decision is made on the major federal action that is the subject of NEPA. Here, we think that is what happened because the Air Force decided it wanted to continue these operations.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So -- well, I guess I'm not sure -- I'm not familiar with situations that would happen like this, where a plan is devised and the Air Force decides to put it forward and then acts on that plan by continuing open detonation at the site by virtue of the extension and then doubles back and does a NEPA analysis after the fact.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So both are necessary conditions. But I think the fact that the submission of the application is a necessary condition is all that is required for a legal consequence for purposes of Bennett prong 2. I don't think this Court's cases have said it has to be a completely sufficient condition on its own. And I think one case that illustrates this is Dalton versus Specter. So, there, of course, the Court ruled that the Secretary's action recommending certain military bases for closure was not final agency action, but the Court did find that the President's action was final action. It's just that he's not an agency. And, there, the process didn't end with the President. There was also -- the President had to submit the base closures to Congress, and there was a 45-day time built in for Congress to essentially veto what the President wanted to do by joint resolution. So, there, you still had a period of -- there was required inaction by another actor, but this Court still found the President's decision to be final action. If there's one thing that I -- or one aspect of my friend's presentation that I would like to clarify, and that is whether or not a finding that there was no final agency action in this case could address the question of whether or not there was a NEPA violation here. So the relevant language in the amended version of NEPA says that there's no obligation to do an EIS if the proposed agency action is not a final agency action. So that means that if the actual operations themselves, once fully authorized and fully permitted, if those aren't a final agency action, then there's no EIS requirement. But I think -- I think it's hard to dispute that the actual operations themselves, once they're being carried out, is final agency action. And so I don't think that is a route to avoid the text of NEPA, which is very clear that NEPA is not displaced in the absence of something like a clear and fundamental conflict or an express exclusion of the kind that Congress has repeatedly done over the years but did not do for -- for RCRA.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes. So I don't -- so, if we were to challenge Guam EPA's decision on a permit, whenever that decision happens, that is done under Guam -- the equivalent of Guam administrative law, so like the Guam APA. And I don't see how we could go --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yeah.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: The Guam EPA has no obligation to police the Air Force's compliance with NEPA. They don't enforce NEPA. There's nothing in RCRA requiring them to ensure that NEPA was required -- was complied with. So we would have no basis to say that Guam EPA did anything wrong with respect to NEPA.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes, I think the same is true of a state EPA because they also don't have a NEPA obligation. And they have the --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, wait a minute. I -- I'm totally lost here. The Guam EPA has to accept an obligation that complies with RCRA law, correct?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: They have to --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And if RCRA law requires an NEPA, wouldn't they be acting ultra vires by approving something without NEPA?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So they have to fulfill all of RCRA's requirements. And I am just saying that because NEPA's a --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And if that includes -- and if that includes that the application must have a NEPA analysis, why isn't the failure subject to Guam review?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Because I don't think there's anything in RCRA that requires --in RCRA itself -- there's certainly something in NEPA -- but I don't think there's anything in RCRA that requires the NEPA analysis. So I don't think that Guam EPA would have the authority to do anything if the Air Force failed to comply with NEPA.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: There's --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: No. I was just going to say 16 states plus D.C. and Puerto Rico have passed their own versions of NEPA in their RCRA obligations. Does Guam need to do that?

turns_pm60.text: Are you referring to the state laws that are sort of the --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I'm not sure about the states requiring their own version of NEPA. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

turns_pm60.text: I think, if this Court found that there was no finality here because there was still some kind of a contingency, I would -- we would respectfully ask that the Court say that there is final agency action once that contingency is resolved so that we could file our federal APA suit against the Air Force then.

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.text: I think there's no difference between the two, and that's why I'm fully comfortable with saying that the final agency action is the submission of the application. turns_pm60.text: I think it --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: May I --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think it reflects the decision to continue these operations past when they otherwise would have ceased because the Air Force was forced to a choice: Do we want to stop when our permit would expire, or do we want to keep going? And, yes, it leads to teeing up this other decision by the regulator, but that doesn't change the Air Force made its own decision.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So no other example comes to mind in this Court's case law, but I would say that it's clear that NEPA attaches to the -- to federal agencies' own operations, so their actions about, you know, like the operations here, what they are doing and not just their actions as a regulator. And so I think the upshot of --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] The Air Force was required to comply with NEPA before choosing to continue open detonation on Tarague Beach. And we can obtain judicial review of that violation now. On the question whether NEPA applies, the government's position is simply atextual. Congress has told us that NEPA is displaced only when it is excluded pursuant to another provision of law or there is a clear and fundamental conflict between NEPA and another law's requirements. That aligns with this Court's precedent, the strong presumption against implied repeals, and Congress's longstanding practice of drafting express exclusions to NEPA when it wants them. The government's response is that RCRA is specifically about hazardous waste. But, because the laws can be harmonized, that observation can't carry the day. Indeed, NEPA is meant to be harmonized with other environmental laws in this way. It is what agencies call an umbrella law. It is meant to consolidate and streamline all required environmental analysis at an early juncture to ensure a better decision and better planning. So, if the Air Force was wrong to ignore NEPA here, the only question should be when Prutehi Guahan can get judicial review of that violation. The Air Force's decision to continue OD at this location and submitting the renewal application was not tentative, and its application implementing the decision had, among other things, the concrete effect of authorizing open detonation operations past the date when they otherwise would have ended. The government is instead pushing a rule where the fact that the Air Force's decision required external sign-off means that it can't be final as a matter of law, perhaps, apparently, not even after that external sign-off occurs. That does not align with this Court's pragmatic approach to finality, and it is especially senseless when it comes to our claim of a procedural violation here. Indeed, this Court has already said in Ohio Forestry Association versus Sierra Club that a litigant with standing can "complain of a NEPA failure at the time it takes place for the claim can never get riper." There is nothing to be gained here by delaying our challenge to the Air Force's own decision-making about its own operations until a non-federal agency has made a different determination under a different law. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.text: -- being able to review the NEPA analysis in that case.

turns_pm60.text: I understand, and I understand that that creates a contingency, but I guess what I would say is that the contingency -- the fact of the contingency shouldn't be determinative. I don't think we would be having a debate about final agency action there, even though it's action about the --the Air Force's own operations. Here, yes, that has to go and get external sign-off from somebody else. But this Court has found final agency action where there is a contingency. For instance --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I don't think so because this Court has been clear that the possibility of revision of the agency's decision, that it might change its mind, is not itself enough to say that a decision where the agency reached the culmination of its decision-making process is non-final. Here, yes, that possibility of revision might come because it's provoked by an outside entity, but I think that was also true in Biden versus Texas, where this Court found final agency action when there was --DHS Secretary issued a memo saying: I am terminating immigration --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well -- so I think it does matter here, and I think it should matter under this Court's pragmatic approach to finality, the kind of legal claim we're bringing here. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Right, but in --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So -- but, to be clear, the NEPA violation, it's clear that it happened before resources were committed in this application. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- the fundamental decision to carry out these --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- open detonations at Tarague Beach. And we know that the Air Force is settled on that decision because it has, in fact, been acting on them past -- you know, by continuing these detonation operations past September 2021, when they otherwise would have ceased.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I am not aware of a basis for us to bring this challenge on review of whatever Guam EPA does. I understand that's what my friend said here today, but Guam EPA has no NEPA obligation. It has no obligation to enforce the Air Force's NEPA obligations. So whatever -- if, you know, we have a basis -- if this permit is granted and we have a basis to challenge it before Guam EPA, that is a separate question.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: No, not against the state permitting agency. Now, you know, it's possible we could just bring the same suit but wait to bring it in federal court against the Air Force until after the permit issues. I think it would be odd to say that that's the point of finality because it would make finality turn on the decision of a non-federal actor. It would somehow make the previous decision by the Air Force non-final. But we do think that there has to be final agency action by the Air Force at some point given that there is a NEPA obligation here and we need to be able to enforce it. We don't think waiting to sue until after the permit issues serves anybody because, if the NEPA, you know, review produces a different application or, in our view, produces a determination not to seek a application from Guam at all because the Air Force decides to treat its waste somewhere else that's not in this location --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- they would have wasted their time.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: They would have -- it would wasted the permitting agency's time to have ruled on that application and have everybody double back at that point.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So that's not the way that the NEPA obligation works. NEPA is very clear that you have to undertake the analysis before proposing a major federal action. And it also talks about bringing entities like Guam EPA to the table as what NEPA calls cooperating agencies, and those are agencies who have jurisdiction by law over some part of the project or some environmental effects involved. And so, if this had been done properly, the Air Force would do its NEPA analysis, bring E -- or Guam EPA in on the process, get their views then, and then, if they decided to go forward with a permit for open detonation on Tarague Beach, submit that permit, which, given that Guam EPA had already been involved, I would assume would -- could be approved readily. But this is exact -- I mean, NEPA, the whole point of NEPA is to make sure that these -- this kind of evaluation is happening before resources -- resources are committed, such as resources in the form of teeing up a plan for an application and before the die is cast. So, no, it would not satisfy NEPA for that to all happen after the Air Force bakes its plan, tees it up, and then says: Okay, wait, now we're going to decide whether -- or we're going to evaluate the environmental effects of what we have already -- you know, the ball we've already started rolling.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So a NEPA challenge, because the route for challenging a NEPA violation is through the APA, it requires final agency action. And so, yes, it often happens that a NEPA analysis is concluded at the same time a decision is made on the major federal action that is the subject of NEPA. Here, we think that is what happened because the Air Force decided it wanted to continue these operations.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So -- well, I guess I'm not sure -- I'm not familiar with situations that would happen like this, where a plan is devised and the Air Force decides to put it forward and then acts on that plan by continuing open detonation at the site by virtue of the extension and then doubles back and does a NEPA analysis after the fact.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So both are necessary conditions. So, there, of course, the Court ruled that the Secretary's action recommending certain military bases for closure was not final agency action, but the Court did find that the President's action was final action. It's just that he's not an agency. And, there, the process didn't end with the President. There was also -- the President had to submit the base closures to Congress, and there was a 45-day time built in for Congress to essentially veto what the President wanted to do by joint resolution. So, there, you still had a period of -- there was required inaction by another actor, but this Court still found the President's decision to be final action. If there's one thing that I -- or one aspect of my friend's presentation that I would like to clarify, and that is whether or not a finding that there was no final agency action in this case could address the question of whether or not there was a NEPA violation here. So that means that if the actual operations themselves, once fully authorized and fully permitted, if those aren't a final agency action, then there's no EIS requirement. But I think -- I think it's hard to dispute that the actual operations themselves, once they're being carried out, is final agency action. And so I don't think that is a route to avoid the text of NEPA, which is very clear that NEPA is not displaced in the absence of something like a clear and fundamental conflict or an express exclusion of the kind that Congress has repeatedly done over the years but did not do for -- for RCRA.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes. So I don't -- so, if we were to challenge Guam EPA's decision on a permit, whenever that decision happens, that is done under Guam -- the equivalent of Guam administrative law, so like the Guam APA. And I don't see how we could go --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: The Guam EPA has no obligation to police the Air Force's compliance with NEPA. They don't enforce NEPA. There's nothing in RCRA requiring them to ensure that NEPA was required -- was complied with. So we would have no basis to say that Guam EPA did anything wrong with respect to NEPA.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes, I think the same is true of a state EPA because they also don't have a NEPA obligation. And they have the --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, wait a minute. I -- I'm totally lost here. The Guam EPA has to accept an obligation that complies with RCRA law, correct?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: They have to --

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: There's --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: No. I was just going to say 16 states plus D.C. and Puerto Rico have passed their own versions of NEPA in their RCRA obligations. Does Guam need to do that?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Are you referring to the state laws that are sort of the --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] The Air Force was required to comply with NEPA before choosing to continue open detonation on Tarague Beach. And we can obtain judicial review of that violation now. On the question whether NEPA applies, the government's position is simply atextual. Congress has told us that NEPA is displaced only when it is excluded pursuant to another provision of law or there is a clear and fundamental conflict between NEPA and another law's requirements. That aligns with this Court's precedent, the strong presumption against implied repeals, and Congress's longstanding practice of drafting express exclusions to NEPA when it wants them. The government's response is that RCRA is specifically about hazardous waste. But, because the laws can be harmonized, that observation can't carry the day. Indeed, NEPA is meant to be harmonized with other environmental laws in this way. It is what agencies call an umbrella law. It is meant to consolidate and streamline all required environmental analysis at an early juncture to ensure a better decision and better planning. So, if the Air Force was wrong to ignore NEPA here, the only question should be when Prutehi Guahan can get judicial review of that violation. The Air Force's decision to continue OD at this location and submitting the renewal application was not tentative, and its application implementing the decision had, among other things, the concrete effect of authorizing open detonation operations past the date when they otherwise would have ended. The government is instead pushing a rule where the fact that the Air Force's decision required external sign-off means that it can't be final as a matter of law, perhaps, apparently, not even after that external sign-off occurs. That does not align with this Court's pragmatic approach to finality, and it is especially senseless when it comes to our claim of a procedural violation here. Indeed, this Court has already said in Ohio Forestry Association versus Sierra Club that a litigant with standing can "complain of a NEPA failure at the time it takes place for the claim can never get riper." There is nothing to be gained here by delaying our challenge to the Air Force's own decision-making about its own operations until a non-federal agency has made a different determination under a different law. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, I can think of one fact pattern in this Court's cases involving another NEPA case, and that was the Winter versus Natural Resources Defense Council case. And, there, the Navy was continuing a series of training exercises for another two years that they had been doing previously, and they did the NEPA analysis before embarking on another two years of exercises. The Court -- you know, finality -- the Court did not decide finality in this case, but nobody seemed to think that there was any issue with --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- being able to review the NEPA analysis in that case.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I understand, and I understand that that creates a contingency, but I guess what I would say is that the contingency -- the fact of the contingency shouldn't be determinative. So say that RCRA required the Air Force to put all of the information it would put in an application and just publish that document. I don't think we would be having a debate about final agency action there, even though it's action about the --the Air Force's own operations. Here, yes, that has to go and get external sign-off from somebody else. But this Court has found final agency action where there is a contingency. For instance --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I don't think so because this Court has been clear that the possibility of revision of the agency's decision, that it might change its mind, is not itself enough to say that a decision where the agency reached the culmination of its decision-making process is non-final. Here, yes, that possibility of revision might come because it's provoked by an outside entity, but I think that was also true in Biden versus Texas, where this Court found final agency action when there was --DHS Secretary issued a memo saying: I am terminating immigration --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well -- so I think it does matter here, and I think it should matter under this Court's pragmatic approach to finality, the kind of legal claim we're bringing here. So our NEPA claim is attached to the -- the process of decision-making the Air Force used before it decided in NEPA's terms to propose this major federal action and should not be --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right, but in --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So -- but, to be clear, the NEPA violation, it's clear that it happened before resources were committed in this application. And because -- excuse me --so, because the NEPA claim there is nothing -- or, sorry, I should say, because any revision that happens by Guam EPA with respect to, you know, particular procedures or something like that, that will not affect whether --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- the fundamental decision to carry out these --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- open detonations at Tarague Beach. And we know that the Air Force is settled on that decision because it has, in fact, been acting on them past -- you know, by continuing these detonation operations past September 2021, when they otherwise would have ceased.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I am not aware of a basis for us to bring this challenge on review of whatever Guam EPA does. I understand that's what my friend said here today, but Guam EPA has no NEPA obligation. It has no obligation to enforce the Air Force's NEPA obligations. So whatever -- if, you know, we have a basis -- if this permit is granted and we have a basis to challenge it before Guam EPA, that is a separate question.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: No, not against the state permitting agency. Now, you know, it's possible we could just bring the same suit but wait to bring it in federal court against the Air Force until after the permit issues. I think it would be odd to say that that's the point of finality because it would make finality turn on the decision of a non-federal actor. It would somehow make the previous decision by the Air Force non-final. But we do think that there has to be final agency action by the Air Force at some point given that there is a NEPA obligation here and we need to be able to enforce it. We don't think waiting to sue until after the permit issues serves anybody because, if the NEPA, you know, review produces a different application or, in our view, produces a determination not to seek a application from Guam at all because the Air Force decides to treat its waste somewhere else that's not in this location --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- they would have wasted their time.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: They would have -- it would wasted the permitting agency's time to have ruled on that application and have everybody double back at that point.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So that's not the way that the NEPA obligation works. NEPA is very clear that you have to undertake the analysis before proposing a major federal action. And it also talks about bringing entities like Guam EPA to the table as what NEPA calls cooperating agencies, and those are agencies who have jurisdiction by law over some part of the project or some environmental effects involved. And so, if this had been done properly, the Air Force would do its NEPA analysis, bring E -- or Guam EPA in on the process, get their views then, and then, if they decided to go forward with a permit for open detonation on Tarague Beach, submit that permit, which, given that Guam EPA had already been involved, I would assume would -- could be approved readily. But this is exact -- I mean, NEPA, the whole point of NEPA is to make sure that these -- this kind of evaluation is happening before resources -- resources are committed, such as resources in the form of teeing up a plan for an application and before the die is cast. So, no, it would not satisfy NEPA for that to all happen after the Air Force bakes its plan, tees it up, and then says: Okay, wait, now we're going to decide whether -- or we're going to evaluate the environmental effects of what we have already -- you know, the ball we've already started rolling.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So a NEPA challenge, because the route for challenging a NEPA violation is through the APA, it requires final agency action. And so, yes, it often happens that a NEPA analysis is concluded at the same time a decision is made on the major federal action that is the subject of NEPA. Here, we think that is what happened because the Air Force decided it wanted to continue these operations.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So -- well, I guess I'm not sure -- I'm not familiar with situations that would happen like this, where a plan is devised and the Air Force decides to put it forward and then acts on that plan by continuing open detonation at the site by virtue of the extension and then doubles back and does a NEPA analysis after the fact.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So both are necessary conditions. But I think the fact that the submission of the application is a necessary condition is all that is required for a legal consequence for purposes of Bennett prong 2. I don't think this Court's cases have said it has to be a completely sufficient condition on its own. And I think one case that illustrates this is Dalton versus Specter. So, there, of course, the Court ruled that the Secretary's action recommending certain military bases for closure was not final agency action, but the Court did find that the President's action was final action. It's just that he's not an agency. And, there, the process didn't end with the President. There was also -- the President had to submit the base closures to Congress, and there was a 45-day time built in for Congress to essentially veto what the President wanted to do by joint resolution. So, there, you still had a period of -- there was required inaction by another actor, but this Court still found the President's decision to be final action. If there's one thing that I -- or one aspect of my friend's presentation that I would like to clarify, and that is whether or not a finding that there was no final agency action in this case could address the question of whether or not there was a NEPA violation here. So the relevant language in the amended version of NEPA says that there's no obligation to do an EIS if the proposed agency action is not a final agency action. So that means that if the actual operations themselves, once fully authorized and fully permitted, if those aren't a final agency action, then there's no EIS requirement. But I think -- I think it's hard to dispute that the actual operations themselves, once they're being carried out, is final agency action. And so I don't think that is a route to avoid the text of NEPA, which is very clear that NEPA is not displaced in the absence of something like a clear and fundamental conflict or an express exclusion of the kind that Congress has repeatedly done over the years but did not do for -- for RCRA.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes. So I don't -- so, if we were to challenge Guam EPA's decision on a permit, whenever that decision happens, that is done under Guam -- the equivalent of Guam administrative law, so like the Guam APA. And I don't see how we could go --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yeah.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: The Guam EPA has no obligation to police the Air Force's compliance with NEPA. They don't enforce NEPA. There's nothing in RCRA requiring them to ensure that NEPA was required -- was complied with. So we would have no basis to say that Guam EPA did anything wrong with respect to NEPA.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes, I think the same is true of a state EPA because they also don't have a NEPA obligation. And they have the --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: They have to --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So they have to fulfill all of RCRA's requirements. And I am just saying that because NEPA's a --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Because I don't think there's anything in RCRA that requires --in RCRA itself -- there's certainly something in NEPA -- but I don't think there's anything in RCRA that requires the NEPA analysis. So I don't think that Guam EPA would have the authority to do anything if the Air Force failed to comply with NEPA.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I certainly want --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I'm sorry. Please.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Are you referring to the state laws that are sort of the --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- equivalent of NEPA? I'm not aware of any requirement for states and territories to pass their own version of NEPA as part of fulfilling their duty under RCRA.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I'm not sure about the states requiring their own version of NEPA. I will say that, as that brief discusses, states find NEPA compliance extremely beneficial to them when they are ruling on RCRA applications because this is a way to, for instance, ensure that the location that is being teed up for RCRA review is the least environmentally destructive because NEPA forces the evaluation of alternatives that we say wasn't -- that didn't happen here, especially with respect to alternative sites.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Speaker A, are you saying that you'll -- I understand your concern about not being able to sue Guam EPA for the NEPA problem of the Navy, and I'm looking forward to hearing [PERSON]'s response to that in rebuttal. But are you saying you would never -- if you should lose here on the question, first question presented, never be able to sue the Navy for a NEPA violation? Are you saying you -- you just don't see any avenue that your client could pursue?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think, if this Court found that there was no finality here because there was still some kind of a contingency, I would -- we would respectfully ask that the Court say that there is final agency action once that contingency is resolved so that we could file our federal APA suit against the Air Force then.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, whether we say that or not, I would think you would take that position, that there's final agency action when the Navy goes ahead and starts engaging in the activities that you think require a NEPA without having secured one.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: We would certainly take that position. I understood my friend to say here today that, no, that's still not federal -- or final agency action by the Air Force, that all -- the only agency action being done here is just by Guam EPA. I think that is strange when you have --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think he's talking about the RCRA -- during the RCRA application process. Put that aside. I -- I didn't hear him say -- and maybe this is another question for [PERSON] on rebuttal -- but I -- I didn't hear him say, I -- I don't think, that there would never be a point at which there could be final agency action by actually engaging in the activity -- Navy's activities once -- once it secures a -- a license to do so.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: If I misunderstood him, I apologize. But we fully agree there has to be final agency action by the Air Force at some point that we can challenge in federal court under the APA. This can't just be -- because, I mean, the Air Force is making a different decision than whatever decision it is that Guam EPA eventually makes under RCRA. And I want to be very clear that our challenge to the Air Force now is about the procedural violation and the Air Force not complying with federal law in reaching the decision to proceed.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Last -- last --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: We're not --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- last question. How about agency action withheld? Have you thought about that as an avenue?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Because they didn't comply with NEPA? Yeah, I think, you know, it's -- we recognize that it's a broader theory to say that, you know, a failure to comply with law is agency action withheld.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Unlawful.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But we -- you know, that isn't something that's been litigated in this case because we -- we thought there was --I mean, there is action here in the form of this application that is --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But that -- that question's not before us whether --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It's not before you. Correct.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It was, but he can correct me.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes. So that regulation is just talking about EPA as the permitting authority, so it's saying that --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, if you look, I think, in context, that becomes apparent. But you can also just look at the notice --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It says when EPA is the permitting authority.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: And when you look at the -- the NPRM and the preamble for the final rule, EPA explains where it got this rule from, and it says we got this from the D.C. Circuit's decision in Portland Cement, which is a functional equivalence case. And that case is very, very clear that the rule the D.C. Circuit was devising applies just to environmental agencies enforcing environmental law. And I think there's another Federal Register rulemaking from 2007 -- it's in our brief -- describing the regulation as applicable to certain EPA actions. So we don't think that touches on the question here about the permitter --the permittee agency, and for that reason, there would be nothing for this Court to give weight to in evaluating the question here. I would also say that this Court said in Epic Systems that the job of reconciling different statutes is a job for courts, not agencies. So I'm not sure this is the kind of topic of how to, you know, interpret NEPA alongside RCRA. That is squarely in the agencies' wheelhouse.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Sure.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right. So I think the alternatives analysis that NEPA requires, which is, like, the heart of NEPA analysis, is important. Here, for instance, we think that alternative -- that NEPA would have required the Air Force to consider not just alternative procedures or modes of treatment but also just doing -- carrying out open detonations somewhere that was not on Guam, like shipping this waste to the mainland and carrying out these operations at another base. That is not something that Guam EPA would be required to consider under RCRA, and I don't think they could deny the permit on that basis because it's not something that RCRA authorizes them to do. The other thing I think is timing. I discussed about how NEPA envisions that this is all done before the plan is teed up, including bringing Guam EPA to the table. But also, the public comment happens at that early stage too. And it would be public comment to the Air Force as decision-maker, not just public comment to Guam EPA, which, yes, RCRA provides for, but, here, our client didn't have a route to speak to the Air Force and the military in trying -- especially in helping to develop or have them evaluate those alternatives.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I do. I think this Court's cases have required a conflict. I think the Reading Law treatise says the same thing, that the specific-general principle is only when there is a conflict to be reconciled. I think Epic Systems, again, is a good example of this. There, there was a specific-general argument being made, and the Court said, no, we can harmonize these statutes and that is where our duty lies.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes, but also certainly here, where Congress has stepped in in NEPA and told us what the ground rules are for displacement and said not just that there has to be a conflict but there has to be a clear and fundamental one. And that comes from this Court's decision in 1976 from Flint Ridge, where the Court said, because NEPA has this language about how agencies must interpret and administer their laws to the fullest extent possible with NEPA, that language was specifically trying to avoid a situation like this, where an agency, as the Court put it, shunts aside the NEPA obligation in the bureaucratic shovel -- shuffle. So, you know, I think, again, NEPA is designed to do this kind of thing. When you look at even the current Department of War NEPA procedures, you can see all the ways in which they say: Integrate review under other environmental laws. Do it all at once. Make sure you don't have duplicative documents. Make sure the documents do cover everything they need to cover and name all the permits that are required and everything like that. But this is -- this is a strength of NEPA, is to make sure that they can cover all the fronts at once and not have duplication because it's just done once.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I don't think that this is going to open the floodgates to more attacks on permitting decisions. So the first thing I'd say is that our -- our position --we -- we fully agree that we can't use this suit as a way to, like, collaterally attack whatever decision Guam EPA makes or to say that this application is deficient under RCRA. So I don't think this is an avenue for suits like that. The other thing I'd say is that our claim is a procedural claim that focuses on the decision-making of the federal entity. So the only kinds of claims that can be brought under a theory like this are ones where there is a law that applies to the decision-maker of the federal agency as the permittee. The other thing I would say is that, if you agree with me that there has to be final agency action at some point by the Air Force in this process, then whatever floodgates there are would already have been opened because that final agency action happens at the point of the permit issuance. So, if people wanted to be suing the permittee agency, they could have been doing so at that point. I think the fact that the government hasn't pointed to those suits is because, you know, you really do have to have the confluence of a claim that attaches to the permittee agency's decision-making that's not just a way to, you know, try another way of complaining about whatever it is the permitting agency, the permitting authority, does.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think there's no difference between the two, and that's why I'm fully comfortable with saying that the final agency action is the submission of the application. I think the application reflects the decision. It's memorialized there. And it also implements it by bringing about the automatic extension but also by binding Air Force personnel to the application's terms upon Guam EPA's approval.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think it --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: May I --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think it reflects the decision to continue these operations past when they otherwise would have ceased because the Air Force was forced to a choice: Do we want to stop when our permit would expire, or do we want to keep going? And I think it reflects the decision to keep going. And I think that is fully the Air Force's decision to make. That's not Guam EPA's decision to make. And, yes, it leads to teeing up this other decision by the regulator, but that doesn't change the Air Force made its own decision.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So no other example comes to mind in this Court's case law, but I would say that it's clear that NEPA attaches to the -- to federal agencies' own operations, so their actions about, you know, like the operations here, what they are doing and not just their actions as a regulator. And so I think the upshot of --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right. And I was -- what I was getting at is that if it were true that there can never be final agency action when the government's own operations are involved and they're not acting as a regulator, you would never be able to bring an action challenging a NEPA violation for the government's own operations, even though that seems like, you know --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- a pretty clear --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes. Our position is that there is because they reached the culmination of their decision-making process about their own operations but about the decision at hand and it produced legal consequences.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I would say Biden versus Texas, the agency was deciding its own policy for immigration enforcement. So the DHS Secretary was making a decision about what DHS employees would do. That's what this Court framed it as, was a determination of what DHS employees would have to do once the injunction in that case -- or if the injunction in that case was lifted. So I do think this Court's finality inquiry is no different when it comes to the federal government's actions, you know, as an entity carrying out its own operations and not just its actions as a regulator.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I guess I'm just a little curious. Do you think you could bring -- I'm repeating myself for both of you. Do you think you could bring an action for agency action unlawfully withheld, and why -- why didn't you try that avenue?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: With apologies, I -- that's not the action we brought here, and I don't want to make commitments about a question when it arose in a different case.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Okay. All right. Thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

turns_pm15.text: Substantively.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Right. So I think the alternatives analysis that NEPA requires, which is, like, the heart of NEPA analysis, is important. Here, for instance, we think that alternative -- that NEPA would have required the Air Force to consider not just alternative procedures or modes of treatment but also just doing -- carrying out open detonations somewhere that was not on Guam, like shipping this waste to the mainland and carrying out these operations at another base. That is not something that Guam EPA would be required to consider under RCRA, and I don't think they could deny the permit on that basis because it's not something that RCRA authorizes them to do. The other thing I think is timing. I discussed about how NEPA envisions that this is all done before the plan is teed up, including bringing Guam EPA to the table. But also, the public comment happens at that early stage too. And it would be public comment to the Air Force as decision-maker, not just public comment to Guam EPA, which, yes, RCRA provides for, but, here, our client didn't have a route to speak to the Air Force and the military in trying -- especially in helping to develop or have them evaluate those alternatives.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: I do. I think this Court's cases have required a conflict. turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Yes, but also certainly here, where Congress has stepped in in NEPA and told us what the ground rules are for displacement and said not just that there has to be a conflict but there has to be a clear and fundamental one. turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: I don't think that this is going to open the floodgates to more attacks on permitting decisions. turns_pm60.text: -- the fundamental decision to carry out these --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- they would have wasted their time.

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think it --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: May I --

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm15.speaker: A

turns_pm60.text: -- equivalent of NEPA? I'm not aware of any requirement for states and territories to pass their own version of NEPA as part of fulfilling their duty under RCRA.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I'm not sure about the states requiring their own version of NEPA. I will say that, as that brief discusses, states find NEPA compliance extremely beneficial to them when they are ruling on RCRA applications because this is a way to, for instance, ensure that the location that is being teed up for RCRA review is the least environmentally destructive because NEPA forces the evaluation of alternatives that we say wasn't -- that didn't happen here, especially with respect to alternative sites.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think, if this Court found that there was no finality here because there was still some kind of a contingency, I would -- we would respectfully ask that the Court say that there is final agency action once that contingency is resolved so that we could file our federal APA suit against the Air Force then.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: We would certainly take that position. I understood my friend to say here today that, no, that's still not federal -- or final agency action by the Air Force, that all -- the only agency action being done here is just by Guam EPA. I think that is strange when you have --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: If I misunderstood him, I apologize. But we fully agree there has to be final agency action by the Air Force at some point that we can challenge in federal court under the APA. This can't just be -- because, I mean, the Air Force is making a different decision than whatever decision it is that Guam EPA eventually makes under RCRA. And I want to be very clear that our challenge to the Air Force now is about the procedural violation and the Air Force not complying with federal law in reaching the decision to proceed.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: We're not --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Because they didn't comply with NEPA? Yeah, I think, you know, it's -- we recognize that it's a broader theory to say that, you know, a failure to comply with law is agency action withheld.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But we -- you know, that isn't something that's been litigated in this case because we -- we thought there was --I mean, there is action here in the form of this application that is --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It's not before you. Correct.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It was, but he can correct me.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes. So that regulation is just talking about EPA as the permitting authority, so it's saying that --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, if you look, I think, in context, that becomes apparent. But you can also just look at the notice --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It says when EPA is the permitting authority.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And when you look at the -- the NPRM and the preamble for the final rule, EPA explains where it got this rule from, and it says we got this from the D.C. Circuit's decision in Portland Cement, which is a functional equivalence case. And that case is very, very clear that the rule the D.C. Circuit was devising applies just to environmental agencies enforcing environmental law. And I think there's another Federal Register rulemaking from 2007 -- it's in our brief -- describing the regulation as applicable to certain EPA actions. So we don't think that touches on the question here about the permitter --the permittee agency, and for that reason, there would be nothing for this Court to give weight to in evaluating the question here. I would also say that this Court said in Epic Systems that the job of reconciling different statutes is a job for courts, not agencies. So I'm not sure this is the kind of topic of how to, you know, interpret NEPA alongside RCRA. That is squarely in the agencies' wheelhouse.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Sure.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Right. So I think the alternatives analysis that NEPA requires, which is, like, the heart of NEPA analysis, is important. Here, for instance, we think that alternative -- that NEPA would have required the Air Force to consider not just alternative procedures or modes of treatment but also just doing -- carrying out open detonations somewhere that was not on Guam, like shipping this waste to the mainland and carrying out these operations at another base. That is not something that Guam EPA would be required to consider under RCRA, and I don't think they could deny the permit on that basis because it's not something that RCRA authorizes them to do. The other thing I think is timing. I discussed about how NEPA envisions that this is all done before the plan is teed up, including bringing Guam EPA to the table. But also, the public comment happens at that early stage too. And it would be public comment to the Air Force as decision-maker, not just public comment to Guam EPA, which, yes, RCRA provides for, but, here, our client didn't have a route to speak to the Air Force and the military in trying -- especially in helping to develop or have them evaluate those alternatives.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I do. I think this Court's cases have required a conflict. I think the Reading Law treatise says the same thing, that the specific-general principle is only when there is a conflict to be reconciled. I think Epic Systems, again, is a good example of this. There, there was a specific-general argument being made, and the Court said, no, we can harmonize these statutes and that is where our duty lies.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes, but also certainly here, where Congress has stepped in in NEPA and told us what the ground rules are for displacement and said not just that there has to be a conflict but there has to be a clear and fundamental one. And that comes from this Court's decision in 1976 from Flint Ridge, where the Court said, because NEPA has this language about how agencies must interpret and administer their laws to the fullest extent possible with NEPA, that language was specifically trying to avoid a situation like this, where an agency, as the Court put it, shunts aside the NEPA obligation in the bureaucratic shovel -- shuffle. So, you know, I think, again, NEPA is designed to do this kind of thing. When you look at even the current Department of War NEPA procedures, you can see all the ways in which they say: Integrate review under other environmental laws. Do it all at once. Make sure you don't have duplicative documents. Make sure the documents do cover everything they need to cover and name all the permits that are required and everything like that. But this is -- this is a strength of NEPA, is to make sure that they can cover all the fronts at once and not have duplication because it's just done once.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I don't think that this is going to open the floodgates to more attacks on permitting decisions. So the first thing I'd say is that our -- our position --we -- we fully agree that we can't use this suit as a way to, like, collaterally attack whatever decision Guam EPA makes or to say that this application is deficient under RCRA. So I don't think this is an avenue for suits like that. The other thing I'd say is that our claim is a procedural claim that focuses on the decision-making of the federal entity. So the only kinds of claims that can be brought under a theory like this are ones where there is a law that applies to the decision-maker of the federal agency as the permittee. The other thing I would say is that, if you agree with me that there has to be final agency action at some point by the Air Force in this process, then whatever floodgates there are would already have been opened because that final agency action happens at the point of the permit issuance. So, if people wanted to be suing the permittee agency, they could have been doing so at that point. I think the fact that the government hasn't pointed to those suits is because, you know, you really do have to have the confluence of a claim that attaches to the permittee agency's decision-making that's not just a way to, you know, try another way of complaining about whatever it is the permitting agency, the permitting authority, does.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think there's no difference between the two, and that's why I'm fully comfortable with saying that the final agency action is the submission of the application. I think the application reflects the decision. It's memorialized there. And it also implements it by bringing about the automatic extension but also by binding Air Force personnel to the application's terms upon Guam EPA's approval.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: And I guess the question is: It reflects the decision to do what? [PERSON] says, from the very beginning, it reflects the decision to make a proposal to another agency that has the authority to say yes or no, et cetera, et cetera. And you said that has no bearing on whether or not we should consider this final agency action?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think it --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I mean, you do agree that it's -- it's the decision to make a proposal?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: May I --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think it reflects the decision to continue these operations past when they otherwise would have ceased because the Air Force was forced to a choice: Do we want to stop when our permit would expire, or do we want to keep going? And I think it reflects the decision to keep going. And I think that is fully the Air Force's decision to make. That's not Guam EPA's decision to make. And, yes, it leads to teeing up this other decision by the regulator, but that doesn't change the Air Force made its own decision.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So no other example comes to mind in this Court's case law, but I would say that it's clear that NEPA attaches to the -- to federal agencies' own operations, so their actions about, you know, like the operations here, what they are doing and not just their actions as a regulator. And so I think the upshot of --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Right. And I was -- what I was getting at is that if it were true that there can never be final agency action when the government's own operations are involved and they're not acting as a regulator, you would never be able to bring an action challenging a NEPA violation for the government's own operations, even though that seems like, you know --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- a pretty clear --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes. Our position is that there is because they reached the culmination of their decision-making process about their own operations but about the decision at hand and it produced legal consequences.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I would say Biden versus Texas, the agency was deciding its own policy for immigration enforcement. So the DHS Secretary was making a decision about what DHS employees would do. That's what this Court framed it as, was a determination of what DHS employees would have to do once the injunction in that case -- or if the injunction in that case was lifted. So I do think this Court's finality inquiry is no different when it comes to the federal government's actions, you know, as an entity carrying out its own operations and not just its actions as a regulator.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: With apologies, I -- that's not the action we brought here, and I don't want to make commitments about a question when it arose in a different case.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.
