turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: While they're different categories of enactments, I think what concerns me about your argument is that you're suggesting that they are separable in some way, which is really not the way in which the guidelines were devised. And I think we sort of have a --a fundamental misunderstanding of how the manual works because the guidelines and commentary are actually inextricably linked. And what I mean by that is that sentencing judges use the Guidelines Manual to do what is essentially a calculation. It's kind of like math, that the guidelines themselves have certain components to them, and the commentary tells you how those pieces fit together, how you are supposed to take them into account. When you are a judge, you're using both to reach the right answer under the guidelines, and there is a right answer as to what the guideline range is. And so what concerns me about your way of framing this is you suggest that the court can somehow look at the guidelines, not take into account the commentary, not defer to it, not use it, and yet still have an accurate guideline calculation, which is really not how the system is designed. So can you -- can you respond to that?

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: Of course. Stinson presumes that the guidelines have a freestanding meaning. Stinson says that the guidelines mean one thing, and if the Commission -- and if the commentary is plainly inconsistent with them, we are to disregard them. So the assumption that the Commission has always been using or should have always been using -- and it has --is that you can determine a meaning from the guidelines alone and resort to the commentary --

The problem arises just when the judge doesn't know what to do because the guidelines say one thing and the commentary says something totally different. turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] For two reasons, the courts below erred in deferring to the commentary when interpreting Guideline 2K2.1. First, the proper rule for deference to guideline commentary is no deference. Nothing in the text of the Sentencing Reform Act suggests that courts must ever defer to commentary when interpreting a guideline, let alone defer on the -- according to the extreme rule of Stinson. That alone should resolve the question presented given the baseline expectation that courts independently determine the meaning of legal provisions. That expectation dates back to Marbury, and it should be especially hard to displace in the criminal setting, where respect for liberty demands that we turn square corners. In fact, the Sentencing Reform Act is affirmatively incompatible with any deference regime. Section -- Section 3553(a)(4) requires that the Commission set forth the range of imprisonment in the guidelines, not elsewhere. And Sections 994 and 995 of Title 28 attach detailed procedural requirements to the amendment of guidelines, which requirements do not apply to guideline commentary. Why would Congress bother to require detailed notice, public comment, 180 days of congressional review, and the approval of four voting commissioners every time the -- the Commission amends a guideline if the Commission could simply bind the courts to a new interpretation of the guideline without going through all of this simply by amending the commentary? The second reason the courts below erred in affording Stinson deference is that if the Sentencing Reform Act leaves room for deference, the proper predicate is genuine ambiguity of the kind that survives every tool of construction, not the mere absence of plain or flat inconsistency, as Stinson suggests. The rule applied below, which requires courts to construe guidelines in ways that they think are wrong, certainly can't be found in the SRA's text, and it is not consistent with the judicial role. I am pleased to take the Court's questions.

As between our position and the amicus's position, we also don't think that it makes a difference in the sense that I don't think that it would mean that the commentary, which we acknowledge is a different species of promulgation from an actual -- actual guideline text or -- or even a policy statement, we don't think that it would affect the amount of deference the commentary should receive. turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Thank you, [ADDRESS] Our position is really the only one that's faithful to this Court's precedents. Stinson interpreted the Sentencing Reform Act to incorporate the same measure of deference for guidelines commentary that Seminole Rock gives to an agency's interpretation of its own rules. Kisor then clarified what Seminole Rock deference means. Add those two decisions together and you get that Kisor applies to guidelines commentary. That said, I don't want to overstate the difference between our position and the position of the amicus here. I -- we believe that even under Kisor, the guidelines are going to continue to be informed and interpreted in most instances by the commentary where there is commentary. Our difference is simply the very small area where the commentary may take an interpretation that is an unreasonable interpretation of an ambiguous guideline or even tries to override unambiguous guidelines text. But we wouldn't think that happens very often. On the other hand, Petitioner wants to swing the pendulum way in the other direction and have a regime of no deference under which individual district judges are just free to interpret for themselves the advice that the Commission is trying to give them, notwithstanding what the Commission is telling them. That would be a massive upheaval that would probably cause some kind of revision to the guidelines that, of course, wouldn't solve all the retroactive problems with the cases that are still in the system. And there's no point. It makes all the sense in the world, when the Commission is reasonably saying what the Commission is trying to say, to listen to the Commission. And that's exactly where our Goldilocks position here lands. Now I've kind of taken Petitioner's counsel to have essentially conceded the point -- I'm sorry, Speaker A.

setting: Excerpt from a recorded institutional proceeding. Exactly one of the two speakers, A and B, holds the more powerful institutional role.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: Speaker B, this argument reminds me of my metaphysics class.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: And that's not necessarily a compliment.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: Let's go back to what this case is about so I can have an under --a complete understanding of how we're looking -- what we're looking at. This is a provision that says -- that enhances the sentence for a large capacity magazine. That's the language, right? Where do we find that definition of what a large capacity magazine is?

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: In the commentary that defines it as a magazine capable of holding more than 15 rounds.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: And if a judge disagrees with that and says, I don't think that a large capacity magazine is -- that that is a large capacity magazine, what is the effect?

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: Well, I think that the authority to interpret what that means has been given in the first instance to the Commission.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] It is emphatically the province of the judiciary to say what the law is, but the advisory sentencing guidelines are not the law. They are advisory. As a result, when interpreting the guidelines, the question is not what the law is but, rather, what is the non-binding advice that the Commission is offering about what type of sentence should be imposed? On that question, the sensible approach is to defer to the Commission on the meaning of its own non-binding advice and then have courts decide for themselves, based on their own independent judgment, whether to follow that advice in deciding what type of sentence they want to impose. Now this type of deference doesn't pose any of the problems that you get when you defer to executive agencies on the meaning of the binding rules that they promulgate and enforce. That creates all kinds of problems for the separation of powers and the rule of law that this Court has cut back on in its recent decisions. But Congress gave us two very clear indications that the Commission is different from executive agencies when it comes to deference. First, Section 706 of the APA, which applies to executive agencies, makes very clear that courts should be the ones to resolve interpretive issues. So anytime you have an executive agency claiming authority for deference, that is a backdrop that's going to require a very clear statement to overcome. Second, instead of Section 706 of the APA, which does not apply to the Sentencing Commission at all, what we have is the text of the Sentencing Reform Act, which does authorize the Commission not only to promulgate guidelines but also to promulgate policy statements that authoritatively interpret the guidelines. And, [PERSON], that is the square holding of Williams, which we can talk about. In Williams, this Court held that when a policy statement interprets a guideline, that is an authoritative interpretation of the guideline. And then, in Stinson, this Court simply recognized that when the Commission uses the label of "commentary" to interpret a guideline, that falls within the same statutory authority. And Stinson starts with Williams, and it doesn't get to Seminole Rock until after it says that there is authority to interpret the guidelines. So, as a result of all of that, the Commission's deference that it gets is based on express statutory text. There's no need to rely here on any fictional presumption of implied delegation. This Court's cases cutting back on that fictional presumption in Loper Bright and Kisor simply don't apply. And the deference that the Commission enjoys rests on express authority that is just as sturdy today as it was when Stinson was decided. Stinson should be upheld. There's no reason to create the chaos that would come from overruling it. And I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: What is --

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: So judges --

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: -- what is the guideline based on then?

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: The guideline is based on the Commission's authority under 994(a)(1) to promulgate a guideline for the enhancement. And then the Commission has been given the authority to interpret that in the first instance through policy statements. And my submission is that it should not make any difference whether the Commission uses the label of "policy statement" or uses the label of "commentary" when it interprets that guideline. So I think it -- you know, you should think about it in two steps. First, has there been authority given to the Commission to interpret what that means? The answer to that is yes. That's Williams and Stinson. And then the second step is, okay, we have authority for the Commission to interpret the guideline. Now what we need to do at step 2 is to police whether the Commission has gone outside the boundaries of that delegated authority. That's what the Stinson test is for. If it's inconsistent with or a plainly erroneous interpretation, the Commission can't go there, but as long as you can put these two provisions together and sensibly read them together to determine what the Commission's non-binding advice is, if they can be reconciled, [ADDRESS], they should be read together to give the authoritative position on what sentence the Commission is recommending. Then, of course, it is up to the courts to exercise their independent discretion, do we want to follow that advice or not? But I think it would be nonsensical to try to interpret the guideline as a standalone statute as if it were something written like a statute that is going to have its own independent legal meaning when, in fact, it was promulgated with the commentary simultaneously to Congress, hey, here is what the guideline says, large capacity magazine, here is what large capacity magazine means. It's all part of the same package through notice and comment. And I think it's very, very different from a statute that's going to be freestanding and have some meaning --

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: -- apart from that.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Absolutely right, [ADDRESS]. I think so. Usually, you discard your precedents when they've been undermined or weakened. But, in this case, Booker has made Stinson a hundred times stronger because now the consequences of deferring are nothing like we get in the executive context, where you're talking about binding law that can have implications for fair notice and all kinds of other problems we get when an agency gets to promulgate, interpret, and enforce its own rules.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Right.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Absolutely. I mean, I think the Court basically dealt with this in Beckles, where it said, yes, some judges may find the guidelines persuasive and may decide to follow them. But the point is it's ultimately the judge's decision. And if you look at the backdrop against the -- you know, the traditional system was Congress prescribes a crime. Congress prescribes the statutory range. And the judge could pick a sentence based on whatever characteristic the judge wants within that range. And that's not a fair notice problem. That's not any kind of separation-of-powers problem or rule-of-law problem. Much less going to be a problem when the Commission recommends a sentence within that range. And that's what makes this very different from all of the executive agency deference cases. You could think there's no legitimate agency difference ever and still think that deference is appropriate here because of the advisory nature of that.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] It is emphatically the province of the judiciary to say what the law is, but the advisory sentencing guidelines are not the law. They are advisory. As a result, when interpreting the guidelines, the question is not what the law is but, rather, what is the non-binding advice that the Commission is offering about what type of sentence should be imposed? On that question, the sensible approach is to defer to the Commission on the meaning of its own non-binding advice and then have courts decide for themselves, based on their own independent judgment, whether to follow that advice in deciding what type of sentence they want to impose. Now this type of deference doesn't pose any of the problems that you get when you defer to executive agencies on the meaning of the binding rules that they promulgate and enforce. That creates all kinds of problems for the separation of powers and the rule of law that this Court has cut back on in its recent decisions. But Congress gave us two very clear indications that the Commission is different from executive agencies when it comes to deference. First, Section 706 of the APA, which applies to executive agencies, makes very clear that courts should be the ones to resolve interpretive issues. So anytime you have an executive agency claiming authority for deference, that is a backdrop that's going to require a very clear statement to overcome. Second, instead of Section 706 of the APA, which does not apply to the Sentencing Commission at all, what we have is the text of the Sentencing Reform Act, which does authorize the Commission not only to promulgate guidelines but also to promulgate policy statements that authoritatively interpret the guidelines. And, Speaker B, that is the square holding of Williams, which we can talk about. In Williams, this Court held that when a policy statement interprets a guideline, that is an authoritative interpretation of the guideline. And then, in Stinson, this Court simply recognized that when the Commission uses the label of "commentary" to interpret a guideline, that falls within the same statutory authority. And Stinson starts with Williams, and it doesn't get to Seminole Rock until after it says that there is authority to interpret the guidelines. So, as a result of all of that, the Commission's deference that it gets is based on express statutory text. There's no need to rely here on any fictional presumption of implied delegation. This Court's cases cutting back on that fictional presumption in Loper Bright and Kisor simply don't apply. And the deference that the Commission enjoys rests on express authority that is just as sturdy today as it was when Stinson was decided. Stinson should be upheld. There's no reason to create the chaos that would come from overruling it. And I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] It is emphatically the province of the judiciary to say what the law is, but the advisory sentencing guidelines are not the law. They are advisory. On that question, the sensible approach is to defer to the Commission on the meaning of its own non-binding advice and then have courts decide for themselves, based on their own independent judgment, whether to follow that advice in deciding what type of sentence they want to impose. Now this type of deference doesn't pose any of the problems that you get when you defer to executive agencies on the meaning of the binding rules that they promulgate and enforce. That creates all kinds of problems for the separation of powers and the rule of law that this Court has cut back on in its recent decisions. But Congress gave us two very clear indications that the Commission is different from executive agencies when it comes to deference. First, Section 706 of the APA, which applies to executive agencies, makes very clear that courts should be the ones to resolve interpretive issues. So anytime you have an executive agency claiming authority for deference, that is a backdrop that's going to require a very clear statement to overcome. Second, instead of Section 706 of the APA, which does not apply to the Sentencing Commission at all, what we have is the text of the Sentencing Reform Act, which does authorize the Commission not only to promulgate guidelines but also to promulgate policy statements that authoritatively interpret the guidelines. And, [PERSON], that is the square holding of Williams, which we can talk about. In Williams, this Court held that when a policy statement interprets a guideline, that is an authoritative interpretation of the guideline. And then, in Stinson, this Court simply recognized that when the Commission uses the label of "commentary" to interpret a guideline, that falls within the same statutory authority. turns_same_span.text: Speaker A, is it your position -- I'm thinking about the limits. Is it your position that any company that has a short up on its website, be it a commercial or whatever, is a video service provider?

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: That's not our position, Speaker B. And I would say the -- the definition of "video tape service provider" in (a)(4), which, by the way, isn't at issue here, is very clear that you have to be engaged in the business of renting, selling, or delivering those audiovisual materials. So it's not everyone who happens to deliver them. It's not everyone who provides a video once. You have to be engaged in that business. And that's another real limitation on liability in (b)(1).

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: Is your theory that 247Sports was in engaged in that business or that Paramount was?

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: Well, in this case, Paramount Global is doing business as --

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: As. Okay.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: -- 247Sports. So I think both is the answer. But, yes, our position is absolutely that Paramount Global is a video tape service provider.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] Outraged by the disclosure of one person's video-watching history, Congress enacted the Video Privacy Protection Act. In Section (b)(1), the Act provides for civil liability when a video tape service provider knowingly discloses personally identifiable information concerning any consumer of such provider. The Act defines three of those terms. At bottom, a video tape service provider is the kind of entity that will owe obligations under the law. Personally identifiable information is the kind of information the statute protects in (b)(1)(D) and (E). And a consumer is the kind of person whose information is protected in Section (b)(1). The Act permits disclosures with a consumer's consent, and in 2013, Congress made that consent easier to obtain, online, in advance, for up to two years. Here, Paramount Global systematically discloses personally identifiable information to Facebook without obtaining consent. These are not one-off disclosures. They happen constantly, instantly, every time someone, including a consumer, watches a video on the website. Paramount has shaped its business around these disclosures. All it needed to avoid liability was its consumers' consent, something it and Facebook agree was easy to get. Paramount just didn't get it. So it asks this Court to narrow the law by imposing an audiovisual limitation on the phrase "goods or services" in the definition of "consumer." But Congress put audiovisual limitations where it wanted them, in the definitions of both "video tape service provider" and "personally identifiable information," not in the definition of "consumer." That choice is dispositive. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Not at all, [PERSON], because, here, we have material variations at every stage of the statute, at every stage of the definitions section. So we start with a "video tape service provider." That definition refers to prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials. That's one subject matter. In (a)(3)'s definition of "personally identifiable information," we have video -- video materials or services. That's a second subject matter that's different in scope from (a)(4)'s definition of a provider. And then, in (a)(1), the "consumer" definition, we have goods or services. And all three subject matters are coming from a video tape service provider. That they're different tells us that a provider can do all three things. It can engage in transactions concerning all three.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: I think we are completely in line with the statutory purpose. And we have no objection, of course, to the Court looking to that purpose. And I don't mean "purpose" in the sense of scouring the legislative history, but look at the text of Section (b)(1), which specifically prohibits the disclosure of personally identifiable information concerning any consumer. We have two different limitations within that section. "Personally identifiable information" is one limitation. "Concerning any consumer" is a second. And the reading, I think the appropriate reading, of those two things together, which exist in (b)(1) but not in other sections of the VPPA, which protect against -- for example, in subsection (D), we've got the admissibility provision. Personally identifiable information won't be admissible unless it's obtained in compliance with the VPPA. In subsection (E), we've got personally identifiable information, an affirmative requirement that providers destroy personally identifiable information after a period of time. In neither location is that personally identifiable information linked to a consumer. It's only in (b)(1) that that link happens, so we know that (b)(1) is protecting less personally identifiable information from disclosure, not more.

turns_pm15.text: Speaker A, is it your position -- I'm thinking about the limits. Is it your position that any company that has a short up on its website, be it a commercial or whatever, is a video service provider?

turns_pm15.speaker: B

turns_pm15.speaker: A

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Well, I guess I want to be very clear because the person who watches videos for free can still be protected by (b)(1)'s disclosure prohibition as long as he's a consumer of something else from that provider. He's rented, purchased, or subscribed to some --

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: I would say I think there are several kind of overlapping reasons that Congress might have preferred the exact regime it enacted. turns_pm15.speaker: A

turns_pm15.speaker: A

turns_pm15.speaker: A

All it needed to avoid liability was its consumers' consent, something it and Facebook agree was easy to get. Paramount just didn't get it. So it asks this Court to narrow the law by imposing an audiovisual limitation on the phrase "goods or services" in the definition of "consumer." But Congress put audiovisual limitations where it wanted them, in the definitions of both "video tape service provider" and "personally identifiable information," not in the definition of "consumer." That choice is dispositive. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Not at all, [PERSON], because, here, we have material variations at every stage of the statute, at every stage of the definitions section. turns_pm15.speaker: A

turns_pm15.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A

So having that window to get consent and, if you look at the 2013 amendments, you've got consent even for a two-year window. So advance consent comes into play. That consumer window is very important in terms of identifying the place to get consent. It could also be that Congress just thought this regime was more fair. You've got a consumer that's exchanged something of value with the provider, and, therefore, they're entitled to the protections and the possibility of liquidated damages. But whatever we -- I don't -- I won't dispute that there is some mystery about why Congress did something different in (b)(1) than it did in, for example, Sections (d) and (e) when it protected personally identifiable information there.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Can you explain exactly how the consent would work in your opinion?

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Absolutely. So consent works by allowing a provider to disclose personally identifiable information, and there are several locations where a provider can get that consent. One is the initiation of the consumer transaction. Another is when the person watches a video, you could have a banner pop up and --

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: A non-video consumer transaction you're talking about there, right?

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: It could be a non-video consumer transaction, or it could be a video consumer transaction. I think the statute is indifferent as to those two possibilities. Or it could be that the provider gets consent just simply before the disclosure is made. I think, again, the statute is indifferent as to when the provider obtains that consent so long as it gets it before the disclosure is made.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: I -- I'm not sure it's true that in 1988 it was inconceivable that someone might watch a video on a computer. I think Congress was very concerned with the changing technological advances and -- and computer technology. But even more in 2013, when Congress stepped back into this statute and revised just the consent provision, I think it was intimately aware -- and, again, this is in the legislative history -- it was intimately aware with the fact that people were streaming all sorts of videos to their phones and to their computers all the time. And I think it's important to note both personally identifiable information in (a)(3) and the consumer relationship in (a)(1) are technology-neutral. Requested or obtained doesn't identify any technology by which you'll request or obtain videos.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Well, I think the -- the -- the definitions are different. We know that for sure because, if you just line them up and look at them, there are a number of material variations between them. As to why they're different -- and this goes back to the point I was trying to make earlier -- there might be some mystery about why they're different. Whether they're different is very clear. And I think we just have to live with that mystery a little bit rather than rewrite the statute. But, again, I think there are good reasons and -- and, in fact, it might close loopholes to have them do different work because a business could structure its relationship with individuals so that you never rent, purchase, or subscribe directly to the video materials. You request or obtain them some other way. And you rent, purchase, or subscribe to something else entirely. Congress wrote this statute so that that sort of clever structure by a provider won't create a loophole that allows a --

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: So I'm not sure I could have said it any better myself. I think you're absolutely right to be focused on the thrust of this statute is about personally identifiable information. Every operative provision of this statute protects some amount of personally identifiable information; (b)(1) just has another limitation so that it protects not all personally identifiable information but just the personally identifiable information concerning a consumer.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: So the parties agree that "personally identifiable information," although it says "includes," requires two strands of information: Something that identifies you and something that identifies the specific video materials or services that you requested or obtained. All the courts of appeals that have addressed that question have reached the exact same conclusion. If you look at the legislative history, Congress actually says why it used the word "includes" instead of "means." And it says we used "includes" there to create a floor, to create a minimum. Personally identifiable information could identify you or -- or identify facts about you in lots of other realms, but, at a minimum, it has to identify you as having requested or obtained those specific video --

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: I think the answer to that question lies in subsection (b)(1), the liability provision, which says it prohibits disclosures of PII to any person. So, if it's identifiable to the "any person" that receives that disclosure, it's personally identifiable information.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] Outraged by the disclosure of one person's video-watching history, Congress enacted the Video Privacy Protection Act. In Section (b)(1), the Act provides for civil liability when a video tape service provider knowingly discloses personally identifiable information concerning any consumer of such provider. The Act defines three of those terms. At bottom, a video tape service provider is the kind of entity that will owe obligations under the law. Personally identifiable information is the kind of information the statute protects in (b)(1)(D) and (E). And a consumer is the kind of person whose information is protected in Section (b)(1). The Act permits disclosures with a consumer's consent, and in 2013, Congress made that consent easier to obtain, online, in advance, for up to two years. Here, Paramount Global systematically discloses personally identifiable information to Facebook without obtaining consent. These are not one-off disclosures. They happen constantly, instantly, every time someone, including a consumer, watches a video on the website. Paramount has shaped its business around these disclosures. All it needed to avoid liability was its consumers' consent, something it and Facebook agree was easy to get. Paramount just didn't get it. So it asks this Court to narrow the law by imposing an audiovisual limitation on the phrase "goods or services" in the definition of "consumer." But Congress put audiovisual limitations where it wanted them, in the definitions of both "video tape service provider" and "personally identifiable information," not in the definition of "consumer." That choice is dispositive. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Not at all, [PERSON], because, here, we have material variations at every stage of the statute, at every stage of the definitions section. So we start with a "video tape service provider." That definition refers to prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials. That's one subject matter. In (a)(3)'s definition of "personally identifiable information," we have video -- video materials or services. That's a second subject matter that's different in scope from (a)(4)'s definition of a provider. And then, in (a)(1), the "consumer" definition, we have goods or services. And all three subject matters are coming from a video tape service provider. That they're different tells us that a provider can do all three things. It can engage in transactions concerning all three.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think we are completely in line with the statutory purpose. And we have no objection, of course, to the Court looking to that purpose. And I don't mean "purpose" in the sense of scouring the legislative history, but look at the text of Section (b)(1), which specifically prohibits the disclosure of personally identifiable information concerning any consumer. We have two different limitations within that section. "Personally identifiable information" is one limitation. "Concerning any consumer" is a second. And the reading, I think the appropriate reading, of those two things together, which exist in (b)(1) but not in other sections of the VPPA, which protect against -- for example, in subsection (D), we've got the admissibility provision. Personally identifiable information won't be admissible unless it's obtained in compliance with the VPPA. In subsection (E), we've got personally identifiable information, an affirmative requirement that providers destroy personally identifiable information after a period of time. In neither location is that personally identifiable information linked to a consumer. It's only in (b)(1) that that link happens, so we know that (b)(1) is protecting less personally identifiable information from disclosure, not more.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That's not our position, [PERSON]. And I would say the -- the definition of "video tape service provider" in (a)(4), which, by the way, isn't at issue here, is very clear that you have to be engaged in the business of renting, selling, or delivering those audiovisual materials. So it's not everyone who happens to deliver them. It's not everyone who provides a video once. You have to be engaged in that business. And that's another real limitation on liability in (b)(1).

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, in this case, Paramount Global is doing business as --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- 247Sports. So I think both is the answer. But, yes, our position is absolutely that Paramount Global is a video tape service provider.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: We would not take that position. And it should come as no surprise that the court that confronted that particular problem found that Chick-fil-A is not a video tape service provider. turns_pm60.text: I -- I think that's exactly right. Our position is yes, but that's a question for remand.

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So, on the first point, I would say, again, Congress wrote a law that isn't technology-specific. By its own admission, Paramount's reading has those two virtually identical phrases mean two radically different things.

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] Outraged by the disclosure of one person's video-watching history, Congress enacted the Video Privacy Protection Act. In Section (b)(1), the Act provides for civil liability when a video tape service provider knowingly discloses personally identifiable information concerning any consumer of such provider. The Act defines three of those terms. At bottom, a video tape service provider is the kind of entity that will owe obligations under the law. Personally identifiable information is the kind of information the statute protects in (b)(1)(D) and (E). And a consumer is the kind of person whose information is protected in Section (b)(1). The Act permits disclosures with a consumer's consent, and in 2013, Congress made that consent easier to obtain, online, in advance, for up to two years. Here, Paramount Global systematically discloses personally identifiable information to Facebook without obtaining consent. These are not one-off disclosures. They happen constantly, instantly, every time someone, including a consumer, watches a video on the website. Paramount has shaped its business around these disclosures. All it needed to avoid liability was its consumers' consent, something it and Facebook agree was easy to get. Paramount just didn't get it. So it asks this Court to narrow the law by imposing an audiovisual limitation on the phrase "goods or services" in the definition of "consumer." But Congress put audiovisual limitations where it wanted them, in the definitions of both "video tape service provider" and "personally identifiable information," not in the definition of "consumer." That choice is dispositive. I welcome the Court's questions.

Personally identifiable information is the kind of information the statute protects in (b)(1)(D) and (E). And a consumer is the kind of person whose information is protected in Section (b)(1). The Act permits disclosures with a consumer's consent, and in 2013, Congress made that consent easier to obtain, online, in advance, for up to two years. Here, Paramount Global systematically discloses personally identifiable information to Facebook without obtaining consent. These are not one-off disclosures. They happen constantly, instantly, every time someone, including a consumer, watches a video on the website. Paramount has shaped its business around these disclosures. All it needed to avoid liability was its consumers' consent, something it and Facebook agree was easy to get. Paramount just didn't get it. So it asks this Court to narrow the law by imposing an audiovisual limitation on the phrase "goods or services" in the definition of "consumer." But Congress put audiovisual limitations where it wanted them, in the definitions of both "video tape service provider" and "personally identifiable information," not in the definition of "consumer." That choice is dispositive. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Not at all, [PERSON], because, here, we have material variations at every stage of the statute, at every stage of the definitions section. So we start with a "video tape service provider." That definition refers to prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials. That's one subject matter. In (a)(3)'s definition of "personally identifiable information," we have video -- video materials or services. That's a second subject matter that's different in scope from (a)(4)'s definition of a provider. And then, in (a)(1), the "consumer" definition, we have goods or services. And all three subject matters are coming from a video tape service provider. That they're different tells us that a provider can do all three things. It can engage in transactions concerning all three.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think we are completely in line with the statutory purpose. And we have no objection, of course, to the Court looking to that purpose. And I don't mean "purpose" in the sense of scouring the legislative history, but look at the text of Section (b)(1), which specifically prohibits the disclosure of personally identifiable information concerning any consumer. We have two different limitations within that section. "Personally identifiable information" is one limitation. "Concerning any consumer" is a second. And the reading, I think the appropriate reading, of those two things together, which exist in (b)(1) but not in other sections of the VPPA, which protect against -- for example, in subsection (D), we've got the admissibility provision. Personally identifiable information won't be admissible unless it's obtained in compliance with the VPPA. In subsection (E), we've got personally identifiable information, an affirmative requirement that providers destroy personally identifiable information after a period of time. In neither location is that personally identifiable information linked to a consumer. It's only in (b)(1) that that link happens, so we know that (b)(1) is protecting less personally identifiable information from disclosure, not more.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That's not our position, [PERSON]. And I would say the -- the definition of "video tape service provider" in (a)(4), which, by the way, isn't at issue here, is very clear that you have to be engaged in the business of renting, selling, or delivering those audiovisual materials. So it's not everyone who happens to deliver them. It's not everyone who provides a video once. You have to be engaged in that business. And that's another real limitation on liability in (b)(1).

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, in this case, Paramount Global is doing business as --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- 247Sports. So I think both is the answer. But, yes, our position is absolutely that Paramount Global is a video tape service provider.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: We would not take that position. And it should come as no surprise that the court that confronted that particular problem found that Chick-fil-A is not a video tape service provider. That's how the motion to dismiss was granted in that case. We have no quarrel with that holding. We don't find it particularly surprising. But that's nothing like what Paramount Global does here.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, I guess I want to be very clear because the person who watches videos for free can still be protected by (b)(1)'s disclosure prohibition as long as he's a consumer of something else from that provider. He's rented, purchased, or subscribed to some --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I would say I think there are several kind of overlapping reasons that Congress might have preferred the exact regime it enacted. I think the clearest one is that the consumer relationship provides an easy window for getting consent, and Congress was very concerned about consent and the -- the consumer controlling the disclosure of personally identifiable information. So having that window to get consent and, if you look at the 2013 amendments, you've got consent even for a two-year window. So advance consent comes into play. That consumer window is very important in terms of identifying the place to get consent. It could also be that Congress just thought this regime was more fair. You've got a consumer that's exchanged something of value with the provider, and, therefore, they're entitled to the protections and the possibility of liquidated damages. But whatever we -- I don't -- I won't dispute that there is some mystery about why Congress did something different in (b)(1) than it did in, for example, Sections (d) and (e) when it protected personally identifiable information there.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Absolutely. So consent works by allowing a provider to disclose personally identifiable information, and there are several locations where a provider can get that consent. One is the initiation of the consumer transaction. Another is when the person watches a video, you could have a banner pop up and --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It could be a non-video consumer transaction, or it could be a video consumer transaction. I think the statute is indifferent as to those two possibilities. Or it could be that the provider gets consent just simply before the disclosure is made. I think, again, the statute is indifferent as to when the provider obtains that consent so long as it gets it before the disclosure is made.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I -- I'm not sure it's true that in 1988 it was inconceivable that someone might watch a video on a computer. I think Congress was very concerned with the changing technological advances and -- and computer technology. But even more in 2013, when Congress stepped back into this statute and revised just the consent provision, I think it was intimately aware -- and, again, this is in the legislative history -- it was intimately aware with the fact that people were streaming all sorts of videos to their phones and to their computers all the time. And I think it's important to note both personally identifiable information in (a)(3) and the consumer relationship in (a)(1) are technology-neutral. Requested or obtained doesn't identify any technology by which you'll request or obtain videos.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, I think the -- the -- the definitions are different. We know that for sure because, if you just line them up and look at them, there are a number of material variations between them. As to why they're different -- and this goes back to the point I was trying to make earlier -- there might be some mystery about why they're different. Whether they're different is very clear. And I think we just have to live with that mystery a little bit rather than rewrite the statute. But, again, I think there are good reasons and -- and, in fact, it might close loopholes to have them do different work because a business could structure its relationship with individuals so that you never rent, purchase, or subscribe directly to the video materials. You request or obtain them some other way. And you rent, purchase, or subscribe to something else entirely. Congress wrote this statute so that that sort of clever structure by a provider won't create a loophole that allows a --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So I'm not sure I could have said it any better myself. I think you're absolutely right to be focused on the thrust of this statute is about personally identifiable information. Every operative provision of this statute protects some amount of personally identifiable information; (b)(1) just has another limitation so that it protects not all personally identifiable information but just the personally identifiable information concerning a consumer.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So the parties agree that "personally identifiable information," although it says "includes," requires two strands of information: Something that identifies you and something that identifies the specific video materials or services that you requested or obtained. All the courts of appeals that have addressed that question have reached the exact same conclusion. If you look at the legislative history, Congress actually says why it used the word "includes" instead of "means." And it says we used "includes" there to create a floor, to create a minimum. Personally identifiable information could identify you or -- or identify facts about you in lots of other realms, but, at a minimum, it has to identify you as having requested or obtained those specific video --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think the answer to that question lies in subsection (b)(1), the liability provision, which says it prohibits disclosures of PII to any person. So, if it's identifiable to the "any person" that receives that disclosure, it's personally identifiable information.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: You -- you said before that "includes" was used to suggest a floor, which makes perfect sense. But I think that the question is, does "includes" -- does that provision with the word "includes" also have a ceiling? I think that that's the question that would give rise to some concern. If you thought "includes" could also mean anything else in the world, then you wouldn't have the limit that you're saying comes from that provision.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think, if you can imagine a disclosure that includes 10 different facts about an individual and just one of them identifies the specific video materials or services that he requested or obtained, Congress is saying that disclosure of that information is personally identifiable information only because of that one strand of information. It might have identified --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I see. But that one strand has to be there?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Absolutely, yes, yes.

turns_pm60.text: That's correct.

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes, it is. And, in fact --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It -- it's very important there that in (a)(4), the definition of "video tape service provider," it says "or similar audiovisual materials."

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Again, it's not a question that's presented here, but you have, I think, several avenues. One way is to say it's similar in that it's prerecorded. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Which is true enough, I guess, and, in fact, when Congress stepped back into the statute in 2013, it acknowledged that video cassette tapes were largely obsolete, Blockbuster was either on its way out or already gone, and everyone was streaming videos directly to their phones. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So, on the first point, I would say, again, Congress wrote a law that isn't technology-specific. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: You're -- you're hypothesizing a prescient Congress, as opposed to a Congress that mistakenly stumbled into broader language than it meant to use.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think that is kind of the foundational premise that this Court indulges at the outset of every statutory interpret -- or interpretation case, namely, that Congress said what it meant and meant what it said when it wrote a statute. turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That's actually -- that -- that's absolutely right, that it was not put up in issue in this case. We argued that in the district court. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That's absolutely right. There is a 2-2 split on the definition of "consumer." turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Absolutely. And, in fact --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- it often is for other reasons. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That -- that's correct, [ADDRESS], yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think this Court's approach is exactly right, that you always look at text in context. We have no quarrel with that methodology because text in context shows you exactly what you normally presume at the outset, which is that Congress meant "goods or services," a broader term, when it said "goods or services" in subsection (a)(1). It did not mean video materials or services, something it said in the same sentence, identically from a video tape service provider. It did not mean prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials. It didn't even mention services at all in the definition, (a)(4)'s definition, of a "provider." It didn't mean those other phrases that it said elsewhere. It meant something different. And I think context absolutely reinforces that point.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think that's an unusual meaning to ascribe to "from" from the outset. That is usually a word that identifies the source of material, not something that identifies the scope. And, here, we know for sure that Congress was looking at "from" as identifying source. And we know that by comparing (a)(1)'s definition of "consumer" to (a)(3)'s definition of "PII." Both identify subject matter that comes from a video tape service provider.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think, in that specific context, that would be a pretty unusual thing to say. But, if we could twist it just a little bit, it would be equally odd to say if we had a statute that defined gas stations a particular way, those that provide fuel, that would be our (a)(4) paradigm. Then we had in the same statute, the same sentence of the same statute, a provision that mentioned fuel materials or services or fuel goods or services. That's (a)(3). And then we had in the same statute, the same sentence, goods or services from a gas station. It would be exceedingly odd to say those three subject matters must be the same thing. Maybe I was feeling really brave at the gas station and I got sushi. That's a good or service from --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- a gas station, but it's not a fuel good or service, and it's certainly not the fuel that you would normally buy at a gas station.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think the courts -- as far as I know at least, the courts are in accord that "or similar audiovisual materials" includes things like streaming videos to a personal device that you would watch in your house. It doesn't require a physicality, you know, necessarily that you're going to have a tape, a physical tape that you play that way. And, again, when you look at, in 2013, Congress stepped back into this statute, it specifically said, we are aware streaming is rampant and we still think this statute covers the -- the personally identifiable information that results from those streaming activities.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Because it's similar in critical ways to a video cassette tape. It allows you to watch that video in the privacy of your home. It allows you to watch it on your own. It allows you to pause, come back later, record -- or, I'm sorry, rewind, and pick it up as you wish. It's -- it's in lots of ways the exact same as the way you would interact with a video cassette tape.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: If we're looking at the technology that was available in 1988, I think the answer has to be no precisely because you couldn't pause and rewind and stop and come back hours later and rewatch things the way that you can now both with a prerecorded video cassette tape and with the exact audiovisual materials that we have at issue here. And I would note too all of this concerns whether Paramount is a video tape service provider, which isn't before the Court today.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] Outraged by the disclosure of one person's video-watching history, Congress enacted the Video Privacy Protection Act. In Section (b)(1), the Act provides for civil liability when a video tape service provider knowingly discloses personally identifiable information concerning any consumer of such provider. The Act defines three of those terms. At bottom, a video tape service provider is the kind of entity that will owe obligations under the law. Personally identifiable information is the kind of information the statute protects in (b)(1)(D) and (E). And a consumer is the kind of person whose information is protected in Section (b)(1). The Act permits disclosures with a consumer's consent, and in 2013, Congress made that consent easier to obtain, online, in advance, for up to two years. Here, Paramount Global systematically discloses personally identifiable information to Facebook without obtaining consent. These are not one-off disclosures. They happen constantly, instantly, every time someone, including a consumer, watches a video on the website. Paramount has shaped its business around these disclosures. All it needed to avoid liability was its consumers' consent, something it and Facebook agree was easy to get. Paramount just didn't get it. So it asks this Court to narrow the law by imposing an audiovisual limitation on the phrase "goods or services" in the definition of "consumer." But Congress put audiovisual limitations where it wanted them, in the definitions of both "video tape service provider" and "personally identifiable information," not in the definition of "consumer." That choice is dispositive. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Not at all, [PERSON], because, here, we have material variations at every stage of the statute, at every stage of the definitions section. So we start with a "video tape service provider." That definition refers to prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials. That's one subject matter. In (a)(3)'s definition of "personally identifiable information," we have video -- video materials or services. That's a second subject matter that's different in scope from (a)(4)'s definition of a provider. And then, in (a)(1), the "consumer" definition, we have goods or services. And all three subject matters are coming from a video tape service provider. That they're different tells us that a provider can do all three things. It can engage in transactions concerning all three.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think we are completely in line with the statutory purpose. And we have no objection, of course, to the Court looking to that purpose. And I don't mean "purpose" in the sense of scouring the legislative history, but look at the text of Section (b)(1), which specifically prohibits the disclosure of personally identifiable information concerning any consumer. We have two different limitations within that section. "Personally identifiable information" is one limitation. "Concerning any consumer" is a second. And the reading, I think the appropriate reading, of those two things together, which exist in (b)(1) but not in other sections of the VPPA, which protect against -- for example, in subsection (D), we've got the admissibility provision. Personally identifiable information won't be admissible unless it's obtained in compliance with the VPPA. In subsection (E), we've got personally identifiable information, an affirmative requirement that providers destroy personally identifiable information after a period of time. In neither location is that personally identifiable information linked to a consumer. It's only in (b)(1) that that link happens, so we know that (b)(1) is protecting less personally identifiable information from disclosure, not more.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That's not our position, [PERSON]. So it's not everyone who happens to deliver them. It's not everyone who provides a video once. You have to be engaged in that business. And that's another real limitation on liability in (b)(1).

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, in this case, Paramount Global is doing business as --

turns_pm60.speaker: A

That's how the motion to dismiss was granted in that case. We have no quarrel with that holding. We don't find it particularly surprising. But that's nothing like what Paramount Global does here.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, I guess I want to be very clear because the person who watches videos for free can still be protected by (b)(1)'s disclosure prohibition as long as he's a consumer of something else from that provider. He's rented, purchased, or subscribed to some --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I would say I think there are several kind of overlapping reasons that Congress might have preferred the exact regime it enacted. I think the clearest one is that the consumer relationship provides an easy window for getting consent, and Congress was very concerned about consent and the -- the consumer controlling the disclosure of personally identifiable information. So having that window to get consent and, if you look at the 2013 amendments, you've got consent even for a two-year window. So advance consent comes into play. That consumer window is very important in terms of identifying the place to get consent. It could also be that Congress just thought this regime was more fair. You've got a consumer that's exchanged something of value with the provider, and, therefore, they're entitled to the protections and the possibility of liquidated damages. But whatever we -- I don't -- I won't dispute that there is some mystery about why Congress did something different in (b)(1) than it did in, for example, Sections (d) and (e) when it protected personally identifiable information there.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Can you explain exactly how the consent would work in your opinion?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Absolutely. So consent works by allowing a provider to disclose personally identifiable information, and there are several locations where a provider can get that consent. One is the initiation of the consumer transaction. Another is when the person watches a video, you could have a banner pop up and --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: A non-video consumer transaction you're talking about there, right?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It could be a non-video consumer transaction, or it could be a video consumer transaction. I think the statute is indifferent as to those two possibilities. Or it could be that the provider gets consent just simply before the disclosure is made. I think, again, the statute is indifferent as to when the provider obtains that consent so long as it gets it before the disclosure is made.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I -- I'm not sure it's true that in 1988 it was inconceivable that someone might watch a video on a computer. I think Congress was very concerned with the changing technological advances and -- and computer technology. But even more in 2013, when Congress stepped back into this statute and revised just the consent provision, I think it was intimately aware -- and, again, this is in the legislative history -- it was intimately aware with the fact that people were streaming all sorts of videos to their phones and to their computers all the time. And I think it's important to note both personally identifiable information in (a)(3) and the consumer relationship in (a)(1) are technology-neutral. Requested or obtained doesn't identify any technology by which you'll request or obtain videos.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, I think the -- the -- the definitions are different. We know that for sure because, if you just line them up and look at them, there are a number of material variations between them. As to why they're different -- and this goes back to the point I was trying to make earlier -- there might be some mystery about why they're different. Whether they're different is very clear. And I think we just have to live with that mystery a little bit rather than rewrite the statute. But, again, I think there are good reasons and -- and, in fact, it might close loopholes to have them do different work because a business could structure its relationship with individuals so that you never rent, purchase, or subscribe directly to the video materials. You request or obtain them some other way. And you rent, purchase, or subscribe to something else entirely. Congress wrote this statute so that that sort of clever structure by a provider won't create a loophole that allows a --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I'm not sure I could have said it any better myself. I think you're absolutely right to be focused on the thrust of this statute is about personally identifiable information. Every operative provision of this statute protects some amount of personally identifiable information; (b)(1) just has another limitation so that it protects not all personally identifiable information but just the personally identifiable information concerning a consumer.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So the parties agree that "personally identifiable information," although it says "includes," requires two strands of information: Something that identifies you and something that identifies the specific video materials or services that you requested or obtained. All the courts of appeals that have addressed that question have reached the exact same conclusion. If you look at the legislative history, Congress actually says why it used the word "includes" instead of "means." And it says we used "includes" there to create a floor, to create a minimum. Personally identifiable information could identify you or -- or identify facts about you in lots of other realms, but, at a minimum, it has to identify you as having requested or obtained those specific video --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think the answer to that question lies in subsection (b)(1), the liability provision, which says it prohibits disclosures of PII to any person. So, if it's identifiable to the "any person" that receives that disclosure, it's personally identifiable information.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think, if you can imagine a disclosure that includes 10 different facts about an individual and just one of them identifies the specific video materials or services that he requested or obtained, Congress is saying that disclosure of that information is personally identifiable information only because of that one strand of information. It might have identified --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Absolutely, yes, yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And the question of PII, even if you prevail on the issue before us, would still be resolved on remand, correct?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That's correct.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It would still be open on remand? We're not resolving that here because there's a big argument, obviously, in the courts of appeals whether this kind of information constitutes PII, correct?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That is correct. And this Court may someday have to resolve that question, but that day is not today.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That -- that's exactly why. There are other arguments that -- that Paramount raised below, and that's why we asked to vacate.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: In the district court, it raised that question, not in the Sixth Circuit.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, it's certainly claiming that the videos are available for free. And our response is, sure, they're delivered for free and you might request or obtain them for free, but that doesn't change the operative provisions of the statute either in --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I -- I think that's exactly right. Our position is yes, but that's a question for remand.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I'm sorry, what -- what do you mean by "prevailed"?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think, if you look at Paramount's brief, it suggests that courts have routinely dismissed VPPA claims.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I -- I think there's --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think there is, unfortunately, some reluctance to -- to believe that Congress actually meant what it said in the context of this statute. It wrote a broad law that is very protective of personally identifiable information. That prohibits a lot of disclosures of that kind of information, and I think --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes, it is. And, in fact --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It -- it's very important there that in (a)(4), the definition of "video tape service provider," it says "or similar audiovisual materials."

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Again, it's not a question that's presented here, but you have, I think, several avenues. One way is to say it's similar in that it's prerecorded. It's similar in that you watch it in the privacy of your home. It's similar in that it can be delivered to you personally; it's not something that you, for example, go to a theater and witness with other people.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Which is true enough, I guess, and, in fact, when Congress stepped back into the statute in 2013, it acknowledged that video cassette tapes were largely obsolete, Blockbuster was either on its way out or already gone, and everyone was streaming videos directly to their phones. Congress saw no need to re-jigger the definitions or to change the provisions at (b)(1)(D) or (E) precisely because they're technology-neutral.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, isn't there a concern about repurposing a statute that was really about public disclosure of what individuals viewed into a statute that regulates data sharing for targeted advertising on the Internet? Those are very different things. And the context here is the data sharing for the targeted advertising.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So, on the first point, I would say, again, Congress wrote a law that isn't technology-specific. It wrote a broad law that spans all kinds of technologies, all kinds of ways that you might obtain those video materials or services, all kinds of ways you might rent, purchase, or subscribe to goods or services. And then the second point, Congress anticipated that this information would be useful for advertising purposes, and it crafted an exception under (b)(2)(D) that specifically allows disclosures of the subject matter of the videos, along with a name and address, when that disclosure is made exclusively or solely for the purpose of advertising goods or services directly to the consumer. And it's important there goods or service -- it says "goods and services" in (b)(2)(D)(ii), that -- that exception, and it says "goods or services" in subsection (a)'s definition of "consumer." Our reading has "goods or services" and "goods and services" mean the same thing. By its own admission, Paramount's reading has those two virtually identical phrases mean two radically different things.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think that is kind of the foundational premise that this Court indulges at the outset of every statutory interpret -- or interpretation case, namely, that Congress said what it meant and meant what it said when it wrote a statute. I think, if you start from the opposite purpose, that maybe Congress accidentally kind of tripped and fell and wrote these words instead of those words, I think, if you indulge that premise, you actually end up landing in the exact same place precisely because, when you walk through (a)(4)'s definition of a "provider," (a)(3)'s definition of "PII," and then (a)(1)'s definition of "consumer," you see that these weren't accidental. The scopes are different every time even though the source is the same.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, the person, I suppose, would be Facebook that got the information, just the largest social media company that exists. But it's also true -- and I think, if you -- if you look closely at the Sixth Circuit's opinion, it actually says all six circuits that have answered that standing question in the context of a VPPA claim are in accord. All of them say, yes, you have standing when there's been a disclosure even to one person of your personally identifiable information without your consent. All six are in accord on that point. The difference with the Eleventh Circuit is, well, what happens in a different context. I believe that was the FDCPA instead of the VPPA. But, in that context, you basically bounced a disclosure from a mail vendor to the consumer, and the court said in that context that's not really a disclosure. You're basically outsourcing kind of who's going to mail the item to the consumer. Here, we've got an exception for disclosures made to the consumer. It's an open question, I guess, whether a similar mail vendor theory would apply to the VPPA, but that's just radically different than the facts we have here.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That's actually -- that -- that's absolutely right, that it was not put up in issue in this case. We argued that in the district court. Paramount abandoned its standing argument in the Sixth Circuit. It addressed it sua sponte. I think you're right that it's a background issue in this case. But it has not been briefed.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That's absolutely right. There is a 2-2 split on the definition of "consumer." And both dismissals here, the -- the district court in Tennessee and the Sixth Circuit, held solely that this complaint should be dismissed because of the particular meaning we're giving to the word "consumer."

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Absolutely. And, in fact --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- it often is for other reasons. If you look at Paramount's brief in opposition to our petition for certiorari, they point to personally identifiable information, disputes about whether someone is a provider. Those are other reasons, and they point to the fact that there are multiple real limitations to liability coexisting at once in subsection (b)(1).

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Is -- the PII, is that a 3-1 split against your position on PII?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That -- that's correct, [ADDRESS], yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think the other side's kind of big-picture argument is that we are a textualist Court but usually not a literalist Court and that we have a lot of principles and doctrines -- major questions, elephants in mouse holes, context, common sense -- you see those terms sprinkled through a lot of our cases, including in this general field, and that we should be thinking about that so that we don't read this statute for all it's worth when the Congress in the 1980s wasn't thinking about data sharing for targeted advertising. So that's a big-picture question for you to tackle.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think this Court's approach is exactly right, that you always look at text in context. We have no quarrel with that methodology because text in context shows you exactly what you normally presume at the outset, which is that Congress meant "goods or services," a broader term, when it said "goods or services" in subsection (a)(1). It did not mean video materials or services, something it said in the same sentence, identically from a video tape service provider. It did not mean prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials. It didn't even mention services at all in the definition, (a)(4)'s definition, of a "provider." It didn't mean those other phrases that it said elsewhere. It meant something different. And I think context absolutely reinforces that point.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think that's an unusual meaning to ascribe to "from" from the outset. That is usually a word that identifies the source of material, not something that identifies the scope. And, here, we know for sure that Congress was looking at "from" as identifying source. And we know that by comparing (a)(1)'s definition of "consumer" to (a)(3)'s definition of "PII." Both identify subject matter that comes from a video tape service provider.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think, in that specific context, that would be a pretty unusual thing to say. But, if we could twist it just a little bit, it would be equally odd to say if we had a statute that defined gas stations a particular way, those that provide fuel, that would be our (a)(4) paradigm. Then we had in the same statute, the same sentence of the same statute, a provision that mentioned fuel materials or services or fuel goods or services. That's (a)(3). And then we had in the same statute, the same sentence, goods or services from a gas station. It would be exceedingly odd to say those three subject matters must be the same thing. Maybe I was feeling really brave at the gas station and I got sushi. That's a good or service from --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- a gas station, but it's not a fuel good or service, and it's certainly not the fuel that you would normally buy at a gas station.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think the courts -- as far as I know at least, the courts are in accord that "or similar audiovisual materials" includes things like streaming videos to a personal device that you would watch in your house. It doesn't require a physicality, you know, necessarily that you're going to have a tape, a physical tape that you play that way. And, again, when you look at, in 2013, Congress stepped back into this statute, it specifically said, we are aware streaming is rampant and we still think this statute covers the -- the personally identifiable information that results from those streaming activities.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Because it's similar in critical ways to a video cassette tape. It allows you to watch that video in the privacy of your home. It allows you to watch it on your own. It allows you to pause, come back later, record -- or, I'm sorry, rewind, and pick it up as you wish. It's -- it's in lots of ways the exact same as the way you would interact with a video cassette tape.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: If we're looking at the technology that was available in 1988, I think the answer has to be no precisely because you couldn't pause and rewind and stop and come back hours later and rewatch things the way that you can now both with a prerecorded video cassette tape and with the exact audiovisual materials that we have at issue here. And I would note too all of this concerns whether Paramount is a video tape service provider, which isn't before the Court today.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Just on the video tape service provider issue, I know that's not before us, but I think you've waved away some of the concerns about every business in America that has video on its website being targeted. But, certainly, the amicus briefs on the other side -- The Retail Litigation Center, the Chamber of Commerce -- point out that your reading would -- and -- and suits have been brought against every sector of the economy -- print media publishers, movie theaters, advocacy groups, sports leagues, health and fitness websites, parenting advice companies, chess websites, crafting websites, professional networking sites, universities -- every other type of defendant under the sun in the words of the amicus brief. And so I think you've waved away some of the concerns about the breadth of your argument on this issue by saying, don't worry, it's not going to apply because of the definition of "video tape service provider." But I don't think other plaintiffs are going to be conceding that in the cases against those businesses, or is the amicus -- are the amicus briefs wrong in saying that that's a legitimate concern?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, I would say a couple of points. One, it's true that those suits have been brought. It's also true that many of them have resulted in district courts saying: Wait a minute, that entity, like Chick-fil-A, is not a video tape service provider. This is the wrong kind of entity. Congress wasn't targeting Chick-fil-A.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And what makes someone a video tape service provider? If they have a video on their business website that, let's say, is three minutes long, are they a video tape service provider?

case: Salazar v. Paramount Global
setting: Excerpt from a recorded institutional proceeding. Exactly one of the two speakers, A and B, holds the more powerful institutional role.
