turns_pm15.text: No. But then would they be in the -- in the business of -- of -- of in commerce for rental, sale, or delivery? That's up to the lower courts, correct?

turns_pm15.text: I -- I think that's exactly right. Our position is yes, but that's a question for remand.

It wrote a broad law that is very protective of personally identifiable information. That prohibits a lot of disclosures of that kind of information, and I think --

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Yes, it is. And, in fact --

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: It -- it's very important there that in (a)(4), the definition of "video tape service provider," it says "or similar audiovisual materials."

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] Outraged by the disclosure of one person's video-watching history, Congress enacted the Video Privacy Protection Act. In Section (b)(1), the Act provides for civil liability when a video tape service provider knowingly discloses personally identifiable information concerning any consumer of such provider. The Act defines three of those terms. At bottom, a video tape service provider is the kind of entity that will owe obligations under the law. Personally identifiable information is the kind of information the statute protects in (b)(1)(D) and (E). And a consumer is the kind of person whose information is protected in Section (b)(1). The Act permits disclosures with a consumer's consent, and in 2013, Congress made that consent easier to obtain, online, in advance, for up to two years. Here, Paramount Global systematically discloses personally identifiable information to Facebook without obtaining consent. These are not one-off disclosures. They happen constantly, instantly, every time someone, including a consumer, watches a video on the website. Paramount has shaped its business around these disclosures. All it needed to avoid liability was its consumers' consent, something it and Facebook agree was easy to get. Paramount just didn't get it. So it asks this Court to narrow the law by imposing an audiovisual limitation on the phrase "goods or services" in the definition of "consumer." But Congress put audiovisual limitations where it wanted them, in the definitions of both "video tape service provider" and "personally identifiable information," not in the definition of "consumer." That choice is dispositive. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Not at all, [PERSON], because, here, we have material variations at every stage of the statute, at every stage of the definitions section. So we start with a "video tape service provider." That definition refers to prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials. That's one subject matter. In (a)(3)'s definition of "personally identifiable information," we have video -- video materials or services. That's a second subject matter that's different in scope from (a)(4)'s definition of a provider. And then, in (a)(1), the "consumer" definition, we have goods or services. And all three subject matters are coming from a video tape service provider. That they're different tells us that a provider can do all three things. It can engage in transactions concerning all three.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think we are completely in line with the statutory purpose. And we have no objection, of course, to the Court looking to that purpose. And I don't mean "purpose" in the sense of scouring the legislative history, but look at the text of Section (b)(1), which specifically prohibits the disclosure of personally identifiable information concerning any consumer. We have two different limitations within that section. "Personally identifiable information" is one limitation. "Concerning any consumer" is a second. And the reading, I think the appropriate reading, of those two things together, which exist in (b)(1) but not in other sections of the VPPA, which protect against -- for example, in subsection (D), we've got the admissibility provision. Personally identifiable information won't be admissible unless it's obtained in compliance with the VPPA. In subsection (E), we've got personally identifiable information, an affirmative requirement that providers destroy personally identifiable information after a period of time. In neither location is that personally identifiable information linked to a consumer. It's only in (b)(1) that that link happens, so we know that (b)(1) is protecting less personally identifiable information from disclosure, not more.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That's not our position, [PERSON]. And I would say the -- the definition of "video tape service provider" in (a)(4), which, by the way, isn't at issue here, is very clear that you have to be engaged in the business of renting, selling, or delivering those audiovisual materials. So it's not everyone who happens to deliver them. It's not everyone who provides a video once. You have to be engaged in that business. And that's another real limitation on liability in (b)(1).

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, in this case, Paramount Global is doing business as --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- 247Sports. So I think both is the answer. But, yes, our position is absolutely that Paramount Global is a video tape service provider.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: We would not take that position. And it should come as no surprise that the court that confronted that particular problem found that Chick-fil-A is not a video tape service provider. That's how the motion to dismiss was granted in that case. We have no quarrel with that holding. We don't find it particularly surprising. But that's nothing like what Paramount Global does here.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: If Congress's interest was the protection of privacy of a person's video tape watching, why would the disclosure of personally identifiable information be limited only to consumers and not to those who watch videos for free?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, I guess I want to be very clear because the person who watches videos for free can still be protected by (b)(1)'s disclosure prohibition as long as he's a consumer of something else from that provider. He's rented, purchased, or subscribed to some --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But the provider has to be in the business of --but -- so why wouldn't Congress just protect at large anyone who's watching videos, free or not free?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I would say I think there are several kind of overlapping reasons that Congress might have preferred the exact regime it enacted. I think the clearest one is that the consumer relationship provides an easy window for getting consent, and Congress was very concerned about consent and the -- the consumer controlling the disclosure of personally identifiable information. So having that window to get consent and, if you look at the 2013 amendments, you've got consent even for a two-year window. So advance consent comes into play. That consumer window is very important in terms of identifying the place to get consent. It could also be that Congress just thought this regime was more fair. You've got a consumer that's exchanged something of value with the provider, and, therefore, they're entitled to the protections and the possibility of liquidated damages. But whatever we -- I don't -- I won't dispute that there is some mystery about why Congress did something different in (b)(1) than it did in, for example, Sections (d) and (e) when it protected personally identifiable information there.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Absolutely. So consent works by allowing a provider to disclose personally identifiable information, and there are several locations where a provider can get that consent. One is the initiation of the consumer transaction. Another is when the person watches a video, you could have a banner pop up and --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It could be a non-video consumer transaction, or it could be a video consumer transaction. I think the statute is indifferent as to those two possibilities. Or it could be that the provider gets consent just simply before the disclosure is made. I think, again, the statute is indifferent as to when the provider obtains that consent so long as it gets it before the disclosure is made.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I -- I'm not sure it's true that in 1988 it was inconceivable that someone might watch a video on a computer. I think Congress was very concerned with the changing technological advances and -- and computer technology. But even more in 2013, when Congress stepped back into this statute and revised just the consent provision, I think it was intimately aware -- and, again, this is in the legislative history -- it was intimately aware with the fact that people were streaming all sorts of videos to their phones and to their computers all the time. And I think it's important to note both personally identifiable information in (a)(3) and the consumer relationship in (a)(1) are technology-neutral. Requested or obtained doesn't identify any technology by which you'll request or obtain videos.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, I think the -- the -- the definitions are different. We know that for sure because, if you just line them up and look at them, there are a number of material variations between them. As to why they're different -- and this goes back to the point I was trying to make earlier -- there might be some mystery about why they're different. Whether they're different is very clear. And I think we just have to live with that mystery a little bit rather than rewrite the statute. But, again, I think there are good reasons and -- and, in fact, it might close loopholes to have them do different work because a business could structure its relationship with individuals so that you never rent, purchase, or subscribe directly to the video materials. You request or obtain them some other way. And you rent, purchase, or subscribe to something else entirely. Congress wrote this statute so that that sort of clever structure by a provider won't create a loophole that allows a --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So I'm not sure I could have said it any better myself. I think you're absolutely right to be focused on the thrust of this statute is about personally identifiable information. Every operative provision of this statute protects some amount of personally identifiable information; (b)(1) just has another limitation so that it protects not all personally identifiable information but just the personally identifiable information concerning a consumer.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So the parties agree that "personally identifiable information," although it says "includes," requires two strands of information: Something that identifies you and something that identifies the specific video materials or services that you requested or obtained. All the courts of appeals that have addressed that question have reached the exact same conclusion. If you look at the legislative history, Congress actually says why it used the word "includes" instead of "means." And it says we used "includes" there to create a floor, to create a minimum. Personally identifiable information could identify you or -- or identify facts about you in lots of other realms, but, at a minimum, it has to identify you as having requested or obtained those specific video --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think the answer to that question lies in subsection (b)(1), the liability provision, which says it prohibits disclosures of PII to any person. So, if it's identifiable to the "any person" that receives that disclosure, it's personally identifiable information.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think, if you can imagine a disclosure that includes 10 different facts about an individual and just one of them identifies the specific video materials or services that he requested or obtained, Congress is saying that disclosure of that information is personally identifiable information only because of that one strand of information. It might have identified --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Absolutely, yes, yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That's correct.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That is correct. And this Court may someday have to resolve that question, but that day is not today.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Is that why you asked us -- is -- is that -- is that why you asked us to vacate instead of remand?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That -- that's exactly why. There are other arguments that -- that Paramount raised below, and that's why we asked to vacate.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: In -- including whether it's a video tape service provider?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: In the district court, it raised that question, not in the Sixth Circuit.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Not in the Sixth Circuit? But it is claiming that these videos are for free and not part of a consumer transaction, correct?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, it's certainly claiming that the videos are available for free. And our response is, sure, they're delivered for free and you might request or obtain them for free, but that doesn't change the operative provisions of the statute either in --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: No. But then would they be in the -- in the business of -- of -- of in commerce for rental, sale, or delivery? That's up to the lower courts, correct?

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I -- I think there's --

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.text: That -- that seems to me to be true. You're delivering it.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But are you engaged --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] Outraged by the disclosure of one person's video-watching history, Congress enacted the Video Privacy Protection Act. In Section (b)(1), the Act provides for civil liability when a video tape service provider knowingly discloses personally identifiable information concerning any consumer of such provider. The Act defines three of those terms. At bottom, a video tape service provider is the kind of entity that will owe obligations under the law. Personally identifiable information is the kind of information the statute protects in (b)(1)(D) and (E). And a consumer is the kind of person whose information is protected in Section (b)(1). The Act permits disclosures with a consumer's consent, and in 2013, Congress made that consent easier to obtain, online, in advance, for up to two years. Here, Paramount Global systematically discloses personally identifiable information to Facebook without obtaining consent. These are not one-off disclosures. They happen constantly, instantly, every time someone, including a consumer, watches a video on the website. Paramount has shaped its business around these disclosures. All it needed to avoid liability was its consumers' consent, something it and Facebook agree was easy to get. Paramount just didn't get it. So it asks this Court to narrow the law by imposing an audiovisual limitation on the phrase "goods or services" in the definition of "consumer." But Congress put audiovisual limitations where it wanted them, in the definitions of both "video tape service provider" and "personally identifiable information," not in the definition of "consumer." That choice is dispositive. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Not at all, [PERSON], because, here, we have material variations at every stage of the statute, at every stage of the definitions section. In (a)(3)'s definition of "personally identifiable information," we have video -- video materials or services. That's a second subject matter that's different in scope from (a)(4)'s definition of a provider. And then, in (a)(1), the "consumer" definition, we have goods or services. And all three subject matters are coming from a video tape service provider. That they're different tells us that a provider can do all three things. It can engage in transactions concerning all three.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think we are completely in line with the statutory purpose. And we have no objection, of course, to the Court looking to that purpose. We have two different limitations within that section. "Personally identifiable information" is one limitation. "Concerning any consumer" is a second. And the reading, I think the appropriate reading, of those two things together, which exist in (b)(1) but not in other sections of the VPPA, which protect against -- for example, in subsection (D), we've got the admissibility provision. Personally identifiable information won't be admissible unless it's obtained in compliance with the VPPA. In subsection (E), we've got personally identifiable information, an affirmative requirement that providers destroy personally identifiable information after a period of time. In neither location is that personally identifiable information linked to a consumer. It's only in (b)(1) that that link happens, so we know that (b)(1) is protecting less personally identifiable information from disclosure, not more.

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It could be a non-video consumer transaction, or it could be a video consumer transaction. I think the statute is indifferent as to those two possibilities. Or it could be that the provider gets consent just simply before the disclosure is made. I think, again, the statute is indifferent as to when the provider obtains that consent so long as it gets it before the disclosure is made.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I -- I'm not sure it's true that in 1988 it was inconceivable that someone might watch a video on a computer. I think Congress was very concerned with the changing technological advances and -- and computer technology. But even more in 2013, when Congress stepped back into this statute and revised just the consent provision, I think it was intimately aware -- and, again, this is in the legislative history -- it was intimately aware with the fact that people were streaming all sorts of videos to their phones and to their computers all the time. And I think it's important to note both personally identifiable information in (a)(3) and the consumer relationship in (a)(1) are technology-neutral. Requested or obtained doesn't identify any technology by which you'll request or obtain videos.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, I think the -- the -- the definitions are different. We know that for sure because, if you just line them up and look at them, there are a number of material variations between them. As to why they're different -- and this goes back to the point I was trying to make earlier -- there might be some mystery about why they're different. Whether they're different is very clear. And I think we just have to live with that mystery a little bit rather than rewrite the statute. But, again, I think there are good reasons and -- and, in fact, it might close loopholes to have them do different work because a business could structure its relationship with individuals so that you never rent, purchase, or subscribe directly to the video materials. You request or obtain them some other way. And you rent, purchase, or subscribe to something else entirely. Congress wrote this statute so that that sort of clever structure by a provider won't create a loophole that allows a --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So I'm not sure I could have said it any better myself. I think you're absolutely right to be focused on the thrust of this statute is about personally identifiable information. Every operative provision of this statute protects some amount of personally identifiable information; (b)(1) just has another limitation so that it protects not all personally identifiable information but just the personally identifiable information concerning a consumer.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So the parties agree that "personally identifiable information," although it says "includes," requires two strands of information: Something that identifies you and something that identifies the specific video materials or services that you requested or obtained. All the courts of appeals that have addressed that question have reached the exact same conclusion. If you look at the legislative history, Congress actually says why it used the word "includes" instead of "means." And it says we used "includes" there to create a floor, to create a minimum. Personally identifiable information could identify you or -- or identify facts about you in lots of other realms, but, at a minimum, it has to identify you as having requested or obtained those specific video --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Personally --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Go ahead, please.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, I was just going to ask: Personally identifiable by whom? By the NSA? I mean, how specific does this have to be?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think the answer to that question lies in subsection (b)(1), the liability provision, which says it prohibits disclosures of PII to any person. So, if it's identifiable to the "any person" that receives that disclosure, it's personally identifiable information.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think, if you can imagine a disclosure that includes 10 different facts about an individual and just one of them identifies the specific video materials or services that he requested or obtained, Congress is saying that disclosure of that information is personally identifiable information only because of that one strand of information. It might have identified --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Absolutely, yes, yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That's correct.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That is correct. And this Court may someday have to resolve that question, but that day is not today.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That -- that's exactly why. There are other arguments that -- that Paramount raised below, and that's why we asked to vacate.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: In the district court, it raised that question, not in the Sixth Circuit.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, it's certainly claiming that the videos are available for free. And our response is, sure, they're delivered for free and you might request or obtain them for free, but that doesn't change the operative provisions of the statute either in --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I -- I think that's exactly right. Our position is yes, but that's a question for remand.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: How have these suits generally prevailed in the lower courts?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I'm sorry, what -- what do you mean by "prevailed"?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Have the plaintiffs won?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think, if you look at Paramount's brief, it suggests that courts have routinely dismissed VPPA claims.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: And why do you think that is? Why do you think these smart lower court judges have rejected the kind of very literal interpretation of the statutory language that you're presenting to us today?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I -- I think there's --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Under every provision of this -- of this statute, why --why have they rejected that?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think there is, unfortunately, some reluctance to -- to believe that Congress actually meant what it said in the context of this statute. It wrote a broad law that is very protective of personally identifiable information. That prohibits a lot of disclosures of that kind of information, and I think --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, it enacted a law that is based on the technology of the 1980s. Suppose we look at (a)(1) and don't consider the statutory definition of "video tape service provider." Is Paramount a video tape service provider in the literal sense of the -- of the term?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes, it is. And, in fact --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: In the literal sense of the term? Are they selling video tapes, VHS tapes?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It -- it's very important there that in (a)(4), the definition of "video tape service provider," it says "or similar audiovisual materials."

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. Okay. That's what I'm saying. But, if we go to that, what does it -- what does its -- what does it mean for it to be similar?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Again, it's not a question that's presented here, but you have, I think, several avenues. One way is to say it's similar in that it's prerecorded. It's similar in that you watch it in the privacy of your home. It's similar in that it can be delivered to you personally; it's not something that you, for example, go to a theater and witness with other people.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But it is not similar in the sense that you go to a Blockbuster store and get a VHS tape.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Which is true enough, I guess, and, in fact, when Congress stepped back into the statute in 2013, it acknowledged that video cassette tapes were largely obsolete, Blockbuster was either on its way out or already gone, and everyone was streaming videos directly to their phones. Congress saw no need to re-jigger the definitions or to change the provisions at (b)(1)(D) or (E) precisely because they're technology-neutral.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So, on the first point, I would say, again, Congress wrote a law that isn't technology-specific. It wrote a broad law that spans all kinds of technologies, all kinds of ways that you might obtain those video materials or services, all kinds of ways you might rent, purchase, or subscribe to goods or services. And then the second point, Congress anticipated that this information would be useful for advertising purposes, and it crafted an exception under (b)(2)(D) that specifically allows disclosures of the subject matter of the videos, along with a name and address, when that disclosure is made exclusively or solely for the purpose of advertising goods or services directly to the consumer. And it's important there goods or service -- it says "goods and services" in (b)(2)(D)(ii), that -- that exception, and it says "goods or services" in subsection (a)'s definition of "consumer." Our reading has "goods or services" and "goods and services" mean the same thing. By its own admission, Paramount's reading has those two virtually identical phrases mean two radically different things.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think that is kind of the foundational premise that this Court indulges at the outset of every statutory interpret -- or interpretation case, namely, that Congress said what it meant and meant what it said when it wrote a statute. I think, if you start from the opposite purpose, that maybe Congress accidentally kind of tripped and fell and wrote these words instead of those words, I think, if you indulge that premise, you actually end up landing in the exact same place precisely because, when you walk through (a)(4)'s definition of a "provider," (a)(3)'s definition of "PII," and then (a)(1)'s definition of "consumer," you see that these weren't accidental. The scopes are different every time even though the source is the same.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, the person, I suppose, would be Facebook that got the information, just the largest social media company that exists. It's an open question, I guess, whether a similar mail vendor theory would apply to the VPPA, but that's just radically different than the facts we have here.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It --

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I mean, there are a lot of examples in which "from" is used in exactly the way [PERSON] tells us, and I -- I don't have to add an additional hypothetical, but I will anyway. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think, in that specific context, that would be a pretty unusual thing to say. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think the courts -- as far as I know at least, the courts are in accord that "or similar audiovisual materials" includes things like streaming videos to a personal device that you would watch in your house. turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.text: But are you engaged --

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I would say I think there are several kind of overlapping reasons that Congress might have preferred the exact regime it enacted. I think the clearest one is that the consumer relationship provides an easy window for getting consent, and Congress was very concerned about consent and the -- the consumer controlling the disclosure of personally identifiable information. You've got a consumer that's exchanged something of value with the provider, and, therefore, they're entitled to the protections and the possibility of liquidated damages. But whatever we -- I don't -- I won't dispute that there is some mystery about why Congress did something different in (b)(1) than it did in, for example, Sections (d) and (e) when it protected personally identifiable information there.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Absolutely. So consent works by allowing a provider to disclose personally identifiable information, and there are several locations where a provider can get that consent. One is the initiation of the consumer transaction. Another is when the person watches a video, you could have a banner pop up and --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It could be a non-video consumer transaction, or it could be a video consumer transaction. I think the statute is indifferent as to those two possibilities. Or it could be that the provider gets consent just simply before the disclosure is made. I think, again, the statute is indifferent as to when the provider obtains that consent so long as it gets it before the disclosure is made.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Could it be also that -- I'm going back to [PERSON]'s question -- that we have a statute that was enacted at a time in which it wasn't really conceivable that you could access videos without purchasing them or renting them? In other words, I'm just wondering whether we have sort of limitations in the facts that we need to think about a little bit in -- in -- in trying to assess what Congress's intent was here?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I -- I'm not sure it's true that in 1988 it was inconceivable that someone might watch a video on a computer. I think Congress was very concerned with the changing technological advances and -- and computer technology. But even more in 2013, when Congress stepped back into this statute and revised just the consent provision, I think it was intimately aware -- and, again, this is in the legislative history -- it was intimately aware with the fact that people were streaming all sorts of videos to their phones and to their computers all the time. And I think it's important to note both personally identifiable information in (a)(3) and the consumer relationship in (a)(1) are technology-neutral. Requested or obtained doesn't identify any technology by which you'll request or obtain videos.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But I guess I'm just trying to go back maybe to even [PERSON]'s first question, which is, what is your theory as to why Congress has a broader category of consumers than the personally identified information and video tape service provider categories?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, I think the -- the -- the definitions are different. We know that for sure because, if you just line them up and look at them, there are a number of material variations between them. As to why they're different -- and this goes back to the point I was trying to make earlier -- there might be some mystery about why they're different. Whether they're different is very clear. And I think we just have to live with that mystery a little bit rather than rewrite the statute. But, again, I think there are good reasons and -- and, in fact, it might close loopholes to have them do different work because a business could structure its relationship with individuals so that you never rent, purchase, or subscribe directly to the video materials. You request or obtain them some other way. And you rent, purchase, or subscribe to something else entirely. Congress wrote this statute so that that sort of clever structure by a provider won't create a loophole that allows a --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah, I mean, I thought your answer was going to be something like, really, the point of this statute was Congress's concern. You started with the concern about the release of video-watching history as it relates to one person. And so, really, the consumer, who is the consumer is not the thrust of this. The thrust of this is the video tape service provider and their activity with respect to releasing or disclosing this information. And Congress wanted to -- or maybe -- maybe wanted to have the consumer relationship for the purposes that you indicated earlier, like consent or whatnot. But, for some of us, it matters why. And -- and mysteries aren't great. So I'm trying to come up with or understand the theory that Congress would have crafted a statute in this way.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I'm not sure I could have said it any better myself. I think you're absolutely right to be focused on the thrust of this statute is about personally identifiable information. Every operative provision of this statute protects some amount of personally identifiable information; (b)(1) just has another limitation so that it protects not all personally identifiable information but just the personally identifiable information concerning a consumer.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So the parties agree that "personally identifiable information," although it says "includes," requires two strands of information: Something that identifies you and something that identifies the specific video materials or services that you requested or obtained. All the courts of appeals that have addressed that question have reached the exact same conclusion. If you look at the legislative history, Congress actually says why it used the word "includes" instead of "means." And it says we used "includes" there to create a floor, to create a minimum. Personally identifiable information could identify you or -- or identify facts about you in lots of other realms, but, at a minimum, it has to identify you as having requested or obtained those specific video --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think the answer to that question lies in subsection (b)(1), the liability provision, which says it prohibits disclosures of PII to any person. So, if it's identifiable to the "any person" that receives that disclosure, it's personally identifiable information.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think, if you can imagine a disclosure that includes 10 different facts about an individual and just one of them identifies the specific video materials or services that he requested or obtained, Congress is saying that disclosure of that information is personally identifiable information only because of that one strand of information. It might have identified --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Absolutely, yes, yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That's correct.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That is correct. And this Court may someday have to resolve that question, but that day is not today.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That -- that's exactly why. There are other arguments that -- that Paramount raised below, and that's why we asked to vacate.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: In the district court, it raised that question, not in the Sixth Circuit.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, it's certainly claiming that the videos are available for free. And our response is, sure, they're delivered for free and you might request or obtain them for free, but that doesn't change the operative provisions of the statute either in --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I -- I think that's exactly right. Our position is yes, but that's a question for remand.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I'm sorry, what -- what do you mean by "prevailed"?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think, if you look at Paramount's brief, it suggests that courts have routinely dismissed VPPA claims.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I -- I think there's --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think there is, unfortunately, some reluctance to -- to believe that Congress actually meant what it said in the context of this statute. It wrote a broad law that is very protective of personally identifiable information. That prohibits a lot of disclosures of that kind of information, and I think --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes, it is. And, in fact --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It -- it's very important there that in (a)(4), the definition of "video tape service provider," it says "or similar audiovisual materials."

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Again, it's not a question that's presented here, but you have, I think, several avenues. One way is to say it's similar in that it's prerecorded. It's similar in that you watch it in the privacy of your home. It's similar in that it can be delivered to you personally; it's not something that you, for example, go to a theater and witness with other people.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Which is true enough, I guess, and, in fact, when Congress stepped back into the statute in 2013, it acknowledged that video cassette tapes were largely obsolete, Blockbuster was either on its way out or already gone, and everyone was streaming videos directly to their phones. Congress saw no need to re-jigger the definitions or to change the provisions at (b)(1)(D) or (E) precisely because they're technology-neutral.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So, on the first point, I would say, again, Congress wrote a law that isn't technology-specific. It wrote a broad law that spans all kinds of technologies, all kinds of ways that you might obtain those video materials or services, all kinds of ways you might rent, purchase, or subscribe to goods or services. And then the second point, Congress anticipated that this information would be useful for advertising purposes, and it crafted an exception under (b)(2)(D) that specifically allows disclosures of the subject matter of the videos, along with a name and address, when that disclosure is made exclusively or solely for the purpose of advertising goods or services directly to the consumer. And it's important there goods or service -- it says "goods and services" in (b)(2)(D)(ii), that -- that exception, and it says "goods or services" in subsection (a)'s definition of "consumer." Our reading has "goods or services" and "goods and services" mean the same thing. By its own admission, Paramount's reading has those two virtually identical phrases mean two radically different things.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think that is kind of the foundational premise that this Court indulges at the outset of every statutory interpret -- or interpretation case, namely, that Congress said what it meant and meant what it said when it wrote a statute. I think, if you start from the opposite purpose, that maybe Congress accidentally kind of tripped and fell and wrote these words instead of those words, I think, if you indulge that premise, you actually end up landing in the exact same place precisely because, when you walk through (a)(4)'s definition of a "provider," (a)(3)'s definition of "PII," and then (a)(1)'s definition of "consumer," you see that these weren't accidental. The scopes are different every time even though the source is the same.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, the person, I suppose, would be Facebook that got the information, just the largest social media company that exists. But it's also true -- and I think, if you -- if you look closely at the Sixth Circuit's opinion, it actually says all six circuits that have answered that standing question in the context of a VPPA claim are in accord. All of them say, yes, you have standing when there's been a disclosure even to one person of your personally identifiable information without your consent. All six are in accord on that point. The difference with the Eleventh Circuit is, well, what happens in a different context. I believe that was the FDCPA instead of the VPPA. But, in that context, you basically bounced a disclosure from a mail vendor to the consumer, and the court said in that context that's not really a disclosure. You're basically outsourcing kind of who's going to mail the item to the consumer. Here, we've got an exception for disclosures made to the consumer. It's an open question, I guess, whether a similar mail vendor theory would apply to the VPPA, but that's just radically different than the facts we have here.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: You all didn't brief standing, right? Is that an issue in this case right now?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I mean, it always is in the sense of our jurisdiction, but I'm just saying, do we have arguments written related to -- to standing?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That's actually -- that -- that's absolutely right, that it was not put up in issue in this case. We argued that in the district court. Paramount abandoned its standing argument in the Sixth Circuit. It addressed it sua sponte. I think you're right that it's a background issue in this case. But it has not been briefed.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And can I ask you a clarifying question just about the lower court dismissals? I -- are they on the consumer issue that is before us now? I thought there was a 2-2 split among the circuits on the definition of "consumer."

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That's absolutely right. There is a 2-2 split on the definition of "consumer." And both dismissals here, the -- the district court in Tennessee and the Sixth Circuit, held solely that this complaint should be dismissed because of the particular meaning we're giving to the word "consumer."

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So, if these have not prevailed in large, it could be for other reasons than that?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Absolutely. And, in fact --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- it often is for other reasons. If you look at Paramount's brief in opposition to our petition for certiorari, they point to personally identifiable information, disputes about whether someone is a provider. Those are other reasons, and they point to the fact that there are multiple real limitations to liability coexisting at once in subsection (b)(1).

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That -- that's correct, [ADDRESS], yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think this Court's approach is exactly right, that you always look at text in context. We have no quarrel with that methodology because text in context shows you exactly what you normally presume at the outset, which is that Congress meant "goods or services," a broader term, when it said "goods or services" in subsection (a)(1). It did not mean video materials or services, something it said in the same sentence, identically from a video tape service provider. It did not mean prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials. It didn't even mention services at all in the definition, (a)(4)'s definition, of a "provider." It didn't mean those other phrases that it said elsewhere. It meant something different. And I think context absolutely reinforces that point.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think that's an unusual meaning to ascribe to "from" from the outset. That is usually a word that identifies the source of material, not something that identifies the scope. And, here, we know for sure that Congress was looking at "from" as identifying source. And we know that by comparing (a)(1)'s definition of "consumer" to (a)(3)'s definition of "PII." Both identify subject matter that comes from a video tape service provider.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think, in that specific context, that would be a pretty unusual thing to say. But, if we could twist it just a little bit, it would be equally odd to say if we had a statute that defined gas stations a particular way, those that provide fuel, that would be our (a)(4) paradigm. Then we had in the same statute, the same sentence of the same statute, a provision that mentioned fuel materials or services or fuel goods or services. That's (a)(3). And then we had in the same statute, the same sentence, goods or services from a gas station. It would be exceedingly odd to say those three subject matters must be the same thing. Maybe I was feeling really brave at the gas station and I got sushi. That's a good or service from --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- a gas station, but it's not a fuel good or service, and it's certainly not the fuel that you would normally buy at a gas station.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think the courts -- as far as I know at least, the courts are in accord that "or similar audiovisual materials" includes things like streaming videos to a personal device that you would watch in your house. It doesn't require a physicality, you know, necessarily that you're going to have a tape, a physical tape that you play that way. And, again, when you look at, in 2013, Congress stepped back into this statute, it specifically said, we are aware streaming is rampant and we still think this statute covers the -- the personally identifiable information that results from those streaming activities.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Because it's similar in critical ways to a video cassette tape. It allows you to watch that video in the privacy of your home. It allows you to watch it on your own. It allows you to pause, come back later, record -- or, I'm sorry, rewind, and pick it up as you wish. It's -- it's in lots of ways the exact same as the way you would interact with a video cassette tape.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: If we're looking at the technology that was available in 1988, I think the answer has to be no precisely because you couldn't pause and rewind and stop and come back hours later and rewatch things the way that you can now both with a prerecorded video cassette tape and with the exact audiovisual materials that we have at issue here. And I would note too all of this concerns whether Paramount is a video tape service provider, which isn't before the Court today.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, I would say a couple of points. One, it's true that those suits have been brought. It's also true that many of them have resulted in district courts saying: Wait a minute, that entity, like Chick-fil-A, is not a video tape service provider. This is the wrong kind of entity. Congress wasn't targeting Chick-fil-A.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I'm not sure the length of the video matters. What will always matter is exactly what (a)(4) says. You have to be engaged in the business of renting, selling, or delivering that audiovisual material.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That -- that seems to me to be true. You're delivering it.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But are you engaged --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I don't think the number of minutes long that a video is.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think it's -- it's exactly what Congress put into (a)(4). Are you engaged in that business? Chick-fil-A is not.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Paramount is.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, I think, if you -- if you imagine the Blockbuster paradigm, it was engaged in the business of delivering those materials because that was what was on offer when you walked into the store. The same is true of a department store. When you walked in those doors, you could rent, purchase --rent or purchase at least those --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: And -- and it might -- it -- it might be that those websites are in the business of delivering those video materials. I don't think that should alarm us so much precisely because (b)(1) has multiple other limitations in it. You also need PII to be collected. You need a knowing disclosure, not an accidental one, a knowing disclosure. You also need a consumer. So I think, even if we lived in a world where, for example, Chick-fil-A someday becomes a video tape service provider, there are lots of other off-ramps for liability included.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I apologize, [PERSON], I'm not sure I have a better answer except to say putting that material on offer in your store, you are driving -- your -- your profit or your business motive is linked to renting, selling, or delivering that material.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Precisely because it is engaged in the business of delivering a whole host of video materials on its website.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Again, I'm not sure that they're similar in terms of length, but, again, it's the profit motive that Paramount has when it makes these deliveries. It doesn't deliver them, you know, for kicks. It delivers them because it sells advertising. It drives business to the website.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think the courts have been very consistent in saying it doesn't bring in every kind of business that incidentally happens to provide a single video on its website. That's certainly not our position either.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So, even if we someday define the universe of video tape service providers because that's not in this case, but even if we define it broadly, can you speak to whether interpreting "consumer" as you have will have the negative consequences? There's a lot of policy arguments in Respondent's brief, and I just wanted to invite you to talk about what the cure for this would be even if this is a broadly interpreted statute.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I don't think it has any real negative consequence here precisely because all of the elements in (b)(1) have to coexist at the same time, so it's not just that you're a video tape service provider and, certainly, that this statute does not prohibit providers from having consumers. It doesn't prohibit them even from collecting or using personally identifiable information. The only thing that triggers liability, the only thing is the disclosure, the knowing disclosure, of personally identifiable information concerning a consumer without consent. And, again, consent is easy to obtain. That's the easiest off-ramp to liability that we have.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So that's -- so the cure is pretty simple. It's not that we have to worry so much about roping in all of these businesses. They would just figure out a way to get consent from people who are watching these videos after they've been disclosed?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Absolutely true. And I would say it's -- it's kind of a technological reality that more businesses are engaged in this business today than were engaged in it in 1988, and that's not a concern for exactly the reasons we just laid out: Consent is such an easy fix.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

Maybe I was feeling really brave at the gas station and I got sushi. That's a good or service from --

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: -- a gas station, but it's not a fuel good or service, and it's certainly not the fuel that you would normally buy at a gas station.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: I think the courts -- as far as I know at least, the courts are in accord that "or similar audiovisual materials" includes things like streaming videos to a personal device that you would watch in your house. It doesn't require a physicality, you know, necessarily that you're going to have a tape, a physical tape that you play that way. And, again, when you look at, in 2013, Congress stepped back into this statute, it specifically said, we are aware streaming is rampant and we still think this statute covers the -- the personally identifiable information that results from those streaming activities.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Because it's similar in critical ways to a video cassette tape. It allows you to watch that video in the privacy of your home. It allows you to watch it on your own. It allows you to pause, come back later, record -- or, I'm sorry, rewind, and pick it up as you wish. It's -- it's in lots of ways the exact same as the way you would interact with a video cassette tape.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: If we're looking at the technology that was available in 1988, I think the answer has to be no precisely because you couldn't pause and rewind and stop and come back hours later and rewatch things the way that you can now both with a prerecorded video cassette tape and with the exact audiovisual materials that we have at issue here. And I would note too all of this concerns whether Paramount is a video tape service provider, which isn't before the Court today.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Just on the video tape service provider issue, I know that's not before us, but I think you've waved away some of the concerns about every business in America that has video on its website being targeted. But, certainly, the amicus briefs on the other side -- The Retail Litigation Center, the Chamber of Commerce -- point out that your reading would -- and -- and suits have been brought against every sector of the economy -- print media publishers, movie theaters, advocacy groups, sports leagues, health and fitness websites, parenting advice companies, chess websites, crafting websites, professional networking sites, universities -- every other type of defendant under the sun in the words of the amicus brief. And so I think you've waved away some of the concerns about the breadth of your argument on this issue by saying, don't worry, it's not going to apply because of the definition of "video tape service provider." But I don't think other plaintiffs are going to be conceding that in the cases against those businesses, or is the amicus -- are the amicus briefs wrong in saying that that's a legitimate concern?

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Well, I would say a couple of points. One, it's true that those suits have been brought. It's also true that many of them have resulted in district courts saying: Wait a minute, that entity, like Chick-fil-A, is not a video tape service provider. This is the wrong kind of entity. Congress wasn't targeting Chick-fil-A.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, I think the -- the -- the definitions are different. And I think we just have to live with that mystery a little bit rather than rewrite the statute. But, again, I think there are good reasons and -- and, in fact, it might close loopholes to have them do different work because a business could structure its relationship with individuals so that you never rent, purchase, or subscribe directly to the video materials. You request or obtain them some other way. And you rent, purchase, or subscribe to something else entirely. Congress wrote this statute so that that sort of clever structure by a provider won't create a loophole that allows a --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So I'm not sure I could have said it any better myself. I think you're absolutely right to be focused on the thrust of this statute is about personally identifiable information. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So the parties agree that "personally identifiable information," although it says "includes," requires two strands of information: Something that identifies you and something that identifies the specific video materials or services that you requested or obtained. Personally identifiable information could identify you or -- or identify facts about you in lots of other realms, but, at a minimum, it has to identify you as having requested or obtained those specific video --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think the answer to that question lies in subsection (b)(1), the liability provision, which says it prohibits disclosures of PII to any person. So, if it's identifiable to the "any person" that receives that disclosure, it's personally identifiable information.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think, if you can imagine a disclosure that includes 10 different facts about an individual and just one of them identifies the specific video materials or services that he requested or obtained, Congress is saying that disclosure of that information is personally identifiable information only because of that one strand of information. It might have identified --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Absolutely, yes, yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: And the question of PII, even if you prevail on the issue before us, would still be resolved on remand, correct?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That's correct.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It would still be open on remand? We're not resolving that here because there's a big argument, obviously, in the courts of appeals whether this kind of information constitutes PII, correct?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That is correct. And this Court may someday have to resolve that question, but that day is not today.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That -- that's exactly why. There are other arguments that -- that Paramount raised below, and that's why we asked to vacate.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: In the district court, it raised that question, not in the Sixth Circuit.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, it's certainly claiming that the videos are available for free. And our response is, sure, they're delivered for free and you might request or obtain them for free, but that doesn't change the operative provisions of the statute either in --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I -- I think that's exactly right. Our position is yes, but that's a question for remand.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I'm sorry, what -- what do you mean by "prevailed"?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think, if you look at Paramount's brief, it suggests that courts have routinely dismissed VPPA claims.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I -- I think there's --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think there is, unfortunately, some reluctance to -- to believe that Congress actually meant what it said in the context of this statute. It wrote a broad law that is very protective of personally identifiable information. That prohibits a lot of disclosures of that kind of information, and I think --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes, it is. And, in fact --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It -- it's very important there that in (a)(4), the definition of "video tape service provider," it says "or similar audiovisual materials."

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Again, it's not a question that's presented here, but you have, I think, several avenues. One way is to say it's similar in that it's prerecorded. It's similar in that you watch it in the privacy of your home. It's similar in that it can be delivered to you personally; it's not something that you, for example, go to a theater and witness with other people.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Which is true enough, I guess, and, in fact, when Congress stepped back into the statute in 2013, it acknowledged that video cassette tapes were largely obsolete, Blockbuster was either on its way out or already gone, and everyone was streaming videos directly to their phones. Congress saw no need to re-jigger the definitions or to change the provisions at (b)(1)(D) or (E) precisely because they're technology-neutral.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, isn't there a concern about repurposing a statute that was really about public disclosure of what individuals viewed into a statute that regulates data sharing for targeted advertising on the Internet? Those are very different things. And the context here is the data sharing for the targeted advertising.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So, on the first point, I would say, again, Congress wrote a law that isn't technology-specific. It wrote a broad law that spans all kinds of technologies, all kinds of ways that you might obtain those video materials or services, all kinds of ways you might rent, purchase, or subscribe to goods or services. By its own admission, Paramount's reading has those two virtually identical phrases mean two radically different things.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think that is kind of the foundational premise that this Court indulges at the outset of every statutory interpret -- or interpretation case, namely, that Congress said what it meant and meant what it said when it wrote a statute. I think, if you start from the opposite purpose, that maybe Congress accidentally kind of tripped and fell and wrote these words instead of those words, I think, if you indulge that premise, you actually end up landing in the exact same place precisely because, when you walk through (a)(4)'s definition of a "provider," (a)(3)'s definition of "PII," and then (a)(1)'s definition of "consumer," you see that these weren't accidental. The scopes are different every time even though the source is the same.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, the person, I suppose, would be Facebook that got the information, just the largest social media company that exists. But it's also true -- and I think, if you -- if you look closely at the Sixth Circuit's opinion, it actually says all six circuits that have answered that standing question in the context of a VPPA claim are in accord. All of them say, yes, you have standing when there's been a disclosure even to one person of your personally identifiable information without your consent. All six are in accord on that point. The difference with the Eleventh Circuit is, well, what happens in a different context. I believe that was the FDCPA instead of the VPPA. But, in that context, you basically bounced a disclosure from a mail vendor to the consumer, and the court said in that context that's not really a disclosure. You're basically outsourcing kind of who's going to mail the item to the consumer. Here, we've got an exception for disclosures made to the consumer. It's an open question, I guess, whether a similar mail vendor theory would apply to the VPPA, but that's just radically different than the facts we have here.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That's actually -- that -- that's absolutely right, that it was not put up in issue in this case. We argued that in the district court. Paramount abandoned its standing argument in the Sixth Circuit. It addressed it sua sponte. I think you're right that it's a background issue in this case. But it has not been briefed.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That's absolutely right. There is a 2-2 split on the definition of "consumer." And both dismissals here, the -- the district court in Tennessee and the Sixth Circuit, held solely that this complaint should be dismissed because of the particular meaning we're giving to the word "consumer."

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Absolutely. And, in fact --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- it often is for other reasons. If you look at Paramount's brief in opposition to our petition for certiorari, they point to personally identifiable information, disputes about whether someone is a provider. Those are other reasons, and they point to the fact that there are multiple real limitations to liability coexisting at once in subsection (b)(1).

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Is -- the PII, is that a 3-1 split against your position on PII?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That -- that's correct, [ADDRESS], yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think the other side's kind of big-picture argument is that we are a textualist Court but usually not a literalist Court and that we have a lot of principles and doctrines -- major questions, elephants in mouse holes, context, common sense -- you see those terms sprinkled through a lot of our cases, including in this general field, and that we should be thinking about that so that we don't read this statute for all it's worth when the Congress in the 1980s wasn't thinking about data sharing for targeted advertising. So that's a big-picture question for you to tackle.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think this Court's approach is exactly right, that you always look at text in context. We have no quarrel with that methodology because text in context shows you exactly what you normally presume at the outset, which is that Congress meant "goods or services," a broader term, when it said "goods or services" in subsection (a)(1). It did not mean video materials or services, something it said in the same sentence, identically from a video tape service provider. It did not mean prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials. It didn't even mention services at all in the definition, (a)(4)'s definition, of a "provider." It didn't mean those other phrases that it said elsewhere. It meant something different. And I think context absolutely reinforces that point.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think that's an unusual meaning to ascribe to "from" from the outset. That is usually a word that identifies the source of material, not something that identifies the scope. And, here, we know for sure that Congress was looking at "from" as identifying source. And we know that by comparing (a)(1)'s definition of "consumer" to (a)(3)'s definition of "PII." Both identify subject matter that comes from a video tape service provider.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think, in that specific context, that would be a pretty unusual thing to say. But, if we could twist it just a little bit, it would be equally odd to say if we had a statute that defined gas stations a particular way, those that provide fuel, that would be our (a)(4) paradigm. Then we had in the same statute, the same sentence of the same statute, a provision that mentioned fuel materials or services or fuel goods or services. That's (a)(3). And then we had in the same statute, the same sentence, goods or services from a gas station. It would be exceedingly odd to say those three subject matters must be the same thing. Maybe I was feeling really brave at the gas station and I got sushi. That's a good or service from --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- a gas station, but it's not a fuel good or service, and it's certainly not the fuel that you would normally buy at a gas station.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think the courts -- as far as I know at least, the courts are in accord that "or similar audiovisual materials" includes things like streaming videos to a personal device that you would watch in your house. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Because it's similar in critical ways to a video cassette tape. It allows you to watch that video in the privacy of your home. It allows you to watch it on your own. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: If we're looking at the technology that was available in 1988, I think the answer has to be no precisely because you couldn't pause and rewind and stop and come back hours later and rewatch things the way that you can now both with a prerecorded video cassette tape and with the exact audiovisual materials that we have at issue here. turns_pm60.text: Just on the video tape service provider issue, I know that's not before us, but I think you've waved away some of the concerns about every business in America that has video on its website being targeted. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, I would say a couple of points. One, it's true that those suits have been brought. It's also true that many of them have resulted in district courts saying: Wait a minute, that entity, like Chick-fil-A, is not a video tape service provider. This is the wrong kind of entity. Congress wasn't targeting Chick-fil-A.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: And what makes someone a video tape service provider? If they have a video on their business website that, let's say, is three minutes long, are they a video tape service provider?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I'm not sure the length of the video matters. What will always matter is exactly what (a)(4) says. You have to be engaged in the business of renting, selling, or delivering that audiovisual material.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: You're delivering it, right, by showing it on your website, correct?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That -- that seems to me to be true. You're delivering it.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Okay. And then what makes you --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But are you engaged --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- what makes you in the business? Two minutes, three minutes, four minutes, 10 minutes? What is it?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I don't think the number of minutes long that a video is.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: What does matter then?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think it's -- it's exactly what Congress put into (a)(4). Are you engaged in that business? Chick-fil-A is not.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I'm trying to -- I'm trying to --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Paramount is.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I understand the words that are used. And I don't mean to be too sharp, but I just want to have some explanation of what you think "engaged in the business" means because I think you waved away some of the concerns by saying, don't worry about Chick-fil-A, and I just want to know why.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, I think, if you -- if you imagine the Blockbuster paradigm, it was engaged in the business of delivering those materials because that was what was on offer when you walked into the store. The same is true of a department store. When you walked in those doors, you could rent, purchase --rent or purchase at least those --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: When you go on a business's website, which is how a lot of people shop, obviously, most people, you'll often see a video quickly and --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And -- and it might -- it -- it might be that those websites are in the business of delivering those video materials. So I think, even if we lived in a world where, for example, Chick-fil-A someday becomes a video tape service provider, there are lots of other off-ramps for liability included.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I still don't think you've told me what a video -- and this is the last time I'm going to ask it -- what on the business's website's video makes it in the business of delivering?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I apologize, Speaker A, I'm not sure I have a better answer except to say putting that material on offer in your store, you are driving -- your -- your profit or your business motive is linked to renting, selling, or delivering that material.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: A video of your product presumably. Okay, thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Precisely because it is engaged in the business of delivering a whole host of video materials on its website.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Again, I'm not sure that they're similar in terms of length, but, again, it's the profit motive that Paramount has when it makes these deliveries. It doesn't deliver them, you know, for kicks. It delivers them because it sells advertising. It drives business to the website.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think the courts have been very consistent in saying it doesn't bring in every kind of business that incidentally happens to provide a single video on its website. That's certainly not our position either.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I don't think it has any real negative consequence here precisely because all of the elements in (b)(1) have to coexist at the same time, so it's not just that you're a video tape service provider and, certainly, that this statute does not prohibit providers from having consumers. It doesn't prohibit them even from collecting or using personally identifiable information. The only thing that triggers liability, the only thing is the disclosure, the knowing disclosure, of personally identifiable information concerning a consumer without consent. And, again, consent is easy to obtain. That's the easiest off-ramp to liability that we have.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Absolutely true. And I would say it's -- it's kind of a technological reality that more businesses are engaged in this business today than were engaged in it in 1988, and that's not a concern for exactly the reasons we just laid out: Consent is such an easy fix.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.
