turns_pm15.text: I apologize, Speaker A, I'm not sure I have a better answer except to say putting that material on offer in your store, you are driving -- your -- your profit or your business motive is linked to renting, selling, or delivering that material.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: A video of your product presumably. Okay, thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It would still be open on remand? We're not resolving that here because there's a big argument, obviously, in the courts of appeals whether this kind of information constitutes PII, correct?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That is correct. And this Court may someday have to resolve that question, but that day is not today.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That -- that's exactly why. There are other arguments that -- that Paramount raised below, and that's why we asked to vacate.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: In the district court, it raised that question, not in the Sixth Circuit.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, it's certainly claiming that the videos are available for free. And our response is, sure, they're delivered for free and you might request or obtain them for free, but that doesn't change the operative provisions of the statute either in --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I -- I think that's exactly right. Our position is yes, but that's a question for remand.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I'm sorry, what -- what do you mean by "prevailed"?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think, if you look at Paramount's brief, it suggests that courts have routinely dismissed VPPA claims.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I -- I think there's --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think there is, unfortunately, some reluctance to -- to believe that Congress actually meant what it said in the context of this statute. It wrote a broad law that is very protective of personally identifiable information. That prohibits a lot of disclosures of that kind of information, and I think --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes, it is. And, in fact --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It -- it's very important there that in (a)(4), the definition of "video tape service provider," it says "or similar audiovisual materials."

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Again, it's not a question that's presented here, but you have, I think, several avenues. One way is to say it's similar in that it's prerecorded. It's similar in that you watch it in the privacy of your home. It's similar in that it can be delivered to you personally; it's not something that you, for example, go to a theater and witness with other people.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Which is true enough, I guess, and, in fact, when Congress stepped back into the statute in 2013, it acknowledged that video cassette tapes were largely obsolete, Blockbuster was either on its way out or already gone, and everyone was streaming videos directly to their phones. Congress saw no need to re-jigger the definitions or to change the provisions at (b)(1)(D) or (E) precisely because they're technology-neutral.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, isn't there a concern about repurposing a statute that was really about public disclosure of what individuals viewed into a statute that regulates data sharing for targeted advertising on the Internet? Those are very different things. And the context here is the data sharing for the targeted advertising.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So, on the first point, I would say, again, Congress wrote a law that isn't technology-specific. It wrote a broad law that spans all kinds of technologies, all kinds of ways that you might obtain those video materials or services, all kinds of ways you might rent, purchase, or subscribe to goods or services. And then the second point, Congress anticipated that this information would be useful for advertising purposes, and it crafted an exception under (b)(2)(D) that specifically allows disclosures of the subject matter of the videos, along with a name and address, when that disclosure is made exclusively or solely for the purpose of advertising goods or services directly to the consumer. And it's important there goods or service -- it says "goods and services" in (b)(2)(D)(ii), that -- that exception, and it says "goods or services" in subsection (a)'s definition of "consumer." Our reading has "goods or services" and "goods and services" mean the same thing. By its own admission, Paramount's reading has those two virtually identical phrases mean two radically different things.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think that is kind of the foundational premise that this Court indulges at the outset of every statutory interpret -- or interpretation case, namely, that Congress said what it meant and meant what it said when it wrote a statute. I think, if you start from the opposite purpose, that maybe Congress accidentally kind of tripped and fell and wrote these words instead of those words, I think, if you indulge that premise, you actually end up landing in the exact same place precisely because, when you walk through (a)(4)'s definition of a "provider," (a)(3)'s definition of "PII," and then (a)(1)'s definition of "consumer," you see that these weren't accidental. The scopes are different every time even though the source is the same.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, the person, I suppose, would be Facebook that got the information, just the largest social media company that exists. But it's also true -- and I think, if you -- if you look closely at the Sixth Circuit's opinion, it actually says all six circuits that have answered that standing question in the context of a VPPA claim are in accord. It's an open question, I guess, whether a similar mail vendor theory would apply to the VPPA, but that's just radically different than the facts we have here.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That's actually -- that -- that's absolutely right, that it was not put up in issue in this case. We argued that in the district court. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That's absolutely right. There is a 2-2 split on the definition of "consumer." And both dismissals here, the -- the district court in Tennessee and the Sixth Circuit, held solely that this complaint should be dismissed because of the particular meaning we're giving to the word "consumer."

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Absolutely. And, in fact --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- it often is for other reasons. If you look at Paramount's brief in opposition to our petition for certiorari, they point to personally identifiable information, disputes about whether someone is a provider. Those are other reasons, and they point to the fact that there are multiple real limitations to liability coexisting at once in subsection (b)(1).

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Is -- the PII, is that a 3-1 split against your position on PII?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That -- that's correct, [ADDRESS], yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think the other side's kind of big-picture argument is that we are a textualist Court but usually not a literalist Court and that we have a lot of principles and doctrines -- major questions, elephants in mouse holes, context, common sense -- you see those terms sprinkled through a lot of our cases, including in this general field, and that we should be thinking about that so that we don't read this statute for all it's worth when the Congress in the 1980s wasn't thinking about data sharing for targeted advertising. So that's a big-picture question for you to tackle.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think this Court's approach is exactly right, that you always look at text in context. We have no quarrel with that methodology because text in context shows you exactly what you normally presume at the outset, which is that Congress meant "goods or services," a broader term, when it said "goods or services" in subsection (a)(1). It did not mean video materials or services, something it said in the same sentence, identically from a video tape service provider. It did not mean prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials. It didn't even mention services at all in the definition, (a)(4)'s definition, of a "provider." It didn't mean those other phrases that it said elsewhere. It meant something different. And I think context absolutely reinforces that point.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think that's an unusual meaning to ascribe to "from" from the outset. That is usually a word that identifies the source of material, not something that identifies the scope. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think, in that specific context, that would be a pretty unusual thing to say. Then we had in the same statute, the same sentence of the same statute, a provision that mentioned fuel materials or services or fuel goods or services. That's (a)(3). And then we had in the same statute, the same sentence, goods or services from a gas station. It would be exceedingly odd to say those three subject matters must be the same thing. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- a gas station, but it's not a fuel good or service, and it's certainly not the fuel that you would normally buy at a gas station.

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: If we're looking at the technology that was available in 1988, I think the answer has to be no precisely because you couldn't pause and rewind and stop and come back hours later and rewatch things the way that you can now both with a prerecorded video cassette tape and with the exact audiovisual materials that we have at issue here. turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, I would say a couple of points. One, it's true that those suits have been brought. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: You're delivering it, right, by showing it on your website, correct?

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.text: Okay. And then what makes you --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- what makes you in the business? Two minutes, three minutes, four minutes, 10 minutes? What is it?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I don't think the number of minutes long that a video is.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: What does matter then?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think it's -- it's exactly what Congress put into (a)(4). Are you engaged in that business? Chick-fil-A is not.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I'm trying to -- I'm trying to --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Paramount is.

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, I think, if you -- if you imagine the Blockbuster paradigm, it was engaged in the business of delivering those materials because that was what was on offer when you walked into the store. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: When you go on a business's website, which is how a lot of people shop, obviously, most people, you'll often see a video quickly and --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And -- and it might -- it -- it might be that those websites are in the business of delivering those video materials. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I still don't think you've told me what a video -- and this is the last time I'm going to ask it -- what on the business's website's video makes it in the business of delivering?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I apologize, Speaker A, I'm not sure I have a better answer except to say putting that material on offer in your store, you are driving -- your -- your profit or your business motive is linked to renting, selling, or delivering that material.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: A video of your product presumably. Okay, thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Precisely because it is engaged in the business of delivering a whole host of video materials on its website.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Again, I'm not sure that they're similar in terms of length, but, again, it's the profit motive that Paramount has when it makes these deliveries. It doesn't deliver them, you know, for kicks. It delivers them because it sells advertising. It drives business to the website.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think the courts have been very consistent in saying it doesn't bring in every kind of business that incidentally happens to provide a single video on its website. That's certainly not our position either.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I don't think it has any real negative consequence here precisely because all of the elements in (b)(1) have to coexist at the same time, so it's not just that you're a video tape service provider and, certainly, that this statute does not prohibit providers from having consumers. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Absolutely true. And I would say it's -- it's kind of a technological reality that more businesses are engaged in this business today than were engaged in it in 1988, and that's not a concern for exactly the reasons we just laid out: Consent is such an easy fix.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

That argument fails at the threshold because the phrase "goods or services" is not unmodified in the statute, but it takes its meaning from the immediate surrounding text. And that immediately surrounding text makes clear that the relevant goods or services are the prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials that one could rent, purchase, subscribe to, from a video tape service provider. So just as one, when referring to goods or services from a medical service provider, would not logically refer to a cup of coffee or valet parking, when one refers to goods or services from a video tape service provider, one does not logically refer to chicken sandwiches or dog bandanas. The alternative of interpreting the statute to create a veritable army of VPPA consumers without any personal information to protect unless and until years or even decades later they watch a free video has nothing to recommend it and underscores that Petitioner is misreading the statute. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] In 1988, Congress addressed a specific problem with a tailored solution, protecting the personally identifiable information of consumers of video tape service providers. For years, the statute worked as designed. Personal protection of video --information of video consumers was protected, and there was virtually no litigation under this statute. Then, however, the plaintiffs' class action bar discovered the VPPA and its statutory and punitive damages. The key to their effort to repurpose the statute is the argument, the claim, that the statute's definition of "consumer" uses the phrase "goods or services" in an unmodified way, so one can become a consumer without ever having rented, purchased, or subscribed to a video. That argument fails at the threshold because the phrase "goods or services" is not unmodified in the statute, but it takes its meaning from the immediate surrounding text. And that immediately surrounding text makes clear that the relevant goods or services are the prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials that one could rent, purchase, subscribe to, from a video tape service provider. So just as one, when referring to goods or services from a medical service provider, would not logically refer to a cup of coffee or valet parking, when one refers to goods or services from a video tape service provider, one does not logically refer to chicken sandwiches or dog bandanas. The alternative of interpreting the statute to create a veritable army of VPPA consumers without any personal information to protect unless and until years or even decades later they watch a free video has nothing to recommend it and underscores that Petitioner is misreading the statute. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So, [PERSON], with all due respect to my friend, I think he gets there the exact same way you would get there in understanding that Chick-fil-A is in the business of delivering videos. It's the same thing. That's not what the website is mostly about, but there -- if you go to the website, the first thing you'll see is, like, a video starts playing. You don't even have to click on anything. It just starts playing. And that's the way that most websites work these days. And -- and most of the websites also have pixels because most of the reason you can get to free content, rather than being behind the pay wall, is because of targeted --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So, I mean, look --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Totally agree with you, [PERSON], as a common-sense matter. But here is I think a little bit of the problem, which is Congress did make it pretty clear that the department store, when it sells the video, is a video tape service provider even though, when it sells furniture and clothes and everything else, it's not a video tape service provider. And the way I think, you know, I would -- the way I understand my friend's position is, yeah, it's all well and good that 247Sports.com is mostly just a sports site, but, because there are videos on it, that's enough to get you in the business of delivering videos. And that's the same way the plaintiffs -- they might not have succeeded, but that's the same way the plaintiffs got to Chick-fil-A, La-Z-Boy, Folger's, Godiva chocolates, and, of course, every newspaper virtually, you know, lots of small newspapers, because all of those newspapers, you know, they're basically in the business of having websites that have news. Some of the news articles are accompanied by videos. And, of course, their theory is not that you become a consumer just by going to the website. That's kind of the weird thing about this theory. Their theory when they sue the newspapers is, well, not everybody that goes there is a consumer, but the people that actually still subscribe to the good old-fashioned paper that comes to your door, they are consumers because they bought a non-video or they subscribed to a non-video product. That gets them in the consumer door. And then maybe five years later, they go to the website --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- and see a video, and all of a sudden we're off to the races.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, it's sort of my job to focus on the easy hypotheticals.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But I think, if you --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, my -- my -- my job is to direct your attention to the easy hypotheticals, I would suppose. But, fair enough, your job is to direct to the harder hypotheticals. But I'm not sure there really are that many hard hypotheticals in the sense that we're not taking the position that if you do -- actually are in the business, you are a video tape service provider, that because you do lots of other things or the --or the rest, that you're not covered. And we think -- I mean, you know, I think we would take the position, though I think [PERSON] raises a good question about streaming services, but we would take the position that Netflix, when you go online to Netflix, that that might still be covered. So I think the core of the -- of the statute is still covered under our view. But what I think what we would say is that this notion that you can just mix --mix and match what makes you a consumer and what gives you the personally identifiable information that the statute protects for consumers, that mismatch doesn't make any sense. So a dog bandana --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, two things, [ADDRESS]. I mean, one, you know, sometimes when that's what you get, maybe you should take another look. And the premise of your question, of course, is that "from a video tape service provider" isn't doing any definitional work in the definition of "consumer." And I would just take issue with that. I mean, you know, "from a video tape service provider," "video tape service provider" is a defined term in the statute. If you plug that definition into the statute, then what you get is "consumer" means any renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from any person engaged in the business in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials. After I'm done plugging that into the statute, I'm left with the conclusion that the goods or service we're talking about here are prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That makes sense --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I guess what I would say is that, you know, no statute pursues its purpose to the ends of the earth. And, here, Congress was very clear that if you don't have a rental, purchaser, or subscription relationship, then you're not covered by this statute. And that's common ground between both parties.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That's because of the way the statute's written. And for those that look at legislative history, that also seems entirely consistent with what Congress said. Congress envisioned the possibility of a department store selling videos and other things, and they were quite clear that they didn't think there was privacy protection for the other things. And then I also --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But, with respect, I think, if Justice Breyer went into the same store, didn't buy the book but still looked at three videos in some cabin and didn't have to subscribe anything to do it, and the reporter asked the same question, he would still fit --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- he would --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right, right. But it's a perfect illustration of how the statute doesn't capture every disclosure of personal identifying information. It requires you to be a consumer. And, logically, the transaction that makes you a consumer is one that involves some personal identifying information. And what's illogical is that you become a consumer on day one, and then there's personal identifiable information doesn't catch up to you --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: What -- what seems --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- until day -- until years later.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: What seems different to me about now from the 1980s is not so much the -- the plaintiffs but the type of personal identifying information. It's not your name being released. It's this data-sharing code, right? And that's quite a bit different. And there are a lot of arguments about PII. And then treating everyone as a video tape service provider, every business as opposed to the ones that are analogous to Blockbuster. But those two arguments, both of which may be raised in future cases in which your side's prevailing in the lower courts for the most part, are not the issues before us. So how do we think about, you know, the sky-is-falling concern in the amicus briefs and it's part of your brief when there are these two other arguments that you may prevail on? And why shouldn't we just follow "consumer" as written and worry about that in a future case?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So a couple of things, Speaker B. I mean, first of all, like, if you're going to tell me that I'm going to win on those other arguments, I mean, great. But we don't know that. My friend has -- you know, thinks that he has great arguments on both PII and on video tape service provider. I also don't think you can really get away from the definition of "video tape service provider" in interpreting the scope of "consumer" because that word, that defined word, is part of the definition of "consumer." But I also want to say there are distinct problems with this expansive definition of "consumer," and it really takes you away from the structure of the statute because this statute operates on the assumption that consumers are going to have personally identifiable information and they are going to be the ones -- the consumers are going to be in the position to consent to the disclosure of that information. And my friend's position breaks that structure of the statute because, even when he answers [PERSON] and says the way this is going to work is we're going to ask for consent from everybody before they go for a website, well, they are going to ask for consent from everybody and they're going to ask for consent from a whole bunch of people who aren't consumers.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, it's going to be overbroad consent, no doubt. But you -- it's a very easy solution for these businesses going forward. And I get the retrospective liability, believe me. But going forward, it's a very easy solution to get consent, isn't it? That's a question. And maybe it's not easy. But --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I'd like --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- tell me the answer going forward.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. I mean, you did point to the two years of liability from the day you decide this case and all of that overhang, but to answer your specific question --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. Or put everything behind a pay wall. That would be great. But I guess what I would say is that --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, I think that's one way that people will try to deal with this. But, as to the question --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Can you answer --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- of whether consent is easy, the -- the statute's set up --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I'm sorry?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Oh, that -- that is --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So, I mean, the -- the problem is the pay wall issue, which is the reason that material is available for "free" on the Internet is precisely because it's being financed by targeted advertisement. And --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right. And --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I guess what I would say to try to answer the question, I'm just not sure the consent is going to be easy as you imagine. Certainly, Congress tried to make consent relatively sort of sticky and said that it had to be in a separate -- a separate formulation. It couldn't be with when you get consent to anything else. And, certainly, the way these cases have been litigated, people have argued that the consent, even when websites have tried to get consent, wasn't clear enough, wasn't unmistakable. That could get --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, that'll always be the argument. But it seems, just technologically, isn't it pretty easy for -- for you all to obtain consent going forward? It'll be a little more hassle for all of us, but --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: For everyone.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. But one --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I know you do that a thousand times a day. I will say that Congress, when it was --when it was setting up this statute, did try to provide the consent, informed written consent. It also said that it has to be provided in a clear and conspicuous manner for the consumer to withdraw on a case-by-case basis. So I -- I -- I think, look, I'm not telling you that it's impossible, but I don't think you should decide this case about the meaning of "consumer" on the assumption that consent is absolutely easy. And I do think what they would do, because they don't know who's a consumer because they don't know who bought a chicken sandwich or who bought a dog bandana, they're going to ask consent from everybody. And right there is a signal that something's off because the statute requires consent from the consumer to the disclosure of the consumer's information.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, the definition might have been under-inclusive back in the day given modern technology, the definition of "consumer." I mean, maybe the -- the real concern Congress had if you translate it to today would be everyone who views the video.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I don't know that that's the case. I mean, I think that's, you know, open to speculation. I mean, that's kind of lunacy. And that's why I think when you get to that kind of result you go back. And then, to the point of --

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A

The point is, though, it shouldn't turn on whether you also subscribed to a free online newsletter, a free email newsletter. See, the --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, here's what I think is an argument for my statute, which is it's undeniable that the statute turns on that happenstance, whether you get the chicken sandwich, whether you subscribe to the free email newsletter, and that doesn't make a lot of sense. So, under their theory, I can buy my chicken sandwich 10 years ago, I can buy my recliner 15 years ago, and then I don't watch a video on the website until a decade later. Congress would never write a statute like that. If they really expected people to be able to -- and I'll say it again --mix and match consumer status with personal information and video watching, they would have put some temporal limit that connected the two.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: And then --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yeah.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So there could be a gap in certain situations, but I think it's a very, like, narrow gap. I don't think you're going to have millions of consumers that are all of a sudden VPPA consumers. But it's also -- there is no gap in this sense. If the initial purchase is a video purchase or, I think, to be more precise, is a prerecorded video cassette tape or similar audiovisual material, there is, under the statute, an immediate opportunity to give advance consent for two years. And so that provision that was added in 2013, even in the somewhat funky hypo I think you're giving me, I mean, that -- that advance consent provision works sensibly from the get-go, whereas, under my friend's position, you could buy a dog bandana and then you could give advance consent to the disclosure of PII before there's any PII under his reading of the statute, and then five years later, when you finally have PII, your advance consent has already expired. And that just shows, like, every provision in this statute is -- makes sense if you tether what makes you a consumer to what generates PII in the first instance. And --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I don't think I'm carving it up more, and I think I'm doing exactly what Congress intended. And Congress -- you know, for those who read Senate reports, Congress focused on this possibility that you could have the department store and they would sell a couple of video tapes and they would sell a lot of -- bunch of other stuff, and they didn't think they wanted to protect the other goods and services. Now my friend will tell you, yeah, that piece of legislative history focused on the PII definition. But here's the thing: It would be pretty weird to have the thing in the statute that does the limiting work to be a definition that by its terms is expressly inclusive. That's not a well-designed tool to do limiting work. What is a well --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So, to me, it makes a ton of sense because what makes you a consumer is a transaction that generates personal identifiable information. And when you buy a book or a dog bandana, under both parties' view of the statute, that doesn't generate any personally identifiable --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: What I'm saying is, if there is a close connection between what makes you a consumer and what generates personally identifiable information, the whole statute, including the consent provisions, work coherently. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So you don't really --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It's both parties' agreed understanding of personally identifiable information until you get specific video information. And speaking of specific video information -- I don't want to sit down before I make this point -- my friend tries to make something of the fact that the word "video" appears in the personally identifiable information definition before the phrase "from a video tape service provider." And he says, aha, they know how to use it. But he ignores that they use two words. They didn't use "video." They used "specific video." And there's a very good reason they did that because there's another provision in the statute, (b)(2)(D), that allows the disclosure of general subject matter information about videos in certain circumstances. So "specific video" is doing work in the "personal identifiable information" definition that there's no analogue to in the definition of "consumer." And here's something else to consider. If you did what my friend wants you to do to make this an easier case, if Congress had put "video" in front of "goods or services," it would have gone a long way to making the phrase "from a video tape service provider" redundant. And my friend tells you we try to avoid redundancy if at all possible. But think of the way the statute works. In order to be a consumer, you have to rent, buy, or subscribe to a video. And if -- no matter what else your business does, if you rent, sell, or deliver videos, prerecorded videos, you are per force a video tape service provider. So, if you had a hypothetical statute that has the word that he wants in it, it said video goods and services from a video tape service provider, at that point, you have two options. Either you admit that "from a video tape service provider" is doing no work, or you do what you might do, which is to struggle to give it some meaning, you would say, ah, you know, there actually are some video goods or services that aren't actually prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials. So take, for example, a blank VCR tape. Now that's clearly a video good or service, but it's not prerecorded and it doesn't involve any personal identifiable information. So, in a hypothetical statute that had the word "video" where my friend wants it, you probably would look to "from a video tape service provider" to limit the scope of -- of video goods or services. But, if you can look to "from a video tape service provider" to limit the scope of video goods or services, I don't know why you can't look to it to limit the scope of goods or services. And I do think that is natural, ordinary meaning, as [PERSON] alluded to, but it also makes particular sense in a statute that's focused on privacy concerns that uniquely arise out of video transactions. Go back to the example I started with with goods or services from a medical service provider. Okay. In ordinary English, I don't think that covers buying a cup of coffee from the hospital. But, in a medical privacy statute, nobody cares whether I got, like, you know, half caf, but what they care about is whether I had an appendectomy or I had plastic surgery or something. So you would naturally in that context say that a consumer of goods or services from a medical service provider talks about people that got actual medical services, not people who got a valet parking service when they got to the -- the medical office. And that's what we're asking to you do here. And my friend's whole position really depends on reading three words in the definition in isolation. But it's a 15-word definition, and the other 12 words all direct you to audiovisual materials that are similar to prerecorded video cassettes because it starts with this triad of terms: Renter, buyer, or subscriber. Weird. It doesn't appear anywhere else in the U.S. Code, but it precisely captures the three ways that you got video tapes in 1988, and it starts with rental, which was the -- was the single most obvious way you would get video tapes in 1988. And then, if you carry through to the definition of a video tape service provider, you see the same triad. You see selling video tapes, renting video tapes, or delivering them. And it all works together as a harmonious whole. And I wouldn't just interpret those three words in splendid isolation and read them to the limits of the world.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I don't think it can mean, unfortunately -- it would help me win this case eventually -- if I thought it meant, like, predominantly or exclusively. But I think that's pretty impossible to square with the idea that Congress plainly wanted to capture department stores that sold videos back in 1988, grocery stores that sold videos in 1988. So I think that if you're engaged in the business, and, you know, there's a reference to interstate or foreign commerce, so I'm thinking they're casting a pretty wide net, and you deliver videos, it seems most naturally read -- and some of you are maybe suggesting I'm most -- not most naturally reading "consumer," but I actually think I'm most naturally reading all 15 words. But I think, most naturally read, this would capture Chick-fil-A, La-Z-Boy, all of these things, because they're certainly in business and they are delivering videos. Now, like, I don't want to put two feet on that because I could be back in some court arguing no, no, no, that, you know, it means something slightly different. But I think it's tough given that Congress clearly wanted to capture the -- the -- the -- the department stores and the grocery stores. And that's why I really think the most natural way to narrow this statute is to get the definition of "consumer" right and limit it to the consumers -- and, again, we're --we're talking about the (a)(4) definition. But the (a)(4) definition's kind of baked right in to the definition of "consumer." And that's why I think it would have been redundant if -- I mean, you know, just to make the redundancy point one more time, I mean, (a)(4) is already baked in and already says a prerecorded video cassette tape or similar audiovisual material. So I suppose what Congress could have said in the definition of "consumer" is consumer means any renter, purchaser, or subscriber of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials from a video tape service provider, which, of course, is a provider of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] In 1988, Congress addressed a specific problem with a tailored solution, protecting the personally identifiable information of consumers of video tape service providers. For years, the statute worked as designed. Personal protection of video --information of video consumers was protected, and there was virtually no litigation under this statute. Then, however, the plaintiffs' class action bar discovered the VPPA and its statutory and punitive damages. The key to their effort to repurpose the statute is the argument, the claim, that the statute's definition of "consumer" uses the phrase "goods or services" in an unmodified way, so one can become a consumer without ever having rented, purchased, or subscribed to a video. That argument fails at the threshold because the phrase "goods or services" is not unmodified in the statute, but it takes its meaning from the immediate surrounding text. And that immediately surrounding text makes clear that the relevant goods or services are the prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials that one could rent, purchase, subscribe to, from a video tape service provider. So just as one, when referring to goods or services from a medical service provider, would not logically refer to a cup of coffee or valet parking, when one refers to goods or services from a video tape service provider, one does not logically refer to chicken sandwiches or dog bandanas. The alternative of interpreting the statute to create a veritable army of VPPA consumers without any personal information to protect unless and until years or even decades later they watch a free video has nothing to recommend it and underscores that Petitioner is misreading the statute. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So, [PERSON], with all due respect to my friend, I think he gets there the exact same way you would get there in understanding that Chick-fil-A is in the business of delivering videos. It's the same thing. That's not what the website is mostly about, but there -- if you go to the website, the first thing you'll see is, like, a video starts playing. You don't even have to click on anything. It just starts playing. And that's the way that most websites work these days. And -- and most of the websites also have pixels because most of the reason you can get to free content, rather than being behind the pay wall, is because of targeted --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So, I mean, look --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Totally agree with you, [PERSON], as a common-sense matter. But here is I think a little bit of the problem, which is Congress did make it pretty clear that the department store, when it sells the video, is a video tape service provider even though, when it sells furniture and clothes and everything else, it's not a video tape service provider. And the way I think, you know, I would -- the way I understand my friend's position is, yeah, it's all well and good that 247Sports.com is mostly just a sports site, but, because there are videos on it, that's enough to get you in the business of delivering videos. And that's the same way the plaintiffs -- they might not have succeeded, but that's the same way the plaintiffs got to Chick-fil-A, La-Z-Boy, Folger's, Godiva chocolates, and, of course, every newspaper virtually, you know, lots of small newspapers, because all of those newspapers, you know, they're basically in the business of having websites that have news. Some of the news articles are accompanied by videos. And, of course, their theory is not that you become a consumer just by going to the website. That's kind of the weird thing about this theory. Their theory when they sue the newspapers is, well, not everybody that goes there is a consumer, but the people that actually still subscribe to the good old-fashioned paper that comes to your door, they are consumers because they bought a non-video or they subscribed to a non-video product. That gets them in the consumer door. And then maybe five years later, they go to the website --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- and see a video, and all of a sudden we're off to the races.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, it's sort of my job to focus on the easy hypotheticals.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But I think, if you --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, my -- my -- my job is to direct your attention to the easy hypotheticals, I would suppose. But, fair enough, your job is to direct to the harder hypotheticals. But I'm not sure there really are that many hard hypotheticals in the sense that we're not taking the position that if you do -- actually are in the business, you are a video tape service provider, that because you do lots of other things or the --or the rest, that you're not covered. And we think -- I mean, you know, I think we would take the position, though I think [PERSON] raises a good question about streaming services, but we would take the position that Netflix, when you go online to Netflix, that that might still be covered. So I think the core of the -- of the statute is still covered under our view. But what I think what we would say is that this notion that you can just mix --mix and match what makes you a consumer and what gives you the personally identifiable information that the statute protects for consumers, that mismatch doesn't make any sense. So a dog bandana --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I don't know if it's mixing and matching. It's following the definitions where they lead. So this definition says "goods and services." It doesn't say "audiovisual goods and services." Other definitions do have the modifier in them. That suggests that the fact that this definition does not have the modifier in it is especially important. And you -- you -- you can't get the modifier from the "from" clause because the "from" clause just tells you what -- where you're getting the goods and services from, but the goods and services are the goods and services not modified in any other way. So mixing and matching, there are three different definitions. You have to put them together. What you get, most naturally read, is the Petitioner's understanding of the statute.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, two things, [ADDRESS]. I mean, one, you know, sometimes when that's what you get, maybe you should take another look. And the premise of your question, of course, is that "from a video tape service provider" isn't doing any definitional work in the definition of "consumer." And I would just take issue with that. I mean, you know, "from a video tape service provider," "video tape service provider" is a defined term in the statute. If you plug that definition into the statute, then what you get is "consumer" means any renter, purchaser, or subscriber of goods or services from any person engaged in the business in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce of rental, sale, or delivery of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials. After I'm done plugging that into the statute, I'm left with the conclusion that the goods or service we're talking about here are prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That makes sense --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I guess what I would say is that, you know, no statute pursues its purpose to the ends of the earth. And, here, Congress was very clear that if you don't have a rental, purchaser, or subscription relationship, then you're not covered by this statute. And that's common ground between both parties.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That's because of the way the statute's written. And for those that look at legislative history, that also seems entirely consistent with what Congress said. Congress envisioned the possibility of a department store selling videos and other things, and they were quite clear that they didn't think there was privacy protection for the other things. And then I also --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But, with respect, I think, if Justice Breyer went into the same store, didn't buy the book but still looked at three videos in some cabin and didn't have to subscribe anything to do it, and the reporter asked the same question, he would still fit --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- he would --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right, right. But it's a perfect illustration of how the statute doesn't capture every disclosure of personal identifying information. It requires you to be a consumer. And, logically, the transaction that makes you a consumer is one that involves some personal identifying information. And what's illogical is that you become a consumer on day one, and then there's personal identifiable information doesn't catch up to you --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- until day -- until years later.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So a couple of things, [PERSON]. I mean, first of all, like, if you're going to tell me that I'm going to win on those other arguments, I mean, great. But we don't know that. My friend has -- you know, thinks that he has great arguments on both PII and on video tape service provider. I also don't think you can really get away from the definition of "video tape service provider" in interpreting the scope of "consumer" because that word, that defined word, is part of the definition of "consumer." But I also want to say there are distinct problems with this expansive definition of "consumer," and it really takes you away from the structure of the statute because this statute operates on the assumption that consumers are going to have personally identifiable information and they are going to be the ones -- the consumers are going to be in the position to consent to the disclosure of that information. And my friend's position breaks that structure of the statute because, even when he answers [PERSON] and says the way this is going to work is we're going to ask for consent from everybody before they go for a website, well, they are going to ask for consent from everybody and they're going to ask for consent from a whole bunch of people who aren't consumers.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I'd like --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. I mean, you did point to the two years of liability from the day you decide this case and all of that overhang, but to answer your specific question --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, this statutory language, you know, it is relatively clear. And you might have been -- be --be charged with having read it. And going forward, you have two very simple solutions. One is to get consent. Easy enough. People do it every day. And the other is to stop selling people's private information. Take your pick.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. Or put everything behind a pay wall. That would be great. But I guess what I would say is that --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Not the same thing.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, I think that's one way that people will try to deal with this. But, as to the question --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- of whether consent is easy, the -- the statute's set up --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I'm sorry?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Oh, that -- that is --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So, I mean, the -- the problem is the pay wall issue, which is the reason that material is available for "free" on the Internet is precisely because it's being financed by targeted advertisement. And --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right. And --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I guess what I would say to try to answer the question, I'm just not sure the consent is going to be easy as you imagine. Certainly, Congress tried to make consent relatively sort of sticky and said that it had to be in a separate -- a separate formulation. It couldn't be with when you get consent to anything else. And, certainly, the way these cases have been litigated, people have argued that the consent, even when websites have tried to get consent, wasn't clear enough, wasn't unmistakable. That could get --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: For everyone.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It's just one of those cookies boxes that comes up, right?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Wouldn't you do it the exact same way?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I mean, we do that a thousand times a day.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I know you do that a thousand times a day. I will say that Congress, when it was --when it was setting up this statute, did try to provide the consent, informed written consent. It also said that it has to be provided in a clear and conspicuous manner for the consumer to withdraw on a case-by-case basis. So I -- I -- I think, look, I'm not telling you that it's impossible, but I don't think you should decide this case about the meaning of "consumer" on the assumption that consent is absolutely easy. And I do think what they would do, because they don't know who's a consumer because they don't know who bought a chicken sandwich or who bought a dog bandana, they're going to ask consent from everybody. And right there is a signal that something's off because the statute requires consent from the consumer to the disclosure of the consumer's information.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I don't know that that's the case. I mean, I think that's, you know, open to speculation. But, as we point out in the brief, I think the one thing that's not open to speculation is that if Congress passes a statute to address the issues with targeted advertisement, they're not going to have coverage turn on the happenstance of where you bought a chicken sandwich or where you bought a dog bandana. I mean, that's kind of lunacy. And that's why I think when you get to that kind of result you go back. And then, to the point of --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But, Speaker A, take this -- the -- the -- the facts of this case, right? So I -- I don't know 247, but there's a sports site and somebody gets a newsletter, purchases a newsletter from that site.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It was a free newsletter, so they don't purchase it. It's free.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Just let's assume that they --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Just the way you sign up for, like, The New York Times.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- they purchase something from that site.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yep.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And then they watch a lot of videos. And let's say a judge does this. And then it turns out that the judge watches some pretty funky sports videos, you know, like a lot of women wrestling or something.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And that's embarrassing. That's embarrassing and exactly the way Congress thought we're passing this statute to prevent disclosure of that information. So why is it like this case? It kind of falls -- you know, a lot of times we get cases that they don't fall within the heartland of the statute, and we say, oh, well, the heartland of the statute isn't the whole statute. The paradigmatic case isn't the only case. But couldn't this case kind of be the paradigmatic case? It's like you can, like, watch lots of embarrassing sports videos that you don't want anybody else to know about. A judge could.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I mean, I think it's hard to watch a lot of embarrassing videos on 247Sports based on my perusal of it. But, like, you know, I don't know, maybe, like, watching, you know, Chicago Bears films is embarrassing in certain parts of the country. I don't know. Maybe it is embarrassing. The point is, though, it shouldn't turn on whether you also subscribed to a free online newsletter, a free email newsletter. See, the --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Maybe that's right. Maybe that's right. Maybe the thing that Congress should do as they look at this again is to take away that limitation. But -- but -- but that wouldn't really serve your purpose, would it? I mean, that's -- that's a limitation that works in your favor, and the fact that it excludes some people who might be embarrassed doesn't seem like an argument for your interpretation of the statute.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, here's what I think is an argument for my statute, which is it's undeniable that the statute turns on that happenstance, whether you get the chicken sandwich, whether you subscribe to the free email newsletter, and that doesn't make a lot of sense. And then the other thing that doesn't make a lot of sense is, because they've untethered the "consumer" definition from "personally identifying information" and from "video tape service provider," then you get the situation where there's no temporal connection whatsoever. So, under their theory, I can buy my chicken sandwich 10 years ago, I can buy my recliner 15 years ago, and then I don't watch a video on the website until a decade later. Congress would never write a statute like that. If they really expected people to be able to -- and I'll say it again --mix and match consumer status with personal information and video watching, they would have put some temporal limit that connected the two.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: And then --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yeah.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So there could be a gap in certain situations, but I think it's a very, like, narrow gap. I don't think you're going to have millions of consumers that are all of a sudden VPPA consumers. But it's also -- there is no gap in this sense. If the initial purchase is a video purchase or, I think, to be more precise, is a prerecorded video cassette tape or similar audiovisual material, there is, under the statute, an immediate opportunity to give advance consent for two years. And so that provision that was added in 2013, even in the somewhat funky hypo I think you're giving me, I mean, that -- that advance consent provision works sensibly from the get-go, whereas, under my friend's position, you could buy a dog bandana and then you could give advance consent to the disclosure of PII before there's any PII under his reading of the statute, and then five years later, when you finally have PII, your advance consent has already expired. And that just shows, like, every provision in this statute is -- makes sense if you tether what makes you a consumer to what generates PII in the first instance. And --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I don't think I'm carving it up more, and I think I'm doing exactly what Congress intended. And Congress -- you know, for those who read Senate reports, Congress focused on this possibility that you could have the department store and they would sell a couple of video tapes and they would sell a lot of -- bunch of other stuff, and they didn't think they wanted to protect the other goods and services. Now my friend will tell you, yeah, that piece of legislative history focused on the PII definition. But here's the thing: It would be pretty weird to have the thing in the statute that does the limiting work to be a definition that by its terms is expressly inclusive. That's not a well-designed tool to do limiting work. What is a well --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So, to me, it makes a ton of sense because what makes you a consumer is a transaction that generates personal identifiable information. And when you buy a book or a dog bandana, under both parties' view of the statute, that doesn't generate any personally identifiable --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: What I'm saying is, if there is a close connection between what makes you a consumer and what generates personally identifiable information, the whole statute, including the consent provisions, work coherently. And that's why I think Congress said that when you buy a video, you're a consumer, but when you buy a book or you buy gasoline or you buy a chicken sandwich, you're not a consumer because, at the moment you buy the book, the -- the chicken sandwich, the gasoline, there's no personally identifiable information.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So you don't really --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It's both parties' agreed understanding of personally identifiable information until you get specific video information. And speaking of specific video information -- I don't want to sit down before I make this point -- my friend tries to make something of the fact that the word "video" appears in the personally identifiable information definition before the phrase "from a video tape service provider." And he says, aha, they know how to use it. But he ignores that they use two words. They didn't use "video." They used "specific video." And there's a very good reason they did that because there's another provision in the statute, (b)(2)(D), that allows the disclosure of general subject matter information about videos in certain circumstances. So "specific video" is doing work in the "personal identifiable information" definition that there's no analogue to in the definition of "consumer." And here's something else to consider. If you did what my friend wants you to do to make this an easier case, if Congress had put "video" in front of "goods or services," it would have gone a long way to making the phrase "from a video tape service provider" redundant. And my friend tells you we try to avoid redundancy if at all possible. But think of the way the statute works. In order to be a consumer, you have to rent, buy, or subscribe to a video. And if -- no matter what else your business does, if you rent, sell, or deliver videos, prerecorded videos, you are per force a video tape service provider. So, if you had a hypothetical statute that has the word that he wants in it, it said video goods and services from a video tape service provider, at that point, you have two options. Either you admit that "from a video tape service provider" is doing no work, or you do what you might do, which is to struggle to give it some meaning, you would say, ah, you know, there actually are some video goods or services that aren't actually prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials. So take, for example, a blank VCR tape. Now that's clearly a video good or service, but it's not prerecorded and it doesn't involve any personal identifiable information. So, in a hypothetical statute that had the word "video" where my friend wants it, you probably would look to "from a video tape service provider" to limit the scope of -- of video goods or services. But, if you can look to "from a video tape service provider" to limit the scope of video goods or services, I don't know why you can't look to it to limit the scope of goods or services. And I do think that is natural, ordinary meaning, as [PERSON] alluded to, but it also makes particular sense in a statute that's focused on privacy concerns that uniquely arise out of video transactions. Go back to the example I started with with goods or services from a medical service provider. Okay. In ordinary English, I don't think that covers buying a cup of coffee from the hospital. But, in a medical privacy statute, nobody cares whether I got, like, you know, half caf, but what they care about is whether I had an appendectomy or I had plastic surgery or something. So you would naturally in that context say that a consumer of goods or services from a medical service provider talks about people that got actual medical services, not people who got a valet parking service when they got to the -- the medical office. And that's what we're asking to you do here. And my friend's whole position really depends on reading three words in the definition in isolation. But it's a 15-word definition, and the other 12 words all direct you to audiovisual materials that are similar to prerecorded video cassettes because it starts with this triad of terms: Renter, buyer, or subscriber. Weird. It doesn't appear anywhere else in the U.S. Code, but it precisely captures the three ways that you got video tapes in 1988, and it starts with rental, which was the -- was the single most obvious way you would get video tapes in 1988. And then, if you carry through to the definition of a video tape service provider, you see the same triad. You see selling video tapes, renting video tapes, or delivering them. And it all works together as a harmonious whole. And I wouldn't just interpret those three words in splendid isolation and read them to the limits of the world.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I don't think it can mean, unfortunately -- it would help me win this case eventually -- if I thought it meant, like, predominantly or exclusively. But I think that's pretty impossible to square with the idea that Congress plainly wanted to capture department stores that sold videos back in 1988, grocery stores that sold videos in 1988. So I think that if you're engaged in the business, and, you know, there's a reference to interstate or foreign commerce, so I'm thinking they're casting a pretty wide net, and you deliver videos, it seems most naturally read -- and some of you are maybe suggesting I'm most -- not most naturally reading "consumer," but I actually think I'm most naturally reading all 15 words. But I think, most naturally read, this would capture Chick-fil-A, La-Z-Boy, all of these things, because they're certainly in business and they are delivering videos. Now, like, I don't want to put two feet on that because I could be back in some court arguing no, no, no, that, you know, it means something slightly different. But I think it's tough given that Congress clearly wanted to capture the -- the -- the -- the department stores and the grocery stores. And that's why I really think the most natural way to narrow this statute is to get the definition of "consumer" right and limit it to the consumers -- and, again, we're --we're talking about the (a)(4) definition. But the (a)(4) definition's kind of baked right in to the definition of "consumer." And that's why I think it would have been redundant if -- I mean, you know, just to make the redundancy point one more time, I mean, (a)(4) is already baked in and already says a prerecorded video cassette tape or similar audiovisual material. So I suppose what Congress could have said in the definition of "consumer" is consumer means any renter, purchaser, or subscriber of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials from a video tape service provider, which, of course, is a provider of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But that would be hopelessly awkward and redundant. And it --it just underscores that if Congress had done both, it would have been redundant, and I think there was a perfectly good reason it left "goods or services" unmodified.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. I -- I must confess I did not understand it either. And I don't think it explains away Chick-fil-A. And just to put it in concrete terms, if you look at the complaint in this case, he alleges that there are over a hundred thousand subscribers to 247Sports.com that he wants to represent in a class action. Now I'm not great at math, but $2500 per plaintiff in a class action that includes at least a hundred thousand people, I think, is $250 million of liability in this case alone. And then you look at the Chamber brief and all those footnotes, you look at The Retail Litigation Center appendix and all of those cases, and there's a reason, I think, as you alluded to, that every district court judge that looks at this thinks this cannot be right, this is crazy. And I would suggest that a careful textual reading of all 15 words in this definition actually gets you to the result that, yes, it's not right.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
