And that's why I think Congress said that when you buy a video, you're a consumer, but when you buy a book or you buy gasoline or you buy a chicken sandwich, you're not a consumer because, at the moment you buy the book, the -- the chicken sandwich, the gasoline, there's no personally identifiable information.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So you don't really --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It's both parties' agreed understanding of personally identifiable information until you get specific video information. And speaking of specific video information -- I don't want to sit down before I make this point -- my friend tries to make something of the fact that the word "video" appears in the personally identifiable information definition before the phrase "from a video tape service provider." And he says, aha, they know how to use it. But he ignores that they use two words. They didn't use "video." They used "specific video." And there's a very good reason they did that because there's another provision in the statute, (b)(2)(D), that allows the disclosure of general subject matter information about videos in certain circumstances. So "specific video" is doing work in the "personal identifiable information" definition that there's no analogue to in the definition of "consumer." And here's something else to consider. If you did what my friend wants you to do to make this an easier case, if Congress had put "video" in front of "goods or services," it would have gone a long way to making the phrase "from a video tape service provider" redundant. And my friend tells you we try to avoid redundancy if at all possible. But think of the way the statute works. In order to be a consumer, you have to rent, buy, or subscribe to a video. And if -- no matter what else your business does, if you rent, sell, or deliver videos, prerecorded videos, you are per force a video tape service provider. So, if you had a hypothetical statute that has the word that he wants in it, it said video goods and services from a video tape service provider, at that point, you have two options. Either you admit that "from a video tape service provider" is doing no work, or you do what you might do, which is to struggle to give it some meaning, you would say, ah, you know, there actually are some video goods or services that aren't actually prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials. So take, for example, a blank VCR tape. Now that's clearly a video good or service, but it's not prerecorded and it doesn't involve any personal identifiable information. So, in a hypothetical statute that had the word "video" where my friend wants it, you probably would look to "from a video tape service provider" to limit the scope of -- of video goods or services. But, if you can look to "from a video tape service provider" to limit the scope of video goods or services, I don't know why you can't look to it to limit the scope of goods or services. And I do think that is natural, ordinary meaning, as [PERSON] alluded to, but it also makes particular sense in a statute that's focused on privacy concerns that uniquely arise out of video transactions. Go back to the example I started with with goods or services from a medical service provider. Okay. In ordinary English, I don't think that covers buying a cup of coffee from the hospital. But, in a medical privacy statute, nobody cares whether I got, like, you know, half caf, but what they care about is whether I had an appendectomy or I had plastic surgery or something. So you would naturally in that context say that a consumer of goods or services from a medical service provider talks about people that got actual medical services, not people who got a valet parking service when they got to the -- the medical office. And that's what we're asking to you do here. And my friend's whole position really depends on reading three words in the definition in isolation. But it's a 15-word definition, and the other 12 words all direct you to audiovisual materials that are similar to prerecorded video cassettes because it starts with this triad of terms: Renter, buyer, or subscriber. Weird. It doesn't appear anywhere else in the U.S. Code, but it precisely captures the three ways that you got video tapes in 1988, and it starts with rental, which was the -- was the single most obvious way you would get video tapes in 1988. And then, if you carry through to the definition of a video tape service provider, you see the same triad. You see selling video tapes, renting video tapes, or delivering them. And it all works together as a harmonious whole. And I wouldn't just interpret those three words in splendid isolation and read them to the limits of the world.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I don't think it can mean, unfortunately -- it would help me win this case eventually -- if I thought it meant, like, predominantly or exclusively. But I think that's pretty impossible to square with the idea that Congress plainly wanted to capture department stores that sold videos back in 1988, grocery stores that sold videos in 1988. So I think that if you're engaged in the business, and, you know, there's a reference to interstate or foreign commerce, so I'm thinking they're casting a pretty wide net, and you deliver videos, it seems most naturally read -- and some of you are maybe suggesting I'm most -- not most naturally reading "consumer," but I actually think I'm most naturally reading all 15 words. But I think, most naturally read, this would capture Chick-fil-A, La-Z-Boy, all of these things, because they're certainly in business and they are delivering videos. Now, like, I don't want to put two feet on that because I could be back in some court arguing no, no, no, that, you know, it means something slightly different. But I think it's tough given that Congress clearly wanted to capture the -- the -- the -- the department stores and the grocery stores. And that's why I really think the most natural way to narrow this statute is to get the definition of "consumer" right and limit it to the consumers -- and, again, we're --we're talking about the (a)(4) definition. But the (a)(4) definition's kind of baked right in to the definition of "consumer." And that's why I think it would have been redundant if -- I mean, you know, just to make the redundancy point one more time, I mean, (a)(4) is already baked in and already says a prerecorded video cassette tape or similar audiovisual material. So I suppose what Congress could have said in the definition of "consumer" is consumer means any renter, purchaser, or subscriber of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials from a video tape service provider, which, of course, is a provider of prerecorded video cassette tapes or similar audiovisual materials.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But that would be hopelessly awkward and redundant. And it --it just underscores that if Congress had done both, it would have been redundant, and I think there was a perfectly good reason it left "goods or services" unmodified.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. I -- I must confess I did not understand it either. And I don't think it explains away Chick-fil-A. And just to put it in concrete terms, if you look at the complaint in this case, he alleges that there are over a hundred thousand subscribers to 247Sports.com that he wants to represent in a class action. Now I'm not great at math, but $2500 per plaintiff in a class action that includes at least a hundred thousand people, I think, is $250 million of liability in this case alone. And then you look at the Chamber brief and all those footnotes, you look at The Retail Litigation Center appendix and all of those cases, and there's a reason, I think, as you alluded to, that every district court judge that looks at this thinks this cannot be right, this is crazy. And I would suggest that a careful textual reading of all 15 words in this definition actually gets you to the result that, yes, it's not right.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I do think there is a fundamental difference between having PII without a consumer and having a consumer that has no PII. Now, as we point out in our brief --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: No, no --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: No, what I'm saying is, actually, under his view as I understand it, if you go into the Blockbuster, the last one, the brick-and-mortar store, you buy your dog bandana, and then you never look at the Blockbuster website, then you are a consumer in his view, but you have no PII. You are an inchoate VPPA consumer. And I think that is far more anomalous than --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, you don't have to buy anything. And that's another anomaly. I don't think that makes any sense. turns_pm60.speaker: B

I mean, your bandanas or your La-Z-Boys, do you think that there's no requirement that the person have requested or obtained video materials or services?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, it's tricky, right, because, if we're going to be literal, I mean, "includes" --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, I want to -- I want to know what you -- you think.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Does it include bandanas and La-Z-Boys?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I would say that it doesn't. But it's hard to get there from a literal reading of the text because the textual definition is just an "includes" definition. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So, if you -- yeah.

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.text: We did. But you know the funny thing about standing arguments, you can't really drop them.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yeah, and maybe that's one more reason to not decide the standing question definitively without more briefing because I do think there is a close relationship between the standing question and the PII question. case: Maxwell v. Dinis
setting: Excerpt from a recorded institutional proceeding. Exactly one of the two speakers, A and B, holds the more powerful institutional role.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: Exhaustion. Absolutely. So we agree that exhaustion is a live issue for remand. In fact, Mr. Maxwell sought to appeal the exhaustion issue, and it was the Fifth Circuit that sua sponte dismissed the case instead on the ground of habeas. turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: Which you could make on remand and not have anything to do with this case. In other words, these issues, exhaustion and, I mean, I guess mootness is here, but the 3621(b) and exhaustion issues are separate and they -- they weren't really litigated below. Is that correct?

turns_same_span.text: Let me ask you about the rule statement that you put forward. turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: That's completely fair, Speaker B. We're happy with a narrow rule here. I think our basic submission is a challenge to a distinct and lower level of custody is cognizable. turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] Mr. Maxwell's claim in this case is that he's being held in prison in violation of federal law because the First Step Act requires his release from prison and transfer to home confinement or to a halfway house. That is a distinct and lower level of custody. That claim falls squarely within the text of the federal habeas statute because it asserts that Respondent, the Warden of Mr. Maxwell's prison, is holding him "in custody in violation of the laws of the United States." It also falls within the core historical province of the Great Writ. And it is materially indistinguishable from this Court's decision in Preiser against Rodriguez, which held that claims seeking release from prison to parole must be brought in habeas. The Fifth Circuit dismissed Mr. Maxwell's case on the ground that habeas is only available where a prisoner seeks complete release. No one defends that rule here. The government, as Respondent, agrees that habeas is the appropriate vehicle and, despite gesturing at a few supposed off-ramps, supports vacatur of the decision below. Even amicus appointed to defend the judgment below does not endeavor to defend the reasoning of the Fifth Circuit. Instead, amicus acknowledges that habeas is available for some level-of-custody claims, but he argues not for Mr. Maxwell's claim here. Amicus's efforts to limit habeas finds no footing in statutory text or in history, and he offers no principled basis for distinguishing the types of claims that are in from those that are out. Perhaps most starkly, amicus cannot distinguish FSA prerelease custody from parole given the legal and practical similarities between the two. Congress put transfer to prerelease custody for prisoners to earn good-time credits at the heart of the First Step Act. When a warden fails to release a prisoner under that authority, habeas is available. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Absolutely, [PERSON]. Happy to address both. To start with the 3621(b) argument, the government, in its brief, raised the possibility that there's a judicial review bar. But that argument -- that provision does not apply to the claims in this case. 3621(b) says not -- a designation of a place of imprisonment under this subsection is not reviewable in any court. That's a determination under 3621(b). Mr. Maxwell's claim in this case is not a challenge to anything the BOP did under 3621(b). It is an assertion under 3624(g) and 3634(d)(4) -- (d)(4)(C), which is the right to be transferred, not BOP's discretionary decision. And I think that the --the First Step Act very clearly treats that as its own distinct form of release. In particular, you can look at 3624(g)(2) and 3624(g)(4) that talk about prisoners placed in prerelease custody pursuant to this subsection as in 3624. So it is a different authority. And we're not invoking the 3621(b). Now, to the extent that the ultimate decision as to which halfway house, Halfway House A or B, still goes through 3621(b), I think that itself is not clear because I think there are regulations that are supposed to adopt the 3621(b) standards pursuant to 3624(c)(6). But, even assuming that is the case, all that means is that Mr. Maxwell cannot dispute being placed in Halfway House A versus Halfway House B, not that he somehow has no ability to obtain judicial review of the decision under a different provision. And the government's cross-reference argument cannot possibly be right because BOP always designates the place of imprisonment under 3621(b), but nobody thinks that a prisoner cannot challenge whether he's sent to prison, whether his conviction is invalid, just because the last step of the determination is which particular prison. And you also asked about mootness, [PERSON]. The -- this case is currently not moot because Mr. Maxwell is in custody, but, in the event the government releases him before the opinion in this case issues, it also would not be moot. So the -- in -- whether he is in custody under 2241 is, of course, measured at the outset of the case. So all that is required at this point is that there be a cognizable case or controversy, that there be some meaningful relief. That is satisfied here because the restoration of Mr. Maxwell's good-time credits, he would argue that that should reduce his time on supervised release because the First Step Act provides that good-time credits can be used towards supervised release, and the Ninth Circuit has held that means it can be used to reduce the term of supervised release. Now I acknowledge there's a circuit conflict on that issue. There is, in fact, a pending cert petition before you about that. But the test for mootness isn't whether you are persuaded by that argument at this stage. Under Chafin versus Chafin, the question is just whether it's not in a substantial argument. It's plainly not in a substantial argument. So a live controversy will remain.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] Mr. Maxwell's claim in this case is that he's being held in prison in violation of federal law because the First Step Act requires his release from prison and transfer to home confinement or to a halfway house. That is a distinct and lower level of custody. That claim falls squarely within the text of the federal habeas statute because it asserts that Respondent, the Warden of Mr. Maxwell's prison, is holding him "in custody in violation of the laws of the United States." It also falls within the core historical province of the Great Writ. And it is materially indistinguishable from this Court's decision in Preiser against Rodriguez, which held that claims seeking release from prison to parole must be brought in habeas. The Fifth Circuit dismissed Mr. Maxwell's case on the ground that habeas is only available where a prisoner seeks complete release. No one defends that rule here. The government, as Respondent, agrees that habeas is the appropriate vehicle and, despite gesturing at a few supposed off-ramps, supports vacatur of the decision below. Even amicus appointed to defend the judgment below does not endeavor to defend the reasoning of the Fifth Circuit. Instead, amicus acknowledges that habeas is available for some level-of-custody claims, but he argues not for Mr. Maxwell's claim here. Amicus's efforts to limit habeas finds no footing in statutory text or in history, and he offers no principled basis for distinguishing the types of claims that are in from those that are out. Perhaps most starkly, amicus cannot distinguish FSA prerelease custody from parole given the legal and practical similarities between the two. Congress put transfer to prerelease custody for prisoners to earn good-time credits at the heart of the First Step Act. And we're not invoking the 3621(b). turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] Federal prisoners typically want two things: better, less restrictive conditions of confinement and earlier release from custody. If Petitioner wins this lawsuit, his term of imprisonment won't be shortened by even a single day, and he will remain subject to control by the Bureau of Prisons. Under the plain terms of this statutory regime, prerelease custody isn't release, and home confinement is a form of confinement. Petitioner isn't suing for release but for a change in the location where he will serve the remainder of his prison sentence. That places this case on the conditions of confinement side of the line and makes habeas the wrong vehicle for Petitioner's claim. The parties treat as self-evident the difference between incarceration in a prison on the one hand and a halfway house or home confinement on the other. But the reality of the federal prison system isn't so simple. A federal prisoner moving from a prison camp to a halfway house may be moving from one facility with dormitory-style housing and no perimeter fence that he leaves to work off site to another facility with all those same attributes. A move between two such facilities is not the sort of quantum change in the level of custody that Preiser and its progeny place at the core of habeas corpus. For that reason, Petitioner's claim to entitlement to credits under the First Step Act may be pursued, if at all, only as a civil rights claim. The Court should affirm the Fifth Circuit's judgment. And I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Would you explain a bit more as to why prerelease is different from other forms of conditional custody?

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: I think the principal difference, Speaker B, is that with prerelease custody --

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: I'm sorry, not conditional custody. Conditional release.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: I under -- if I understand the -- [ADDRESS]'s question correctly --

turns_pm15.text: Yeah.

turns_pm15.text: Exactly.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: I think the principal distinction is the -- the fact that with a prisoner who's in prerelease custody, they're still under the ultimate control of the Bureau of Prisons. That's the -- the fundamental distinction that this Court drew in the Koray case in a related context, and I think it's a very important distinction. And -- and just to think about two -- two people who are in the same halfway house, subject to the same rules in the halfway house, the one that's in prerelease custody, that person, if they violate the rules, they commit a serious infraction of the rules in the halfway house, they're going to get routed through the Bureau of Prisons' process. It's ultimately going to be a disciplinary hearing officer in the Bureau of Prisons that's deciding what the consequences of that rules violation will be. The same situation, but if you have someone in supervised release, in contrast, that's something that's going to be an issue for the probation office, and, ultimately, that will go to a federal district judge, the sentencing court. And --

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Parole, [ADDRESS], doesn't exist in the federal system.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: That's --

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: That's correct. It was an agency within the executive branch, but it was a distinct body. You -- you did not have, with the old federal parole system, a situation where people were being released on parole and it was literally the same prison officials who were deciding, you know, which of multiple prisons someone would serve their time of incarceration in also deciding what to do about somebody violating the conditions of their parole. And so I think it's really important here to focus on that fact that you have literally the same government officials who are designating a place of incarceration across the federal prison system and who are overseeing the people who are in prerelease custody. Another point I'd make here that I think is quite significant is that the federal escape statute has been understood to apply to people who are in prerelease custody. Somebody who's serving the remainder of their time in prison -- of incarceration in a halfway house or on home confinement, if they walk away and they're in prerelease custody, they could be prosecuted for escape the same way that a prisoner who escapes from a federal prison can be prosecuted for escape. That's not true for somebody who's on supervised release. And so that's another way in which these two categories are -- are -- are different and distinct in -- in important ways. And then the last point I'd make is that the restraints on liberty in the mine run of cases are going to be quite different for someone who's on parole or supervised release on the one hand versus in prerelease custody on the other. Now, admittedly, there's overlap. You can have people in supervised release who are basically detained in the same halfway house as someone who's in prerelease custody. But that's -- that's the exception. Typically, kind of the core -- there's a core concept of what parole is or what supervised release is, and, typically, these are people who are able to come and go from -- from where they live as they please. They're not required to get permission to sign out from -- from where they live or only permitted to -- to leave their place where they live for very specific, specified reasons. So that's another way in which this is -- the -- the prerelease custody is just fundamentally and, I think, categorically different.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Yes, [ADDRESS]. And I agree with the government that someone moving from medium to minimum security can't bring a habeas claim. I think that follows from this Court's --

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Yeah. I -- I do think one consequence is the next case you're going to hear is a case where somebody is saying, I'm entitled to be moved from a medium-or a low-security prison to a prison camp. Prison camps look, I think, as a factual matter, in a lot of relevant ways quite similar to the typical halfway house. And so that -- that is something to -- to really worry about. I -- I take the government's response to that largely to just rely on labeling. They say, well, it's obvious that one of these facilities is "a prison" and the other is not. But I would submit that it's not that obvious when we look at a statutory regime that contemplates people serving a term of imprisonment in a halfway house or on a --

turns_pm15.text: I think --

turns_same_span.text: But it used to? It wasn't BOP, but it was a similar --it was an agency. It was a --

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: That's --

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: -- agency within the executive branch.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: That's correct. It was an agency within the executive branch, but it was a distinct body. You -- you did not have, with the old federal parole system, a situation where people were being released on parole and it was literally the same prison officials who were deciding, you know, which of multiple prisons someone would serve their time of incarceration in also deciding what to do about somebody violating the conditions of their parole. And so I think it's really important here to focus on that fact that you have literally the same government officials who are designating a place of incarceration across the federal prison system and who are overseeing the people who are in prerelease custody. Another point I'd make here that I think is quite significant is that the federal escape statute has been understood to apply to people who are in prerelease custody. Somebody who's serving the remainder of their time in prison -- of incarceration in a halfway house or on home confinement, if they walk away and they're in prerelease custody, they could be prosecuted for escape the same way that a prisoner who escapes from a federal prison can be prosecuted for escape. That's not true for somebody who's on supervised release. And so that's another way in which these two categories are -- are -- are different and distinct in -- in important ways. And then the last point I'd make is that the restraints on liberty in the mine run of cases are going to be quite different for someone who's on parole or supervised release on the one hand versus in prerelease custody on the other. Now, admittedly, there's overlap. You can have people in supervised release who are basically detained in the same halfway house as someone who's in prerelease custody. But that's -- that's the exception. Typically, kind of the core -- there's a core concept of what parole is or what supervised release is, and, typically, these are people who are able to come and go from -- from where they live as they please. They're not required to get permission to sign out from -- from where they live or only permitted to -- to leave their place where they live for very specific, specified reasons. So that's another way in which this is -- the -- the prerelease custody is just fundamentally and, I think, categorically different.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] Federal prisoners typically want two things: better, less restrictive conditions of confinement and earlier release from custody. If Petitioner wins this lawsuit, his term of imprisonment won't be shortened by even a single day, and he will remain subject to control by the Bureau of Prisons. Under the plain terms of this statutory regime, prerelease custody isn't release, and home confinement is a form of confinement. Petitioner isn't suing for release but for a change in the location where he will serve the remainder of his prison sentence. That places this case on the conditions of confinement side of the line and makes habeas the wrong vehicle for Petitioner's claim. The parties treat as self-evident the difference between incarceration in a prison on the one hand and a halfway house or home confinement on the other. But the reality of the federal prison system isn't so simple. A federal prisoner moving from a prison camp to a halfway house may be moving from one facility with dormitory-style housing and no perimeter fence that he leaves to work off site to another facility with all those same attributes. A move between two such facilities is not the sort of quantum change in the level of custody that Preiser and its progeny place at the core of habeas corpus. For that reason, Petitioner's claim to entitlement to credits under the First Step Act may be pursued, if at all, only as a civil rights claim. The Court should affirm the Fifth Circuit's judgment. And I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: I think the principal difference, [PERSON], is that with prerelease custody --

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: I under -- if I understand the -- [ADDRESS]'s question correctly --

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: -- the -- it's the distinction between prerelease custody and supervised release or parole.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: I think the principal distinction is the -- the fact that with a prisoner who's in prerelease custody, they're still under the ultimate control of the Bureau of Prisons. That's the -- the fundamental distinction that this Court drew in the Koray case in a related context, and I think it's a very important distinction. And -- and just to think about two -- two people who are in the same halfway house, subject to the same rules in the halfway house, the one that's in prerelease custody, that person, if they violate the rules, they commit a serious infraction of the rules in the halfway house, they're going to get routed through the Bureau of Prisons' process. It's ultimately going to be a disciplinary hearing officer in the Bureau of Prisons that's deciding what the consequences of that rules violation will be. The same situation, but if you have someone in supervised release, in contrast, that's something that's going to be an issue for the probation office, and, ultimately, that will go to a federal district judge, the sentencing court. And --

turns_pm15.text: And parole?

turns_pm15.text: Parole, [ADDRESS], doesn't exist in the federal system.

turns_pm15.text: -- agency within the executive branch.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Yes, [ADDRESS]. And I agree with the government that someone moving from medium to minimum security can't bring a habeas claim. I think that follows from this Court's --

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Yeah. turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: I think --

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Yeah, I guess what I'd say to that, [PERSON], is maybe worry less about the future habeas case where somebody is invoking a federal statutory right to be moved between prison facilities and worry more about sort of the due process type of claim that's pernicious.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: The -- the Meachum case rejects the due process claim. turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Yeah. [PERSON], I think the Court fundamentally needs to draw a line in one of two places. I would just note that the -- the Congress here, it has drawn a line between prerelease custody and just generally being in prison, but it's also drawn, I would submit, a sharper line between prerelease custody on the one hand and supervised release on the other. And this claim belongs on the conditions-of-confinement side of the line, but however the Court decides this case, it's not going to change the fundamental reality that, you know, to the extent there's confusion about, you know, if a prisoner wants to bring a complaint, you know, complaining about the overcrowding in his -- in his prison cell or about the food that he's being served in prison, think of a classic conditions-of-confinement claim, that's -- there's going to be this analytical problem of figuring out what the right cause of action is for the federal prisoner to use. turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Because -- for several reasons. One, parole involves a --

turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] Federal prisoners typically want two things: better, less restrictive conditions of confinement and earlier release from custody. If Petitioner wins this lawsuit, his term of imprisonment won't be shortened by even a single day, and he will remain subject to control by the Bureau of Prisons. Under the plain terms of this statutory regime, prerelease custody isn't release, and home confinement is a form of confinement. Petitioner isn't suing for release but for a change in the location where he will serve the remainder of his prison sentence. That places this case on the conditions of confinement side of the line and makes habeas the wrong vehicle for Petitioner's claim. The parties treat as self-evident the difference between incarceration in a prison on the one hand and a halfway house or home confinement on the other. But the reality of the federal prison system isn't so simple. A federal prisoner moving from a prison camp to a halfway house may be moving from one facility with dormitory-style housing and no perimeter fence that he leaves to work off site to another facility with all those same attributes. A move between two such facilities is not the sort of quantum change in the level of custody that Preiser and its progeny place at the core of habeas corpus. For that reason, Petitioner's claim to entitlement to credits under the First Step Act may be pursued, if at all, only as a civil rights claim. The Court should affirm the Fifth Circuit's judgment. And I welcome the Court's questions.

It's ultimately going to be a disciplinary hearing officer in the Bureau of Prisons that's deciding what the consequences of that rules violation will be. Now, admittedly, there's overlap. You can have people in supervised release who are basically detained in the same halfway house as someone who's in prerelease custody. turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Thank you, [ADDRESS] Pleading an affirmative defense is ordinarily a precondition for invoking that defense to bar or limit a claim. Kontrick held that ordinarily, under the civil rules, a defense is lost if it's not included in an amended plain -- complaint -- in an amended defense or in the original defense. There's no reason to depart in this case from those established rules. The Eleventh Circuit's Hassan decision improperly permits a defendant to invoke an affirmative defense which it has never pled. It has several fatal flaws. First, it effectively rewrites Rules 8 and 12 to create categories of affirmative defenses that do not have to be pled, despite the fact that the plain text of those rules provide that any affirmative defense and every affirmative defense must be pled. Secondly, if a defendant has not yet included an affirmative defense in its answer and the deadline under a scheduling order for amending the answer has passed, a defendant would normally have to meet the good cause standard in Rule 16(b)(4). But, under Hassan, a defendant can -- is exempt itself from that rule simply by moving for summary judgment. Third, where a defendant has inadvertently omitted an affirmative defense, Rules 15(a)(2) and 16(b)(4) establish the standard for nonetheless raising that affirmative defense. Hassan substitutes a no-prejudice standard for that. In addition, in -- in its justifications for the Hassan rule or some version of it, the defendant has offered arguments that reach far beyond just the question of what happens with an unpled affirmative defense and raises a host of issues about the -- about the issue -- the standards that would emerge. A ruling for us would simply apply the established rules and -- and standards in Rules 15(a)(2) and 16(b)(4). It would not require the Court to become embroiled in fashioning new standards, as was aired in the previous case. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.text: Thank you, [ADDRESS] Pleading an affirmative defense is ordinarily a precondition for invoking that defense to bar or limit a claim. Kontrick held that ordinarily, under the civil rules, a defense is lost if it's not included in an amended plain -- complaint -- in an amended defense or in the original defense. First, it effectively rewrites Rules 8 and 12 to create categories of affirmative defenses that do not have to be pled, despite the fact that the plain text of those rules provide that any affirmative defense and every affirmative defense must be pled. Third, where a defendant has inadvertently omitted an affirmative defense, Rules 15(a)(2) and 16(b)(4) establish the standard for nonetheless raising that affirmative defense. Hassan substitutes a no-prejudice standard for that. A ruling for us would simply apply the established rules and -- and standards in Rules 15(a)(2) and 16(b)(4). It would not require the Court to become embroiled in fashioning new standards, as was aired in the previous case. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] Petitioner Younge's Title VII claim fails because, as her own testimony helped to establish, she was undisputably personal staff to an elected official. That includes Rule 61, but it also includes the numerous rules that provide specific consequences like waiver, like bars on raising arguments from 12(h) to 71.1, 72(a). turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] Petitioner Younge's Title VII claim fails because, as her own testimony helped to establish, she was undisputably personal staff to an elected official. Now, to be sure, the DA's office mistakenly failed to plead this defense in its answer. But the failure to comply with the pleading rules and the consequences for that mistake are two separate issues. And nothing in the federal rules holds, not 15 or 16 or anything else, that the consequence for this type of pleading mistake is that a litigant cannot raise a legal argument at summary judgment on an undisputable record where there's no prejudice to the plaintiff because nothing would have been materially different without the mistake. To the contrary, the text, structure, background principles support a prejudice test, a strict prejudice test but a prejudice test in these circumstances. That includes Rule 61, but it also includes the numerous rules that provide specific consequences like waiver, like bars on raising arguments from 12(h) to 71.1, 72(a). And conspicuously missing here is anything like that. And that silence is especially compelling because the rules used to provide that a defendant waives all defenses and objections not included in the answer. But that was removed in 1966. Younge would reinsert that atextually into the rules. Younge essentially insists that a defendant must first amend the pleadings to raise a legal argument at summary judgment. But that's not just wrong. It misunderstands what pleadings are and what they do. They provide notice of factual issues to be worked out, discovered, investigated, and ultimately tried. But legal arguments are the province of motions. And so demanding an amendment here, where the record is already set, would be empty paper-shuffling. That's what the prejudice test got you to. We have a record. What's the right answer? I think the Court should affirm. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_same_span.speaker: B

I mean, my understanding is that there are many religious schools that the -- the -- not only does the State seek to have religious schools as a part of this program but that many religious schools even in the same faith have chosen to participate, have followed the mandate. So what -- what do we do with that?

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: Mm- hmm. [ADDRESS], I think it's telling that neither of the courts below found the -- the argument compelling. And this is at JA 155. But, essentially, the testimony from the superintendent of Catholic schools was that Catholic Charities, which operates these Head Start programs, which do participate in the program, they have a very different mission and ministry. Their ministry is to serve those most in need. So you can think of that akin to Catholic Charities running a soup kitchen. They don't ask people if they're Catholic.

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: They're the ones that are in the program?

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: They're the ones that are in the program, [ADDRESS].

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: Mm-hmm.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: And on the flip side, you have parish preschools, and the role of the parish preschools is different. They have a different mission. Their mission is to support parents in the Catholic education of their children. And so they -- they ask all families who seek to enroll to affirm in good faith the statement of community beliefs.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] The Archdiocese of Denver schools exist to pass on the faith to the next generation. To do this, they ask all families who enroll to be open to and supportive of the church's teachings. Because of this sincere religious exercise, the State has denied Colorado families the ability to use Universal Preschool funding at Catholic schools. Under this Court's public benefits cases, that triggers strict scrutiny. The Tenth Circuit was wrong to cabin that precedent that this Court reaffirmed in Carson to explicit religious exclusions only. That can't be reconciled with Sherbert, [PERSON], or Mahmoud. Nor can it be reconciled with this Court's instruction in Carson to look to the operation and the effect of the law, not for magic words. After rejecting Carson, the Tenth Circuit applied Smith, but this too was wrong. When Colorado allows over a thousand schools to turn families away for a variety of different reasons, it has created a flexible and customizable program, nothing like the generally applicable across-the-board laws that Smith envisioned. And Colorado's inconsistent and contradictory arguments further confirm the State's actions are anything but generally applicable. Colorado has flexibly interpreted the mandate to accommodate important secular interests, but it's called the same law a hard limit when Petitioners sought a religious accommodation. And Colorado has discretion via the catch-all exemption to permit preschools to organize around "specific competencies or interests" and to serve "specific communities." Yet it has refused to extend that flexible treatment to Petitioners. Finally, this is not a zero-sum game. Letting families use Universal Preschool funding at Catholic schools won't take away a single seat from the over 2,000 preschools already participating in the program. In fact, letting Catholic schools in will create more seats for everyone, even for families who disagree with Catholic teachings. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: I think the rule this Court applied in Carson when it discussed Sherbert and [PERSON] is on all fours with this case. Both Sherbert and [PERSON] involved facially neutral laws, and that's my understanding of where this Court derived the public benefits rule it applied in Carson. I would also look to the holding that this Court articulated at the end of its opinion in Carson, which says, "Regardless of how the benefit and restriction are described, the program operates to identify and exclude otherwise eligible schools on the basis of their religious exercise." So that's how I understand this Court's decision in Carson. And I also think the focus of the way that this Court resolved Carson was to look at, you know, what is happening to the religious believer? It didn't focus on the text of the law in Maine. It focused on whether schools are being excluded on account of their religious exercise.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS], a few points. I don't think we're actually asking for a very broad principle. And I think it is the principle that this Court articulated previously in Sherbert and [PERSON] and then reaffirmed in Mahmoud. In all three of those cases, the law on its face was neutral. But, to also talk about the scope of this rule, when we're talking about public benefits, it's -- it's a relatively small category of things we're talking about. This Court has applied the public benefits precedent when we're talking about welfare benefits and education funding predominantly, and I don't think this rule would -- would change much beyond that.

And -- and whatever is cited there, you know, oh, look, there's a citation to Sherbert, Carson really followed from those two other cases or -- or, you know, the Court understood it that way, and it was a nondiscrimination principle. It was religious people are not being treated the same way as non-religious people here in each of those three cases. And I think what you're asking us to do is something far beyond that. It's saying, even though religious people are being treated the same way -- and this puts aside Question 1 a little bit, you know, where you have some argument on -- on the neutrality front, but -- but I just want to focus on your main argument, which is, even though religious people are being treated the same way on the face of the statute, that's not enough. turns_same_span.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] The Archdiocese of Denver schools exist to pass on the faith to the next generation. To do this, they ask all families who enroll to be open to and supportive of the church's teachings. Because of this sincere religious exercise, the State has denied Colorado families the ability to use Universal Preschool funding at Catholic schools. Under this Court's public benefits cases, that triggers strict scrutiny. The Tenth Circuit was wrong to cabin that precedent that this Court reaffirmed in Carson to explicit religious exclusions only. That can't be reconciled with Sherbert, [PERSON], or Mahmoud. Nor can it be reconciled with this Court's instruction in Carson to look to the operation and the effect of the law, not for magic words. After rejecting Carson, the Tenth Circuit applied Smith, but this too was wrong. When Colorado allows over a thousand schools to turn families away for a variety of different reasons, it has created a flexible and customizable program, nothing like the generally applicable across-the-board laws that Smith envisioned. And Colorado's inconsistent and contradictory arguments further confirm the State's actions are anything but generally applicable. Colorado has flexibly interpreted the mandate to accommodate important secular interests, but it's called the same law a hard limit when Petitioners sought a religious accommodation. And Colorado has discretion via the catch-all exemption to permit preschools to organize around "specific competencies or interests" and to serve "specific communities." Yet it has refused to extend that flexible treatment to Petitioners. Finally, this is not a zero-sum game. Letting families use Universal Preschool funding at Catholic schools won't take away a single seat from the over 2,000 preschools already participating in the program. In fact, letting Catholic schools in will create more seats for everyone, even for families who disagree with Catholic teachings. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] The Archdiocese of Denver schools exist to pass on the faith to the next generation. Nor can it be reconciled with this Court's instruction in Carson to look to the operation and the effect of the law, not for magic words. After rejecting Carson, the Tenth Circuit applied Smith, but this too was wrong. When Colorado allows over a thousand schools to turn families away for a variety of different reasons, it has created a flexible and customizable program, nothing like the generally applicable across-the-board laws that Smith envisioned. Colorado has flexibly interpreted the mandate to accommodate important secular interests, but it's called the same law a hard limit when Petitioners sought a religious accommodation. Letting families use Universal Preschool funding at Catholic schools won't take away a single seat from the over 2,000 preschools already participating in the program. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, just to interrupt for a moment, would it not in your view apply to things like driver's licenses, employment benefits, Social Security? I'm not quite sure how you limit the applicability of your principle.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. [ADDRESS], I think it would apply to situations where the government is subsidizing private conduct. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Mm- hmm. [ADDRESS], I think it's telling that neither of the courts below found the -- the argument compelling. And this is at JA 155. Their ministry is to serve those most in need. So you can think of that akin to Catholic Charities running a soup kitchen. They don't ask people if they're Catholic.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: They're the ones that are in the program, [ADDRESS].

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: And on the flip side, you have parish preschools, and the role of the parish preschools is different. They have a different mission. turns_pm60.text: Well, [ADDRESS], my read of this Court's decision in Carson is that it roots the rule in Sherbert and [PERSON], not in Smith. And I think the Tenth Circuit was right about one thing. They were right to say -- yes, [ADDRESS]?

turns_pm60.text: Well, [ADDRESS], at the end of --

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.text: Yeah, two responses, [ADDRESS], one practical, and, hopefully, the second one, doctrinal, is more satisfying. The practical one is just that's what Smith did, as you described. But the doctrinal answer, which I think will hopefully be more satisfying, is that if you look at it from the perspective of Smith, Smith is focused on the government's interest, and the government's interest is at its zenith when you're talking about criminal laws. Smith was concerned about every man becoming a law unto himself. It was concerned about having to give these broad exemptions to criminal prohibitions. That interest is not as strong when it comes to public benefits when the underlying conduct is lawful. One other way to just explain it is Smith looked at this from the government's perspective. Sherbert and [PERSON] looked at this from the religious believers' perspective. And I think that's one way to understand it. I would also point to what this Court said in Carson. In Carson, this Court made clear that when it comes to public benefits, you have to be particularly strict and look carefully at how the program is set up because it's really easy for the government to try to tweak the way the program works to kind of subsume the challenged condition within the scope of the program. You can't do that when it comes to criminal laws. There's the Rule of Lenity. There's other procedural protections that criminal defendants have. Just to give one more example, you know, in this case, after we filed our complaint, you know, at that time, the catch-all exception wasn't written into the regulations. It was just an online form. Preschools could submit the form and ask for an exception. There was no, you know, restrictions on it. This is in the record at JA 828. It was only on the second day of trial that Colorado introduced brand-new regulations trying to put restrictions on the catch-all exception to make it look more generally applicable. That's what this is -- that's what Smith is encouraging governments to do.

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.text: And just to be clear, we agree those are important. We just want the same treatment.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes, yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yeah, two responses, [ADDRESS], one practical, and, hopefully, the second one, doctrinal, is more satisfying. The practical one is just that's what Smith did, as you described. But the doctrinal answer, which I think will hopefully be more satisfying, is that if you look at it from the perspective of Smith, Smith is focused on the government's interest, and the government's interest is at its zenith when you're talking about criminal laws. Smith was concerned about every man becoming a law unto himself. It was concerned about having to give these broad exemptions to criminal prohibitions. That interest is not as strong when it comes to public benefits when the underlying conduct is lawful. One other way to just explain it is Smith looked at this from the government's perspective. Sherbert and [PERSON] looked at this from the religious believers' perspective. And I think that's one way to understand it. I would also point to what this Court said in Carson. In Carson, this Court made clear that when it comes to public benefits, you have to be particularly strict and look carefully at how the program is set up because it's really easy for the government to try to tweak the way the program works to kind of subsume the challenged condition within the scope of the program. It was only on the second day of trial that Colorado introduced brand-new regulations trying to put restrictions on the catch-all exception to make it look more generally applicable. That's what this is -- that's what Smith is encouraging governments to do.

Even in their brief before this Court, at pages 41 and 51, they state their government interest, and it's just in enforcing the mandate regardless of the protected characteristic. At the same time, they let other preschools favor families based on those protected characteristics if there's a good or important reason. And I think it's telling that Colorado doesn't say, you know, we're not spending 10 pages of our brief kind of engaged in the work of statutory interpretation. They spend 10 pages explaining why it's really important to grant these secular accommodations.

turns_pm60.text: I think Sherbert is much closer to the original meaning than Smith, for sure. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So you see it as an implementing doctrine that's close to how it would have been implemented at the time of the founding?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think that's right, yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.text: This was after the statute was passed, [ADDRESS].

turns_pm60.text: After the statute was passed.

turns_pm60.text: I see.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: So, I guess, going back to [PERSON]'s points, as I understand your Carson theory, it appears to threaten school funding programs, conditions, benefits, nationwide by giving religious entities and individuals a special preferred status. And I think her point and mine too is that that sort of takes this out of, at least conceptually, the Carson line, where it was clear that the Court was concerned about treating religious entities worse. Everybody else got access to this benefit, but the religious entity did not. Yet, here, it seems like you are saying the religious entity has to be treated specially. So let me give you a hypothetical. Suppose Colorado imposes certain educational standards on a school that receives state funding. As a benefit, you have to have certain educational marks; for example, the requirement that a student attains a particular level of proficiency in math. But a religious school might believe under its tenets that, say, female students aren't -- aren't allowed or shouldn't be allowed to learn math at all. Wouldn't your Carson theory require the state to exempt that school on the basis of their religious belief, even though that educational standard is being applied across the board and they're just -- they, the state, are just asking that condition of receiving this fund -- this funding is that this school, like every other school, teach math to all its students?

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: [ADDRESS], I think that would be a public benefit. So, under Carson, it would trigger strict scrutiny. The government could come forward and say we have a good reason, and it could come forward.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: But wouldn't it only strict -- wouldn't it only trigger strict scrutiny under Carson to the extent that it was treating the religious entity worse? That's my point. The strict scrutiny comes from the discrimination. And what I worry about in the way that you're framing this, sort of as a big picture, is that we've got two lines of precedent here that seem relevant to your claim. One says that when the state is handing out public benefits, it can't discriminate or disfavor religious entities. And that's Carson, Trinity, Espinoza. The other line says that if a state has a rule, but it's handing out exclusions, it's exempting people from that rule, then it can't refuse to do so for similar religious conduct. I think that this actually doesn't fit in either of those buckets, and that's what I'm worried about. I think you're asking us to do something more. In the first instance, this -- this religious entity would be treated better than everybody else who has to follow this rule. And in the second, the kinds of things you're talking about, the preferences that the -- Colorado has allowed is not similar. I mean, here, your schools want to discriminate by exclusion. Nobody else is allowed to do that. There's nothing in this record that shows that any other kind of school is allowed to discriminate by exclusion. I know, in theory, you know, some people might have testified. But that's not actually happening. And, certainly, the preferences aren't operating to discriminate by -- by exclusion. So why are you asking us to do something new and different in this case that certainly wasn't brought to the fore by these previous doctrines that, as I've described, are pretty narrow and make perfect sense?

turns_pm60.text: Well, [ADDRESS], strict scrutiny would still apply here. We're not -- we're not saying this is just straight to we get to participate in the program. If the government is -- is excluding someone from a public benefit solely on account of their religious exercise, that would trigger strict scrutiny. And then the government can come forward and say we have a really good reason for this. And we just don't think they've done that in this case.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS], I think the question at the end of the day is, should this Court apply the Smith line of cases, which looks at it from the perspective of the government, or should it apply what I think Carson applied, which is it cited back to Sherbert and [PERSON]? Those cases look at the burden on religion from the perspective of the religious believer. So, in Thomas, the government defended its law in the same way. It said this is -- this law applies to everybody. In Sherbert, the government said everybody has to work on Saturday, whether you're religious or not. And Ms. Sherbert came back and said, well, my sabbath is the Saturday, and so I can't work on Saturday. This Court credited the religious --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, [ADDRESS], I think, at the end of the day, the question is, are Sherbert and [PERSON] still good law in the public benefits space? Because I don't take Smith to be overturning those cases. They distinguish those cases twice. And so, when it comes to conduct that the state has made unlawful, that's covered by Smith. But there's no question these Catholic schools can continue their teachings if they don't take this benefit. We think this is a coercive benefit, you know, a 20 percent decline in enrollment in these Catholic preschools. But my view is Sherbert and [PERSON] remain good law at least in the context of public benefits. And I think this Court's decision in Carson confirms that. And my -- my submission is I just don't see any difference between this case and those cases.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I don't think much would be, [ADDRESS].

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think that's probably right, yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Absolutely. It's not just Colorado that's done this. In Maine itself, after this Court's decision in Carson, before the ink was even dry in Carson, Maine changed its laws to look more like the laws here, where they don't explicitly call out religion, but they still exclude the same families and the same schools. So I think there's no question that if this Court doesn't address the Carson issue here, you're going to have other states trying to do the same thing, trying to exclude religious schools, just without using religious terminology. I think that is a serious problem.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, you know, I'm not the one to -- to say that, [ADDRESS], but I -- I think, you know, the -- I think Maine seems to think that. They -- they seem to think they could get around it. I -- I tend to think that's the -- the situation.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I -- I completely agree, [ADDRESS].

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That is correct, [ADDRESS].

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS], I don't doubt that that's true. At the end of the day, it's a question for the Archbishop in --in Denver to -- to decide on the religious teaching. And I think every diocese can make their own decision about where exactly that line is. The requirement to affirm the statement of community beliefs has been in place in the Archdiocese long before this program started. And I think it's -- it's their thoughtful attempt to say, we're creating a Catholic community, so we want to ensure that everybody who participates in the school, whether it's a parent who volunteers or whatever the situation might be, is acting consistent with -- with the responsibility we've been given as parents to teach these kids the Catholic faith.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That's correct.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah, two responses, [ADDRESS], one practical, and, hopefully, the second one, doctrinal, is more satisfying. The practical one is just that's what Smith did, as you described. And the concurrence in Smith makes exactly the same point. The concurrence says, why are we treating benefits better than direct prohibitions? And the majority doesn't respond to that. But the doctrinal answer, which I think will hopefully be more satisfying, is that if you look at it from the perspective of Smith, Smith is focused on the government's interest, and the government's interest is at its zenith when you're talking about criminal laws. Smith was concerned about every man becoming a law unto himself. It was concerned about having to give these broad exemptions to criminal prohibitions. That interest is not as strong when it comes to public benefits when the underlying conduct is lawful. One other way to just explain it is Smith looked at this from the government's perspective. Sherbert and [PERSON] looked at this from the religious believers' perspective. And I think that's one way to understand it. I would also point to what this Court said in Carson. In Carson, this Court made clear that when it comes to public benefits, you have to be particularly strict and look carefully at how the program is set up because it's really easy for the government to try to tweak the way the program works to kind of subsume the challenged condition within the scope of the program. You can't do that when it comes to criminal laws. There's the Rule of Lenity. There's other procedural protections that criminal defendants have. Just to give one more example, you know, in this case, after we filed our complaint, you know, at that time, the catch-all exception wasn't written into the regulations. It was just an online form. Preschools could submit the form and ask for an exception. There was no, you know, restrictions on it. This is in the record at JA 828. It was only on the second day of trial that Colorado introduced brand-new regulations trying to put restrictions on the catch-all exception to make it look more generally applicable. That's what this is -- that's what Smith is encouraging governments to do.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. Succinctly, [ADDRESS], yes. Yeah, there's two main points under general applicability. The first is kind of our -- our broadest argument. This is just not the type of across-the-board, generally applicable law that Smith envisioned. This Court in Kennedy described what -- what it need -- what you need to have to have an across-the-board prohibition. And when you have, you know, all these different preschools getting to limit their enrollment in all these different ways, that's a problem. But then, even if you zoom in on the mandate specifically, which is where Colorado focuses, and that's what they pointed to when they said these Catholic schools are not allowed to participate, there are some problems there as well. So the one thing that Colorado has been consistent on throughout this case is that their government interest is in the mandate, enforcing the mandate uniformly. It's a hard limit. Even in their brief before this Court, at pages 41 and 51, they state their government interest, and it's just in enforcing the mandate regardless of the protected characteristic. At the same time, they let other preschools favor families based on those protected characteristics if there's a good or important reason. And I think it's telling that Colorado doesn't say, you know, we're not spending 10 pages of our brief kind of engaged in the work of statutory interpretation. They spend 10 pages explaining why it's really important to grant these secular accommodations.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And just to be clear, we agree those are important. We just want the same treatment.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes, yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes, [ADDRESS]. Essentially, it was push-back on this common schools movement. You had public schools, government-funded schools that were teaching the King James Bible and were not accommodating different Catholic beliefs. And -- and some of this is spelled out in the Barkley amicus brief as well. But, essentially, these Catholic schools were a response to their exclusion from the common school system.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: We'd be making different arguments. I don't think that would be a Carson case because I do think that's what this Court was addressing to some extent in Smith. It said --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, I think we'd have to look at how the -- how the restriction was described, what it covered --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, I think, [ADDRESS], we'd still have church autonomy, the right of these schools to continue to inculcate the faith without government interference. There might be a parental rights Mahmoud argument. So I think there are other arguments we could make. I just don't think it would be a kind of Carson public benefits case.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think Sherbert is much closer to the original meaning than Smith, for sure. I don't -- I don't think the original meaning of free exercise of religion would -- would kind of care how the government treats non-religious groups or how the law is written. And I do think strict scrutiny in particular makes some sense if you look at these peace and safety provisos that lots of state constitutions had at the time. There was some understanding that, you know, we're going to protect the free exercise of religion up and to a -- up until a particular point, and that's when the government can come in and say we have this really important interest. I don't think peace and safety means anytime something's unlawful. It has to be -- you know, I think a close approximation is probably the strict scrutiny analysis this Court has adopted.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think that's right, yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes, [ADDRESS]. There's a few points there. Colorado quickly responds and says, no, the mandate's a hard limit, we cannot accommodate you. Tracy -- Tracy Seul, who's the -- who was the preschool director, did participate in this religious working group. That's in the record at JA 233. And she raised these concerns. Ms. Cooke's testimony at trial was that she understood their concerns went specifically to sexual orientation and gender identity.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: This was after the statute was passed, [ADDRESS].

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: While Colorado was working on the exception. So they had all these enrollment criteria that they were developing at the time.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So, yes, all of this is implementing the way the program operated. And I think it's even telling the district court in this case said it wasn't inconsistent for the Catholic schools to participate in those programs but to have a religious objection to UPK.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So, I guess, going back to [PERSON]'s points, as I understand your Carson theory, it appears to threaten school funding programs, conditions, benefits, nationwide by giving religious entities and individuals a special preferred status. And I think her point and mine too is that that sort of takes this out of, at least conceptually, the Carson line, where it was clear that the Court was concerned about treating religious entities worse. Everybody else got access to this benefit, but the religious entity did not. Yet, here, it seems like you are saying the religious entity has to be treated specially. So let me give you a hypothetical. Suppose Colorado imposes certain educational standards on a school that receives state funding. As a benefit, you have to have certain educational marks; for example, the requirement that a student attains a particular level of proficiency in math. But a religious school might believe under its tenets that, say, female students aren't -- aren't allowed or shouldn't be allowed to learn math at all. Wouldn't your Carson theory require the state to exempt that school on the basis of their religious belief, even though that educational standard is being applied across the board and they're just -- they, the state, are just asking that condition of receiving this fund -- this funding is that this school, like every other school, teach math to all its students?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS], I think that would be a public benefit. So, under Carson, it would trigger strict scrutiny. The government could come forward and say we have a good reason, and it could come forward.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But wouldn't it only strict -- wouldn't it only trigger strict scrutiny under Carson to the extent that it was treating the religious entity worse? That's my point. The strict scrutiny comes from the discrimination. And what I worry about in the way that you're framing this, sort of as a big picture, is that we've got two lines of precedent here that seem relevant to your claim. One says that when the state is handing out public benefits, it can't discriminate or disfavor religious entities. And that's Carson, Trinity, Espinoza. The other line says that if a state has a rule, but it's handing out exclusions, it's exempting people from that rule, then it can't refuse to do so for similar religious conduct. I think that this actually doesn't fit in either of those buckets, and that's what I'm worried about. I think you're asking us to do something more. In the first instance, this -- this religious entity would be treated better than everybody else who has to follow this rule. And in the second, the kinds of things you're talking about, the preferences that the -- Colorado has allowed is not similar. I mean, here, your schools want to discriminate by exclusion. Nobody else is allowed to do that. There's nothing in this record that shows that any other kind of school is allowed to discriminate by exclusion. I know, in theory, you know, some people might have testified. But that's not actually happening. And, certainly, the preferences aren't operating to discriminate by -- by exclusion. So why are you asking us to do something new and different in this case that certainly wasn't brought to the fore by these previous doctrines that, as I've described, are pretty narrow and make perfect sense?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, [ADDRESS], I wouldn't say what we're asking for is new and different. I think it's going back to Sherbert and [PERSON], to what this Court has already said. The way you've described it is -- is similar. It's on all fours with Sherbert and [PERSON]. And I think that better reflects what the free exercise --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: You disagree with -- with what [PERSON] said and how some people have read the doctrine, which was that Smith actually displaced the Sherbert and [PERSON] concept of just because it burdens a religious activity, it gets strict scrutiny? You don't think that's right?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I don't think that's right when it comes to public benefits. And I think the language in Smith is telling. It says, you know, whether or not Sherbert and [PERSON] are limited, they at least have nothing to do with an across-the-board criminal prohibition on a particular form --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: One final question. Doesn't Smith's concern about individuals and entities becoming a law unto themself arise if we interpret what you're saying? I mean, I understand you're trying to move Smith to the side, but it had some really serious concerns about religious entities not having to follow the law that everybody else is just because they hold sincerely held religious beliefs. It was like, how are you going to have a society where all people live and work together? And, here, we have a particular concern, as [PERSON] pointed out, because what the religious entity would like to do is discriminate against a class of people. So we've got a conflict at some level between, like, the First Amendment right of the religious entity and potentially the Fourteenth Amendment right of certain individuals who would have the right not to be discriminated against. And so your -- your rule is, like, not allowing our society to have all people live together because it's preferencing the religious entity's ability to discriminate against others.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, [ADDRESS], our rule is the one that promotes pluralism. So these are private religious schools. They're not subject to the Fourteenth Amendment. But it's Colorado that's denying Catholic families equal access to this benefit also based on a protected characteristic, their religious exercise. And in terms of the practicalities of this case, 41 jurisdictions, including the federal government, are already subject to heightened scrutiny for any substantial burden on religion. And I think the federal government's probably the biggest provider of public benefits in the world, and they're functioning just fine.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: You can also -- thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But these --

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] There are two main paths to reversal. First, this Court could hold that public benefits programs that condition eligibility for benefits on foregoing otherwise lawful religious exercise trigger strict scrutiny. That's the rule Carson distilled from Sherbert, and that rule makes particular sense for educational benefits given the Court's longstanding recognition that religious education is vital to many faiths. Second, this Court could hold that Colorado's pre -- pre-K benefits regime triggers strict scrutiny under any approach because it isn't generally applicable. Either way, Colorado can't satisfy strict scrutiny. The better path in our view, though, would be to go with the first course, as Petitioner has emphasized. At this point, the doctrine is at a point where the Court should decide whether Sherbert survives. Carson puts that in sharp relief. And the Court's most recent decision in Mahmoud creates an especially untenable situation in the educational context because parents have strict scrutiny in this context and yet religious schools would not in many of the same claims. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm15.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] Colorado welcomes religious preschools to UPK. The only thing Colorado asks is that they comply with the same conditions that every publicly funded preschool must meet, religious and secular alike. UPK is neutral towards religion. Well before this Court's decision in Carson, Colorado made three key choices. First, it expanded free high-quality preschool to every four-year-old in the state when, before, its predecessor program focused only on low-income and disabled children. Second, it replaced its public school-only approach with a public/private partnership that welcomes private schools, including religious schools that teach religious education. And, third, it holds all participating preschools to the same standards, including student-teacher ratios, class sizes, teacher training obligations, and equal opportunity. Under this program, faith-based preschools remain free to teach their religious beliefs, including their beliefs about sex or gender or marriage, free to teach them while receiving public funding. Under this program, publicly funded preschools choose their curriculum, and families, regardless of their protected class status, choose what schools to attend. But families have no right to change a school's curriculum. Finally, UPK's equal opportunity requirements are generally applicable. The statute requires that disabled and low-income children receive additional and specialized services because having a disability or living in poverty directly interferes with those children's ability to benefit from preschool at all. UPK does not devalue religion by allowing preschools to remove these barriers. The judgment below should be affirmed. I welcome this Court's questions.

turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] Colorado welcomes religious preschools to UPK.
