Well before this Court's decision in Carson, Colorado made three key choices. First, it expanded free high-quality preschool to every four-year-old in the state when, before, its predecessor program focused only on low-income and disabled children. Second, it replaced its public school-only approach with a public/private partnership that welcomes private schools, including religious schools that teach religious education. And, third, it holds all participating preschools to the same standards, including student-teacher ratios, class sizes, teacher training obligations, and equal opportunity. Under this program, faith-based preschools remain free to teach their religious beliefs, including their beliefs about sex or gender or marriage, free to teach them while receiving public funding. Under this program, publicly funded preschools choose their curriculum, and families, regardless of their protected class status, choose what schools to attend. But families have no right to change a school's curriculum. Finally, UPK's equal opportunity requirements are generally applicable. The statute requires that disabled and low-income children receive additional and specialized services because having a disability or living in poverty directly interferes with those children's ability to benefit from preschool at all. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] Colorado welcomes religious preschools to UPK. First, it expanded free high-quality preschool to every four-year-old in the state when, before, its predecessor program focused only on low-income and disabled children. Second, it replaced its public school-only approach with a public/private partnership that welcomes private schools, including religious schools that teach religious education. And, third, it holds all participating preschools to the same standards, including student-teacher ratios, class sizes, teacher training obligations, and equal opportunity. Under this program, faith-based preschools remain free to teach their religious beliefs, including their beliefs about sex or gender or marriage, free to teach them while receiving public funding. Under this program, publicly funded preschools choose their curriculum, and families, regardless of their protected class status, choose what schools to attend. But families have no right to change a school's curriculum. Finally, UPK's equal opportunity requirements are generally applicable. The statute requires that disabled and low-income children receive additional and specialized services because having a disability or living in poverty directly interferes with those children's ability to benefit from preschool at all. UPK does not devalue religion by allowing preschools to remove these barriers. The judgment below should be affirmed. I welcome this Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Not at all, [ADDRESS]. And it's Colorado's position that the equal opportunity requirements help religious families. turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.text: Very quickly, I just wanted to touch on the Tandon line of argument here. Does Colorado's preference program undermine the equal opportunity mandate or discriminate in a similar way as what these preschools would like to do?

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Thank you. [ADDRESS] AEDPA's restrictions on second or successive habeas applications reflect the balance struck by Congress between finality and error correction. turns_pm60.text: Thank you. [ADDRESS] AEDPA's restrictions on second or successive habeas applications reflect the balance struck by Congress between finality and error correction. And Respondent relied on Atkins versus Virginia in his initial federal habeas application. The rule of Atkins is not a new rule of constitutional law that was previously unavailable to him under Section 2244(b)(2)(A). And Moore versus Texas, which was a legal change following Respondent's initial federal habeas application, has not been made retroactive to cases on collateral review by this Court. Nor can Respondent pass through the gateway of Section 2244(b)(2)(B) because the facts underlying his claim are unrelated to his guilt for the underlying offense. This Court should defer to Congress's policy choices, correct the Fifth Circuit's interpretation of Section 2244(b)(2)(A), and reverse. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. I guess what I'm suggesting is that Atkins is more -- there -- there's more than one Atkins rule. turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.text: And he now believes that he has a way to establish his intellectual disability.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: We respectfully disagree, [ADDRESS], as we see that perhaps going to the availability of the claim but not to the availability of the rule of Atkins, that the Constitution prohibits the imposition of capital punishment on the intellectually disabled. [PERSON], let me return to your question, and I think the helpful way of thinking about this is what the Court recognized in Montgomery versus Louisiana, that when the Constitution prohibits a particular form of punishment for a class of persons, an affected prisoner receives a procedure through which he can show that he belongs to the protected class. So we have a substantive rule in Atkins protecting a class of persons, the intellectually disabled. And then what we have is Hall and Moore perhaps modifying the procedures by which a person can prove that he would belong to the protected class. But, under Edwards versus Vannoy, those procedures wouldn't be new rules of constitutional law applied retroactively, and this Court certainly hasn't made them so.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But why are you saying there that it's a modification of the procedures? It is a substantive change in who belongs in the class. It's not about, you know, evidence, right? It's not a change in what Mr. Johnson can offer to show that he's intellectually disabled. It is a substantive change in the criteria of the people who constitute that class.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So, first, every circuit that has recognized Moore as a new rule has treated Moore as a new procedural rule that is not retroactive.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But why are you talking about Moore? I'm talking about Atkins, right? Atkins says you can't execute the intellectually disabled. And, in the context of that very case, we indicated that who qualifies as intellectually disabled is keyed to medical standards and that medical standards might vary in -- throughout the country. It might evolve over time. I don't understand why that's characterized as a procedural determination.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Atkins did leave the definition of "intellectual disability" to the states. And then, even in Hall, where this Court placed a greater emphasis legally on updated medical definitions, it still reiterated that the legal determination of intellectual disability is distinct from a medical diagnosis.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: No, I understand. But I -- it's -- it's -- so let me ask you this. The problem, I think, with your interpretation is that, as you said, we're supposed to be giving effect to the -- Congress's policy choices. And as I understood this set of provisions, Congress's policy choice was to give individuals one clear shot at bringing their constitutional claims. This is what the whole scheme is about. You can't bring a second or successive claim if you had the opportunity before and you didn't do it. The way you're interpreting this, Mr. Johnson will never get that opportunity because the criteria that makes him eligible for claiming that he's intellectually disabled came after his original habeas petition, but you're saying that because it relates to the rule that we had laid out before, he's foreclosed. And -- and that seems like a really incongruous consequence given Congress's policy determination in this case.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Respectfully, [ADDRESS], I disagree with the premise of the question.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Okay.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think what you articulated was essentially the common law abuse-of-the-writ doctrine that preceded AEDPA. And what we see in 2244(b)(2) is Congress restricting the abuse of the writ, taking away opportunities. And the best way of looking at that is the limitation that we see in 2244(b)(2)(B)(ii). We know that Congress didn't intend to allow prisoners to raise any previously unavailable claim because that limitation in (ii) means that if a prisoner uncovers a new factual predicate for a claim that is unrelated to whether they would have been found guilty of the underlying offense, they do not have an opportunity to bring that claim. So we don't look at this as Congress attempting to provide a full opportunity. We look at this as Congress placing strict limitations on second or successive applications and favoring finality.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS], when I look at the PLRA, Booth versus Churner recognizes that the meaning of a phrase involving "available" depends heavily on what must be available. In that case, the Court had to determine what it meant for a remedy to be available. I'll note that Booth rejects a futility exception under the PLRA. And Ross versus Blake, when it talks about what might make an administrative remedy unavailable under the PLRA, identifies procedural impediments to the filing of that sort of claim, the inability to take advantage of it by even asserting those sorts of arguments, not the fact that it would have been non-meritorious.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: When we look at Ross, that "dead end" phrase, I think the Court explained it involved officers unable or consistently unwilling to provide any relief to aggrieved inmates. I think that would be a circumstance where, for example, you might have a -- a district clerk who had simply refused to file a petition --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: What we would say is it was capable of being used, simply not useful. Perhaps the usage by this Court in Perry versus New Hampshire, referring to constitutional safeguards available to defendants, including compulsory process -- compulsory process remains a constitutional safeguard available to a defendant even who doesn't --one who doesn't have any use for it. So, in this case, we think of the two pieces of a claim. If the prisoner has the legal rule available to him that he can bring to court that would serve as a rule of decision, even if he doesn't have the factual predicate for that claim, that rule is available. And that's consistent with how we see the structure of 2244(b)(2).

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS], we think that is a difficult question that is not presented on the facts of this case and that you don't need to address in order to resolve this case. However --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. Yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: We agree with the Eleventh Circuit's interpretation in Bowles. That's what we have consistently argued for. If a prisoner can say, even though this Court announced the rule while I had an initial federal habeas petition or a federal habeas petition pending, I could not have actually brought that rule before the district court, I was not in a position to invoke that rule, I would not have been permitted to invoke it and --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS], I think of an extreme hypothetical: If this Court were to announce a new rule of constitutional law made retroactive to cases on collateral review the day that a district court enters final judgment or the day before a district court enters final judgment, the Court could adopt a bright-line rule based on Banister and Rivers, but we might acknowledge that under some circumstances such as those, a prisoner would be able to say that rule was not available to me, even though, theoretically, if I had been able to amend my pending petition the day before final judgment, it would not have constituted a second or successive application.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes, [ADDRESS], you could. Now the State's asking you to resolve it based on "previously unavailable," in part because of the pending Cathey case that we have. In Cathey, Atkins was a new rule because it was announced after his conviction became final on direct appeal. And that would still leave the acknowledged split between at least the Fifth and the Eleventh Circuits.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I suspect that would go a bit too far, [ADDRESS]. It -- we can -- certainly, we would say, if it was announced before the filing of the initial federal habeas application, we do agree that it would have been available. I don't think we would say that every rule announced after the filing of the initial federal habeas petition would be unavailable. This Court did, in Banister and Rivers, recognize that filings before the entry of final judgment during a pending federal habeas application are not second or successive. We certainly think, in the mine run of cases, a prisoner is going to be able to take advantage of a new rule announced while a pending -- excuse me -- while a federal habeas petition is pending.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think what you would write is to say the question presented in this case -- and we tried to narrow it slightly in the merits brief -- was to talk about this is a rule that had been announced before the filing of the -- of the Petitioner's initial federal habeas application and made retroactive to cases on collateral review. We conclude --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes, [ADDRESS]. You could do that. And that's going to solve, we think, 99 percent of the cases. Certainly, just adopting our understanding of "previously unavailable" is going to avoid the problems that might result with publication of, say, the DSM-6 when new prisoners would come forward saying, I am now intellectually disabled when I wasn't previously.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: We would characterize Respondent's argument the same way. Their theory is that a claim is -- as I understand the argument, it is that a rule is unavailable when a claim is unavailable or a claim would lack merit, and a claim -- and it would be futile to raise that claim. So I think they still are tying in the availability of a rule to the futility of asserting a claim under that rule.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Can I just get clarification on that? What -- so the rule -- they say the rule is unavailable if I could not take advantage of it. And your argument in response to that is what? It's still available if it just existed?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: The rule is available to be used for whatever purpose the prisoner could make use of it. So, as we define "rule that is capable of being used," it is not necessarily useful to a particular prisoner. So the way of thinking of it here is there are two pieces of a claim. There is the legal predicate for the claim and the factual predicate. The prisoner may well have the legal rule available to him. He can always make any use of it that he wants to. And, indeed, Respondent used that rule in his initial federal habeas application, not the same way he's using it now, but he did rely on, cite Atkins, urge a court to follow it and account for it in the arguments he was making. What he lacked at the time of that initial federal habeas application was the factual predicate, the diagnosis.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Right. So what do you do with the fact that we've sort of rejected -- I -- your -- I noted that your brief didn't cite Panetti versus Quarterman, but the same kind of analysis came up with respect to Ford claims. This is kind of what [PERSON] was exploring with you. A Ford claim is one in which we said that the -- that states are prohibited from executing people when they can't understand why they're being killed, and that kind of factual circumstance arises later. And the government in Ford said too bad, you needed to make the claim originally because it was available to you because Ford existed, and the fact that you didn't have that factual predicate, you know, sorry. And we said, no, that doesn't really make sense because it doesn't enable this defendant to ever make the claim. And, here, similarly, I think the same kind of thing is happening.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: And, [ADDRESS], we see those as qualitatively different claims, that Panetti and Ford are about the defendant's competence to be executed, which is focused on the defendant's status at the moment of execution, whereas an Atkins claim concerns the defendant's status at the time of the crime and conviction, the onset of disability -- of the intellectual disability during the developmental period.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But, if the standards change as to whether or not, at the time of the initial conviction, he was intellectually disabled, you're saying that doesn't matter? He didn't have the factual predicate at the relevant time?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That's correct, [ADDRESS]. If it's a change in the medical standards, if it's a change in the legal standards, then we would say that would need to be a change that's a new rule of constitutional law made retroactive to cases on collateral review by this Court.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But -- but those would be -- and I guess I'm just a little concerned that if we -- that we have two timing issues in this statute. We have "previously unavailable," which is particular to the Petitioner, but it's not clear to me that Congress intended for the phrase "new rule" in the way that it exists in the other part of the statute to also do that work because you could end up with a situation in which you have such overlap that one part of the statute is superfluous if we read it in the way that you're talking about. Can you speak to that?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Do we have evidence that that's what Congress intended, that that's what they were doing in this statute?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: What if the Court said so and made it prospective? What if the Court said: We are announcing this rule and, in the future, if the category changes per state law, we intend for that to be applied retroactively?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Would they have to just do it every time there's -- is --is your position that it only satisfies the retroactive part of this statute if the Supreme Court rubber stamps each change in the DSM?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And that's because, I think, right, what -- what you're saying is that, really, we have to take the whole phrase, that we don't just isolate, like, what does it mean to be new. It is a new rule of constitutional law made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court. And those are the rare circumstances in which the Supreme Court makes an announcement and determines that this thing that it is announcing is so significant that even defendants with closed cases should be able to benefit from it. In -- in that framing, as you say, Atkins was a new rule. And any other circumstance in the past in which the Supreme Court made that kind of announcement related to the significance of its ruling is a new rule. It's not about the timing of it. It's about the character of it.

turns_pm15.text: Well, I think a few responses to that, [PERSON]. One is that I think it's -- it's difficult to imagine Congress enacting a law that would allow the American Psychiatric Association, without independent action of this Court, to create a new rule of constitutional law.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Sure. turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] Respondent seeks prospective application of an old rule that was available when he filed his first habeas application 15 years ago. That claim does not satisfy AEDPA's bar on second or successive habeas applications. Atkins is not a new rule with respect to Respondent because it was decided five years before his conviction. He cannot seek retroactive application of a constitutional rule that existed and applied before he even committed his crimes. And the Atkins rule was previously un -- was previously available during his first habeas application. Atkins was the law of the land, and he used it to advance a different claim in that same application. Respondent's contrary reading, which would allow successive habeas applications anytime doctors change their understanding of intellectual disability, would seriously undermine Congress's choice in AEDPA to prioritize finality over successive habeas applications spanning decades. This Court should reverse. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think this Court could resolve it on either prong. I think it would be most helpful to address both and address the statute holistically. So just to discuss the new rule issue to begin, I think, to address, I think, [PERSON]'s questions about whether "new rule" encompasses a concept of the sorts of rules that the Court has in -- at one time deemed a new rule that was important enough to --to make retroactive, I think that is inconsistent with the way this Court has, in dozens of cases, described what it means for a rule to be new. It's consistently described the concept of a new rule as with respect to the particular defendant who is invoking the rule. And that's in cases both pre-and post-AEDPA. You have cases pre-AEDPA like Saffle, you have cases post-AEDPA like Whorton v. Bockting, all of which --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes. So I think I would point to a few things. One is, for example, this Court in Magwood described Section (b) -- Subsection (b)(2)(A) as requiring intervening case law, and I think that puts a really fine point on it. This is not just a rule that was new at the time it was decided. This is a rule that is -- has intervened in the time between the individual's conviction and this -- this application. And so that, I think, is -- is some evidence of what the Court --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, I think, by incorporating language that very, very closely tracks Teague and that -- and given that Teague was describing when these rules can apply on collateral review, it would be exceedingly unusual for the Court to use the same framework that Teague adopted but divorce it from the rule that Teague was actually applying, which requires that it be new with respect to the particular defendant.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, I think a few responses to that, [PERSON]. One is that I think it's -- it's difficult to imagine Congress enacting a law that would allow the American Psychiatric Association, without independent action of this Court, to create a new rule of constitutional law.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Sure. I -- I think, looking at Atkins, the substantive rule that Atkins announced was that individuals who were intellectually disabled at the time they committed their crime cannot be sentenced to -- to -- to death for that because they lack the culpability necessary to warrant execution. That rule isn't changed by the adoption of a new DSM. That is the underlying rule of Atkins. That's what Hall described the rule of Atkins as. And so the DSM updating who falls within the definition of "intellectually disabled" or who might be diagnosed as intellectually disabled isn't creating a new rule of constitutional law. The rule of constitutional law is the same.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Sure. I -- I think Atkins, to the extent it incorporated the DSM and updated psychological understandings of intellectual disability, it also incorporated state processes for determining intellectual disability. It expressly said that states would be responsible for developing the method of determining intellectual disability. And I don't think that it would make a lot of sense for there to be an available successive application anytime the relevant state had a -- a new case, a new state supreme court case, for example, or even a state lower court case that changed the framework that the state was using. I think that would run contrary to the structure of the law, which is the structure of (b)(2)(A), which says that it has to be a new rule of constitutional law made retroactive to cases on collateral review by this Court. And I think that when the update that renders the rule available on Respondent's view is the DSM or, for that matter, some state court decision that's changing the way that a court is to assess an IQ score or a -- a type of adaptive functioning, then that can't possibly trigger (b)(2)(A) because it's not a new rule of constitutional law made retroactive by this Court.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: If the --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think, if -- if the Court -- if this Court says now the DSM is the governing standard, then I think that's a procedural change. And so I -- I don't know that that -- I suppose, if this Court said it is retroactive anyway, then that would satisfy it. I don't think it would ordinarily be considered retroactive under the way -- you know, after Edwards and the way this Court conceptualizes what it means for a rule to be substantive versus procedural and therefore retroactive. But, if this Court expressly said we think that the substance of an Atkins claim depends on the DSM-5 and that is retroactive, then that could be the basis for a second or successive.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes. So I -- I agree with -- with [PERSON] that there's no need to address the particular circumstances in this case. It's not presented by this case. But, if this Court wanted to wade into exactly when during the first habeas the rule would have to be announced, I do think that a final judgment rule makes sense. I think it accords with this Court's approach in Rivers, and it accords with the availability of -- you know, habeas actions are generally, for most purposes in the civil rules, considered civil actions. You can amend your application once as of right. You can also amend it again if justice requires. And so, in that circumstance, if this Court were to announce something that really is a new rule, retroactive on collateral review, then that would provide -- [ADDRESS], may I?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That would provide an opportunity to address it on first habeas.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think your latter formulation captures what the -- the Atkins Eighth Amendment rule was.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I'm not altogether sure I understood your answer to [PERSON].

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Okay.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: You are taking the position that -- do you want to limit this -- you -- you said to [PERSON] earlier that you wanted to go under both prongs, but your colleague wanted to limit this to -- that it can't be a new rule if it was announced before the filing of the first petition.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Speaker B, I -- our position certainly --and I understand [PERSON]'s position to be that it cannot be a new rule if it was announced after -- it cannot be a new rule with respect to a particular applicant if it was announced after that applicant -- before that applicant's conviction.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I thought he said it differently. I took down what he said. It can't be a new rule if it was announced before filing of the first petition. He didn't say before the final conviction, because there is a final conviction the moment you file a habeas. You're trying to undo the final conviction.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I suppose I'm best speaking just for -- for our own position. I think that it is a new rule -- the -- the timing of a new rule is defined with respect to when the particular defendant's conviction becomes final. The timing for previous availability is tied to the first habeas application, and --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Now you're -- now you're doing two different -- that makes no sense to me. I mean, I understand the General's position, but yours makes no sense. Why would you have two different timeframes?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think that -- that --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: New rule announced before this but not before the -- but not previously available until the first habeas?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think that accounts for why the statute has two different terms that both have reference to timing. So "new" is incorporating the concept from Teague, which is tied to the time of conviction. And then "previously unavailable" should be tied to the first habeas application or the -- the immediately preceding habeas application because we're dealing with second or successive habeas applications specifically. So the question in a second or successive is whether it could have been raised in the first or the immediately preceding. And so that's -- that's how we would justify the -- the two different timing questions, one for a new rule and the other for previous unavailability.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: You're not unhappy with the General's suggest -- suggestion earlier?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I -- I didn't understand us to be advancing different positions, but to the extent that they are --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: We'll both listen to the transcript.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think that's what she said.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Could you reprise for me the (2)(B)(ii) argument on why you think the First Circuit was wrong on not considering a factual change? I think the General said that you can't succeed under (2)(B)(ii) because it doesn't go to your --to your guilt of the crime. It just makes you a class of people. turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: In our view, Atkins was new at the time it was decided.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: We're talking about now, though.

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: That -- we believe that Atkins was new based off of the character of the decision in 2002 and that it remains new now.

turns_same_span.speaker: A

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: Every rule was certainly new at some point and is --

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] The Fifth Circuit correctly interpreted the federal successor statute. It did so according to the ordinary meaning of that statute's words. Under that interpretation, a rule is new when the case in question announced a novel legal standard. It's retroactive when this Court has said so. And a claim relying on that rule is previously unavailable if it had no possibility of merit under the governing legal standard. In contrast, the Petitioner and the United States assert that a rule is available simply when it's been announced. But existence and availability aren't the same thing. Many things exist that aren't necessarily available to us. This Court's decisions in Booth and Ross strongly support the Fifth Circuit's rule here. There, this Court held that "available" means "capable of use" and that it requires the possibility of some relief. Importantly, in those cases, that was relief to the specific prisoner in question, not just whether the grievance system generally was capable of providing relief. Much has been discussed regarding the clinical standards of intellectual disability as being facts, and while that's certainly true in some sense, there are also facts with important legal significance. This Court has described those standards as the fundamental premise of its Atkins decision. When those standards change, the Eighth Amendment's protected class potentially changes as well. And in those rare circumstances, that can render a rule legally available for the first time, as it does here for Mr. Johnson. But those changes are, in fact, rare. Mr. Johnson is the only individual who has been authorized to proceed based off of the changes in 2013 in the DSM-5. And when the DSM was again updated in 2022, no one has been authorized to proceed under those changes. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Does Atkins ever stop being a new rule?

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: In our view, Atkins was new at the time it was decided.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: We're talking about now, though.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: That -- we believe that Atkins was new based off of the character of the decision in 2002 and that it remains new now.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: What about Marbury versus Madison?

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Every rule was certainly new at some point and is --

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: When does it ever stop being new?

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Under our reading, the rule is just new based off of what this Court did at the time. And then, while that -- while that provision of the statute does little work, the next prong, retroactivity, is a significant limiter on which rules petitioners can use to proceed under the statute. And then prior unavailability continues to narrow the field down farther.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: We view the word "new" in the statute as doing very little work at the end of the day in anyone's definition. Certainly, with ours, it gets wrapped into the retroactivity assessment, as I believe [PERSON] was alluding to in questioning before. In the Petitioner and the United States' view, it just simply moves a different timing window that already exists. So I think all versions of "new," it's doing very little work in terms of the statutory construction here.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Absolutely, [PERSON].

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Respectfully, [PERSON], we disagree with that position. We think both "new" and "retroactivity" go to the character of the rule and also to this Court's decision, and then the courts look to see whether that rule was, in fact, available or capable of being used by the petitioner in question.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: [PERSON], we took the position in the lower court that the statute of limitations began to run with the publication of the DSM-5.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] The Fifth Circuit correctly interpreted the federal successor statute. It did so according to the ordinary meaning of that statute's words. Under that interpretation, a rule is new when the case in question announced a novel legal standard. It's retroactive when this Court has said so. And a claim relying on that rule is previously unavailable if it had no possibility of merit under the governing legal standard. In contrast, the Petitioner and the United States assert that a rule is available simply when it's been announced. But existence and availability aren't the same thing. Many things exist that aren't necessarily available to us. This Court's decisions in Booth and Ross strongly support the Fifth Circuit's rule here. There, this Court held that "available" means "capable of use" and that it requires the possibility of some relief. Importantly, in those cases, that was relief to the specific prisoner in question, not just whether the grievance system generally was capable of providing relief. Much has been discussed regarding the clinical standards of intellectual disability as being facts, and while that's certainly true in some sense, there are also facts with important legal significance. This Court has described those standards as the fundamental premise of its Atkins decision. When those standards change, the Eighth Amendment's protected class potentially changes as well. And in those rare circumstances, that can render a rule legally available for the first time, as it does here for Mr. Johnson. But those changes are, in fact, rare. Mr. Johnson is the only individual who has been authorized to proceed based off of the changes in 2013 in the DSM-5. And when the DSM was again updated in 2022, no one has been authorized to proceed under those changes. I welcome the Court's questions.

And, certainly, the fact that there are alternative remedial structures that Carlson didn't consider and that Congress has legislated in this area since, that is going to, under the framework, mean that Carlson claims are no longer viable.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] The power to create damages remedies belongs to Congress, not federal courts. Bivens, Davis, and Carlson departed from that principle, and this Court has spent the last 45 years trying to set things straight. It has repeatedly explained that Bivens claims are disfavored, that they strain the separation of powers, and that they cannot proceed if there is any reason to think that Congress might be better suited to weigh the costs and benefits of a damages remedy. The Court has rejected Bivens claim after Bivens claim after Bivens claim. But the Ninth Circuit allowed a Bivens remedy here anyway. The Court may conclude that it's time to end the Bivens experiment and hand accountability for providing damages remedies back to Congress, where it belongs. But the claim here also fails under a straightforward application of this Court's Bivens framework, as Watanabe concedes his claim cannot proceed if it presents a new context, that is, if there is any meaningful difference between his case and Carlson. There are at least three. First, unlike Carlson and Bivens and Davis, this case is not damages or nothing. Watanabe not only could but did pursue administrative and injunctive relief. Second, Congress could see a meaningful difference between the inmate's rapid death in Carlson and the less severe injury Watanabe alleges here both in terms of proper deterrence and in the risk of disruption that would be posed by extending Carlson to less severe but far more common conditions like that alleged here. Third, this case implicates special factors not considered in Carlson, including alternative remedial structures and post-Carlson legislation, where Congress has declined to provide a damages remedy for federal prisoners. Those are exactly the kinds of differences this Court has repeatedly held to present a new context and to foreclose a Bivens remedy as recently as last year's summary reversal in Goldey. Reversal should follow here too. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] The power to create damages remedies belongs to Congress, not federal courts. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] The power to create damages remedies belongs to Congress, not federal courts. Bivens, Davis, and Carlson departed from that principle, and this Court has spent the last 45 years trying to set things straight. It has repeatedly explained that Bivens claims are disfavored, that they strain the separation of powers, and that they cannot proceed if there is any reason to think that Congress might be better suited to weigh the costs and benefits of a damages remedy. The Court has rejected Bivens claim after Bivens claim after Bivens claim. But the Ninth Circuit allowed a Bivens remedy here anyway. The Court may conclude that it's time to end the Bivens experiment and hand accountability for providing damages remedies back to Congress, where it belongs. But the claim here also fails under a straightforward application of this Court's Bivens framework, as Watanabe concedes his claim cannot proceed if it presents a new context, that is, if there is any meaningful difference between his case and Carlson. There are at least three. First, unlike Carlson and Bivens and Davis, this case is not damages or nothing. Watanabe not only could but did pursue administrative and injunctive relief. Second, Congress could see a meaningful difference between the inmate's rapid death in Carlson and the less severe injury Watanabe alleges here both in terms of proper deterrence and in the risk of disruption that would be posed by extending Carlson to less severe but far more common conditions like that alleged here. Third, this case implicates special factors not considered in Carlson, including alternative remedial structures and post-Carlson legislation, where Congress has declined to provide a damages remedy for federal prisoners. Those are exactly the kinds of differences this Court has repeatedly held to present a new context and to foreclose a Bivens remedy as recently as last year's summary reversal in Goldey. Reversal should follow here too. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.text: Well, I -- I think --

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.text: -- specific ones would not apply in Bivens.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. So medical negligence -- so the --the discretionary act or discretionary function exception generally applies to things in the nature of policy. turns_pm60.text: Yeah.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Hmm?

And I don't think it's clear at all. And I think the -- all the evidence actually tends to show that that's not what Congress has done. It's been differing --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Congress could have done something. But, in Loper Bright and other decisions, this Court --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And I think the difference with those stat- -- is that they are statutes. And this has a constitutional overlay where the Court purported to derive these causes of action directly under the Constitution itself, and that creates uncertainty as to whether -- what Congress really could have done.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So I think what it would be was the -- it would be the broader principle at stake, which is separation of powers means that courts should not be creating damages remedies directly under the Constitution. And that would apply to Bivens as well. But the Court, of course, does have other options. It could follow the existing framework and say: Well, under that framework, Carlson claims are no longer viable, or it could even say that under the particular facts of this particular case, there is at least one meaningful difference that creates a new context.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So, in -- in that situation, as long as state survival law allowed the claim to proceed under the FTCA, yes, that would be available.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I don't believe so. There may be some instances where state law, which Congress has allowed to govern under the FTCA, may limit the amount of recovery, but, for the most part, state survival statutes allow these kinds of torts to survive death.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think, if it bothers anyone, it should bother Congress and the people who could ask Congress to change that. I don't think that it would be a -- provide a -- a warrant for this Court to recognize a damages remedy that properly isn't within the judicial function.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So it sounds to me like your answer to every question is there is no remaining Carlson claim, because I don't understand why it matters that state survival statutes would allow for this if your underlying theory is that, you know, we have a separation-of-powers problem whenever the federal courts recognize a -- a implied cause of action, whether that's based on state survival theory or -- survival statutes or not. So why -- why can't you just say that your -- your bottom line, your through line, is that there will be no more kind of Carlson claim as a result of your rule?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So -- so, if the Court overrules Carlson and Bivens, yes, we agree with that. I think, if the Court applies the existing framework and finds that the existence of alternative remedial structures in post-Carlson legislation creates a new context from Carlson, that will also be the effect that Carlson claims don't come. But there are some of the other distinctions that we have, like that the death in Carlson is different from --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right. I understand you have those distinctions.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So let me just -- let me ask you about -- going back to [PERSON]'s question: What is the overstep here in this case? We have the same kind of alleged violation as in Carlson. We have the same constitutional right brought under the same legal framework by the same kind of defendant who's housed in the same kind of federal institution. So, with respect to all major indicia of sameness, this case is Carlson. This person is bringing an Eighth Amendment deliberate indifference claim for what he says is abuse in prison. I appreciate that a death occurred in Carlson and not here, but why do you say it would be an extension of the judicial power from a separation-of-powers standpoint in this case but not in Carlson?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. So the Court in Ziglar said we don't just look --it's the same right, it's the same method, mechanism of injury, and so we have to look for not just what similarities can we tote up but also what differences are there. And, here, there is --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: All of them have to be relative to your argument that this would be an extension of the separation of powers. So whatever sameness and difference, it has to relate to your concern that in one case, you'd be improperly extending the judicial authority, and in another case, you wouldn't. And so that's what I don't understand --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. And so the question --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- distinguishes this case.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And so the question there is, is this something that Congress could think meaningful from a policy/legislative perspective when weighing the costs and benefits of affording a damages remedy? And if it could adjust that balance, then courts should let Congress make the call rather than asserting that the cause of action is available in that situation. And, here, Congress has created statutes that provide additional deterrence where death results. And Carl--- Bivens is supposed to be all about deterrence. And -- and Egbert held that deterrence is properly for Congress to calibrate. And so, if Carlson presented a stronger case for deterrence than this case does because there was a death there and not here, that is something a rational legislature could consider, and that's the kind of meaning --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Notwithstanding that the in-depth -- in -- in -- excuse me -- in the deliberate indifference factors don't turn on death, deliberate -- you -- you have a claim for deliberate indifference based on the actions or inactions of the prison officials in both cases.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. So I don't think it goes by the strict -- you know, the elements of the cause of action. I don't think an excessive-force claim has an element that it's not a national security case like in Egbert or in Hernandez. It really is, are there circumstances involved where Congress could think that this is a pol--- different from a policy decision?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Can I just ask one last thing, which is, if we do what you would like us to do in this case, my concern is that we would be not actually taking into account the factors that we ordinarily look at when we are overruling a case. You're essentially asking us to implicitly overrule Carlson if not explicitly. So what about things like whether this was egregiously wrong when it was initially determined, whether there are reliance interests? You've spoken a little bit, I guess, on the workability, but that depends on whether or not we agree with you that the two factors -- the -- the two steps should be collapsed. So can you -- can you speak to us as though you are making a case for overruling under our traditional factors?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Certainly. And that's -- that's our kind of alternative argument, that the Court could overrule Bivens and with it Carlson. You know, it created a damages remedy directly under the Constitution that no court had recognized for two centuries after the Bill of Rights' enactment. And the Court has now come to appreciate that that offends the separation of powers because Congress is properly the -- the right body to be making the policy considerations that go into creating a damages remedy.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: What about reliance? Fifty years we've had Carlson.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. And there has been precious few Carlson and Bivens claims that have actually led to relief. We --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Does that help you or hurt you?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Hmm?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Does that help you or hurt you?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, I -- I think there's been a lot more litigation. So I think the -- the toll that those -- that litigation in those cases take has been quite great. But, in terms of the -- the payoff for the beneficiaries, the plaintiffs, the -- the Mason and Smith article cited in the last footnote of our reply says, in the last 20 years, only one Bivens claim was actually upheld after judgment on appeal. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So there are remedies that exist.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I have a statistic I came across that said something like 75 percent of all Bivens actions are Carlson claims. Do you have information to that effect?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So that would have a pretty significant impact if -- if we agreed that there -- that they no longer exist on -- on the universe of Bivens claims?

turns_same_span.text: No, Speaker A. In our view, there are no viable Carlson claims anymore. Now there may be statutes that people could point to in the Fourth Amendment area, but that would be something that would have to be litigated. turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] Our brief has offered three ways in which this Court could resolve the case. First, it could apply its existing standards and recognize that Carlson is now obsolete. We stand by all three of those arguments, but we would respectfully urge that the Court adopt one of the first two options, either of which would abrogate Carlson, fully resolve the circuit conflicts that it has created, and end the severe practical problems that it creates for prison administration. setting: Excerpt from a recorded institutional proceeding. Exactly one of the two speakers, A and B, holds the more powerful institutional role.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: You suggest in your brief that -- that Congress has ratified this line of cases, Bivens, Carlson, Davis. Precisely how did they do that?

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: I think our argument is more specific to Carlson.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: Mm-hmm.

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: I think it is in two ways. It's first through the Westfall Act, which I would characterize more as a form of reliance rather than ratification because Congress, as we've discussed, was taking something away that had existed since the founding but was doing so only with the express understanding that the constitutional claims recognized under Bivens and Carlson would remain. But the PLRA, I think, is where we have real validation and ratification of the Carlson remedy. And it bears going back to the dialogue between the Court and Congress that led up to that. Before McCarthy, before the PLRA, the administrative exhaustion provision requirement applied only to Section 1983 claims. This Court in McCarthy construed that narrowly and declined to impose a similar exhaustion requirement for Carlson claims as a matter of federal common law. Congress then responded with McCar- -- with the PLRA, which this Court has three times recognized was a direct response to McCarthy, and extended that administrative exhaustion requirement to all federal claims brought by prisoners. Now my friend has argued that that is not validation of a ratification because the PLRA applies more broadly, not just to Carlson claims. But the problem is that was also true of the PSLRA, which this Court held in Stoneridge ratified and validated the 10(b) implied private right of action under the Exchange Act. That statute also applies to Section 9 claims and Section 18 claims, which are express private rights of action. But this Court still said that the PSLRA was best understood as ratifying what the Court had said about 10(b) at the same time that Congress was expressing its view that this Court should not go further and expand that implied private right of action. And we think, consistent with Abbasi and Stoneridge, that's the white -- right way to understand the PLRA as well.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] "This far and no further" has been the Court's consistent message for Bivens and Carlson over the past decade. "No further" means we should not extend those precedents. But "this far" means also that Carlson remains settled law within its core context and should not be reduced to a null set. We ask only that the Court adhere to that approach. For more than four decades, Carlson has empowered federal prisoners to vindicate their constitutional rights against prison officers who wantonly inflict pain and suffering, and Congress has twice validated that remedy. First, in the Westfall Act, it eliminated the traditional state-law remedy against federal officers that had existed since the founding, but, at the same time, it expressly preserved claims brought for violations of the Constitution. And then, second, through the PLRA, Congress imposed an administrative exhaustion requirement on Carlson claims in direct response to this Court's decision in McCarthy. My friend and the United States nonetheless asks this Court to reinterpret its precedent and have now conceded that their approach would render Carlson claims -- or foreclose Carlson claims in all possible circumstances, even those arising under the precise same facts as Carlson itself. That is nothing less than a request to overrule precedent, and it is unjustifiable in view of the decades-long interbranch dialogue on this issue. Indeed, to overrule Carlson now would disregard Congress's measured judgment in this area and eliminate a crucial bulwark against the encroachment on the constitutional rights of some of society's most vulnerable members. We do not ask this Court to extend Carlson beyond its context, to reassess its criticism of that precedent, or to alter the new context framework. We ask only that the Court reaffirm what it has said: "This far and no further." I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: The first thing I would say is that Congress has already told us through the Westfall Act that it views the FTCA and constitutional came -- claims as complementary and not mutually exclusive.

turns_pm15.speaker: B

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Yes, [ADDRESS]. So the first thing I would say is that the FTCA, as the Court recognized not just in Carlson but has held also in FDIC v. Meyer and then again in Malesko, the virtue of a Carlson claim, its principal virtue, is the deterrent effect on the individual officer. And this Court in FDIC declined to extend Bivens to allow a claim against a federal agency precisely because doing so would eviscerate that deterrent effect. So that's not simply Carlson's rationale. That's the rationale that this Court has offered for why Carlson and Bivens claims are necessary in the first place. More specifically, on whether or not a plaintiff would have an FTCA claim here, there are, I think, a couple of problems with relying on the FTCA in this respect. The first is that we know the plaintiff in Carlson v. Green would not have had a cause of action under the FTCA because of Indiana's survivorship statute. For more than four decades, Carlson has empowered federal prisoners to vindicate their constitutional rights against prison officers who wantonly inflict pain and suffering, and Congress has twice validated that remedy. First, in the Westfall Act, it eliminated the traditional state-law remedy against federal officers that had existed since the founding, but, at the same time, it expressly preserved claims brought for violations of the Constitution. And then, second, through the PLRA, Congress imposed an administrative exhaustion requirement on Carlson claims in direct response to this Court's decision in McCarthy. My friend and the United States nonetheless asks this Court to reinterpret its precedent and have now conceded that their approach would render Carlson claims -- or foreclose Carlson claims in all possible circumstances, even those arising under the precise same facts as Carlson itself. That is nothing less than a request to overrule precedent, and it is unjustifiable in view of the decades-long interbranch dialogue on this issue. Indeed, to overrule Carlson now would disregard Congress's measured judgment in this area and eliminate a crucial bulwark against the encroachment on the constitutional rights of some of society's most vulnerable members. We do not ask this Court to extend Carlson beyond its context, to reassess its criticism of that precedent, or to alter the new context framework. We ask only that the Court reaffirm what it has said: "This far and no further." I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think our argument is more specific to Carlson.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think it is in two ways. It's first through the Westfall Act, which I would characterize more as a form of reliance rather than ratification because Congress, as we've discussed, was taking something away that had existed since the founding but was doing so only with the express understanding that the constitutional claims recognized under Bivens and Carlson would remain. But the PLRA, I think, is where we have real validation and ratification of the Carlson remedy. And it bears going back to the dialogue between the Court and Congress that led up to that. Before McCarthy, before the PLRA, the administrative exhaustion provision requirement applied only to Section 1983 claims. This Court in McCarthy construed that narrowly and declined to impose a similar exhaustion requirement for Carlson claims as a matter of federal common law. Congress then responded with McCar- -- with the PLRA, which this Court has three times recognized was a direct response to McCarthy, and extended that administrative exhaustion requirement to all federal claims brought by prisoners. Now my friend has argued that that is not validation of a ratification because the PLRA applies more broadly, not just to Carlson claims. But the problem is that was also true of the PSLRA, which this Court held in Stoneridge ratified and validated the 10(b) implied private right of action under the Exchange Act. That statute also applies to Section 9 claims and Section 18 claims, which are express private rights of action. But this Court still said that the PSLRA was best understood as ratifying what the Court had said about 10(b) at the same time that Congress was expressing its view that this Court should not go further and expand that implied private right of action. And we think, consistent with Abbasi and Stoneridge, that's the white -- right way to understand the PLRA as well.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think there's a few responses there. Maybe the best response is that, as we've discussed, Carlson itself depended on the conclusion that the individual himself, Mr. Jones, had a personal injury claim. That's the only reason the survivorship analysis even arose, was because it first had to conclude that there was a claim and then determine what the federal rule was going to be for survivorship of that claim. The other response I would offer is that Congress, through the PLRA, clearly contemplated that Carlson claims other than those resulting in death would be allowed because, as [PERSON] mentioned, it is only those claims that don't result in death that administrative remedies are even accessible to the plaintiff. So, if -- if it is correct that Carlson claims do not exist outside of the death context, then Congress's response to McCarthy in the PLRA is essentially rendered moot because that administrative exhaustion requirement will never apply to a Carlson claim.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think a big theme of what you heard from counsel on the other side was that you don't need Carlson or Bivens, they said, at least [PERSON], because the FTCA provides a remedy in meritorious cases that would otherwise merit recovery under Carlson or Bivens. So what's your response to that? Because, if that's true, that does seem to negate the need.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: The first thing I would say is that Congress has already told us through the Westfall Act that it views the FTCA and constitutional came -- claims as complementary and not mutually exclusive.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, that's a -- I get that response. But -- but, as a practical matter, I think they were saying --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- meritorious Carlson or Bivens claims would prevail under the FTCA in some form to provide some remedy in meritorious cases. So I think you need to respond to that.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes, [ADDRESS]. So the first thing I would say is that the FTCA, as the Court recognized not just in Carlson but has held also in FDIC v. Meyer and then again in Malesko, the virtue of a Carlson claim, its principal virtue, is the deterrent effect on the individual officer. And this Court in FDIC declined to extend Bivens to allow a claim against a federal agency precisely because doing so would eviscerate that deterrent effect. So that's not simply Carlson's rationale. That's the rationale that this Court has offered for why Carlson and Bivens claims are necessary in the first place. More specifically, on whether or not a plaintiff would have an FTCA claim here, there are, I think, a couple of problems with relying on the FTCA in this respect. The first is that we know the plaintiff in Carlson v. Green would not have had a cause of action under the FTCA because of Indiana's survivorship statute. So that case itself would have come out differently. But there are also other differences in state law. For example, the doctrine of contributory or comparative negligence could apply and, in some states, requires only 1 percent negligence on the part of the plaintiff to bar a remedy in its entirety, notwithstanding that the defendant there in those cases might have violated and intentionally violated their constitutional rights. And I think that all goes back to what this Court said in Carlson, that there is an inherent virtue in having a uniform body of federal law. This Court recognized it again in Abbasi, the reliance interest that follows not just for individual plaintiffs but for officers themselves who know what they're going to be held accountable for and in what circumstances. And that, I think, is all reason why the FTCA, while it might provide a remedy in some circumstances, it provides a qualitatively different remedy and may not even provide that remedy in all cases.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I think we actually agree that there are factual distinctions here that a hypothetical legislator could -- could take into account. The problem is the Court has never articulated the new context test in that way. It's never applied it in that way. And as my friends have now conceded today, the United States conceded in its brief, that approach would render every claim a new context claim. There are always going to be some factual distinctions. There are always going to be some differences --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I think, as we -- the way we understand the Court's new context test is this, which is we're looking for a difference that's meaningful in the way in which it raises new separation-of-powers questions, not simply that it raises new facts that a -- that Congress could consider but that it actually qualitatively changes the separation-of-powers analysis. That was what happened in Abbasi, where the claim there was being used to challenge executive-level policy following a historic terrorist attack, and the Court was understandably uncomfortable with the idea of using a damages claim in that way because you would be intruding on the executive's prerogative there to determine that policy. So the -- the factual distinctions that [ADDRESS] has raised, I think they are things that Congress could care about, but they're not qualitatively different from Carlson in terms of the separation-of-powers question of who was best equipped to actually make those determinations.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I think a couple of things there, [ADDRESS]. First off, I -- I -- I -- I read Abbasi a little bit differently. I don't think it's suggesting that a new context arises anytime there's a factual distinction that Congress could think is -- is relevant. And the reason why I think that's the case is because Abbasi says very clearly that nothing in the opinion is intended to cast doubt on the force or necessity of Bivens within its context. So, if -- if the test that the Court was laying out in Abbasi allows us to find a new context anytime there's any factual distinction -- and there's always going to be some factual distinction that could be relevant. I mean, Congress sets statute of limitations, right.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I think, in -- in large part, the questions, for example, about knowledge, affirmative conduct, they actually factor into the substantive standard, the Eighth Amendment standard for whether or not a claim can be brought here at all and then, again, perhaps in the qualified-immunity analysis of asking whether there's a clearly established precedent here. So understanding or evaluating whether someone has acted deliberately or negligently is already a part of the analysis, but it's not at the Carlson step. It's at the substantive Eighth Amendment step. And so, when this Court in Carlson recognized an Eighth Amendment claim, it was necessarily incorporating into that standard all those considerations about what level of recklessness versus knowledge versus deliberate indifference is required for a claim to be asserted.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I agree with that, [ADDRESS]. And it's particularly significant, again, because Congress has legislated in response, right? At the time Congress is passing the PLRA, it knows that McCarthy was a Carlson case where there was no death, where there was no acute emergency, and this Court was declining to impose an administrative exhaustion requirement. So Congress, in passing the PLRA, understood the class of Carlson claims that were being brought yet, instead of overruling it, erected a procedural structure around it. Same at the time of the Westfall Act. Again, for the vast better part of four decades, there's never been any question among the lower courts that a claim like Mr. Watanabe's arose in the prototypical Carlson context. That dispute came about only over the past few years after some courts, we believe, have started to misinterpret this Court's decision in Egbert as essentially foreclosing all of these claims. So this has not proven, actually, to be an unworkable or challenging exercise up until recently.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes, [ADDRESS].

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think it is also the case that there's a conceptual mismatch between using "death is different" as a distinguishing factor and the substantive Eighth Amendment claim that is being brought here because the remedy or -- sorry, excuse me -- the injury that's being remedied there is the pain and suffering attendant to the deliberate indifference, not the ultimate consequence, right? It is the actual suffering that has occurred. And it also runs into the deterrence problem.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: And I think, actually, for Eighth Amendment purposes, we would describe that violation as more egregious, not less, because it extends the pain and suffering even further, and --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: No, please.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Just that that is another way, I think, in which there's a mismatch between the substantive standard and the distinction that they've offered here.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: For -- not more serious, but, for purposes of the Eighth Amendment, what the -- what the Eighth Amendment is concerned with is the pain and suffering that leads up to the death, not the death itself. And so for them to draw the line in this way I actually think is kind of backwards as a matter of Eighth Amendment law.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It's a more serious constitutional violation, but -- but -- but --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yeah, yeah, I mean, as a -- as a matter of sort of common sense and tort law, yes, I would say death is very significant. But the problem is the mismatch between the Eighth Amendment and the distinction that they're drawing.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I don't think it would be an irrational line for a hypothetical Congress to do that. But I think we should start by asking ourselves: What has Congress actually done here, right? When it passed the Westfall Act, there was no notion that Carlson was limited to claims in which the prisoner died. And yet Congress still took the additional step, after enacting a -- an extensive and sweeping preemption provision, to then except from that Carlson claims and Bivens claims. And then, in the PLRA, again, Congress set up an administrative exhaustion scheme that only makes sense for Carlson claims if claims can be pursued by prisoners who did not die from their injury. So, yes, I understand that -- that that is a possible route that Congress could go, but I think we should be focusing on what is it that Congress has actually done and told us in this area about what types of claims it thinks are sustainable.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think, with -- with respect to Mr. Watanabe's claim, I mean that it has not seriously been disputed that a claim like this arises in the prototypical Carlson --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think it has. And I think also the Court's statement that the two steps sometimes collapse into each other, which I believe is correct but for a different reason than my -- than my friend does.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I -- I do, [ADDRESS], yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That is correct.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think a large problem is the -- the pro se litigants not knowing about the FTCA claims and also not knowing how to navigate the administrative procedures that you have to go through in order to assert an FTCA claim. There are obviously administrative exhaustion requirements for a Carlson claim, but those are within the walls of the prison. Everybody understands how those work at a general level. And I think there are practical challenges with pursuing an FTCA claim on a pro se basis.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That is our understanding of the precedent. And, yes, we agree with that.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, so two things. First off, I think I understand the PATRIOT Act to apply simply to all Department of Justice divisions, which include the Bureau of Prisons but is not specifically narrowed to that. But I -- I do think that this Court has recognized over time that there is something uniquely powerful about the threat of individual liability that serves an important and additional deterrence purposes. We're not suggesting that Carlson is the only thing out there that prevents officers from acting unconstitutionally. Of course, there's many other motivations for doing that. But this Court has consistently recognized that this type of claim has a special role in that place. And I -- I think it's especially important for a plaintiff of this type. Prisoners have been long understood as uniquely vulnerable within our common-law tradition, and there's unique responsibilities and obligations on the jailer that flow from that. And so, if we're going to hold deterrence up in any place, I think it has to be in this context, where we know these individuals are uniquely susceptible to constitutional violations.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I don't think it's -- I think it's actually contradicted by the Westfall Act because Congress is clearly contemplating there that there's going to be two remedies. There's going to be the FTCA and there's going to be the constitutional claim. So I wouldn't just say it's unsupported. I think it's actually foreclosed by what Congress has done. And -- and I would add also to that the PLRA, which describes administrative remedies as a prerequisite to and not a substitute for other claims, such as a Carlson claim or a 1983 claim.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.
