turns_pm60.text: [PERSON], I just want to make sure I understand the full panoply of your arguments. What you're saying is, regardless of whether we explicitly reverse Carlson, do a typical stare decisis analysis and reverse it, regardless of whether we do that, there are no viable Carlson claims on your view because there are new special factors --the PLRA, the ARP -- that have come into play since Carlson that make Carlson obsolete so that we can kind of bypass the traditional stare decisis inquiry and just say, because of the passage of the PLRA, et cetera, Carlson is obsolete anyway, good-bye, no Carlson claims. Is that correct?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Okay. If we put all of that aside and we say, no, we really are looking for meaningful differences, what principally or what in the entirety do you think is a meaningful difference?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, I mean here. I mean here.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It's a very harsh rule, right? If you say to somebody, well, if he dies, that's one thing, but, if there's a life-long, extremely severe disability, that's in a different box entirely, and Congress would treat it as such or at least potentially would treat it as such?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: You were asked whether Congress could change anything we did, and you said yes. I know the Justice Department, you know, would typically think of something -- a question to the effect of, is -- is what we're asking the Court to do essentially a dare to Congress to change it? Have you thought about that?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] "This far and no further" has been the Court's consistent message for Bivens and Carlson over the past decade. "No further" means we should not extend those precedents. But "this far" means also that Carlson remains settled law within its core context and should not be reduced to a null set. We ask only that the Court adhere to that approach. For more than four decades, Carlson has empowered federal prisoners to vindicate their constitutional rights against prison officers who wantonly inflict pain and suffering, and Congress has twice validated that remedy. First, in the Westfall Act, it eliminated the traditional state-law remedy against federal officers that had existed since the founding, but, at the same time, it expressly preserved claims brought for violations of the Constitution. And then, second, through the PLRA, Congress imposed an administrative exhaustion requirement on Carlson claims in direct response to this Court's decision in McCarthy. My friend and the United States nonetheless asks this Court to reinterpret its precedent and have now conceded that their approach would render Carlson claims -- or foreclose Carlson claims in all possible circumstances, even those arising under the precise same facts as Carlson itself. That is nothing less than a request to overrule precedent, and it is unjustifiable in view of the decades-long interbranch dialogue on this issue. Indeed, to overrule Carlson now would disregard Congress's measured judgment in this area and eliminate a crucial bulwark against the encroachment on the constitutional rights of some of society's most vulnerable members. We do not ask this Court to extend Carlson beyond its context, to reassess its criticism of that precedent, or to alter the new context framework. We ask only that the Court reaffirm what it has said: "This far and no further." I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think our argument is more specific to Carlson.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think it is in two ways. It's first through the Westfall Act, which I would characterize more as a form of reliance rather than ratification because Congress, as we've discussed, was taking something away that had existed since the founding but was doing so only with the express understanding that the constitutional claims recognized under Bivens and Carlson would remain. But the PLRA, I think, is where we have real validation and ratification of the Carlson remedy. And it bears going back to the dialogue between the Court and Congress that led up to that. Before McCarthy, before the PLRA, the administrative exhaustion provision requirement applied only to Section 1983 claims. This Court in McCarthy construed that narrowly and declined to impose a similar exhaustion requirement for Carlson claims as a matter of federal common law. Congress then responded with McCar- -- with the PLRA, which this Court has three times recognized was a direct response to McCarthy, and extended that administrative exhaustion requirement to all federal claims brought by prisoners. Now my friend has argued that that is not validation of a ratification because the PLRA applies more broadly, not just to Carlson claims. But the problem is that was also true of the PSLRA, which this Court held in Stoneridge ratified and validated the 10(b) implied private right of action under the Exchange Act. That statute also applies to Section 9 claims and Section 18 claims, which are express private rights of action. But this Court still said that the PSLRA was best understood as ratifying what the Court had said about 10(b) at the same time that Congress was expressing its view that this Court should not go further and expand that implied private right of action. And we think, consistent with Abbasi and Stoneridge, that's the white -- right way to understand the PLRA as well.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think there's a few responses there. Maybe the best response is that, as we've discussed, Carlson itself depended on the conclusion that the individual himself, Mr. Jones, had a personal injury claim. That's the only reason the survivorship analysis even arose, was because it first had to conclude that there was a claim and then determine what the federal rule was going to be for survivorship of that claim. The other response I would offer is that Congress, through the PLRA, clearly contemplated that Carlson claims other than those resulting in death would be allowed because, as [PERSON] mentioned, it is only those claims that don't result in death that administrative remedies are even accessible to the plaintiff. So, if -- if it is correct that Carlson claims do not exist outside of the death context, then Congress's response to McCarthy in the PLRA is essentially rendered moot because that administrative exhaustion requirement will never apply to a Carlson claim.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: The first thing I would say is that Congress has already told us through the Westfall Act that it views the FTCA and constitutional came -- claims as complementary and not mutually exclusive.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes, [ADDRESS]. So the first thing I would say is that the FTCA, as the Court recognized not just in Carlson but has held also in FDIC v. Meyer and then again in Malesko, the virtue of a Carlson claim, its principal virtue, is the deterrent effect on the individual officer. And this Court in FDIC declined to extend Bivens to allow a claim against a federal agency precisely because doing so would eviscerate that deterrent effect. So that's not simply Carlson's rationale. That's the rationale that this Court has offered for why Carlson and Bivens claims are necessary in the first place. More specifically, on whether or not a plaintiff would have an FTCA claim here, there are, I think, a couple of problems with relying on the FTCA in this respect. The first is that we know the plaintiff in Carlson v. Green would not have had a cause of action under the FTCA because of Indiana's survivorship statute. So that case itself would have come out differently. But there are also other differences in state law. For example, the doctrine of contributory or comparative negligence could apply and, in some states, requires only 1 percent negligence on the part of the plaintiff to bar a remedy in its entirety, notwithstanding that the defendant there in those cases might have violated and intentionally violated their constitutional rights. And I think that all goes back to what this Court said in Carlson, that there is an inherent virtue in having a uniform body of federal law. This Court recognized it again in Abbasi, the reliance interest that follows not just for individual plaintiffs but for officers themselves who know what they're going to be held accountable for and in what circumstances. And that, I think, is all reason why the FTCA, while it might provide a remedy in some circumstances, it provides a qualitatively different remedy and may not even provide that remedy in all cases.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Speaker A --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I'm wondering, Speaker A, whether you think there might be other factual differences besides the death versus all other injuries one that you've been asked about. So I can think of a couple if I look at the facts of Carlson and I look at the facts here. In Carlson, there was a view that the prison officials had actively contributed to the injury, and there was also a view that the prison officials knew exactly what was happening while it was happening. So knowledge and contribution seem actually the kinds of factual circumstances which Congress might be interested in if it's thinking about what kind of tort remedy to create. Why isn't that the case?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I think we actually agree that there are factual distinctions here that a hypothetical legislator could -- could take into account. The problem is the Court has never articulated the new context test in that way. It's never applied it in that way. And as my friends have now conceded today, the United States conceded in its brief, that approach would render every claim a new context claim. There are always going to be some factual distinctions. There are always going to be some differences --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But the -- the -- the ones that I just gave you is not like, you know, what color uniform was the official wearing. These are meaningful things with respect to the proper scope of a tort remedy, knowledge, contribution. These are the kinds of things courts think about and Congress, you know, anybody that creates a remedy would think about when it decides how far the remedy goes. I guess one other -- a different way of saying the same thing is that this looks like a pretty standard medical malpractice case, bad but standard, where --where the -- the factual circumstances in Carlson look like something a good deal more than that.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I think, as we -- the way we understand the Court's new context test is this, which is we're looking for a difference that's meaningful in the way in which it raises new separation-of-powers questions, not simply that it raises new facts that a -- that Congress could consider but that it actually qualitatively changes the separation-of-powers analysis. That was what happened in Abbasi, where the claim there was being used to challenge executive-level policy following a historic terrorist attack, and the Court was understandably uncomfortable with the idea of using a damages claim in that way because you would be intruding on the executive's prerogative there to determine that policy. So the -- the factual distinctions that [ADDRESS] has raised, I think they are things that Congress could care about, but they're not qualitatively different from Carlson in terms of the separation-of-powers question of who was best equipped to actually make those determinations.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah. I mean, I think there really is a question here as to how far we've suggested these factual -- these differences go. I mean, one way to understand these differences is to say, is it a different claim based on a different constitutional provision? Is it a different set, category of defendants? Is it even, like, something that is just so obviously a different context, like, we're dealing with national security issues, we're dealing with border issues? You know, but -- but we also have suggested in a couple of these recent cases it's anything Congress could reasonably be concerned about when thinking about fashioning a remedy. What's our knowledge standard? What's our contribution standard? Exactly the kinds of differences that exist between this case and Carlson.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I think a couple of things there, [ADDRESS]. First off, I -- I -- I -- I read Abbasi a little bit differently. I don't think it's suggesting that a new context arises anytime there's a factual distinction that Congress could think is -- is relevant. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I think, in -- in large part, the questions, for example, about knowledge, affirmative conduct, they actually factor into the substantive standard, the Eighth Amendment standard for whether or not a claim can be brought here at all and then, again, perhaps in the qualified-immunity analysis of asking whether there's a clearly established precedent here. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I agree with that, [ADDRESS]. And it's particularly significant, again, because Congress has legislated in response, right? Same at the time of the Westfall Act. Again, for the vast better part of four decades, there's never been any question among the lower courts that a claim like Mr. Watanabe's arose in the prototypical Carlson context. That dispute came about only over the past few years after some courts, we believe, have started to misinterpret this Court's decision in Egbert as essentially foreclosing all of these claims. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes, [ADDRESS].

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think it is also the case that there's a conceptual mismatch between using "death is different" as a distinguishing factor and the substantive Eighth Amendment claim that is being brought here because the remedy or -- sorry, excuse me -- the injury that's being remedied there is the pain and suffering attendant to the deliberate indifference, not the ultimate consequence, right? turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: And I think, actually, for Eighth Amendment purposes, we would describe that violation as more egregious, not less, because it extends the pain and suffering even further, and --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: No, please.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Just that that is another way, I think, in which there's a mismatch between the substantive standard and the distinction that they've offered here.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: For -- not more serious, but, for purposes of the Eighth Amendment, what the -- what the Eighth Amendment is concerned with is the pain and suffering that leads up to the death, not the death itself. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It's a more serious constitutional violation, but -- but -- but --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yeah, yeah, I mean, as a -- as a matter of sort of common sense and tort law, yes, I would say death is very significant. But the problem is the mismatch between the Eighth Amendment and the distinction that they're drawing.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I don't think it would be an irrational line for a hypothetical Congress to do that. But I think we should start by asking ourselves: What has Congress actually done here, right? turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think, with -- with respect to Mr. Watanabe's claim, I mean that it has not seriously been disputed that a claim like this arises in the prototypical Carlson --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I -- I do, [ADDRESS], yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That is correct.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think a large problem is the -- the pro se litigants not knowing about the FTCA claims and also not knowing how to navigate the administrative procedures that you have to go through in order to assert an FTCA claim. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That is our understanding of the precedent. And, yes, we agree with that.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Well, so two things. We're not suggesting that Carlson is the only thing out there that prevents officers from acting unconstitutionally. Of course, there's many other motivations for doing that. Prisoners have been long understood as uniquely vulnerable within our common-law tradition, and there's unique responsibilities and obligations on the jailer that flow from that. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I don't think it's -- I think it's actually contradicted by the Westfall Act because Congress is clearly contemplating there that there's going to be two remedies. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

turns_pm60.text: So I think, as we -- the way we understand the Court's new context test is this, which is we're looking for a difference that's meaningful in the way in which it raises new separation-of-powers questions, not simply that it raises new facts that a -- that Congress could consider but that it actually qualitatively changes the separation-of-powers analysis. turns_pm60.text: Well, [PERSON] is not talking about just any old distinction. She is talking about specific differences. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I think, in -- in large part, the questions, for example, about knowledge, affirmative conduct, they actually factor into the substantive standard, the Eighth Amendment standard for whether or not a claim can be brought here at all and then, again, perhaps in the qualified-immunity analysis of asking whether there's a clearly established precedent here. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] "This far and no further" has been the Court's consistent message for Bivens and Carlson over the past decade. "No further" means we should not extend those precedents. But "this far" means also that Carlson remains settled law within its core context and should not be reduced to a null set. We ask only that the Court adhere to that approach. For more than four decades, Carlson has empowered federal prisoners to vindicate their constitutional rights against prison officers who wantonly inflict pain and suffering, and Congress has twice validated that remedy. First, in the Westfall Act, it eliminated the traditional state-law remedy against federal officers that had existed since the founding, but, at the same time, it expressly preserved claims brought for violations of the Constitution. And then, second, through the PLRA, Congress imposed an administrative exhaustion requirement on Carlson claims in direct response to this Court's decision in McCarthy. My friend and the United States nonetheless asks this Court to reinterpret its precedent and have now conceded that their approach would render Carlson claims -- or foreclose Carlson claims in all possible circumstances, even those arising under the precise same facts as Carlson itself. That is nothing less than a request to overrule precedent, and it is unjustifiable in view of the decades-long interbranch dialogue on this issue. Indeed, to overrule Carlson now would disregard Congress's measured judgment in this area and eliminate a crucial bulwark against the encroachment on the constitutional rights of some of society's most vulnerable members. We do not ask this Court to extend Carlson beyond its context, to reassess its criticism of that precedent, or to alter the new context framework. We ask only that the Court reaffirm what it has said: "This far and no further." I welcome the Court's questions.

Before McCarthy, before the PLRA, the administrative exhaustion provision requirement applied only to Section 1983 claims. This Court in McCarthy construed that narrowly and declined to impose a similar exhaustion requirement for Carlson claims as a matter of federal common law. Congress then responded with McCar- -- with the PLRA, which this Court has three times recognized was a direct response to McCarthy, and extended that administrative exhaustion requirement to all federal claims brought by prisoners. Now my friend has argued that that is not validation of a ratification because the PLRA applies more broadly, not just to Carlson claims. But the problem is that was also true of the PSLRA, which this Court held in Stoneridge ratified and validated the 10(b) implied private right of action under the Exchange Act. That statute also applies to Section 9 claims and Section 18 claims, which are express private rights of action. But this Court still said that the PSLRA was best understood as ratifying what the Court had said about 10(b) at the same time that Congress was expressing its view that this Court should not go further and expand that implied private right of action. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] "This far and no further" has been the Court's consistent message for Bivens and Carlson over the past decade. "No further" means we should not extend those precedents. But "this far" means also that Carlson remains settled law within its core context and should not be reduced to a null set. We ask only that the Court adhere to that approach. For more than four decades, Carlson has empowered federal prisoners to vindicate their constitutional rights against prison officers who wantonly inflict pain and suffering, and Congress has twice validated that remedy. First, in the Westfall Act, it eliminated the traditional state-law remedy against federal officers that had existed since the founding, but, at the same time, it expressly preserved claims brought for violations of the Constitution. And then, second, through the PLRA, Congress imposed an administrative exhaustion requirement on Carlson claims in direct response to this Court's decision in McCarthy. My friend and the United States nonetheless asks this Court to reinterpret its precedent and have now conceded that their approach would render Carlson claims -- or foreclose Carlson claims in all possible circumstances, even those arising under the precise same facts as Carlson itself. That is nothing less than a request to overrule precedent, and it is unjustifiable in view of the decades-long interbranch dialogue on this issue. Indeed, to overrule Carlson now would disregard Congress's measured judgment in this area and eliminate a crucial bulwark against the encroachment on the constitutional rights of some of society's most vulnerable members. We do not ask this Court to extend Carlson beyond its context, to reassess its criticism of that precedent, or to alter the new context framework. We ask only that the Court reaffirm what it has said: "This far and no further." I welcome the Court's questions.

Before McCarthy, before the PLRA, the administrative exhaustion provision requirement applied only to Section 1983 claims. This Court in McCarthy construed that narrowly and declined to impose a similar exhaustion requirement for Carlson claims as a matter of federal common law. Congress then responded with McCar- -- with the PLRA, which this Court has three times recognized was a direct response to McCarthy, and extended that administrative exhaustion requirement to all federal claims brought by prisoners. Now my friend has argued that that is not validation of a ratification because the PLRA applies more broadly, not just to Carlson claims. turns_pm15.text: I -- I do, [ADDRESS], yes.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Yes.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: That is correct.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: I think a large problem is the -- the pro se litigants not knowing about the FTCA claims and also not knowing how to navigate the administrative procedures that you have to go through in order to assert an FTCA claim. There are obviously administrative exhaustion requirements for a Carlson claim, but those are within the walls of the prison. Everybody understands how those work at a general level. And I think there are practical challenges with pursuing an FTCA claim on a pro se basis.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS], you agree that Congress could eliminate Bivens actions tomorrow if it wanted?

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: That is our understanding of the precedent. And, yes, we agree with that.

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: Okay. One other question. Your friends on the other side point to the PATRIOT Act as a subsequent legislative development. And I confess, on the question of whether that's an alternative remedy and a cause of action, I don't find the existence of that statute really neither here -- I think it's neither here nor there. But you were emphasizing deterrence before and the importance of Bivens actions in deterring unconstitutional conduct by prison officials. The PATRIOT Act, as I understand it, does tighten up prison regulations and provide for discipline of officials that do violate regulations in federal law. Would that bear on whether it's appropriate to have a Carlson remedy here given that there are other mechanisms Congress has put in place for purposes of deterrence?

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Well, so two things. First off, I think I understand the PATRIOT Act to apply simply to all Department of Justice divisions, which include the Bureau of Prisons but is not specifically narrowed to that. turns_pm15.speaker: B

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: B

Before McCarthy, before the PLRA, the administrative exhaustion provision requirement applied only to Section 1983 claims. This Court in McCarthy construed that narrowly and declined to impose a similar exhaustion requirement for Carlson claims as a matter of federal common law. Congress then responded with McCar- -- with the PLRA, which this Court has three times recognized was a direct response to McCarthy, and extended that administrative exhaustion requirement to all federal claims brought by prisoners. That statute also applies to Section 9 claims and Section 18 claims, which are express private rights of action. turns_pm60.text: The first thing I would say is that Congress has already told us through the Westfall Act that it views the FTCA and constitutional came -- claims as complementary and not mutually exclusive.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes.

turns_pm60.text: No, please.

turns_pm60.text: Just that that is another way, I think, in which there's a mismatch between the substantive standard and the distinction that they've offered here.

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It's a more serious constitutional violation, but -- but -- but --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yeah, yeah, I mean, as a -- as a matter of sort of common sense and tort law, yes, I would say death is very significant. But the problem is the mismatch between the Eighth Amendment and the distinction that they're drawing.

case: Hoffmann v. WBI Energy Transmission, Inc.
setting: Excerpt from a recorded institutional proceeding. Exactly one of the two speakers, A and B, holds the more powerful institutional role.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: Could you give me some examples of your argument or your approach being applied in recent years?

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: I think our approach is exactly the approach this Court took last term in Hencely, [ADDRESS], which is that even-handed state laws --

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: In pipeline case -- in eminent domain cases.

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: Well, [ADDRESS], this Court has yet to decide really a private condemnor case, so this Court's cases are all about the United States as sovereign taking property.

turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: So, if the U.S. delegates its power, its authority to --of eminent domain, you're saying that it brings with it state law trappings of just compensation?

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: I think we're saying it doesn't preempt state just compensation law that would otherwise apply, [ADDRESS], because --

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] The Natural Gas Act authorizes private companies to ask courts to order the forced sale of private property, but it says nothing about the substantive law those courts should use to determine what that property is worth. That silence matters because, on its own, authorizing companies to file condemnations does nothing to preempt state laws defining the measure of compensation. As this Court held in Jones and as Congress and the courts would have known in 1947, the right of eminent domain is just the power to take property. It's separate from an individual's right to just compensation, which flows from a different source. North Dakota law provides that source here. On its face, it imposes even-handed obligations on anyone who condemns land in that state, including WBI. The Fifth Amendment places a floor on that compensation but not a ceiling. Now, to be sure, North Dakota law wouldn't apply to the United States if it took land in its own name, but that's not because of some special trait of the federal eminent domain cause of action. It's because the United States is sovereign. And private companies aren't sovereign. They're private delegees. And this Court has consistently said that distinction matters. Nothing in the statute extends the United States' sovereign immunity to private companies, and that means they don't have it. That's what Congress would have expected in 1947, which was just three years after this Court in Davies Warehouse reaffirmed its longstanding custom of looking to state law to give meaning and content to federal statutes. Silence meant state law then. Silence means state law today. North Dakota law controls unless Congress preempts it or the Kimbell Foods factors demand a uniform federal rule. We read this statute to do what Congress meant for it to do, ensure that pipeline companies had access to an eminent domain cause of action in all 50 states. That's all the statute says. That's all contemporaneous courts believed it did, and that's because that's all it does. It delegates the power to take property, but it leaves the law of just compensation where it found it, with the states. I welcome this Court's questions.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: I -- I don't think so, [ADDRESS], for two reasons. One, this distinction between the United States as condemnor and a private party that's been vested with the eminent domain power is a longstanding one, and it goes back -- it's articulated in this Court's decision in United States v. Carmack, but it's a longstanding common-law principle that when Congress delegates the eminent domain power to an arm of the United States Government, that carries with it all of the United States' powers, but when it delegates it to a private party, that's necessarily a grant of limited powers. It doesn't include -- I'll stop.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: No, I think that's right, [ADDRESS], and I think it matters whether the United States is the party or whether this is a delegation of public power into private hands, which this Court has always read more narrowly. And even in my friend's eminent domain cases, this Court seems to be drawing exactly that distinction. I -- I'd point the Court to 93.97 Acres, which is, I think, the strongest statement of federal law controlling where the government is condemning for important federal interests. But the cases this Court cites in 93.97 are cases where the United States is taking land, and then it cites Clearfield Trust, where the Court said that the federal law merchant controls questions about federal commercial paper, and Parnell for --

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Yes, [ADDRESS].

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Yes, [ADDRESS].

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Yes, [ADDRESS].

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: Because I think it matters whether the United States is doing things as sovereign or whether a private delegee is doing it. The -- the same could be said of Hencely last term, [ADDRESS]. If the United States puts itself in charge of base security in war zones, no one thinks that you can use state law to sue the United States for its on-base security. But, in Hencely, this Court said that state tort law was not preempted. And I think the same analysis applies here. It matters whether the sovereign is acting. And I think that is throughout this Court's eminent domain cases. It's throughout this Court's preemption cases.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] The Natural Gas Act authorizes private companies to ask courts to order the forced sale of private property, but it says nothing about the substantive law those courts should use to determine what that property is worth. That silence matters because, on its own, authorizing companies to file condemnations does nothing to preempt state laws defining the measure of compensation. It's separate from an individual's right to just compensation, which flows from a different source. North Dakota law provides that source here. On its face, it imposes even-handed obligations on anyone who condemns land in that state, including WBI. The Fifth Amendment places a floor on that compensation but not a ceiling. Now, to be sure, North Dakota law wouldn't apply to the United States if it took land in its own name, but that's not because of some special trait of the federal eminent domain cause of action. It's because the United States is sovereign. And private companies aren't sovereign. They're private delegees. And this Court has consistently said that distinction matters. Nothing in the statute extends the United States' sovereign immunity to private companies, and that means they don't have it. That's what Congress would have expected in 1947, which was just three years after this Court in Davies Warehouse reaffirmed its longstanding custom of looking to state law to give meaning and content to federal statutes. Silence meant state law then. Silence means state law today. North Dakota law controls unless Congress preempts it or the Kimbell Foods factors demand a uniform federal rule. We read this statute to do what Congress meant for it to do, ensure that pipeline companies had access to an eminent domain cause of action in all 50 states. That's all the statute says. That's all contemporaneous courts believed it did, and that's because that's all it does. It delegates the power to take property, but it leaves the law of just compensation where it found it, with the states. I welcome this Court's questions.

turns_pm60.text: I think it may well have, [ADDRESS], and I think it matters that Congress is very clearly not trying to --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Seventy- one, yes, [ADDRESS]. I think that language today is not enforced. But I do think it shows that Congress isn't trying to change anything about how these proceedings go. turns_pm60.text: So I think that we deal with Miller by pointing out that in Miller, the United States was the condemnor, and so Miller says that the measure of compensation --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: And I think that --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: No, go ahead, [ADDRESS].

turns_pm60.text: Different --

turns_pm60.text: For the United States?

turns_pm60.speaker: A

That's the correct reading of the statute. Thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, but I think that leads to my second answer, [ADDRESS], which is, really, Congress is free, if it wants to, to oust state just compensation law, but nothing in the text or legislative history says anything about changing the existing background rule that state compensation law was controlling here. Now it may be that energy cost concerns have changed in the decades since 1947. I'd certainly concede that. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Thank you.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: No, [ADDRESS]. It comes up in a variety of other contexts where states have made nuanced judgments that the fair market value standard isn't meeting the realities in their state. Some states have different rules about valuing rural property, which the states have determined isn't best value through a pure fair market value analysis. Different states have rules about how you value an ongoing business that's on the land, whether that's a separate piece of property or whether that collapses into the land. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Because the condemnor in United States versus Miller is the United States. And, again, this Court makes clear in its eminent domain cases that the United States' sovereign immunity is what's doing work in those cases. It's why the only measure of compensation is the constitutional minimum. And Miller comes out, again, the same term as United States v. Carmack in 1946, where this Court says things are different when Congress delegates eminent domain into private hands. That's a narrower delegation. We're more skeptical of that. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Can you connect the dots between the issue presented and the cost issue that your brief identifies, the cost for consumers?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Has that been a real problem in the areas governed by different circuit precedent?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Just three points in rebuttal, [ADDRESS]. turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: So, to start with, the relevance would be, was there some uniform, well-understood background against which Congress was legislating in 1947? And I think the answer to that is clearly no. I -- I recognize the Feltz case of the Eighth Circuit out of 1942, and then another case decided by the same panel with the same dispute a couple weeks later in Fairchild has a single sentence that says Nebraska law applies. It was not disputed. It does not appear that it had any dispositive outcome. It was a simple sentence that I don't think was -- there was no reasoning. My -- my friends in the yellow brief agree there was no reasoning. So, to start with, that's not the kind of universal consensus in the lower courts that we think, well, Congress must have been aware of this and incorporated it. But I think there's much better evidence, which is what Congress was aware of, is what this Court did in 1943, construing the Condemnation Act of 1888. I've talked about that. And then there were at least six courts of appeals cases between 1943 and when Congress acted in 1947 understanding the implications of Miller. So I think, if we're trying to -- to use that frame of analysis as to what the state of judicial affairs was in 1947 and what Congress would have understood, Congress would have known that if it did the same thing it did in the 1888 Act in the 1947 amendment, it would have a clear conclusion, the conclusion this Court had already drawn for it in 1943. And, again, I don't think there's much of a surprise because, just the year prior, Congress wanted a different result in the General Bridge Act, and it had the language at hand. I don't think it matters that the General Bridge Act had a pedigree going back decades. It just means that Congress had two different mechanisms to choose from. It had one set of language when it felt like in its policy judgment that the compensation measure should model state law. It had language for that. It had other language that this Court had already construed to say when we want the just --the federal just compensation standard, that's the one that we're going to use. And -- and Congress made that choice.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] As PennEast explained, Congress delegated to pipelines the federal government's eminent domain power. The question here is the remedy. Did Congress intend the federal remedy that controls when the federal government takes property or the state remedy that governs when states take property? It makes most sense to conclude that Congress intended for the federal compensation standard. When Congress enacted 7(h), it resembled the Condemnation Act of 1888, which the Court in Miller had construed just four years earlier as adopting the federal measure of compensation. This was in stark contrast to the General Bridge Act enacted a year prior, where Congress explicitly incorporated state compensation law. In 7(h) itself, Congress used state law in one specific way, for practice and procedure. When Congress wanted state law to apply, it said so. Ultimately, Petitioner's argument requires the Court to conclude that in creating this new federal cause of action for pipelines, Congress explicitly adopted state law for procedure, but it silently adopted state law for remedy. I want to turn for a moment to my colleague's argument on sovereign immunity because I think that's the linchpin to their argument. They assert that but for sovereign immunity, state law would govern a federal taking. That's fundamentally wrong. State law applies to state takings. Federal law governs federal takings. This Court said that clearly in Kohl and in 93.97 Acres. It's just the same that states don't get to regulate the federal government's power of war. The states don't get to regulate the federal government's eminent domain authority. That's the authority that has been delegated to pipelines. Congress can decide that that authority should be or that measure of compensation should be incorporated into federal law if Congress chooses. It chose to do so in the General Bridge Act. It did not do so, however, in 7(h). That is the choice that should be respected. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS], I think the most simple answer is it is not sovereign immunity that's doing the work for the federal government. The federal government's power, as this Court said in Kohl and in 93.97 Acres, is not subject to state regulation. So it is simply not a -- a sovereign immunity issue. Now, if a state says, well, we don't like how the government is --is using its federal domain power, the --the federal government would not say, well, we're immune from the state law. They would say the state law is without force for reasons of the Supremacy Clause, that this is the federal power and states are -- do not have the authority to restrict the state power. And to Speaker A's point earlier about, well, what do we think about state practice and procedure, the -- the -- the -- the Act that Miller was construing, the Condemnation Act, had the exact same terms that practice and procedure in 1888 would also govern the Condemnation Act, but that didn't factor into the Court's analysis that, sure, procedure will -- will follow state law, but the compensation, this critical compensation question, is a matter solely of federal law.

turns_pm15.text: Well, [ADDRESS], I don't think we have a gap. turns_same_span.speaker: A
turns_same_span.text: Speaker B, is there still judgment required in determining how to figure out just compensation? In other words, does the Fifth Amendment just solve that question on its own, or do federal courts have to develop some sort of common law or flesh out what it means for fair market value? How do you know what the fair market value is? Because, presumably, there will be some times, even putting aside special rules for heritage sites, et cetera, there are presumably going to be some times where states say this is how you figure out what fair market value is.

turns_same_span.speaker: B
turns_same_span.text: Yes. So this Court obviously has expounded on what kinds of things are -- are in and out, but then, even in terms of determining fair market value, there is a pretty robust body of federal law and guidance in terms of, you know, do you look at the before-and-after value, do you look at comparisons to other arm's-length transactions. There is something called the Yellow Book, it's kind of a -- a -- a guidance document for -- for federal takings. And, obviously, these takings come up in the Court of Federal Claims when -- when the United States takes land and --and we litigate those issues. So there is a whole kind of ready-made body of law here. I think that's actually another reason why resorting to state law doesn't make a lot of sense. My friends have talked in their briefs about instances in which the court will kind of borrow state law when it comes to interpreting statutes that have to do with property, and that's often because there is a ready-made body of state property law and there isn't really the same kind of thing for federal property rules. And so judicial humility sort of counsels in favor of -- of borrowing the ready-made law rather than just making something up. But that's not a situation we have here because the Fifth Amendment standard is -- is a well-developed standard. And federal, you know, land valuation standards exist and all the rest.

turns_same_span.speaker: A

turns_same_span.speaker: B

I would also point out that some of the courts might not have appreciated the extent to which this is a categorical delegation. A lot of these cases were decided before PennEast. The Eleventh Circuit revisited this case after PennEast but -- but felt bound by prior Fifth Circuit precedent. And then the Eighth Circuit considers this issue afresh after PennEast and I think appreciates the -- the categorical nature of the delegation.

turns_pm15.speaker: A

turns_pm15.speaker: B
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] When the federal government takes land, it must pay just compensation under the Fifth Amendment unless Congress affirmatively requires more. When the federal government exercises its eminent domain power through a delegee, the same default rule applies. That rule resolves this case because the Natural Gas Act does not require compensation above the Fifth Amendment standard. Petitioners' contrary default rule makes little sense. State compensation laws do not apply of their own force in federal condemnation actions, so Congress had no need to expressly displace them in the NGA. Nor did Congress silently adopt state compensation laws in granting pipelines the federal power of eminent domain. That kind of mismatch is especially implausible for this delegation, whose very purpose was to make interstate pipelines less dependent on state eminent domain laws. Finally, the statute leaves no gap to fill through judicial lawmaking. But, even if it did, the Court should choose the Fifth Amendment's standard. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm15.speaker: B

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] When a federal statutory claim resembles common-law actions and remedies, this Court presumes private rights are at stake and that Article III adjudication is required. But, as Jarkesy reaffirmed, that presumption is overcome when the federal claim fits within historical categories of public rights. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: [ADDRESS] When a federal statutory claim resembles common-law actions and remedies, this Court presumes private rights are at stake and that Article III adjudication is required. But, as Jarkesy reaffirmed, that presumption is overcome when the federal claim fits within historical categories of public rights. Here, two historical public rights categories overlap: sovereign control of immigration and government-granted privileges. The government is exercising its plenary immigration power on the employer's behalf to grant aliens visas and allow them to stay and work for that employer. In exchange, the employer agrees to comply with the government's conditions spelled out in 8 U.S.C. 1188 and the implementing regulations. Those ensure that importing particular aliens for particular work won't distort U.S. wages or working conditions for those jobs. Agencies, not just courts, unquestionably adjudicate violations of those conditions. Even Respondent seemingly agrees that the agency could adjudicate every claim at issue if the remedy was just kicking the employer out of the H-2A program. Imposing civil penalties and back wages doesn't change the answer. Indeed, Oceanic Steam and Lloyd Sabaudo upheld near- identical remedies a century ago in similar circumstances. Respondent instead argues that only courts can adjudicate civil penalties. But Oceanic Steam rejected that very theory. Respondent is also wrong that the agency is enforcing contracts between employers and aliens. The agency is adjudicating the employer's violations of its regulatory promises to the government. That classic public rights dispute doesn't convert to private rights just because the government requires employers to embed those federal regulations in their contracts as a further enforcement mechanism. The government requires the same of Medicare program participants, federal contractors, and federal student loan providers. This Court should not upend those programs based on an ahistorical and artificial objection. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm60.text: How would that work out? I would encourage you to first start with conceiving of the nature of the privilege, as the Court did in Oil States. It's --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: The privilege is importing goods, and so I think you can draw lines between what does that specific privilege look like, as the way the Court did in Oil States, patents versus other public --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right. And so the way I think that works out is, for the foreign commerce privilege, I think you could draw a different line, which is the foreign commerce privilege, unlike the immigration rights, does, at a certain point, vest in the person -- like, in -- you have to draw a line between --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Because the -- of the difference between foreign commerce and interstate commerce. And I think the Court's Footnote 1 in Jarkesy draws this distinction pretty well. You have to look at --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I think the way you could do it that would be on the permissible side of the line is you are banning importation of goods that are defective in some way or that you think don't meet labor standards, the good itself. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: And you could say at -- at -- for those goods, if you thought that those goods at the moment of importation would have a bad effect on whatever it is in the country, you could say: I'm banning those goods from the country.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: If you try to import them, civil penalties --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right. And I think --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think it's too far removed specific to the tradition of foreign commerce and the way that power works.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: And here's why. The Court has distinguished between the scope of the privilege to control importation of goods for foreign commerce purposes and the point at which you're past the importer, the sort of a private right to the good vests, and you're trying to regulate at the back end --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- which is what I think your hypothetical taking --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think immigration power is different, and this Court's cases actually --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It -- it -- it is always a conditional privilege.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It ends at the point when someone's status changes.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, that -- that begs the question of the other side says that the immigration power stops at the border basically. That stops at the border. But that's not true --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- because we've had plenty of cases, Fong Yue Ting, where an alien was here for years, and we said you can deport him in administrative process, correct?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Exactly. And that's why that -- that public right is different from foreign commerce.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So -- exactly. But now let's put -- where I think [PERSON] is talking about. You concede, don't you, that there are some things that would not be sufficiently related to immigration, following conditions of securities trading, for example? Do you concede that wouldn't be within the immigration power of the United States to put into administrative proceedings?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes, insofar as it's something different from just saying you can't break the law. Like, if it's --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: All right.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- if it's -- if it's something more than that. And I think I would also concede there's a lot of other conditions you can't do on employers. You can't say the condition of getting an alien is you have to submit to all of your torts or all of your employment practices in agency adjudications. You can't attach extraneous conditions. There's a germaneness requirement.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Germaneness, that's your test. So do you have a way of defining what "germaneness" means? Is it related to the terms and conditions of employment or what -- what --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think it has to relate to the -- the public right and the privilege itself. The privilege is, here, a combination of the sovereign power over immigration. So it's relating to the historical tradition of being able to control the terms and conditions under which aliens are allowed to enter and remain in the United States. And the employer's reciprocal obligations relate to that. It is -- everything in this program is geared towards preventing there being adverse effects from doing that thing, allowing the alien into the country to work for you, the employer, and under specified conditions. And the employer knows all of those conditions at the outset. That's the whole point of the certification process.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: You gave up on Atlas -- Atlas Roofing in this case. But I looked at the terms and conditions. We keep talking about them as an employment contract almost, but this is the most unusual employment contract I've ever seen, although you do have terms on wages, terms on pest control, not charging people for -- certain amounts for things they buy. It's an unusual -- it's not the general employment contract that employees sign with their employers.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That's exactly correct because it's dictated by the -- entirely dictated by the Labor Secretary's findings under the program that these are the conditions necessary to prevent adverse effects on U.S. labor and working conditions.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: When we impose tariffs, we impose it for a lot of reasons, correct?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Not just the -- so the fact that this might have a limitation on immigration, which we want to respect, we can also want to protect American workers, correct?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes, because it's sort of a one-to-one. By importing foreign labor, you are trying to prevent a situation in which you have a tradeoff with people who would otherwise be working --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But I go back to Atlas Roofing. This very much is more like safety and health regulation that really is not in the common law than it is a contract dispute.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So here is what I would say about Atlas Roofing. The reason we don't think that it's at issue in this case is because this case, unlike Atlas Roofing, involves historical areas of public rights. And that's sort of what we're resting on. And it doesn't involve traditional contracts in that sense. You can have lots of other areas of public rights that might look like, at the surface level, 40,000-foot level, they involve contracts. That's true of certainly government contracts, like one of the classic areas of public rights. That's true of the Oceanic Steam case obviously involved negligence or sort of contract actions. Just because you have that threshold resemblance cannot be dispositive. Atlas Roofing was a little different because it did not involve any common law analog at all, but it also didn't involve a historical tradition of public rights.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: We have not relied on Atlas Roofing.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: We did not rely on Atlas Roofing because the Court has said it had cast doubt on Atlas Roofing.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So a couple things. I think the basic answer is yes with some caveats with respect to some of your specific hypothetical. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: The way, like the INA -- one classic example in the INA itself is for illegal entry. There are civil penalty provisions for illegal entry. So you -- you do something that you're not allowed to do as a matter of the INA, you may face civil penalties. You violated a condition. Some of your conditions, we could talk about whether they're germane to, like, how much -- how much the federal government can control, like, what you're doing in the country.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But yeah.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Because I think, respectfully, that's not the correct reading of Oceanic Steam or the way the Court treated Oceanic Steam in Jarkesy. Like, that was what the respondent was arguing in that case. turns_pm60.text: -- you know, not just talking about a large part of the INA and other things; you're talking about, you know, utilizing --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I'm not resisting that. turns_pm60.text: Yes. We've identified multiple lines on this. I think germaneness is one. And --

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: No, that cannot possibly be right or you would have to overturn Oceanic Steam, where the Court confronted exactly that question and exactly that argument and said that that would be completely incorrect and rejected that argument as magnifying the judicial to the detriment of all other departments of the government, disregarding many previous adjudications of this Court, and ignoring practices often manifested and hitherto deemed to be free from any possible constitutional question. turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So what's the best way for you to lose? What's the most narrow way for you to lose if you --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And that's not to suggest that you will.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: No, understood.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: No, no, no, no. I'm not -- I don't intend to make that suggestion at all. But, if you were to lose, what would be the most narrow way not to affect all of these other things?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Then I would say take the statutory path, which we haven't talked about. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: We have schemes where agencies determine the penalty or have an administrative proc- -- process -- process for penalties but then go to court and the factual issues are decided de novo.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Would that satisfy you? But this statute's not created that way.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: This statute's not created that way. You could -- you could leave open that that was a reading --sort of a severability-type reading as one way of doing it. Again, don't love that for this program, but if I had to pick a --a particular poison, that would definitely be on the menu.
