But what we have here is heartland: You violated conditions to the federal government that you had to embed in contracts. That involves public rights the same way that other contractual suits do.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So I disagree with that, and the reason is it's all bound up together. As a condition of getting your alien in the entire workforce, the way this program works is you have to agree at the start as the employer, you're going to agree to specific terms and conditions to continue to enjoy that privilege that relate specifically to accounting for the potential distorting effects on the U.S. labor market of importing those particular aliens in your workforce. And so that is the whole gist of the program. It's all bound up with: You're getting a special privilege in the immigration context that depends on the federal government's grace and its exercise of disciplinary power.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And -- and that's why it can't just be conceived of as a mere condition on entry, although entry alone, I think, as [PERSON]'s question suggests, does a lot of work. I mean, you're agreeing to conditions on them.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: How would that work out? I would encourage you to first start with conceiving of the nature of the privilege, as the Court did in Oil States. It's --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: The privilege is importing goods, and so I think you can draw lines between what does that specific privilege look like, as the way the Court did in Oil States, patents versus other public --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Right. And so the way I think that works out is, for the foreign commerce privilege, I think you could draw a different line, which is the foreign commerce privilege, unlike the immigration rights, does, at a certain point, vest in the person -- like, in -- you have to draw a line between --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Because the -- of the difference between foreign commerce and interstate commerce. And I think the Court's Footnote 1 in Jarkesy draws this distinction pretty well. You have to look at --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So I think the way you could do it that would be on the permissible side of the line is you are banning importation of goods that are defective in some way or that you think don't meet labor standards, the good itself. And that has a long history. The Buttfield case is a good example of that with --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And you could say at -- at -- for those goods, if you thought that those goods at the moment of importation would have a bad effect on whatever it is in the country, you could say: I'm banning those goods from the country.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: If you try to import them, civil penalties --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Right. And I think --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think it's too far removed specific to the tradition of foreign commerce and the way that power works.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And here's why. The Court has distinguished between the scope of the privilege to control importation of goods for foreign commerce purposes and the point at which you're past the importer, the sort of a private right to the good vests, and you're trying to regulate at the back end --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- which is what I think your hypothetical taking --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think immigration power is different, and this Court's cases actually --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It -- it -- it is always a conditional privilege.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It ends at the point when someone's status changes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Right.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Exactly. And that's why that -- that public right is different from foreign commerce.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes, insofar as it's something different from just saying you can't break the law. Like, if it's --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- if it's -- if it's something more than that. And I think I would also concede there's a lot of other conditions you can't do on employers. You can't say the condition of getting an alien is you have to submit to all of your torts or all of your employment practices in agency adjudications. You can't attach extraneous conditions. There's a germaneness requirement.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I think it has to relate to the -- the public right and the privilege itself. The privilege is, here, a combination of the sovereign power over immigration. So it's relating to the historical tradition of being able to control the terms and conditions under which aliens are allowed to enter and remain in the United States. And the employer's reciprocal obligations relate to that. It is -- everything in this program is geared towards preventing there being adverse effects from doing that thing, allowing the alien into the country to work for you, the employer, and under specified conditions. And the employer knows all of those conditions at the outset. That's the whole point of the certification process.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: That's exactly correct because it's dictated by the -- entirely dictated by the Labor Secretary's findings under the program that these are the conditions necessary to prevent adverse effects on U.S. labor and working conditions.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes, because it's sort of a one-to-one. By importing foreign labor, you are trying to prevent a situation in which you have a tradeoff with people who would otherwise be working --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So here is what I would say about Atlas Roofing. The reason we don't think that it's at issue in this case is because this case, unlike Atlas Roofing, involves historical areas of public rights. And that's sort of what we're resting on. And it doesn't involve traditional contracts in that sense. You can have lots of other areas of public rights that might look like, at the surface level, 40,000-foot level, they involve contracts. That's true of certainly government contracts, like one of the classic areas of public rights. That's true of the Oceanic Steam case obviously involved negligence or sort of contract actions. Just because you have that threshold resemblance cannot be dispositive. Atlas Roofing was a little different because it did not involve any common law analog at all, but it also didn't involve a historical tradition of public rights.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Speaker B, can I --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: We have not relied on Atlas Roofing.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: We did not rely on Atlas Roofing because the Court has said it had cast doubt on Atlas Roofing.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Speaker B, can I ask you a question about the imposition of fines on the aliens themselves? You said there are lots of places where that's permissible, and I wonder if you could tell me a little bit more about that. And maybe I can do it through a hypothetical drawn from the facts of this case. What if -- I think we -- let's just posit for now I agree that Sun Valley could be kicked out of the program, out of the H-2A program, and I think we agree that the aliens could be removed pursuant to our immigration tradition without an Article III court. But the fines, I'm wondering if they're different. So what if there were conditions on the aliens here rather than on the employer, like the alien had to work a certain number of hours, that the alien had to enroll children in school, or the alien, you know, couldn't leave the country or couldn't leave a certain radius, whatever? Is it the government's position that then fines could be imposed on the alien for breaching those conditions without a jury trial? Let's say it's a $50,000 penalty.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So a couple things. I think the basic answer is yes with some caveats with respect to some of your specific hypothetical. The aliens can face civil penalties for various violations of the conditions of coming into the United States and staying here, and that would be permissible, I think, within the language of Oceanic Steam and the way that these have been conceived of.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: The way, like the INA -- one classic example in the INA itself is for illegal entry. There are civil penalty provisions for illegal entry. So you -- you do something that you're not allowed to do as a matter of the INA, you may face civil penalties. You violated a condition. Some of your conditions, we could talk about whether they're germane to, like, how much -- how much the federal government can control, like, what you're doing in the country.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right. I mean, I was trying to come up with --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But yeah.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- conditions that might be sort of mirror images of these, but -- but the point being, I mean, Oceanic Steam also says -- and I know part of this, like in Wong Wing, if you're talking about a misdemeanor -- take criminal law out of it. It also says that if there's going to be a forfeiture of the alien's property, that would be a different thing, that there might need to be an Article III court or that there would need to be an Article III court. So I'm -- I'm wondering here why that wouldn't be the case for the alien. If the alien violated some sort of condition on the H-2A visa, why wouldn't the alien be entitled to an Article III court before the alien had to pay that kind of a fine?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Because I think, respectfully, that's not the correct reading of Oceanic Steam or the way the Court treated Oceanic Steam in Jarkesy. The Court there is distinguishing between things that look like criminal punishment or other forms of punishment from that case itself rejecting the proposition that anytime you impose civil penalties, you necessarily have to be in an Article III court with a jury. Like, that was what the respondent was arguing in that case. And the Court emphatically rejected the proposition that in the -- and said, in the area of immigration, like in tax, like in other areas where civil penalties have been imposed, the nature of the power is special. Congress has the ability to say that there's going to be executive adjudication and that there will be civil penalties. And I think that has to make sense if you think about just the theoretical framework of public rights in this area and the way other public rights work. This is an area -- area of combined --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Wong Wing does talk about also confiscating a property, but I don't think that can be fairly read to mean any civil penalties are out, or you would have to, I think, overrule Oceanic Steam and you would also have problems with, like, Murray's Lessee itself. If the idea is you can never have, in -- in a non-Article III setting, some sort of consequences for property, then you're not just talking about this --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- you know, not just talking about a large part of the INA and other things; you're talking about, you know, utilizing --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I'm not resisting that. What I'm saying is there's a difference between civil penalties that are being attached to you for violating conditions of coming into the country versus things that I think implicate other rights of, let's say, someone who's been here for a while. You're confiscating their property as punishment. There are limits, we would say, on obviously the kinds of --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes. We've identified multiple lines on this. I think germaneness is one. And --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Germaneness is one, and what are the others?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: The others are a careful look at the nature of the privilege and public right at the outset, which I think you have to say it has to be immigration. It is relating to the entry and continued presence of the alien, and that does tie into germaneness. But I think a careful look at the scope of the privilege and -- and right on a right-by-right basis is quite important in this context to distinguish things like foreign commerce or other areas. And then the third thing I would say is that there are also limits from the Due Process Clause. The Court's always recognized that in any form of adjudication, due process is going to be an important limit. And we think that that is quite important as well.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But that's a limit that doesn't need to be satisfied by an Article III court. So the limits I was asking you about are limits on the need for a jury, the need to go to an Article III court.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Right. And then the final limit I would just say is I think it is quite important and goes to [PERSON]'s question, that the adjudication itself here involves federal enforcement of the conditions vis- -vis the employer in the program, and you're not taking the additional step of saying you're adjudicating essentially two private parties' rights in a final binding and conclusive way, the way you would be doing in, say, Granfinanciera or some of the bankruptcy cases that involved actually conclusively adjudicating a state law common --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- counterpoint.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: A public rights case involves rights that are vested in the sovereign for the public at large or privileges that are extended by the sovereign as a matter of grace. And that sounds like it might involve any Article I plenary powers, so I would just give an additional cut on that, which is the Court said in Jarkesy correctly that history and tradition are --also help you zoom in on the distinctive areas involving governmental prerogatives that historically could have been determined exclusively by the political branches.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes. Private rights are things that sort of the -- you -- the Court's commonly said the stuff of Westminster, the stuff -- you know, the stuff of traditional actions at common law. I think the best definition is Blackstone. It's the rights of the individual qua the individual versus rights for the public at large.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: No, that cannot possibly be right or you would have to overturn Oceanic Steam, where the Court confronted exactly that question and exactly that argument and said that that would be completely incorrect and rejected that argument as magnifying the judicial to the detriment of all other departments of the government, disregarding many previous adjudications of this Court, and ignoring practices often manifested and hitherto deemed to be free from any possible constitutional question. So that's pretty emphatic over a century ago saying absolutely not, it's not a bright-line rule. Civil penalties equals Article III courts. And, otherwise, you know, have at it.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes. So let me just talk about the different ways of disruption. One, if the Court were to say civil penalties always have to be in Article III courts, that's kind of the nuclear option. Civil penalties are imposed by the government in all kinds of contracts. We've been relying on Oceanic Steam and this long tradition of public rights in all sorts of areas, in -- in all sorts of areas that are modern benefits programs like Medicare, in all sorts of historical programs that stem from immigration, just across the board. There are tons of civil penalty programs that we think are very justifiable even post-Jarkesy. Now, if the Court were to instead say there's something wrong with the contractual setup, it too much looks like a contract, that too would be quite disruptive for the government. If that's the breaking point, the point at which these cases have to be adjudicated in an Article III court, that imperils the way we do Medicare and Medicaid penalties, the way federal contracts work because we often require federal contractors to embed in their contracts with subcontractors these same regulatory requirements as a method of enforcement. The federal student loan program also does that. So those are big deals to us. Now, if the option is immigration is something that only ends at the border, I think that would have highly disruptive consequences for immigration law. Like, we would be quite troubled by that result because --not just because there are a lot of penalty programs that involve imposing penalties on aliens for overstaying -- for staying too long, for not voluntarily departing, for violating the term -- sort of being -- for illegal entry or other things, but, for these H-2A and H-2B programs, they're really important mechanisms of making sure the government, when it's bargaining and giving a condition for employers to do certain things, has to live by them.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: No, understood.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Then I would say take the statutory path, which we haven't talked about. Say that -- say that for this particular statutory scheme, if we could not impose -- we could not impose penalties in a non-Article III adjudication because you don't think the statute is clear enough or something and leave open to us being able to seek penalties in court. I think that would be the narrowest. It would be fairly unsatisfying for the government, though, because I think the other thing I want to highlight is we really don't -- we don't want to lose, but what we want even less is a lack of clarity on the scope of public versus private rights in this context. We have, as I just told you, a lot of different schemes involving civil penalties, and clarity is quite important to us.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: This statute's not created that way. You could -- you could leave open that that was a reading --sort of a severability-type reading as one way of doing it. Again, don't love that for this program, but if I had to pick a --a particular poison, that would definitely be on the menu.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: The government's response would be twofold. One is part of Article II prerogatives do involve when it's permissible to use agency adjudication. We do care deeply about exercising that means of enforcing the law. That has traditionally been a means of exercising executive power that we care about that. But two is, why do we care about this as a practical matter? Because there are hundreds of enforcement proceedings in a given year for just this program, and for -- across the government, for these kinds of programs, the numbers, you know, keep adding zeros. And the idea that the Department of Justice would be having to then pursue every single one of these in federal court would be a choice that -- would be a choice that would raise massive concerns about under-enforcement of the law just given resource constraints.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I mean, how would it work in the immigration context if the proposition were that the only types of things that could be in executive adjudication are things that happen at the border? I think it would be catastrophic. I mean, just the volume of -- of immigration-related cases for the aliens themselves for things that make you inadmissible after you enter the country, like, huge, enormous numbers. And that's why I think the everything-stops-at-the-border theory is utterly untenable, not to mention completely contrary to the way the Court has conceived of this power in its cases, so you have a stare decisis problem on top of that.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Thoughts? I think this statute is still quite close to that because what we're talk --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Would I agree the other statutes are closer?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I'm sorry.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Would I try to distinguish those statutes going forward if we were to lose this case? I mean, I think it depends on how. It seems to be the proposition of the immigration power stopping at the border would --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I don't think I would. I mean, I think even Respondents agree that things that are closely related would include things like employer verification or other things that relate to the alien's ability to stay in -- in the country and the conditions under which you're allowed to have someone, and that's what this program is.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: But you're also then enjoying -- like, then you're also then employing them. And here, on top of that, the -- unlike the employer verification setting, you're an employer who's expressly getting a privilege from the government at the outset. You are agreeing: I promise I will comply with all these regulatory commissions -- conditions. I get this special sovereign benefit no one else gets to bring an alien in and continue to have them here at the government's grace.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: You could look at it as a way through the problem. We haven't relied on it in the way that Respondents are suggesting because we're not suggesting in this case, if this case were to involve --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: We think there is consent here.

turns_pm60.text: The privilege is importing goods, and so I think you can draw lines between what does that specific privilege look like, as the way the Court did in Oil States, patents versus other public --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, but let's say Congress says it's really important to have these wage and -- and liability regimes in order to protect the American worker and prevent a flood of cheap imports.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right. And so the way I think that works out is, for the foreign commerce privilege, I think you could draw a different line, which is the foreign commerce privilege, unlike the immigration rights, does, at a certain point, vest in the person -- like, in -- you have to draw a line between --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So, at some point, it stops, you think?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Because the -- of the difference between foreign commerce and interstate commerce. And I think the Court's Footnote 1 in Jarkesy draws this distinction pretty well. You have to look at --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So what if it were just the product liability and wages of those who are actually importing from abroad?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So I think the way you could do it that would be on the permissible side of the line is you are banning importation of goods that are defective in some way or that you think don't meet labor standards, the good itself. And that has a long history. The Buttfield case is a good example of that with --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: No, not -- not -- not abroad. I'm talking about wages and product liability issues here in this country.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: And you could say at -- at -- for those goods, if you thought that those goods at the moment of importation would have a bad effect on whatever it is in the country, you could say: I'm banning those goods from the country.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: No, no, not banning the goods.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: If you try to import them, civil penalties --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: No, no, we all agree you could -- you could ban these people from participating in the program. I'm talking about setting up -- maybe my question is not clear enough -- setting up a whole product liability regime in this country for goods that are imported and minimum wage laws with respect to people who are involved in -- in -- domestically involved in importing the goods.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right. And I think --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It seems to me you either say it's -- yes, it's part of the comprehensive regime and the Department of Commerce can adjudicate those things without an Article III court involved anywhere -- that's one option -- or you say, well, no, it's too far removed, which is your other option. And I'm guessing -- I'm just wondering, which is it?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think it's too far removed specific to the tradition of foreign commerce and the way that power works.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Okay.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: And here's why. The Court has distinguished between the scope of the privilege to control importation of goods for foreign commerce purposes and the point at which you're past the importer, the sort of a private right to the good vests, and you're trying to regulate at the back end --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: If -- if that's true --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- which is what I think your hypothetical taking --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- if that's true, would you also agree the immigration power ends at some point too?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think immigration power is different, and this Court's cases actually --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: It never ends?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It -- it -- it is always a conditional privilege.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Always? Okay.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: It ends at the point when someone's status changes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Okay.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Exactly. And that's why that -- that public right is different from foreign commerce.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes, insofar as it's something different from just saying you can't break the law. Like, if it's --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- if it's -- if it's something more than that. And I think I would also concede there's a lot of other conditions you can't do on employers. You can't say the condition of getting an alien is you have to submit to all of your torts or all of your employment practices in agency adjudications. You can't attach extraneous conditions. There's a germaneness requirement.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think it has to relate to the -- the public right and the privilege itself. The privilege is, here, a combination of the sovereign power over immigration. So it's relating to the historical tradition of being able to control the terms and conditions under which aliens are allowed to enter and remain in the United States. And the employer's reciprocal obligations relate to that. It is -- everything in this program is geared towards preventing there being adverse effects from doing that thing, allowing the alien into the country to work for you, the employer, and under specified conditions. And the employer knows all of those conditions at the outset. That's the whole point of the certification process.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: That's exactly correct because it's dictated by the -- entirely dictated by the Labor Secretary's findings under the program that these are the conditions necessary to prevent adverse effects on U.S. labor and working conditions.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes, because it's sort of a one-to-one. By importing foreign labor, you are trying to prevent a situation in which you have a tradeoff with people who would otherwise be working --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So here is what I would say about Atlas Roofing. The reason we don't think that it's at issue in this case is because this case, unlike Atlas Roofing, involves historical areas of public rights. And that's sort of what we're resting on. And it doesn't involve traditional contracts in that sense. You can have lots of other areas of public rights that might look like, at the surface level, 40,000-foot level, they involve contracts. That's true of certainly government contracts, like one of the classic areas of public rights. That's true of the Oceanic Steam case obviously involved negligence or sort of contract actions. Just because you have that threshold resemblance cannot be dispositive. Atlas Roofing was a little different because it did not involve any common law analog at all, but it also didn't involve a historical tradition of public rights.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: We have not relied on Atlas Roofing.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: We did not rely on Atlas Roofing because the Court has said it had cast doubt on Atlas Roofing.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So a couple things. I think the basic answer is yes with some caveats with respect to some of your specific hypothetical. The aliens can face civil penalties for various violations of the conditions of coming into the United States and staying here, and that would be permissible, I think, within the language of Oceanic Steam and the way that these have been conceived of.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: The way, like the INA -- one classic example in the INA itself is for illegal entry. There are civil penalty provisions for illegal entry. So you -- you do something that you're not allowed to do as a matter of the INA, you may face civil penalties. You violated a condition. Some of your conditions, we could talk about whether they're germane to, like, how much -- how much the federal government can control, like, what you're doing in the country.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But yeah.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Because I think, respectfully, that's not the correct reading of Oceanic Steam or the way the Court treated Oceanic Steam in Jarkesy. The Court there is distinguishing between things that look like criminal punishment or other forms of punishment from that case itself rejecting the proposition that anytime you impose civil penalties, you necessarily have to be in an Article III court with a jury. Like, that was what the respondent was arguing in that case. And the Court emphatically rejected the proposition that in the -- and said, in the area of immigration, like in tax, like in other areas where civil penalties have been imposed, the nature of the power is special. Congress has the ability to say that there's going to be executive adjudication and that there will be civil penalties. And I think that has to make sense if you think about just the theoretical framework of public rights in this area and the way other public rights work. This is an area -- area of combined --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I'm sorry -- I'm sorry to interrupt here, but just to follow up on this before we lose track of it. I -- I thought Wong Wing said confiscating property goes to an Article III court for -- when you're trying to confiscate property from aliens.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Wong Wing does talk about also confiscating a property, but I don't think that can be fairly read to mean any civil penalties are out, or you would have to, I think, overrule Oceanic Steam and you would also have problems with, like, Murray's Lessee itself. If the idea is you can never have, in -- in a non-Article III setting, some sort of consequences for property, then you're not just talking about this --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So -- so --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- you know, not just talking about a large part of the INA and other things; you're talking about, you know, utilizing --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: No, I understand penalties associated with entry, but I'm -- I'm trying to draw on [PERSON]'s hypothetical, and it's a little further afield, right, less immediately about the entry and you're seeking to confiscate the alien's property. I -- I -- I thought we decided a long time ago that you've got to go to an Article III court. Are -- are you resisting that?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I'm not resisting that. What I'm saying is there's a difference between civil penalties that are being attached to you for violating conditions of coming into the country versus things that I think implicate other rights of, let's say, someone who's been here for a while. You're confiscating their property as punishment. There are limits, we would say, on obviously the kinds of --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So there is an outer bound then with respect to the alien on how far you can go with this immigration exception? You -- you agree?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes. We've identified multiple lines on this. I think germaneness is one. And --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: The others are a careful look at the nature of the privilege and public right at the outset, which I think you have to say it has to be immigration. It is relating to the entry and continued presence of the alien, and that does tie into germaneness. But I think a careful look at the scope of the privilege and -- and right on a right-by-right basis is quite important in this context to distinguish things like foreign commerce or other areas. And then the third thing I would say is that there are also limits from the Due Process Clause. The Court's always recognized that in any form of adjudication, due process is going to be an important limit. And we think that that is quite important as well.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right. And then the final limit I would just say is I think it is quite important and goes to [PERSON]'s question, that the adjudication itself here involves federal enforcement of the conditions vis- -vis the employer in the program, and you're not taking the additional step of saying you're adjudicating essentially two private parties' rights in a final binding and conclusive way, the way you would be doing in, say, Granfinanciera or some of the bankruptcy cases that involved actually conclusively adjudicating a state law common --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- counterpoint.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: A public rights case involves rights that are vested in the sovereign for the public at large or privileges that are extended by the sovereign as a matter of grace. And that sounds like it might involve any Article I plenary powers, so I would just give an additional cut on that, which is the Court said in Jarkesy correctly that history and tradition are --also help you zoom in on the distinctive areas involving governmental prerogatives that historically could have been determined exclusively by the political branches.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes. Private rights are things that sort of the -- you -- the Court's commonly said the stuff of Westminster, the stuff -- you know, the stuff of traditional actions at common law. I think the best definition is Blackstone. It's the rights of the individual qua the individual versus rights for the public at large.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: No, that cannot possibly be right or you would have to overturn Oceanic Steam, where the Court confronted exactly that question and exactly that argument and said that that would be completely incorrect and rejected that argument as magnifying the judicial to the detriment of all other departments of the government, disregarding many previous adjudications of this Court, and ignoring practices often manifested and hitherto deemed to be free from any possible constitutional question. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes. So let me just talk about the different ways of disruption. One, if the Court were to say civil penalties always have to be in Article III courts, that's kind of the nuclear option. Civil penalties are imposed by the government in all kinds of contracts. We've been relying on Oceanic Steam and this long tradition of public rights in all sorts of areas, in -- in all sorts of areas that are modern benefits programs like Medicare, in all sorts of historical programs that stem from immigration, just across the board. There are tons of civil penalty programs that we think are very justifiable even post-Jarkesy. Now, if the Court were to instead say there's something wrong with the contractual setup, it too much looks like a contract, that too would be quite disruptive for the government. If that's the breaking point, the point at which these cases have to be adjudicated in an Article III court, that imperils the way we do Medicare and Medicaid penalties, the way federal contracts work because we often require federal contractors to embed in their contracts with subcontractors these same regulatory requirements as a method of enforcement. The federal student loan program also does that. So those are big deals to us. Now, if the option is immigration is something that only ends at the border, I think that would have highly disruptive consequences for immigration law. Like, we would be quite troubled by that result because --not just because there are a lot of penalty programs that involve imposing penalties on aliens for overstaying -- for staying too long, for not voluntarily departing, for violating the term -- sort of being -- for illegal entry or other things, but, for these H-2A and H-2B programs, they're really important mechanisms of making sure the government, when it's bargaining and giving a condition for employers to do certain things, has to live by them.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: No, understood.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Then I would say take the statutory path, which we haven't talked about. Say that -- say that for this particular statutory scheme, if we could not impose -- we could not impose penalties in a non-Article III adjudication because you don't think the statute is clear enough or something and leave open to us being able to seek penalties in court. I think that would be the narrowest. It would be fairly unsatisfying for the government, though, because I think the other thing I want to highlight is we really don't -- we don't want to lose, but what we want even less is a lack of clarity on the scope of public versus private rights in this context. We have, as I just told you, a lot of different schemes involving civil penalties, and clarity is quite important to us.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: This statute's not created that way. You could -- you could leave open that that was a reading --sort of a severability-type reading as one way of doing it. Again, don't love that for this program, but if I had to pick a --a particular poison, that would definitely be on the menu.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: The government's response would be twofold. One is part of Article II prerogatives do involve when it's permissible to use agency adjudication. We do care deeply about exercising that means of enforcing the law. That has traditionally been a means of exercising executive power that we care about that. But two is, why do we care about this as a practical matter? Because there are hundreds of enforcement proceedings in a given year for just this program, and for -- across the government, for these kinds of programs, the numbers, you know, keep adding zeros. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I mean, how would it work in the immigration context if the proposition were that the only types of things that could be in executive adjudication are things that happen at the border? turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I looked at your seven examples in the immigration statutes, and they all seemed a lot closer to the core of admission, expulsion, or deportion -- deportation than this one. Thoughts?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Thoughts? I think this statute is still quite close to that because what we're talk --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Do you --would you agree the others are closer?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Would I agree the other statutes are closer?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And, certainly, wouldn't you take that position going forward?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I'm sorry.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: And, certainly, wouldn't you take that position if you were to lose in this case?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Would I try to distinguish those statutes going forward if we were to lose this case? I mean, I think it depends on how. It seems to be the proposition of the immigration power stopping at the border would --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I didn't say that. I said those were closer to the core immigration powers. Would you agree with that?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I don't think I would. turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: I would have thought employer verification is a lot closer. You have to verify that you can bring somebody in.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: But you're also then enjoying -- like, then you're also then employing them. turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: You could look at it as a way through the problem. We haven't relied on it in the way that Respondents are suggesting because we're not suggesting in this case, if this case were to involve --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: You don't have consent here, but what if you sought it --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: We think there is consent here.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, you didn't argue that.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Correct. We're not presenting this as a case about consent.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So -- so, in the next case involving all of these others, that would be available too, right?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I think it depends on what the Court says because, if the proposition is this case involves private rights, then the question would be: Can you consent to non-Article III adjudication of these things? turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, if it was so clear, why didn't you argue it? turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Yes.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Then it says you can impose penalties. Very similar language we had last year in FCC/AT&T case. turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Because the statute there expressly provided for recovery only in de novo circuit -- in de novo civil suits. So the statutory language, as the Court did say in FCC v. AT&T, is context-specific. And the context here is different from the statutory context there because, again, there, there is an express mention of the de novo civil suits.

turns_pm60.speaker: B

turns_pm15.speaker: A
turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] This Court in Jarkesy made clear that the public rights exception is an atextual exception to Article III that must be applied carefully and with close attention to history. Yet the government here identifies no history extending the immigration adjudication tradition to the types of claims and remedies at issue here. The government invokes the idea of immigration, but it points to no history extending the immigration adjudication doctrine to the imposition of what amounts to a judgment imposing penalties and back wages on a breach-of-contract theory or involving labor issues more generally. Oceanic Steam, the government's key case, involves penalties that were imposed based on a finding that aliens were ineligible for admission and that were collected as an exaction upon the defendant recrossing the border. In other words, both the claim and the remedy involved the exercise of the executive's power to control who could or could not cross the border into the country. That is a far cry from a case about labor issues at a farm in New Jersey with a mix of foreign and domestic workers. The government also invokes history from a range of disparate contexts, including tax, militia service, and the jurisdiction of the Court of Claims. But that blunderbuss approach to history is the opposite of the close analysis that Jarkesy requires, and given the broad range of privileges and benefits that are controlled by the executive, it threatens to badly erode Article III. Indeed, even the government says in its brief that it can adjudicate penalties imposed as a condition of access to the mail. Under such a theory, little would be left of this Court's decision in Jarkesy. Separately, the government points to no statutory language authorizing the penalties here. To be sure, the statute contemplates penalties, but it says nothing about where those penalties should be adjudicated. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns_pm15.text: [ADDRESS] This Court in Jarkesy made clear that the public rights exception is an atextual exception to Article III that must be applied carefully and with close attention to history. Yet the government here identifies no history extending the immigration adjudication tradition to the types of claims and remedies at issue here. Oceanic Steam, the government's key case, involves penalties that were imposed based on a finding that aliens were ineligible for admission and that were collected as an exaction upon the defendant recrossing the border. In other words, both the claim and the remedy involved the exercise of the executive's power to control who could or could not cross the border into the country. That is a far cry from a case about labor issues at a farm in New Jersey with a mix of foreign and domestic workers. The government also invokes history from a range of disparate contexts, including tax, militia service, and the jurisdiction of the Court of Claims. But that blunderbuss approach to history is the opposite of the close analysis that Jarkesy requires, and given the broad range of privileges and benefits that are controlled by the executive, it threatens to badly erode Article III. Indeed, even the government says in its brief that it can adjudicate penalties imposed as a condition of access to the mail. Under such a theory, little would be left of this Court's decision in Jarkesy. Separately, the government points to no statutory language authorizing the penalties here. To be sure, the statute contemplates penalties, but it says nothing about where those penalties should be adjudicated. I welcome the Court's questions.

I think in a case about -- you know, if the allegation is that the -- the worker was unlawfully employed, fundamentally, the allegation is this worker was not lawfully in the country.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So, to be clear, I think my position of what the best reading here is that I would focus both on the nature of the claim and the remedy because I --I do think, when you're only looking at the claim, that is -- there is a certain risk that it gets a little bit indeterminate. So, you know, I think, if you look at the nature of the remedy, that that's -- that really -- the fact that Oceanic was --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So I do think it's different. I think that my view would be the question is, is it -- is the claim about whether somebody is lawfully in the country or not, or is it otherwise about sort of the process of determining whether someone is lawfully in the country or not? I think that's different from germaneness, which I take to be kind of more of like what is the degree of separation, which, you know, I -- I don't think is an administrable standard because I don't know, you know, is that a rational basis test? Is it some sort of more tight test? I don't know what germaneness really means.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: So are foreign workers who are brought into the country pursuant to a set of conditions that are subsequently violated lawfully in the country?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So they would be, yes. So an H-2A --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: They would be?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So an H- 2A worker, if they come into the country under --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Pursuant to a set of conditions that allows for their entry that are subsequently violated --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- they are lawfully in the country?

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: Well, so, you know, I guess maybe I'm not understanding the question right. If your question is --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: No, I think you understand the question. I think it just really highlights why "lawfully in the country" can't be the right line for --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- determining whether or not this is an immigration case.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- if an H-2A worker is working at a farm that has violated these terms and conditions, the H-2A worker is not in the country unlawfully. The H-2A worker could, you know, if the -- if the government is -- the government has a choice, to -- to debar someone from the program --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: I thought the government could expel them. They -- if you agree that the government could expel them, it would be because the conditions are violated and, therefore, they are not in the country lawfully, right?

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Let me ask you another question. I hear you setting up a test for identifying public rights that turns on the nature or the claim -- of the claim or the remedies. You've said it many times. That's like how we should tell courts to go about doing this. What I don't understand is where those particular criteria come from because, in the historical cases, those were not the metric. You just seem to be looking at the historical cases and picking out certain facts and telling us that today we should have a new test that relates to those facts. But we have many, many cases in which public route -- rights were applied and found by this Court even though the government imposed monetary liability. So it was not tied to the remedy as to whether or not you would find a public right. We have many cases that resembled common-law claims, and the Court still found that there were public rights involved. So help me to understand whether you are asking us to just fashion a new test based on some facts that you see in the historical cases. Surely, this is not what we were doing traditionally because those cases would have come out differently.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So I think that there are -- that most of the cases that you're referencing arise in a distinct historical tradition bucket, you might say.

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right. But they don't turn on the factors that you're now saying we should apply. That's my -- I'm trying to help the courts that [PERSON] says are going to be confused. So I want to have a rule, like, what do you look for to determine whether or not this is a public rights case or a private rights case? And you have offered us one. You say: Look at the nature of the claim and the type of remedy. And I say: Ha, that rule's not going to work consistent with all the public right -- rights cases that we have traditionally had because those cases wouldn't be public rights if your test is -- is -- is the right test. So I guess I'm just trying to understand what you're asking us to do and isn't it novel.

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: So I don't think it's novel. I think, if you actually look at those historical cases, they do turn on distinct considerations. So, for instance, just to pick one, the government cites McElrath, which is a case about the dispute between the government and a government employee and whether the Court of Claims could adjudicate counterclaims, and it's about -- the case is about the importance of the government's sovereign immunity, that, you know, there's particular considerations --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: Right, but you're --

turns_pm60.speaker: B
turns_pm60.text: -- involving government employees --

turns_pm60.speaker: A
turns_pm60.text: -- not asking us to look at those considerations. I'm just trying to figure out where you're getting your test from, but I think I have the answer. Thank you.
